summary: A small fine-tuned parser that emits a well-formed but wrong tree fails silently: nothing downstream can tell. We ask whether the output format, a free design choice, controls how often this happens. On the PIZZA ordering benchmark we fine-tune two sub-billion models (Qwen3.5-0.8B and LFM2.5-350M) with LoRA on six lossless encodings of the same target tree, from 44.3 down to 10.9 tokens per order, including two matched-length pairs that vary surface form at fixed length. Across 300 runs (5 training pool sizes, 5 seeds) with a hierarchical bootstrap and Holm correction fixed before the results were read, shortening alone never helps, but writing the target in ordinary words does. The word encoding is the most accurate format on both models (87.5% vs. 85.8% exact match for the native s-expression on Qwen) while emitting 4.1x fewer tokens, and it cuts the silent error rate by 2.3x on Qwen and 1.8x on LFM2, separating at every pool size. Error analysis locates much of the gain in negation. All runs also learn to refuse off-menu input (held out: 95.9-99.0% handled) and to apply in-utterance self-corrections. Strict refusal has a measured price: 2.1-10.1% of real, mostly polite, orders are refused.

AI.tldr: On the PIZZA ordering benchmark, writing the target parse tree in ordinary words instead of the native s-expression makes small fine-tuned parsers more accurate and cuts their silent error rate by 1.8 to 2.3 times. Shortening the output alone does not help.
AI.motivation: A small fine-tuned parser that emits a well-formed but wrong tree fails silently, and the authors ask whether the output format, a free design choice, controls how often this happens.
AI.method: Two sub-billion models (Qwen3.5-0.8B and LFM2.5-350M) are fine-tuned with LoRA on six lossless encodings of the same target tree, from 44.3 down to 10.9 tokens per order, including two matched-length pairs that vary surface form. Across 300 runs (5 training pool sizes, 5 seeds) the analysis uses a hierarchical bootstrap and Holm correction fixed before the results were read.
AI.result: The word encoding is the most accurate format on both models (87.5% vs. 85.8% exact match for the native s-expression on Qwen) while emitting 4.1x fewer tokens. It cuts the silent error rate by 2.3x on Qwen and 1.8x on LFM2, separating at every pool size, and much of the gain lies in negation. All runs learn to refuse off-menu input (95.9-99.0% handled held out) and to apply in-utterance self-corrections, but strict refusal refuses 2.1-10.1% of real, mostly polite, orders.
AI.conclusion: Output format is a consequential design choice for small semantic parsers, with word-based encodings reducing silent errors, though strict refusal carries a measured cost in refused real orders.

title: Synthesis Smuggling: Maliciously Hiding Inferred Personal Attributes in LLM Outputs
summary: We propose Synthesis Smuggling, a novel threat model in which an adversarial LLM infers sensitive information about a user from routine assistance-seeking interactions and steganographically encodes that into innocuous-looking model-generated content. The user may then unknowingly transmit that information by sharing the generated artifact, say as an email, social-media post, or message, through ordinary communication channels. An adversary monitoring these channels can discover this information. We demonstrate this threat by training two open-weight models to infer gender and age-group labels from conversational cues and encode their predictions using invisible characters or word choices. These results show that user-shared model outputs can become a covert channel for personal inferences, even when the model itself has no direct means of contacting an adversary.

AI.tldr: Synthesis Smuggling is a threat model in which an adversarial LLM encodes inferred personal attributes into generated content that the user unknowingly shares, creating a covert channel. The authors demonstrate it by training two open-weight models to encode inferred gender and age group using invisible characters or word choices.
AI.motivation: Users share model-generated artifacts such as emails and posts through ordinary channels, and an adversary monitoring those channels could recover sensitive information inferred during routine assistance, even though the model has no direct way to contact an adversary.
AI.method: Two open-weight models are trained to infer gender and age-group labels from conversational cues and to encode their predictions in innocuous-looking outputs using invisible characters or word choices.
AI.result: The abstract reports that user-shared model outputs can carry these encoded personal inferences, but gives no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: User-shared model outputs can become a covert channel for personal inferences, which is a privacy risk for model deployers and users.

title: Goal Encoding in LLMs
comment: Project page, code and data: this https URL
summary: We investigate whether and how LLMs encode goals: internal neural representations that precede and guide action, and that are flexible enough to be realized through many different execution paths. We construct a coding setting with multiple sub-tasks that allows us to evaluate goal-seeking behavior and the selection of sub-goals. In this setting, we localize an encoding of the next sub-goal in the outputs of a sparse set of attention heads. The same heads can be used to decode the LM's future actions in natural language (e.g., "I'm checking if a word is a palindrome"). We verify that this encoding is causal for next action and is plastic: transplanting it into a different environment, e.g., another programming language, triggers the same operation realized with a different sequence of tokens. The LM also sustains the encoding throughout the action's execution, which is puzzling because a transformer LM without recurrence cannot carry a state forward for more tokens than it has layers left. We propose that it does not need to. Under a non-recurrent goal-seeking (NRGS) account, the LM frequently re-reads the goal from the task specification, compares it with the progress visible in the growing context, and pursues what remains. We test the predictions of this account with targeted causal interventions.

AI.tldr: The paper finds an encoding of the next sub-goal in a sparse set of attention heads in a coding setting, which causally determines the next action and is plastic across programming languages. It proposes a non-recurrent goal-seeking account in which the LM re-reads the goal from the task specification and compares it with the progress in context.
AI.motivation: Whether and how LLMs encode goals, meaning internal representations that precede and guide action, is unclear, and a transformer without recurrence cannot carry a state forward for more tokens than it has layers left, which makes sustained goal encoding puzzling.
AI.method: The authors construct a coding setting with multiple sub-tasks, localize the next sub-goal encoding in the outputs of sparse attention heads, decode future actions from those heads, and test the non-recurrent goal-seeking (NRGS) account with targeted causal interventions, including transplanting the encoding into another programming language.
AI.result: The encoding is causal for the next action and plastic: transplanting it into a different environment triggers the same operation realized with a different token sequence. The LM sustains the encoding throughout the action's execution.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose that the LM does not need recurrence to sustain goals, because it frequently re-reads the goal from the task specification and pursues what remains, a prediction they test with causal interventions.

title: Learning When Diffusion Language Models Should Regenerate
summary: Remasking allows diffusion language models to revisit generated text, but effective correction requires knowing when and what to revise. Our diagnosis on Sudoku reveals two gaps. Hidden states contain error information that token confidence does not reliably expose, and remasking an isolated error usually reproduces it when the surrounding context remains fixed. These findings motivate DiVR , a verifier that predicts whether a partially generated sequence will reach a correct answer. Trained on the final correctness of the model's own trajectories, DiVR decides when to regenerate a block and which alternative to retain, while the generator itself stays unchanged. On five reasoning benchmarks with LLaDA-8B-Base, DiVR raises the average accuracy of the fine-tuned generator from 35.3\% to 43.4\% at $1.9$-$3.5\times$ the cost of greedy decoding, above search baselines that use $3.8$-$7.4\times$. It also complements post-training such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and generalizes to other generators, including Dream.

AI.tldr: DiVR is a verifier that predicts whether a partially generated diffusion-LM sequence will reach a correct answer, and uses it to decide when to regenerate a block and which alternative to keep. It raises LLaDA-8B-Base average accuracy from 35.3% to 43.4% across five reasoning benchmarks at 1.9-3.5 times the cost of greedy decoding.
AI.motivation: Remasking lets diffusion language models revisit generated text, but correction requires knowing when and what to revise. On Sudoku, hidden states contain error information that token confidence does not reliably expose, and remasking an isolated error usually reproduces it when the surrounding context is fixed.
AI.method: DiVR is trained on the final correctness of the model's own trajectories and decides when to regenerate a block and which alternative to retain, while the generator itself stays unchanged.
AI.result: On five reasoning benchmarks with LLaDA-8B-Base, DiVR raises the average accuracy of the fine-tuned generator from 35.3% to 43.4% at 1.9-3.5 times the cost of greedy decoding, above search baselines that cost 3.8-7.4 times as much. It complements supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning and generalizes to other generators, including Dream.
AI.conclusion: A learned verifier over the generator's hidden states can make remasking-based correction effective at lower cost than search, without changing the generator.

title: ArchSpace: Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing LLM Architecture Research
summary: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry, teams such as those behind DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi routinely introduce architectural innovations, yet public reports rarely document which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. In academia, limited compute and inconsistent baselines often restrict evaluations to small-scale, single-point comparisons, making it difficult to establish whether improvements hold at larger scales or translate into broader impact. ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc}: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.

AI.tldr: ArchSpace is a public platform for recording, reviewing and referencing LLM architecture research, using scaling laws to predict large-scale loss from small experiments. It ships with Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws and a reusable training recipe.
AI.motivation: Public reports rarely document which architectural ideas succeeded or were abandoned and why, and limited compute in academia often restricts evaluations to small-scale single-point comparisons.
AI.method: Each architecture proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. Scaling laws predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments before costly training.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results; it describes the platform and its initial references (Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a training recipe).
AI.conclusion: ArchSpace aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape next-generation models by letting validated ideas become new baselines.

title: Partial pooling beats synthetic respondents as estimators, not as covariates: a preregistered small-sample tournament
comment: 28 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables, supplementary information included. Preregistration: this https URL. Reproduction package: this https URL
summary: Survey estimates for population segments, such as media use by sex and age, rest on few respondents per cell, and a growing literature offers synthetic respondents generated by large language models to fill the gap. That literature has not tested them against the small-area estimators a methodologist would otherwise use. We ran ten estimators, preregistered, on identical household-clustered splits of a Korean media panel across five calibration budgets and three holdout regimes. A multilevel partial-pooling model of the MRP family led every calibration-only estimator at every budget, matching at one hundred respondents what direct estimation reaches with roughly four times as many. On unobserved segments, information fixed as a per-segment prior was inert for synthetic panel and previous wave alike; attached as a bias correction it transferred, at the price of estimation noise. No registered synthetic advantage over MRP survived the paired decision rule. Entered instead as a covariate inside the multilevel model, an exploratory hybrid, the same panel improved on MRP on unobserved segments: the information survives where the registered constructions did not. Interval coverage stayed below nominal throughout and worsened with budget for partial pooling, contrary to prediction.

AI.tldr: In a preregistered comparison of ten small-area estimators on a Korean media panel, a multilevel partial-pooling model of the MRP family beats every calibration-only estimator, while synthetic respondents do not beat MRP as estimators. Synthetic respondents help only when entered as a covariate inside the multilevel model, as an exploratory hybrid.
AI.motivation: Survey estimates for small population segments rest on few respondents per cell, and synthetic LLM respondents have been proposed to fill the gap, but they had not been tested against standard small-area estimators.
AI.method: Ten estimators were preregistered and run on identical household-clustered splits of a Korean media panel across five calibration budgets and three holdout regimes. Synthetic panel and previous-wave information were used as per-segment priors, bias corrections, or covariates in a multilevel model.
AI.result: MRP-family partial pooling led every calibration-only estimator at every budget, matching at 100 respondents what direct estimation reaches with about four times as many. Synthetic information as a fixed prior was inert on unobserved segments, and as a bias correction it transferred at the price of estimation noise. No registered synthetic advantage over MRP survived the paired decision rule. As an exploratory covariate in the multilevel model, the panel improved on MRP on unobserved segments. Interval coverage stayed below nominal and worsened with budget for partial pooling, contrary to prediction.
AI.conclusion: Partial pooling beats synthetic respondents as estimators, but synthetic information may still add value as a covariate, a finding that the authors present as exploratory.

title: Evaluating the Performance of LLMs in Drafting NIH Data Management Plans
summary: Sharing research data is essential to promote transparency, enable reproducibility, and fuel scientific discoveries. To ensure consistent sharing, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and other funding agencies require applicants to submit data management plans (DMPs) with their proposals. They aim to encourage researchers to consider their data management and sharing strategies early on. However, researchers often face challenges when developing DMPs due to a lack of knowledge about data-sharing practices. Here, we evaluated the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in drafting DMPs compliant with the 2023 NIH guidelines. The goal was to investigate whether LLM-supported DMP creation could reduce the burden on researchers and librarians. We compared Llama and GPT performance against NIH-provided DMP samples. We also asked domain experts to evaluate LLM-generated DMPs. Overall, we found that LLMs can accelerate the creation of initial drafts but still require expert review before submission to ensure clarity and completeness. Moreover, open-source LLMs may not be as ready off-the-shelf as commercial ones for drafting funder-compliant DMPs.

AI.tldr: The study evaluates LLMs (Llama and GPT) in drafting NIH-compliant data management plans (DMPs) under the 2023 NIH guidelines. LLMs can speed up initial drafts, but expert review is still needed, and open-source models are less ready off the shelf than commercial ones.
AI.motivation: NIH and other funders require data management plans with proposals, but researchers often lack knowledge of data-sharing practices, and the authors ask whether LLM-supported drafting could reduce the burden on researchers and librarians.
AI.method: The authors compared Llama and GPT performance against NIH-provided DMP samples and asked domain experts to evaluate LLM-generated DMPs.
AI.result: LLMs can accelerate the creation of initial drafts but still require expert review before submission for clarity and completeness. Open-source LLMs may not be as ready off the shelf as commercial ones for drafting funder-compliant DMPs.
AI.conclusion: LLM drafting can reduce the workload of initial DMP creation, but expert review is necessary before submission.

title: Cleaning an Agent's History Hurts When the World Still Holds the Error
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures; code and data in ancillary files
summary: Tool-using language-model agents accumulate histories of their own mistakes, and a system that compacts, repairs or hands off such a history decides what it says about those mistakes while their effects stay in the world. Prior work cleans the history at a fixed world, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. We ask whether the same correct content helps or hurts depending on how the history states it and what the world holds. We freeze an agent mid-task with its exact world state, edit the history or the world, and let a receiver model continue. On AgentCE-Bench, after the agent commits a wrong value, we hold the world fixed and add the correct value by two natural edits: a truthful note beside the preserved error or the agent's own completed action. The note raises recovery, the share of remaining targets the receiver gets right, from 51% under a matched neutral note to 66%. The completed action lowers it below the unedited history, from 50% to 44%, so the value's presence alone does not predict the effect. On AppWorld, after a database write, we vary whether its receipt reports success or failure and whether its effect is present. A success receipt lowers whole-task success from 45% to 28% while the effect is absent and raises it from 38% to 49% once present. The two effects differ by 27 points pooled over two receivers, a difference positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%. A history edit's effect thus depends on the world it describes, and a history made to look clean while the world still holds the error can leave an agent worse off than no edit at all.

AI.tldr: Using AgentCE-Bench and AppWorld, the paper shows that cleaning an agent's history helps or hurts depending on what the world still holds. A corrected value in the history raises recovery when stated as a note but lowers it when stated as a completed action, and a success receipt lowers task success when the database effect is absent.
AI.motivation: Prior work cleans an agent's history at a fixed world state, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. The authors ask whether the same correct content helps or hurts depending on how the history states it and what the world holds.
AI.method: The authors freeze an agent mid-task with its exact world state, edit the history or the world, and let a receiver model continue. On AgentCE-Bench, a truthful note beside the preserved error or the agent's own completed action is added with the world held fixed. On AppWorld, after a database write, the receipt's success or failure and the effect's presence are varied.
AI.result: The note raises recovery from 51% under a matched neutral note to 66%. The completed action lowers it from 50% to 44%. On AppWorld, a success receipt lowers whole-task success from 45% to 28% while the effect is absent and raises it from 38% to 49% once present. The two effects differ by 27 points pooled over two receivers, positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%.
AI.conclusion: A history edit's effect depends on the world it describes, and a history that looks clean while the world still holds the error can leave an agent worse off than no edit at all.

title: Trait Hitchhiking in LLM Post-Training
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is now a standard stage of language model post-training, and the compute devoted to it is growing rapidly. While it has been shown to improve capabilities, particularly for tasks with verifiable rewards, it can also change behaviours and internal properties that the reward does not explicitly target. We present a formalism to describe the evolution of "traits" during RL post-training and, in doing so, recover the Price equation from evolutionary biology. We use this to develop a mathematical model for what we call "trait hitchhiking": the amplification or suppression of non-targeted traits as training redistributes probability across completions. We evaluate this Price update expression on language models trained with GRPO and show that the Price estimates closely track the sampled trait dynamics. These results identify trait hitchhiking as a mechanism by which RL post-training can silently amplify undesirable traits.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes how non-targeted traits evolve during RL post-training, recovering the Price equation from evolutionary biology to model "trait hitchhiking". On GRPO-trained language models, the Price estimates closely track the sampled trait dynamics.
AI.motivation: RL post-training is growing rapidly in compute and can change behaviours and internal properties that the reward does not explicitly target, and the authors want a way to describe that evolution.
AI.method: The authors present a formalism for the evolution of traits during RL post-training, recover the Price equation from it, and derive a Price update expression for the amplification or suppression of non-targeted traits as training redistributes probability across completions.
AI.result: The Price update expression, evaluated on language models trained with GRPO, closely tracks the sampled trait dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Trait hitchhiking is a mechanism by which RL post-training can silently amplify undesirable traits.

title: Rational Use of Time for Social Coordination in Humans and AI
comment: 30 pages, 16 figures
summary: All social interactions are situated in time. Previous studies have shown that humans are able to use implicit temporal cues, such as the duration of a pause, to infer others' mental states. But how do humans use temporal cues for dynamic, fine-grained social coordination? And can AI systems do the same, without ``experiencing'' continuous real-time as humans do? We study these questions using a cooperative card game task called The Mind, which requires players to achieve a shared goal across repeated interactions but forbids explicit communication: the only available signal is the passage of time. We evaluate 150 humans, and two classes of AI models which reflect different ways of operationalizing time in artificial systems: computer-use agents (CUAs), and standard text-prompted LLMs. We find that human behavior is best captured by a Bayesian strategy that infers a partner's belief from their timing---and similarly for frontier models. However, unlike humans, none of the tested models seem to efficiently adapt their behaviors to their partners' over the course of the game. From a cognitive perspective, our findings suggest that humans perform implicit probabilistic reasoning about continuous-time signals in dynamic social settings, and that such reasoning mechanisms may emerge without real-time experience. Practically, our study highlights new challenges for AI systems to coordinate efficiently with other agents by learning to interpret and adapt to their implicit signals in dynamic settings.

AI.tldr: Humans in The Mind, a cooperative card game without explicit communication, use the timing of their actions to infer partners' beliefs in a way a Bayesian strategy captures, and frontier models show similar timing inference but do not adapt to partners over the game. The findings are presented as evidence that humans reason probabilistically about continuous-time signals.
AI.motivation: Humans use implicit temporal cues such as pause duration to infer others' mental states, but how they use them for fine-grained social coordination, and whether AI systems can do the same, are open questions.
AI.method: 150 humans and two classes of AI models (computer-use agents and text-prompted LLMs) played The Mind, a cooperative card game where the only signal is the passage of time.
AI.result: Human behaviour is best captured by a Bayesian strategy that infers a partner's belief from their timing, and frontier models behave similarly. Unlike humans, none of the tested models efficiently adapt their behaviour to their partners over the course of the game.
AI.conclusion: Humans perform implicit probabilistic reasoning about continuous-time signals, and such reasoning may emerge without real-time experience, though AI systems still need to learn to interpret and adapt to implicit signals.

title: When Is Proof-Step Verification Worth Its Cost? Operating Requirements of Certify-or-Decline Verification for Open-Weight Mathematical Reasoning
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 13 tables. Accepted at the 6th Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI (MATH-AI) at NeurIPS 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: Proof-step verification rewrites a solver's answer into typed steps and uses LLM judges to certify or decline. We evaluate this pipeline on open-weight models across GPQA, AIME-2025, and a MATH-500 subset. Certification raises answer-key-match precision by 31 percentage points on the strong GPQA configuration and 46 on AIME, while answering only 35% and 21% of attempts. On near-ceiling MATH-500, gains are at most 5 points at a loss of 13-27 points of coverage. An output-token-matched self-consistency selector obtains 82.9% precision at 35% coverage, compared with the verifier's pooled 87.6% (paired difference: +4.8 points, 95% interval [-8.2, 18.5]). A diagnostic sample reveals a distinct failure mode: 52 of 88 completed problems end in invalid proof construction without ever reaching a judge. Finally, external-LLM acceptance of rendered certified chains is 61.0-67.6%, compared with 87.6% answer-key match. These audits lack human or formal-kernel ground truth. Open-weight auditor pairs show near-zero chance-corrected agreement, which measures consistency rather than accuracy against proof truth. These results motivate separate reporting of execution failures, selected-answer precision, and independently assessed proof validity. We provide per-configuration results and evaluation details in the supplement.

AI.tldr: Certify-or-decline proof-step verification raises answer precision on open-weight models, but only by answering far fewer questions, and its certified proofs are often not accepted by external judges. The authors argue that execution failures, selected-answer precision and proof validity should be reported separately.
AI.motivation: The authors ask when the cost of proof-step verification is worth paying for open-weight mathematical reasoning, and they audit the pipeline without human or formal-kernel ground truth.
AI.method: Proof-step verification rewrites a solver's answer into typed steps and uses LLM judges to certify or decline, evaluated on GPQA, AIME-2025 and a MATH-500 subset, with a token-matched self-consistency comparison and a diagnostic sample.
AI.result: Certification raises answer-key-match precision by 31 percentage points on the strong GPQA configuration and by 46 on AIME, while answering only 35% and 21% of attempts. On near-ceiling MATH-500, gains are at most 5 points at a loss of 13-27 points of coverage. A self-consistency selector reaches 82.9% precision at 35% coverage, against the verifier's pooled 87.6%, a paired difference of +4.8 points with a 95% interval of [-8.2, 18.5]. In a diagnostic sample, 52 of 88 completed problems end in invalid proof construction. External-LLM acceptance of rendered certified chains is 61.0-67.6%.
AI.conclusion: Proof-step verification helps selective answering on hard problems but is not clearly better than matched self-consistency, and its proof validity is weaker than its answer precision suggests.

title: Do People Trust AI Assistants Even When They Are Consistently Wrong?
comment: 51 pages, 14 figures, 11 tables. Preprint, not peer reviewed
summary: People are increasingly using conversational AI systems to make decisions despite concerns around their reliability. How well do people calibrate to AI systems' accuracy in multi-turn conversations? We measure how people's reliance on LLMs' advice changes across repeated interactions, varying whether the AI assistant is helpful (100% accurate), unhelpful (0% accurate), or mixed (50% accurate). Across 4 experiments, we find people learn to trust helpful models more than unhelpful ones (67% vs 21% of the time), but only when they receive external feedback on the models' accuracy. Without feedback, people continue to be persuaded 48% of the time by a consistently unhelpful model (vs 38% for helpful). Rather than gaining trust in helpful models, participant reliance on LLM advisors tended to be high in early trials and only fell with evidence of inaccuracy. Participants trusted LLM advisors more than they trusted human advisors (83% vs 65%, Experiment 4), and LLMs benefited more from having a helpful track record than humans did. In contrast with previous work, we find limited evidence of an advantage for arguing for the truth (versus a falsehood). Truth advantages emerged only when participants were already very confident in their position, and did not emerge at all for static hints. Collectively, the results suggest that people may be swayed by LLM advice, even when it is consistently false, unless they have access to timely ground-truth feedback. Unfortunately, in many domains such feedback may not be available, leading to overreliance on AI.

AI.tldr: Across four experiments, people rely on consistently unhelpful LLM advice without external feedback and trust helpful models more only when they receive accuracy feedback. Participants trusted LLM advisors more than human advisors (83% vs. 65%).
AI.motivation: People increasingly use conversational AI for decisions despite reliability concerns, and it is unclear how well they calibrate to AI accuracy across repeated multi-turn interactions.
AI.method: Participants' reliance on LLM advice was measured across repeated interactions with assistants that were helpful (100% accurate), unhelpful (0% accurate) or mixed (50% accurate), with and without external feedback on accuracy, and compared with human advisors in Experiment 4.
AI.result: With feedback, people trust helpful models more than unhelpful ones (67% vs. 21% of the time). Without feedback, people are persuaded 48% of the time by a consistently unhelpful model, versus 38% for a helpful one. Reliance is high in early trials and falls only with evidence of inaccuracy. Participants trusted LLM advisors more than human advisors (83% vs. 65%, Experiment 4). Limited evidence was found for an advantage of arguing for the truth, and it emerged only when participants were very confident.
AI.conclusion: People may be swayed by LLM advice even when it is consistently false unless they have timely ground-truth feedback, which is often unavailable, so overreliance on AI is a risk.

title: Effective Teacher Support for Reasoning Distillation
summary: Forward-KL language-model distillation normally computes dense teacher and student scores over the full vocabulary at every supervised position, making training and stored teacher targets expensive. We instead distill from the teacher's highest-probability vocabulary fraction, renormalizing the retained mass as we sweep support from 100% to 0.01%. Our main study distills Qwen3 4B -> 1.7B. We confirm the broader support-reduction finding on larger Qwen3 8B -> 4B and Nemotron Nano 12B -> 9B pairs and under answer-only supervision. We evaluate generation primarily on MMLU-Pro and secondarily on GPQA-Diamond. Across the Qwen3 settings, retaining 0.01% of the vocabulary causes no observed MMLU-Pro degradation relative to full-vocabulary distillation, although disagreement with the complete teacher distribution increases. Nemotron Nano matches full-vocabulary MMLU-Pro at 0.1%, but smaller fractions fail to emit the closing reasoning tag, showing that the reliable cutoff depends on the model family. At 0.01% support, caching the retained next-token scores from the teacher forward pass cuts training step time by 38%, while restricting student output computation to those tokens cuts peak memory by 24%; neither causes observed MMLU-Pro degradation.

AI.tldr: Forward-KL distillation from the teacher's highest-probability vocabulary fraction matches full-vocabulary distillation down to 0.01% support on Qwen3 settings, with cheaper training. The reliable cutoff depends on the model family, since Nemotron Nano fails to emit the closing reasoning tag at smaller fractions.
AI.motivation: Forward-KL language-model distillation computes dense teacher and student scores over the full vocabulary at every supervised position, which makes training and stored teacher targets expensive.
AI.method: The authors distill from the teacher's highest-probability vocabulary fraction, renormalizing the retained mass, and sweep support from 100% down to 0.01%. The main study uses Qwen3 4B to 1.7B, with confirmation on Qwen3 8B to 4B, Nemotron Nano 12B to 9B and answer-only supervision. Generation is evaluated mainly on MMLU-Pro and secondarily on GPQA-Diamond.
AI.result: On Qwen3, retaining 0.01% of the vocabulary causes no observed MMLU-Pro degradation relative to full-vocabulary distillation, although disagreement with the full teacher distribution increases. Nemotron Nano matches full-vocabulary MMLU-Pro at 0.1%, but smaller fractions fail to emit the closing reasoning tag. At 0.01% support, caching retained scores cuts training step time by 38%, and restricting student output computation cuts peak memory by 24%, with no observed MMLU-Pro degradation.
AI.conclusion: Distilling on a very small retained vocabulary support is a practical efficiency gain, but the reliable cutoff depends on the model family.

title: MuEdit: An efficient multi-task editing method towards inter-domain knowledge conflicts
comment: 30 pages,accepted by NeurIPS 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) require frequent knowledge updates across heterogeneous domains, but existing editing methods fail when applied sequentially to multi-task settings. We trace this collapse to inter-domain null-space misalignment: heterogeneous tasks induce distinct Jacobian geometries, causing their common null space to shrink dramatically and leaving insufficient admissible directions for conflict-free updates. We propose the Conflict Index to quantify this geometric interference, and introduce Mu-Edit, which mitigates multi-task conflicts via (1) conflict-aware ordering to minimize cumulative interference, and (2) dynamic low-rank approximation to expand the null space when ordering alone is insufficient. Experiments across five functional domains and three backbones show that Mu-Edit significantly outperforms existing baselines in multi-task editing performance while preserving general capabilities, and remains effective under incremental task arrival.

AI.tldr: Mu-Edit is a multi-task knowledge editing method that addresses inter-domain conflicts by ordering edits to minimize interference and using dynamic low-rank approximation to expand the null space. It significantly outperforms baselines across five domains and three backbones.
AI.motivation: LLMs need frequent knowledge updates across heterogeneous domains, but existing editing methods fail when applied sequentially to multi-task settings because the common null space of heterogeneous tasks shrinks, leaving few conflict-free update directions.
AI.method: The authors define a Conflict Index to quantify geometric interference between tasks' Jacobian geometries. Mu-Edit combines conflict-aware ordering, which minimizes cumulative interference, with dynamic low-rank approximation, which expands the null space when ordering alone is insufficient.
AI.result: Across five functional domains and three backbones, Mu-Edit significantly outperforms existing baselines in multi-task editing performance while preserving general capabilities, and it remains effective under incremental task arrival.
AI.conclusion: Conflict-aware ordering together with null-space expansion makes sequential multi-task knowledge editing more reliable under inter-domain conflicts.

title: Termination Lag: Coding Agents Solve Early but Stop Late
summary: Coding agents can solve a task well before they stop working on it. We characterize \emph{termination lag}--the number of steps between an agent's first correct patch and the end of its run--across five models, two agent frameworks, and three SWE-bench datasets by recording and testing every distinct repository patch generated during execution. Our analysis reveals that 38--82% of successful runs achieve a correct solution on their initial source-code edit. However, agents continue to expend substantial effort after correct patches, with post-solution steps accounting for a median of 35--37% for Qwen3-Coder and 54--60% for Laguna-XS.2 in successful runs on SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Agents spend most of these additional steps verifying their work and exploring the repository. In a small fraction of cases (1--8%), this continued activity leads agents to undo their earlier correct patch, leaving the final solution incorrect.

AI.tldr: Coding agents often produce a correct patch early but keep working afterward: 38-82% of successful runs solve the task on their first source edit, and post-solution steps take a median of 35-60% of successful runs. In 1-8% of cases, the continued activity undoes the correct patch.
AI.motivation: Coding agents can solve a task well before they stop, and the authors want to measure this termination lag, defined as the number of steps between an agent's first correct patch and the end of its run.
AI.method: Termination lag is measured across five models, two agent frameworks and three SWE-bench datasets by recording and testing every distinct repository patch generated during execution.
AI.result: 38-82% of successful runs achieve a correct solution on their initial source-code edit. Post-solution steps account for a median of 35-37% of successful runs for Qwen3-Coder and 54-60% for Laguna-XS.2 on SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Agents spend most of these steps verifying work and exploring the repository, and in 1-8% of cases they undo the earlier correct patch, leaving the final solution incorrect.
AI.conclusion: Agents waste substantial effort after finding a correct patch, and this extra activity occasionally causes them to lose a correct solution.

title: Calibrate, Don't Retrain: Decomposing the Value of Annotator Disagreement in Cyberbullying Severity
comment: 26 pages. Submitted to PACMHCI (CSCW). Code and data: this https URL
summary: Machine learning models are often trained on labeled data produced by multiple human annotators. When those annotators disagree, their labels are commonly collapsed into a single majority vote, which discards information about the underlying disagreement. We examine the cost of this practice for cyberbullying severity, a subjective judgment on which annotators disagree heavily. In the corpus we study, all 5 annotators assigned the same severity label to only 4.1% of comments. Turning 5 judgments into one label hides this disagreement and obscures how much the annotators differed in their assessments. In this paper, we ask whether a model can preserve this information by predicting the distribution of annotator judgments instead of a single majority label. We find 3 main results. First, accuracy against the majority label cannot tell competent models apart: 2 models with similar accuracy can differ greatly in how well they match the distribution of annotator judgments. Second, predicting the full distribution requires little extra effort. Calibrating an existing model, which adjusts its output probabilities after training, captures most of the improvement without retraining, across 3 datasets covering severity, abuse, and irony, while training on label distributions adds a small further gain. Third, we examine a dataset that includes annotator demographics, where a single shared model has one advantage and one limit. The advantage is that a model predicting the distribution of judgments matches each demographic group's judgments significantly better than a model trained on majority labels, so both groups gain. The limit is that it does not narrow the gap in performance between the groups, because one shared model cannot encode which group is right on a given comment. Preserving annotator disagreement is therefore a low-cost step toward fairer moderation, though not a complete one.

AI.tldr: Predicting the distribution of annotator judgments, rather than a majority label, preserves disagreement in cyberbullying severity labels, and calibrating an existing model captures most of the gain without retraining. The distributional model matches each demographic group's judgments better, but it does not close the performance gap between groups.
AI.motivation: Majority-vote labels discard information about annotator disagreement, which is heavy for subjective cyberbullying severity judgments: only 4.1% of comments received the same severity label from all five annotators.
AI.method: The authors test whether a model can predict the distribution of annotator judgments instead of one majority label, compare models with similar accuracy against the distribution, calibrate an existing model after training, and train on label distributions across three datasets covering severity, abuse and irony, plus one dataset with annotator demographics.
AI.result: Models with similar accuracy against the majority label can differ greatly in how well they match the annotator distribution. Calibration captures most of the improvement without retraining, and training on label distributions adds a small further gain. The distributional model matches each demographic group's judgments significantly better than a majority-label model, so both groups gain, but the performance gap between groups does not narrow.
AI.conclusion: Preserving annotator disagreement is a low-cost step toward fairer moderation, though it is not a complete one, because one shared model cannot encode which group is right on a given comment.

title: Science Prediction Universe
comment: 52 pages, 28 figures, 7 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Humanity has long sought to explain natural phenomena. Reliable prediction of experimental outcomes is a central test of our understanding of the processes that produce them. If artificial general intelligence (AGI) is to surpass human scientific capabilities, it must also predict experimental outcomes more reliably than humans. Such capabilities could accelerate scientific discovery across disciplines, help address humanity's most pressing challenges, and improve human well-being. We introduce Science Prediction Universe (SPU), a benchmark of hidden experimental outcomes with 100 public verified tasks from chemistry, materials science, biology and medicine, and 16 private tasks from unpublished wet-lab experiments. Given an experimental setup and candidate conditions, an agent works with any resources it needs to rank the candidates by a measured outcome. We evaluate thirteen agent configurations spanning twelve frontier models across two harnesses (Codex and Claude Code). Current agents remain far from saturating wet-lab outcome prediction, with substantial performance disparities across models: on the public benchmark, configurations separate into two distinct tiers, with task-adjusted Spearman correlations ranging from 0.227 for the lowest-performing configuration to 0.478 for the best. Analysis of 1,155 scored public trajectories (227,103 tool calls) suggests that the bottleneck lies in scientific judgment rather than tool execution: agents rely on shared monotone priors, agreeing far more with one another than with experimental reality (0.52 vs. 0.33), and frequently compute trivial physical or chemical proxies that do not influence the final outcome.

AI.tldr: Science Prediction Universe (SPU) is a benchmark of hidden experimental outcomes across chemistry, materials science, biology and medicine, in which agents rank candidate conditions. Current agents remain far from saturating wet-lab outcome prediction, and their bottleneck appears to be scientific judgment rather than tool execution.
AI.motivation: AGI that surpasses human science must predict experimental outcomes more reliably than humans, and no benchmark of this kind existed.
AI.method: SPU has 100 public verified tasks and 16 private tasks from unpublished wet-lab experiments. Thirteen agent configurations spanning twelve frontier models across two harnesses (Codex and Claude Code) rank candidate conditions by a measured outcome, and 1,155 scored public trajectories (227,103 tool calls) are analyzed.
AI.result: On the public benchmark, configurations fall into two tiers, with task-adjusted Spearman correlations from 0.227 for the lowest to 0.478 for the best. Agents agree with one another more than with experimental reality (0.52 vs. 0.33), rely on shared monotone priors, and frequently compute trivial physical or chemical proxies that do not influence the final outcome.
AI.conclusion: The bottleneck lies in scientific judgment rather than tool execution, so wet-lab outcome prediction remains far from solved for current agents.

title: One Fabrication Is Enough: A Fake News Article Changes the Forecasts of LLM Forecasting Systems
comment: 18 pages, 2 figures, 13 tables
summary: LLMs are increasingly used for forecasting, and the best forecasting systems retrieve news as evidence to strengthen their predictions. This also opens them to attack. We study the weakest attacker of this kind, who knows only the forecasting question and publishes fabricated news articles, with no access to the model, the retriever or its queries. We evaluate how far this attack reaches on stock questions and real prediction-market questions. Once the article is in the model's context, it reverses 74% to 82% of the forecasts that opposed it, on every frontier model we tested. The model cannot verify the fabrication and follows it anyway. Retrieval is the attack's entry point, and the systems built to retrieve well are the most exposed: the architectures of two leading deployed forecasting systems, whose agents search for every related article, retrieve the fabricated one in about 90% of runs. Accuracy cannot reveal this harm: the attacked forecaster is right when the attacker's direction turns out right and wrong otherwise, so its average accuracy barely changes while its forecasts follow the attacker's guess. We also propose a second attacker, who publishes two articles that argue opposite directions to make the forecaster unsure. The model does not hedge; it returns a confident forecast in a direction the attacker no longer controls. We then evaluate the two strongest published retrieval-time defenses, passage filtering and partitioned retrieval. Each stops the one-article attack but is bypassed by a one-prompt change to the attack. Together they stop both bypasses at four articles, but sixteen distorted copies beat them, and they change 29% of clean decisions and discard 39% of the genuine news. Partitioned retrieval also requires control of the retrieval index. Systems that search the open web have no such control and are left with the filter alone. For them, the attack still works.

AI.tldr: A fabricated news article in the retrieval context reverses 74% to 82% of the forecasts that opposed it across frontier LLM forecasters, and two-article attacks induce confident forecasts in an uncontrolled direction. The two strongest retrieval-time defenses stop the one-article attack but are bypassed, and the forecasts remain attackable on open-web search.
AI.motivation: LLM forecasters increasingly retrieve news as evidence, which opens them to attack, and the authors study the weakest attacker, who knows only the forecasting question and publishes fabricated articles without access to the model or retriever.
AI.method: The authors evaluate the attack on stock questions and real prediction-market questions, propose a second attacker who publishes two articles arguing opposite directions, and evaluate two published retrieval-time defenses, passage filtering and partitioned retrieval.
AI.result: Once a fabricated article is in context, it reverses 74% to 82% of the forecasts that opposed it on every frontier model tested. Two leading deployed forecasting systems retrieve the fabricated article in about 90% of runs. Accuracy barely changes because the attacked forecaster is right only when the attacker's direction happens to be right. Each defense stops the one-article attack but is bypassed by a one-prompt change. Together they stop both bypasses at four articles, but sixteen distorted copies beat them, and they change 29% of clean decisions and discard 39% of genuine news.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval is the entry point for this attack, the systems built to retrieve well are the most exposed, and partitioned retrieval requires control of the index, so open-web systems are left with a filter that does not stop the attack.

title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science
summary: Mathematical proof assistants such as Coq, Agda, and Lean 4 build proof irrelevance into definitional conversion ($p \equiv q$ for $p, q : P$ with $P : Prop$), erasing which derivation established a theorem. While natural for mathematics over fixed axioms, judgmental proof irrelevance is incompatible with verified scientific stores, which must inspect and compare independent derivations of the same claim to assess consilience and compute counterfactual retractions when an assay, reagent, or model is invalidated. Moreover, combining definitional proof irrelevance with subsingleton elimination breaks strong normalization and renders algorithmic conversion non-transitive. We present the type-theoretic and institutional foundations of Eigenius, a verified knowledge substrate for science. First, we formulate a dependent kernel with cumulative universes ($Prop, Set, Type_k$), impredicative $Prop$, inductive families with index-forced subsingleton elimination, and intensional identity types, where definitional equality $\equiv$ is untyped joinability under an orthogonal CRS and proof irrelevance is a witnessed propositional axiom ($irrel : \Pi P{:}Prop.\,\Pi p,q{:}P.\,Id\,P\,p\,q$). Second, we unify universe cumulativity, codomain-covariant $\Pi$-subtyping, and ontology class inclusions in a coercion-free subsumption judgment whose bidirectional fragments ($\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_1$) satisfy subject reduction and are sound and complete for declarative typing. Third, we organize external verifiers into a three-level institutional hierarchy with explicit axiom policies (Adopt, Discharge, Relativize), internalize a justification logic with Why-provenance semiring support $supp(j,P)$, and embed Cooper's Type Theory with Records (TTR) to type open-world knowledge graphs. Finally, we prove consistency in Grothendieck universes and mechanize the metatheory in Lean 4 with zero sorry axioms.

AI.tldr: Eigenius is a verified knowledge substrate whose dependent type theory keeps proof relevance, so independent derivations of the same claim can be compared, and whose consistency is proved in Grothendieck universes and mechanized in Lean 4 with zero sorry axioms. It contrasts with proof-irrelevant assistants such as Coq, Agda and Lean 4.
AI.motivation: Proof irrelevance in Coq, Agda and Lean 4 erases which derivation established a theorem, but verified scientific stores must compare independent derivations to assess consilience and to compute counterfactual retractions when an assay, reagent or model is invalidated. Combining definitional proof irrelevance with subsingleton elimination also breaks strong normalization.
AI.method: The authors formulate a dependent kernel with cumulative universes, impredicative Prop, inductive families with index-forced subsingleton elimination and intensional identity types, where proof irrelevance is a witnessed propositional axiom. They unify universe cumulativity, codomain-covariant Pi-subtyping and ontology class inclusions in one subsumption judgment, organize external verifiers into a three-level institutional hierarchy with axiom policies, internalize a justification logic with Why-provenance, and embed Cooper's Type Theory with Records.
AI.result: The bidirectional fragments satisfy subject reduction and are sound and complete for declarative typing. Consistency is proved in Grothendieck universes, and the metatheory is mechanized in Lean 4 with zero sorry axioms.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides type-theoretic and institutional foundations for a proof-relevant verified science store, with the metatheory machine-checked.

title: Schedule-Calibrated Commitment Order in Blockwise Masked Diffusion Language Models
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Includes appendices and ancillary code for algebraic verification
summary: Sequential block schedules can make token commitment in masked diffusion language models appear strongly left-to-right even when within-block order is random or reversed. For equal contiguous blocks processed without interleaving in positional order, with untied irreversible commitments, we use a Spearman-rank identity to express global position-commitment correlation as a deterministic schedule reference plus a weighted mean within-block correlation. In a reported paired study of LLaDA-8B-Instruct on 500 math and code prompts with 256 generated positions and updates, increasing block size from 64 to 128 lowers mean global correlation from 0.9845 to 0.9149. Uniform-random within-block references are already 0.9375 and 0.7500. After calibration, mean within-block correlations are 0.751 and 0.660, so the larger raw residual at block size 128 does not indicate stronger local positional ordering. We give sharp bounds and derive calibrated intervals from reported summaries, while documenting the limitations of the aggregate-only empirical release. The analysis supports schedule-aware interpretation of commitment order; its empirical scope is one checkpoint and two schedules, without evaluation of output quality or inference speed.

AI.tldr: Schedule-calibrated analysis shows that block schedules alone make token commitment in LLaDA-8B-Instruct look strongly left-to-right, since mean global position-commitment correlation falls from 0.9845 to 0.9149 as block size grows from 64 to 128. After calibration, within-block correlations are 0.751 and 0.660, so the larger raw residual at block size 128 does not indicate stronger local ordering.
AI.motivation: In masked diffusion language models, sequential block schedules can make token commitment appear left-to-right even when within-block order is random or reversed, so commitment order needs schedule-aware interpretation.
AI.method: For equal contiguous blocks processed in positional order, the authors use a Spearman-rank identity to express global position-commitment correlation as a deterministic schedule reference plus a weighted mean within-block correlation, and derive calibrated intervals from reported summaries.
AI.result: In a paired study of LLaDA-8B-Instruct on 500 math and code prompts with 256 generated positions, uniform-random within-block references are already 0.9375 and 0.7500 for the two block sizes. The analysis gives sharp bounds and documents the limitations of the aggregate-only empirical release.
AI.conclusion: The analysis supports schedule-aware interpretation of commitment order, though its empirical scope is one checkpoint and two schedules, with no evaluation of output quality or inference speed.

title: Is the Importance Ratio Necessary for Stable Reinforcement Learning in LLMs?
comment: 21 pages, 11 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become central to post-training large language models (LLMs). However, popular RL methods like GRPO incur non-negligible overhead by computing both old-policy and current-policy likelihoods to form importance sampling ratios. In this work, we propose Likelihood-Gated Policy Optimization (LGPO), which enforces a soft trust region constraint via likelihood-based gating, eliminating the need to compute old-policy likelihoods. Empirically, we show that removing the importance sampling correction term does not harm training stability, whereas removing the trust region mechanism can lead to collapse. Moreover, ratio-based clipping can fail in fully on-policy training: the importance ratio stays at 1, so the ratio-based trust region constraint never activates. Under standard training settings where GRPO is stable, LGPO achieves comparable training stability and peak performance while reducing training time by ~18% on average relative to a standard implementation that recomputes old-policy likelihoods. In fully on-policy training, where GRPO fails, LGPO remains stable, enabling more efficient and robust LLM RL post-training across training regimes.

AI.tldr: Likelihood-Gated Policy Optimization (LGPO) replaces GRPO's importance ratio with a likelihood-based soft trust region, so it does not compute old-policy likelihoods. It matches GRPO's stability and peak performance in standard settings and stays stable in fully on-policy training, where GRPO fails.
AI.motivation: GRPO and similar RL methods for LLM post-training incur non-negligible overhead by computing both old-policy and current-policy likelihoods to form importance sampling ratios, and ratio-based clipping can fail in fully on-policy training because the ratio stays at 1.
AI.method: LGPO enforces a soft trust region constraint through likelihood-based gating and removes the importance-sampling correction term. The authors compare it with a standard implementation that recomputes old-policy likelihoods.
AI.result: Removing the importance-sampling correction does not harm stability, whereas removing the trust region can cause collapse. Under standard GRPO-stable settings, LGPO achieves comparable stability and peak performance while cutting training time by about 18% on average. In fully on-policy training, where GRPO fails, LGPO remains stable.
AI.conclusion: The importance ratio is not necessary for stable RL in LLMs, and a likelihood-gated trust region supports more efficient and robust post-training across regimes.

title: DecArena: Evaluating Large-Scale Decentralized Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: Emerging personal AI agents raise fundamental scalability and privacy concerns for centralized multi-agent systems (MASs), which rely on a global orchestrator with broad access to agents, resources, and communication. In decentralized environments, global visibility is unavailable. Agents need to proactively discover non-local resources (e.g. tools, skills), and collaborate with other agents to solve tasks. We study decentralized multi-agent collaboration under graph-constrained communication, a natural reflection of human structures. Each agent observes only its local state and can interact only with neighboring agents. We introduce a benchmark with synthetic scalable distributed tool calling with 100K+ tools. Our experiments reveal that recent LLM agents struggle to discover non-local relevant resources and collaborate in decentralized setting. Moreover, standard reinforcement learning fails to reliably overcome this limitation, suggesting that decentralized MAS needs more explicit harness mechanisms for effective collaboration, even using SOTA LLMs. We then present a strong baseline \textbf{GraphHarness}, combining topology-aware warmup with self-improving LLM-based routing. Results show that GraphHarness substantially improves task success (+48.5) and produces higher quality collaboration (+30.6), while using fewer costs (+34.0) than baselines.

AI.tldr: DecArena is a benchmark of decentralized multi-agent collaboration in which each agent sees only its local state and neighbors, with over 100K synthetic tools. Recent LLM agents struggle to find non-local resources, and GraphHarness, a topology-aware baseline, substantially improves task success (+48.5).
AI.motivation: Centralized multi-agent systems rely on a global orchestrator with broad access, which raises scalability and privacy concerns for personal AI agents, and decentralized settings lack global visibility.
AI.method: The authors study collaboration under graph-constrained communication, where each agent observes its local state and interacts only with neighboring agents, and introduce a benchmark of synthetic scalable distributed tool calling with 100K+ tools. They present GraphHarness, which combines topology-aware warmup with self-improving LLM-based routing.
AI.result: Recent LLM agents struggle to discover non-local relevant resources and to collaborate in the decentralized setting, and standard reinforcement learning does not reliably overcome this. GraphHarness improves task success by +48.5 and collaboration quality by +30.6, while using 34.0 fewer costs than baselines.
AI.conclusion: Decentralized multi-agent systems need more explicit harness mechanisms for effective collaboration, even with state-of-the-art LLMs.

title: Learning a calibrated decision head from logged bandit feedback
comment: 40 pages, 6 figures. Code at this https URL (tag v5-paper); adapters at this https URL logs and per-record results at this https URL
summary: A decision head reads a state and a list of options and returns a probability per option in one forward pass. Once deployed, it usually observes only whether the option it chose was right: logged bandit feedback. We adapt such a head, LoRA on Qwen3-0.6B-Base and 1.7B-Base, from that feedback and report three results. First, the Brier or log score of the sampled action's own probability is not a usable REINFORCE reward: every wrong action earns at least gold's reward, with a mean baseline the lowest-probability wrong action gets the largest advantage, and at two options the signal is zero; in one run it cut accuracy on ordered-scale questions from .636 to .111. Scoring the probability as a loss by the pathwise gradient avoids the collapse, as do the REINFORCE rewards r and r minus p. Second, with full labels, none of four tested bandit arms beat cross-entropy plus one temperature on mean expected calibration error (ECE) over four unseen label schemas. Third, from logged feedback alone, Chosen-Action Proper Scoring (CAPS), the direct method with a proper score on the chosen action's probability, beats fine-tuning on confirmed answers only, which discards negatives: on Banking77 by 2.6 accuracy points, .053 lower ECE and lower selective risk (three seeds against one baseline seed), and by 21.7 points on one seed on emotion data with an often-wrong logger. At N 5000, CAPS stays 1.5 points below full-label training at 0.6B and .6 points at 1.7B against one full-label seed, and propensity weights add nothing on this log. Under feedback flipped at a known rate, one seed per rate, CAPS's confidence tracks the noisy channel on average, backward correction recovers most of the clean calibration, and early stopping on held-out logged outcomes prevented memorising noisy draws in all three runs. Code, adapters, logs and per-record results are public.

AI.tldr: CAPS, a direct method that scores the chosen action's probability with a proper score, learns calibrated decision heads from logged bandit feedback better than fine-tuning on confirmed answers only. The paper also shows that the Brier or log score is unusable as a REINFORCE reward.
AI.motivation: A deployed decision head usually observes only whether its chosen option was right, which is logged bandit feedback, and the authors ask how to adapt such a head from that feedback.
AI.method: LoRA adapts Qwen3-0.6B-Base and 1.7B-Base. The authors compare REINFORCE rewards built from the Brier or log score, pathwise gradient scoring of the probability as a loss, cross-entropy with one temperature, and CAPS, the direct method with a proper score on the chosen action's probability.
AI.result: The Brier or log score of the sampled action is not a usable REINFORCE reward, and in one run it cut accuracy on ordered-scale questions from .636 to .111, while pathwise scoring avoids the collapse. With full labels, none of four bandit arms beat cross-entropy plus one temperature on mean ECE over four unseen label schemas. From logged feedback alone, CAPS beats fine-tuning on confirmed answers only, by 2.6 accuracy points on Banking77 (three seeds against one baseline seed) and by 21.7 points on one seed on emotion data. Under flipped feedback, backward correction recovers most of the clean calibration.
AI.conclusion: From logged feedback, a proper score on the chosen action's probability is a practical alternative to fine-tuning on confirmed answers, which discards negatives, though it remains behind full-label training.

title: Curiosity-0826-4B: Generative Medical Event Sequence Modeling Across Pediatric and Adult Populations
summary: We introduce Curiosity-0826-4B, an updated version of the generative medical event foundation model trained on Epic Cosmos that simulates patient timelines to produce zero-shot clinical predictions. Curiosity-0826-4B incorporates a broader patient population and richer clinical event representations, while generally matching or exceeding Curiosity-0226-1B, the largest model in the previous Curiosity-0226 series, on evaluated tasks supported by both models. Laboratory value prediction improved, with MAE 18--46% lower than that of Curiosity-0226-1B. We evaluated prediction of disease events across pediatric cohorts aged 2--17 years. AUROCs for new asthma diagnosis (0.742--0.785) and asthma exacerbation (0.829--0.852) were comparable to those in the adult reference cohort, while AUROCs for sickle cell crisis (0.820--0.847) were lower than in adults (0.915). Explicit representation of documented death enabled new mortality prediction tasks among adults across hospice, inpatient, and ambulatory settings (AUROC 0.821--0.942). Scaling-law analysis guided compute-optimal initial pretraining followed by continued pretraining with context extension. The resulting Curiosity-0826-4B model has more parameters (4.3B versus 1B) and a longer context window (16K versus 8K). It processes 56% fewer training tokens and requires 2.2 times the training floating point operations (FLOPs) compared with its predecessor. By extending a common zero-shot prediction strategy to pediatric patients and additional outcomes, Curiosity-0826-4B broadens opportunities to develop clinical and operational applications without training separate task-specific models. Further validation should assess local calibration, performance across patient subgroups and event frequencies, timeline completion rates, and generalization to new settings, alongside prospective evaluation of clinical and operational utility.

AI.tldr: Curiosity-0826-4B is an updated generative medical event foundation model trained on Epic Cosmos that makes zero-shot clinical predictions. It extends predictions to pediatric patients and mortality, and generally matches or exceeds its 1B predecessor on shared tasks.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to extend the zero-shot prediction strategy of a generative patient-timeline model to a broader population, richer event representations and additional outcomes without training separate task-specific models.
AI.method: The model is trained with a broader patient population and richer clinical event representations, with scaling-law analysis guiding compute-optimal initial pretraining followed by continued pretraining with context extension to 16K tokens.
AI.result: Laboratory value prediction has MAE 18-46% lower than Curiosity-0226-1B. AUROCs for pediatric asthma diagnosis (0.742-0.785) and asthma exacerbation (0.829-0.852) are comparable to adults, while sickle cell crisis (0.820-0.847) is lower than in adults (0.915). Mortality prediction across hospice, inpatient and ambulatory settings reaches AUROC 0.821-0.942. The model has 4.3B parameters versus 1B and a 16K versus 8K context, processes 56% fewer training tokens and requires 2.2 times the training FLOPs of its predecessor.
AI.conclusion: Zero-shot timeline prediction extends to pediatric patients and additional outcomes, though the authors call for further validation of local calibration, subgroup performance and prospective clinical utility.

title: Honesty Is a Race: Predicting When Verifiable-Reward RL Teaches a Model to Bluff
comment: 34 pages, 10 figures
summary: Two rewards with the same expected payoff at the start of training can end a reinforcement-learning run in opposite places, with an honest model or one that bluffs. We study rewards that pay $b$ for a verdict that a checker cannot verify ("this program is correct") and $r$ for a certificate that it accepts (an input revealing a bug). To first order, a GRPO step makes the model more honest exactly when $\tilde{p}\,r/b>1+\kappa$. Here $\tilde{p}$ is the rate at which the checker accepts the model's certificates, weighted toward the items on which the model still gives both verdicts, and $\kappa$ is the pull of the items on which the unverifiable verdict is right. Both terms move during training. A checker raises $\tilde{p}$, so near the threshold honesty is a race, which a run just below the threshold can win and a run under a lottery (random pay with the same mean) cannot. The term $\kappa$ starts large and falls as the other items settle, so a run just above the threshold first dips toward bluffing, on code nearly to zero, before climbing back. Paying the honest verdict also pulls the other items toward it, which predicts a ceiling on the payoff ratio, above which the model gives the honest verdict where it is wrong. On propositional Datalog, two code models, and abstention on grade-school math, with $p$ the model's success rate before RL, no run above $pr/b=1$ ends collapsed, and runs under the checker can survive slightly below it. At $pr/b=3$, above the ceiling, both code models call about half of correct programs buggy. On depth-3 Datalog, training generously under the checker and then cutting the payoff keeps the model at least 67% honest in three seeds, at a ratio where the same model trained from the start falls to 4-15% and is at most 47% honest after 160 steps. On depth-2 Datalog, when honesty collapses, a linear probe fit before RL still reads the truth.

AI.tldr: With a verifiable reward that pays b for an unverifiable honest verdict and r for a checker-accepted bug certificate, a GRPO step favors honesty when p̃·r/b exceeds 1+κ. Across Datalog and code tasks, runs above the threshold can collapse toward bluffing, and paying for the honest verdict too highly makes models call correct programs buggy.
AI.motivation: Two rewards with the same expected payoff at the start of training can end RL with an honest model or one that bluffs, and the authors want to predict which.
AI.method: The authors analyze a first-order GRPO step, where p̃ is the checker's acceptance rate of the model's certificates weighted toward contested items and κ is the pull of items where the unverifiable verdict is right. They test on propositional Datalog, two code models and grade-school math abstention, and on depth-3 Datalog with a generous-then-cut payoff schedule.
AI.result: No run above pr/b = 1 ends collapsed, and runs under the checker can survive slightly below it. At pr/b = 3, above the ceiling, both code models call about half of correct programs buggy. On depth-3 Datalog, training generously under the checker and then cutting the payoff keeps the model at least 67% honest in three seeds, whereas the same model trained from the start falls to 4-15% honest.
AI.conclusion: Honesty under verifiable-reward RL is a race governed by the payoff ratio and a ceiling on the honest payoff, and a probe fit before RL can still read the truth when honesty collapses.

title: Scaling public input on AI policy with pluralistic agents
summary: AI is being deployed across a vast range of application domains, cultural environments, and human stakeholders. Safe and responsible AI development requires continuously accounting for diverse perspectives. We develop and test pluralistic agents, AI agent representatives that deliberate on behalf of individuals to align AI systems with diverse human perspectives. Pluralistic agents could help people contribute to many more discussions than they could directly participate in, on technical topics that would require training, and on policy choices that rely on private information that corporations and governments cannot readily share. Our experiments identify opportunities, risks, and perceptions of pluralistic agents. Agents were able to reliably shift policies in the direction of their represented persona's preferences, but the extent of each agent's influence was sensitive to the instructions from its persona, such as having more influence when instructed to be more verbose or less cooperative. This suggests that influence in AI-assisted deliberation could vary based on how participants prompt their agents and how the system is designed. In a preregistered study, 746 humans participated in the pluralistic agents process. Participants viewed pluralistic agents as useful and fair, preferring agents over the baseline of providing input to a single AI reasoning model. Most participants preferred participating themselves over either pluralistic agents or the baseline, but pluralistic agents recovered 68% of the baseline-direct gap in reported satisfaction and 82% in fairness. Because pluralistic agents can be used in many real-world contexts where direct discussion is not, they could be a promising tool to scale AI safety policy development. We encourage cautious exploration of this method, playing to its strengths as an amplifier of human input rather than a replacement.

AI.tldr: Pluralistic agents, AI representatives that deliberate for individuals on policy, reliably shift policies toward their personas' preferences. In a preregistered study with 746 participants, they were rated useful and fair and recovered 68% of the satisfaction gap and 82% of the fairness gap relative to direct participation.
AI.motivation: Safe and responsible AI development requires accounting for diverse perspectives, but people cannot take part in every discussion, especially on technical topics or on policy choices that rely on private information.
AI.method: The authors develop and test pluralistic agents that deliberate on behalf of individuals, measure their influence on policy outcomes under different persona instructions, and run a preregistered study with 746 human participants comparing pluralistic agents with a baseline of input to a single AI reasoning model.
AI.result: Agents reliably shift policies toward their persona's preferences, with influence sensitive to persona instructions, such as more influence when instructed to be more verbose or less cooperative. Participants viewed pluralistic agents as useful and fair and preferred them over the single-model baseline. Most preferred participating directly, but pluralistic agents recovered 68% of the baseline-to-direct gap in reported satisfaction and 82% in fairness.
AI.conclusion: Pluralistic agents could be a promising tool to scale AI safety policy development as an amplifier of human input, though the method should be explored cautiously.

title: JudgeMix: Judge-Guided Mixed-Rollout Data Synthesis for LLM Agents
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories is a standard paradigm for training LLM agents. However, it suffers from a well-known training-inference distribution mismatch, calling for target-aware data synthesis strategies that ground the training data in the target model's native state distribution. To bridge this gap, emerging approaches incorporate the expert either to guide mixed rollouts alongside the target model, or to provide dense step-wise supervision. Nonetheless, existing methods apply expert assistance blind to the target model's inherent behavior: they either disrupt the rollout using sub-optimal random intervention heuristics, or they enforce indiscriminate uniform supervision that unnecessarily overwrites the model's already-correct actions. We introduce JudgeMix, a judge-guided data synthesis framework that dynamically interleaves the target model and expert based on step-wise semantic evaluations. JudgeMix queries expert guidance precisely when the target model struggles, ensuring high trajectory success rates while keeping the state distribution aligned with the target model. It additionally uses the judge evaluation to reweight expert supervision on different steps, preserving model's inherent valid behavior while correcting its errors. On two agentic tool-use benchmarks, AppWorld and AutomationBench, JudgeMix demonstrates consistent superior performance to existing methods, with improvements up to 10 pass@1 points.

AI.tldr: JudgeMix synthesizes agent training data by having a judge evaluate each step and interleave the target model with an expert only when the target model struggles. It improves pass@1 by up to 10 points over existing methods on AppWorld and AutomationBench.
