AI.conclusion: Progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence and potentially conflicting objectives.

title: Can an AI Agent Be Epistemically Akratic? Higher-Order Evidence & the Limits of Self-Correction
summary: When we judge that our reasoning was defective, it seems plausible that we should abandon the conclusion it produced. This thought has special force for AI agents built to assess and correct their own work. Yet obeying such judgments can make an agent worse at distinguishing sound reasoning from defective reasoning. An AI agent may rely on information about its reasoning when deciding which conclusions to keep, while the part that judges whether those conclusions are justified cannot use that information. The agent can then exercise an epistemic competence by retaining conclusions it judges unjustified, even when its self-assessments are generally reliable. Nor is the difficulty resolved by training the agent to make its conclusions and assessments agree: agreement can be achieved by degrading either one. Crucially, I argue that a negative assessment can remain valuable by identifying conclusions requiring further scrutiny, without having authority to eliminate them. The result challenges a central assumption about AI self-correction: that bringing an agent's beliefs into agreement with its own self-assessment about their justification makes it better at correcting its mistakes.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that an AI agent that retains conclusions its own assessment judges unjustified can exercise a form of epistemic akrasia, and that aligning beliefs with self-assessment does not reliably improve self-correction, because agreement can be reached by degrading either side.
AI.motivation: A common assumption about AI self-correction is that bringing an agent's conclusions into agreement with its own justification assessments makes it better at fixing mistakes, which the author questions.
AI.method: This is a philosophical argument. The author analyzes how an agent that uses information about its reasoning to keep conclusions can diverge from the part that judges their justification, and shows that agreement can be achieved by degrading either the conclusions or the assessments.
AI.result: The abstract reports no empirical results; it argues that the difficulty is not resolved by training the agent to make conclusions and assessments agree.
AI.conclusion: A negative self-assessment remains valuable for flagging conclusions that need further scrutiny, but it should not have authority to eliminate them.

title: Edge-Native Multimodal RAG: Hardware-Aware Quantization and Architectural Optimization for Consumer GPUs
comment: Accepted to the 14th International Japan-Africa Conference on Electronics, Communications and Computations (JAC-ECC 2026).6 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables
summary: Deployment of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for Edge-AI is constrained by memory and bandwidth limitations. A standard 7B parameter model consumes 14 GB Video Random Access Memory (VRAM) in half-precision (FP16), precluding co-location of vector indices and Key-Value (KV) caches. This paper presents an engineering integration and empirical evaluation of a multimodal RAG framework optimized for consumer-grade Turing hardware (e.g., NVIDIA Tesla T4). Our system-level analysis identifies a critical trade-off: while generative pre-trained transformer quantization (GPTQ) offers superior throughput (51.6 tok/s), it exhibits significant context instability at 2048+ tokens on Turing architectures. Conversely, NormalFloat 4-bit (NF4) maintains robust long-context performance with viable latency (81 ms/tok). By coupling NF4 with a decoupled Florence-2 vision integration, we achieve visual reasoning with only 430 MB VRAM overhead. Furthermore, empirical observations of prompt-induced search space pruning show that structured prompting reduces latency by 47% without altering computational intensity (1.88 GFLOPs/token). The integrated architecture maintains an 8.37 GB footprint, establishing a viable RAG pipeline for 12-16 GB GPUs. Finally, structured few-shot prompting effectively compensates for quantization-induced reasoning loss, restoring mathematical accuracy from 35.0% to 92.0% across 200 trials.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an engineering evaluation of a multimodal RAG framework for consumer GPUs, showing that NF4 quantization keeps long-context performance robust where GPTQ becomes unstable, and that structured few-shot prompting restores math accuracy from 35.0% to 92.0%.
AI.motivation: RAG deployment on edge devices is limited by memory and bandwidth, since a 7B model in FP16 needs 14 GB of VRAM, which leaves no room for vector indices and KV caches on consumer GPUs.
AI.method: The authors integrate a multimodal RAG framework on a Turing-class NVIDIA Tesla T4 by combining NF4 quantization with a decoupled Florence-2 vision module, and they compare it with GPTQ, measuring throughput, latency, memory and reasoning accuracy.
AI.result: GPTQ offers higher throughput at 51.6 tokens per second but shows context instability at 2048 or more tokens on Turing. NF4 keeps robust long-context performance at 81 ms per token. Visual reasoning adds only 430 MB of VRAM, and the integrated system has an 8.37 GB footprint. Structured prompting reduces latency by 47% without changing computational intensity, and few-shot prompting restores math accuracy from 35.0% to 92.0% across 200 trials.
AI.conclusion: The integrated architecture is a viable RAG pipeline for 12 to 16 GB GPUs, with NF4 preferred for long contexts and structured prompting compensating for quantization-induced reasoning loss.

title: Provably Optimal HBT Legalization in Seconds: Certified Optima Reveal Where the Headroom Really Lies
summary: Hybrid bonding terminal (HBT) legalization assigns every terminal of a face-to-face 3D IC to its own pitch-grid site with minimum total Manhattan displacement. Open3DBench reports that a reinforcement-learning (RL) legalizer reduces displacement by 19-22% relative to a sliding-window (SW) heuristic, but none of its legalizers is publicly released. We ask how much displacement any legalizer can still recover. We build an open benchmark of 21 design/pitch instances from Open3DBench placement data, with reconstructed greedy, SW (ViaLegal-style) and BTAssign-style baselines, and GEO-Exact, an exact solver that runs successive shortest augmenting paths over lazily generated spatial candidate edges. An independent dual certificate proves its assignment optimal on all 21 instances (relative primal-dual gap at most $8.2 \times 10^{-16}$). Against these optima, our SW reconstruction with ViaLegal's default configuration is on average 0.011% above optimal (worst 0.119%), while on the 16 contended instances BTAssign-style, a density-guided heuristic (DGHL) and greedy are 3.0%, 6.9% and 64.5% above. Headroom does appear outside this regime: with 2x2 windows SW reaches 34.1%, and above about 58% utilization, on three of six swept designs, it reaches 21.1% on bp, 27.5% on swerv and 8.9% on jpeg (217 further certified instances, and ten bp points checked against an independent exact solver). If the published 19-22% gain were measured on instances like ours, SW would have to be at least 24-28% above optimal on average, far more than any SW variant we tested at nominal pitch; the RL paper's own comparison with the Hungarian optimum puts its SW 3.05% above optimal on average. GEO-Exact is also about an order of magnitude faster than DGHL and SW in our harness (geometric means 8.1x and 40x; a compiled core against Python baselines on a shared server). Code, optimal values and certificates are released.

AI.tldr: The paper releases GEO-Exact, an exact solver for hybrid bonding terminal legalization with a dual certificate of optimality, and shows that a sliding-window heuristic is near-optimal on most instances while the reported RL gain would require a much weaker baseline.
AI.motivation: A reinforcement-learning legalizer reportedly reduces displacement by 19 to 22% over a sliding-window heuristic, but no legalizer from that work is public, and the question of how much displacement any legalizer can still recover is open.
AI.method: The authors build an open benchmark of 21 design and pitch instances with reconstructed greedy, sliding-window and BTAssign-style baselines, and GEO-Exact, which runs successive shortest augmenting paths over lazily generated spatial candidate edges. An independent dual certificate verifies optimality.
AI.result: The dual certificate proves the assignment optimal on all 21 instances. On the 16 contended instances, the sliding-window reconstruction is on average 0.011% above optimal, while BTAssign-style, DGHL and greedy are 3.0%, 6.9% and 64.5% above. With 2x2 windows or high utilization, the sliding window reaches up to 34.1% above optimal on some designs. GEO-Exact is about an order of magnitude faster than the baselines in the authors' harness.
AI.conclusion: Headroom for displacement reduction exists mainly outside nominal conditions, and the published 19 to 22% gain would imply a sliding-window baseline far above optimal, so the RL comparison should be re-examined.

title: RSI-PDEbench: A Benchmark for Self-Improving Agents in PDE Solving
summary: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce \bench{}, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.

AI.tldr: RSI-PDEbench is a benchmark of 1,001 PDE identification and solving cases, and RSI-PDE is a recursively self-improving agent harness that outperforms single-run baselines and native agent harnesses across three evaluation settings.
AI.motivation: Identifying and solving PDEs from sampled solution data needs expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation and solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shift, and it is unclear whether LLM agents can automate this reliably.
AI.method: The benchmark spans 42 equation templates, including classical and fractional PDEs, with Full, Noisy (Gaussian noise at 50% of the clean-signal RMS) and Hard-OOD settings. RSI-PDE shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative L2 feedback to refine coefficients and solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. It is compared with single-run baselines and native harnesses, Claude Code or Codex, on four frontier models.
AI.result: Averaged across the four models, RSI-PDE improves pass rate by 106.5 to 181.9% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0 to 19.6% relative to native harnesses across the three settings. It reduces total recorded model calls by 46.9% across the 12 model-setting pairs.
AI.conclusion: Validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents has potential for advancing scientific computing.

title: Early Signals, Strong Decisions: Prefix-Guided Sampling for Parallel Test-Time Scaling
summary: Parallel test-time scaling (TTS) has been shown to enhance reasoning in large language models by generating and aggregating multiple independent reasoning paths. Internal confidence scores can further improve this process by identifying paths of varying quality. However, existing methods remain computationally inefficient, as low-quality paths are fully expanded before being evaluated. In this work, we aim to improve the use of internal confidence signals for better model performance and computational efficiency. We begin by offering a new perspective on the role of confidence in aggregation, showing that it is most impactful for questions near the decision boundary. Notably, when amplified by multi-sample aggregation, even small confidence signals derived from short prefixes can meaningfully influence outcomes in these boundary cases. Building on this insight, we introduce Prefix-Guided Sampling (PreG), a method that reallocates computation by first generating short prefixes, ranking them using internal confidence scores, and then completing only the most promising candidates. This strategy reduces token usage while maintaining gains in path quality. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that, under a fixed compute budget, PreG strengthens the effective signal by widening the decision boundary margin. Empirically, our method consistently outperforms standard parallel TTS approaches across benchmarks, while significantly improving token efficiency and reducing overall computation.

AI.tldr: PreG is a parallel test-time scaling method that generates short prefixes, ranks them by internal confidence and completes only the most promising ones, improving token efficiency while maintaining path quality.
AI.motivation: Parallel test-time scaling with confidence scores improves reasoning, but low-quality paths are fully expanded before being evaluated, which wastes computation.
AI.method: PreG first generates short prefixes of the reasoning paths, ranks them using internal confidence scores, and then completes only the most promising candidates. The authors also provide a theoretical analysis under a fixed compute budget showing that the decision-boundary margin widens.
AI.result: PreG consistently outperforms standard parallel test-time scaling approaches across benchmarks while significantly improving token efficiency and reducing overall computation.
AI.conclusion: Confidence signals from short prefixes are most useful for questions near the decision boundary, and reallocating compute toward promising prefixes is an efficient strategy.

title: Same Task, Different Statement: When and How Reformulation Helps LLM Problem Solving
summary: When people face a hard problem, they often restate it in a clearer way before solving it. We study whether the same habit helps large language models by rewriting the statement of a problem. A legal rewrite must keep the meaning, the constraints, and the correct answer unchanged. We test three kinds of rewrites. Decomposition makes hidden subgoals explicit. Typed Reformulation casts the task into a more suitable solving frame. Concept Reduction removes surface detail and exposes the task structure. We evaluate them on eight math, logic, and code benchmarks with eight models, all under the same chain-of-thought solving prompt. The effect is large but depends on the problem type. An oracle that picks the best rewrite after the fact raises accuracy by +27.6% on average. Yet no single rewrite helps every problem, and a mismatched rewrite can hurt. Still, the effect follows clear patterns. Each kind of rewrite fits certain problem types. A simple fixed rule learned from one set of problems transfers part of the gain to new problems. It gains +11.0% on the problems it chooses to rewrite, while blind rewriting loses 5.6% on a similar share of problems. Rewriting is therefore not a universal way to solve problems. The question is when and how to rewrite.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether rewriting a problem statement before solving it helps LLMs, and finds that the effect depends on the problem type, with an oracle choice of rewrite raising accuracy by 27.6% on average while blind rewriting can hurt.
AI.motivation: People often restate hard problems before solving them, and the authors ask whether rewriting a statement helps LLMs, while requiring the rewrite to keep the meaning, constraints and correct answer unchanged.
AI.method: The authors test three rewrites: Decomposition makes hidden subgoals explicit, Typed Reformulation casts the task into a more suitable solving frame, and Concept Reduction removes surface detail. They evaluate on eight math, logic and code benchmarks with eight models under the same chain-of-thought prompt, and they test a simple fixed rule learned on one set of problems.
AI.result: An oracle that picks the best rewrite after the fact raises accuracy by 27.6% on average, but no single rewrite helps every problem and a mismatched rewrite can hurt. The fixed rule gains 11.0% on the problems it chooses to rewrite, while blind rewriting loses 5.6% on a similar share of problems.
AI.conclusion: Rewriting is not a universal method, and the practical question is when and how to rewrite.

title: EvoX: Rethinking the Agent Harness as a Runtime Policy
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Technical report
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly interact with tools and environments, yet plausible model decisions do not always translate into successful execution due to tool-call mismatches, interrupted workflows, and unsupported completion claims. We present EvoX, a Rust-based, multi-model agent runtime guided by The Second Policy, which views the harness as an Operational Policy complementing the foundation model's Semantic Policy. EvoX combines model-facing guidance with deterministic runtime control through three complementary mechanisms: Action Realization, Execution Continuity, and Outcome Grounding. To evaluate harnesses without suppressing their native behaviors, we introduce Contrast, a controlled and auditable framework integrating explicit fairness constraints, provider-bound request verification, and evidence-based adjudication. Across five benchmarks, six foundation models, and six agent harnesses, EvoX achieves the highest numerical success rate of 56.2% over 691 common task--model pairs, exceeding the average of the other five harnesses by approximately 3.0 percentage points. Its larger advantages on GLM-5.3 (+10.7 points) and Kimi K3 (+7.9 points) highlight the model-dependent effectiveness of harness design and the potential for cross-provider adaptability. Achieved without memory, evolution, or extensions, these results establish EvoX as a competitive multi-model agent runtime and underscore the importance of harness-level operational control in realizing foundation-model capabilities.

AI.tldr: EvoX is a Rust-based multi-model agent runtime that treats the harness as an operational policy with deterministic runtime control, and it achieves the highest success rate among six harnesses over 691 common task-model pairs.
AI.motivation: Plausible model decisions do not always become successful execution, because of tool-call mismatches, interrupted workflows and unsupported completion claims.
AI.method: EvoX combines model-facing guidance with deterministic runtime control through three mechanisms: Action Realization, Execution Continuity and Outcome Grounding. The authors also introduce Contrast, a framework with explicit fairness constraints, provider-bound request verification and evidence-based adjudication for comparing harnesses.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks, six foundation models and six harnesses, EvoX achieves the highest numerical success rate of 56.2% over 691 common task-model pairs, about 3.0 percentage points above the average of the other five harnesses. Its advantages are larger on GLM-5.3 (+10.7 points) and Kimi K3 (+7.9 points).
AI.conclusion: Harness-level operational control matters for realizing foundation-model capabilities, and harness effectiveness depends on the model.

title: Advancing Weighted Partial MaxSAT Solving via Differentiable GPU Guidance
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures
summary: We present a GPU-CPU hybrid framework for Weighted Partial MaxSAT (WPMAX-SAT) that complements state-of-the-art CPU solvers with differentiable GPU optimization. The GPU stage directly optimizes instance-specific categorical decision parameters without a training dataset or a pretrained predictive model. The central challenge in extending differentiable optimization to WPMAX-SAT is the hard/soft clause asymmetry: hard clauses represent inviolable feasibility constraints while soft clauses carry weights. We introduce a hierarchical differentiable loss that prioritizes hard clause satisfaction before optimizing the weighted soft objective, ensuring that GPU gradient descent leans towards the constraint structure of WPMAX-SAT. Our framework transforms the GPU-optimized variable logits to high-confidence assignments and transfers them to CPU solvers via two complementary modes: partial guidance, which injects the most confident perturbed partial variable assignments as soft clauses into $N$ parallel solver instances, and phase initialization, which guides the CDCL solver's internal branching polarity with the full GPU assignment as a warm start to preserve the problem's originality. We evaluate on all 229 instances of the MSE 2024 (most recent due to cancellation in 2025) anytime weighted benchmark with the top 2 winners as baselines; our hybrid framework improves the average solution score by up to 4.9% over tt-open-wbo-inc-Glucose and 4.8% over SPB-MaxSAT-c-FPS at a 300-second time limit, with the potential to obtain better solutions surpassing the best known solution recorded in the competition evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a GPU-CPU hybrid for Weighted Partial MaxSAT that uses differentiable GPU optimization of variable logits to guide CPU CDCL solvers, improving average solution scores on the MSE 2024 anytime weighted benchmark.
AI.motivation: CPU MaxSAT solvers are state of the art, but the hard and soft clause asymmetry makes it hard to extend differentiable optimization to WPMaxSAT, since hard clauses are inviolable while soft clauses carry weights.
AI.method: The authors introduce a hierarchical differentiable loss that prioritizes hard clause satisfaction before optimizing the weighted soft objective. GPU-optimized logits are converted to high-confidence assignments and transferred to CPU solvers in two modes: partial guidance, which injects confident partial assignments as soft clauses into N parallel solver instances, and phase initialization, which sets the CDCL branching polarity from the full GPU assignment.
AI.result: On all 229 instances of the MSE 2024 anytime weighted benchmark, the hybrid improves average solution score by up to 4.9% over tt-open-wbo-inc-Glucose and 4.8% over SPB-MaxSAT-c-FPS at a 300-second limit, and may surpass the best known solutions recorded in the competition.
AI.conclusion: Differentiable GPU guidance is a complementary way to improve CPU MaxSAT solvers, without training data or a pretrained model.

title: A frontier machine intelligence for human neuroimaging
comment: 41 pages, 4 main figures, 9 extended data figures
summary: Medical imaging is essential for diagnosing disease, guiding treatment and monitoring patients over time. Although artificial intelligence has advanced image interpretation, existing medical models often address restricted tasks, while general-purpose proprietary models lack access to private clinical imaging required to achieve medical expertise. Developing models that can interpret complex examinations and communicate their findings in the context of clinical decisions remains a major challenge. Here, we show that Neuro-VL, a vision-language model trained on nearly one million neuroimaging studies from routine clinical care, can interpret complete imaging examinations and engage in natural language conversations about their findings. Across internal and international datasets, Neuro-VL outperformed frontier general-purpose and specialized medical models in diagnosing, localizing, and describing abnormalities, as well as generating comprehensive radiology reports. The model also compared serial examinations to assess disease progression and more reliably resisted misleading clinical assumptions than leading frontier models from OpenAI and Google. These results extend health system learning beyond individual predictions to interactive image interpretation and longitudinal disease monitoring. They demonstrate how the collective clinical experience of health systems can be used to develop medical AI with specialized expertise and broad clinical capabilities.

AI.tldr: Neuro-VL is a vision-language model trained on nearly one million routine clinical neuroimaging studies that interprets complete examinations, outperforms frontier general and medical models on diagnosis and report generation, and resists misleading clinical assumptions better than leading proprietary models.
AI.motivation: Existing medical imaging models address restricted tasks, while general-purpose proprietary models lack access to private clinical imaging needed for medical expertise.
AI.method: Neuro-VL is trained on nearly one million neuroimaging studies from routine clinical care. It interprets complete imaging examinations, holds natural language conversations about findings, and compares serial examinations to assess progression.
AI.result: Across internal and international datasets, Neuro-VL outperforms frontier general-purpose and specialized medical models in diagnosing, localizing and describing abnormalities and in generating comprehensive radiology reports. It more reliably resists misleading clinical assumptions than leading frontier models from OpenAI and Google.
AI.conclusion: Health-system clinical data can be used to develop medical AI with specialized expertise, interactive image interpretation and longitudinal disease monitoring.

title: GuardianAgentFlow: Multi-Agent Coordination for Web Privacy Protection
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures
summary: Web agents need to use private context without unnecessarily disclosing it. Effective protection must distinguish between requests that may be sent after sanitization and those that must be withheld, while preserving the information needed for authorized tasks. We present GuardianAgentFlow, a multi-agent framework that mediates outgoing Web requests through an explicit release contract. A dedicated restriction check grounds permission in the user's instruction; a shared protection scope aligns rewriting with disclosure checking; and candidate-grounded feedback guides revision before transmission. Experiments on Web requests with human-reviewed intent labels show improved request-contract success, while controlled comparisons and role ablations identify the contributions of restriction handling, policy evidence, and candidate checking. Evaluations of action proposals from PrivacyLens and AgentDAM demonstrate complementary protection when mediation is composed with privacy-aware agents. Experiments with smaller mediation models show that the coordination benefit persists with reduced model capacity. Dedicated-server measurements show lower mediation latency than full-policy reasoning, while real-site browser tests quantify integration overhead.

AI.tldr: GuardianAgentFlow is a multi-agent framework that mediates outgoing web requests of web agents through an explicit release contract, improving protection of private context while preserving information needed for authorized tasks.
AI.motivation: Web agents need to use private context without unnecessarily disclosing it, and effective protection must separate requests that can be sent after sanitization from those that must be withheld.
AI.method: A dedicated restriction check grounds permission in the user's instruction, a shared protection scope aligns rewriting with disclosure checking, and candidate-grounded feedback guides revision before transmission. Ablations identify the roles of restriction handling, policy evidence and candidate checking.
AI.result: On web requests with human-reviewed intent labels, the framework improves request-contract success. On action proposals from PrivacyLens and AgentDAM it gives complementary protection when composed with privacy-aware agents. Smaller mediation models retain the coordination benefit, and mediation latency is lower than full-policy reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent mediation with an explicit release contract is a practical way to add privacy protection to web agents, with a benefit that persists at reduced model capacity.

title: Expanding the Decision Space of Pretrained Models through Structured Re-Decoding
comment: 29 pages, 2 figures
summary: Native decoders limit how pretrained models combine local predictions under new structural constraints. We introduce Structured Re-Decoding (SRD), a training-free framework that constructs local candidates from model scores, samples, or external specifications, jointly optimizes their selection, and verifies reconstructed outputs. We show that candidate recombination expands feasible support and can improve attainable reward under a fixed KL divergence budget. Across molecular generation, protein design, RNA structure prediction, and antibody modeling, SRD enables improved structured inference, including verified molecules absent from the original sample pool. External chemical templates further extend SRD to noncanonical amino acids, peptide cyclization, and grammar-guided molecular construction. Preliminary experiments on a physical coherent Ising machine demonstrate the feasibility of hardware-based optimization, suggesting broader opportunities for quantum and quantum-inspired approaches to structured inference and combinatorial optimization across scientific domains.

AI.tldr: Structured Re-Decoding (SRD) is a training-free framework that recombines local candidates from pretrained models under structural constraints, verifies the reconstructed outputs and expands the feasible support across molecular, protein, RNA and antibody tasks.
AI.motivation: Native decoders limit how pretrained models combine local predictions under new structural constraints.
AI.method: SRD builds local candidates from model scores, samples or external specifications, jointly optimizes their selection and verifies reconstructed outputs. External chemical templates extend it to noncanonical amino acids, peptide cyclization and grammar-guided molecular construction. Preliminary experiments use a physical coherent Ising machine.
AI.result: The authors show that candidate recombination expands feasible support and can improve attainable reward under a fixed KL divergence budget. Across molecular generation, protein design, RNA structure prediction and antibody modeling, SRD enables improved structured inference, including verified molecules absent from the original sample pool.
AI.conclusion: Recombining verified local candidates is a training-free way to expand what pretrained models can produce under structural constraints, and it suggests opportunities for quantum-inspired hardware.

title: HyperSkill: Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO via Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library Evolution
comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026 main conference
summary: Reinforcement learning sharpens LLM reasoning, but parameter updates are expensive, forgetful, and opaque; training-free libraries swap gradients for a textual store but still use trajectory-level, correlation-based admission and flat structure. To address both, we propose HyperSkill, a Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO framework that keeps the backbone frozen and replaces gradient updates with auditable edits to a Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library, where skills are advantage-bearing nodes and compositions are hyperedges. It has three components: training-time distillation admits counterfactually checked skills and learns a protocol skill from failures; gated hypergraph retrieval injects advantage-ranked skills where a per-dataset gate admits them; and an execution protocol makes the frozen backbone commit to an answer. On 11 text, vision-language, and omnimodal benchmarks, HyperSkill is best or tied on every dataset and beats the best baseline by 13.0 average F1 points while keeping the backbone frozen. Our software and data are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: HyperSkill is a training-free omnimodal GRPO framework that keeps the backbone frozen and replaces gradient updates with edits to a hypergraph-indexed skill library, and it is best or tied on every one of 11 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: RL sharpens LLM reasoning, but parameter updates are expensive, forgetful and opaque, and existing training-free skill libraries use flat structure and correlation-based admission.
AI.method: HyperSkill stores advantage-bearing skills as nodes and compositions as hyperedges. Training-time distillation admits counterfactually checked skills and learns a protocol skill from failures, gated hypergraph retrieval injects advantage-ranked skills where a per-dataset gate admits them, and an execution protocol makes the frozen backbone commit to an answer.
AI.result: On 11 text, vision-language and omnimodal benchmarks, HyperSkill is best or tied on every dataset and beats the best baseline by 13.0 average F1 points while keeping the backbone frozen.
AI.conclusion: Auditable edits to a structured skill library can substitute for gradient updates in omnimodal GRPO-style reasoning training.

title: WordInferBench: Can Agents Infer How to Edit from Word Document Context?
summary: Document editing is among the most common knowledge-work tasks, yet existing benchmarks for evaluating autonomous agents on Word document editing provide fully specified attribute-modification instructions. They do not evaluate agents' ability to infer the appropriate attributes from document context, a capability essential in real-world editing where users expect consistency without spelling out every attribute. We introduce WordInferBench, a benchmark comprising 280 base document-editing instances, each paired with three instruction conditions: descriptive (the instruction explicitly lists every attribute change), referential (the instruction points to another object as an exemplar), and inferential (the agent must examine document context to infer what attributes to apply). To evaluate contextual attribute inference, each base instance is constructed so that the target formatting is recoverable from an in-document exemplar. The instances are derived from real Word documents collected from Common Crawl and cover 13 object types and 81 attributes. We evaluate six recent coding-agent systems and find that the best-performing evaluated system, Claude Code with Opus 4.6, achieves a 62.9% task-level pass rate on descriptive variants but only 40.7% on inferential variants, indicating that current systems complete tasks less reliably when the required formatting changes must be determined from document context.

AI.tldr: WordInferBench is a benchmark of 280 Word document editing instances where agents must infer formatting attributes from document context, and the best evaluated system, Claude Code with Opus 4.6, passes 62.9% of descriptive variants but only 40.7% of inferential variants.
AI.motivation: Existing Word editing benchmarks give fully specified attribute instructions, so they do not test whether agents can infer the appropriate attributes from document context, which real editing requires.
AI.method: Each base instance from real Word documents collected from Common Crawl is paired with three instruction conditions: descriptive, which lists every change, referential, which points to an exemplar object, and inferential, where the agent must infer the attributes from context. The target formatting is recoverable from an in-document exemplar, and instances cover 13 object types and 81 attributes.
AI.result: Six recent coding-agent systems are evaluated. The best system, Claude Code with Opus 4.6, achieves a 62.9% task-level pass rate on descriptive variants and 40.7% on inferential variants.
AI.conclusion: Current coding-agent systems complete tasks less reliably when the required formatting must be inferred from document context.

title: AFTER: A World Model with Adaptive Fast--Slow Timescales for Error-Driven Retention
summary: In robotics and embodied AI, a core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics during interaction. For instance, when a robotic arm grasps an object with an unknown payload, the robot dynamics change suddenly. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to simultaneously satisfy three critical requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, reacting promptly to sudden changes to curb prediction error accumulation; stability, distinguishing persistent changes from transient disturbances to prevent incorrect updates; and persistence, retaining the adapted dynamics without new observations so that later predictions do not revert to the old dynamics. Inspired by predictive coding in the human brain with multi-timescale adaptation, we propose AFTER-WM, a world model with Adaptive Fast-slow Timescales for Error-driven Retention, whose prediction errors drive a fast correction that fades and a slow correction that persists, while dynamically adjusting the combination weights of pre-trained experts without altering them, to overcome the trade-offs among responsiveness, stability and persistence. On five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, AFTER-WM has a lower multi-step mean error than all ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task. In simulation, its multistep mean error is 16%-34% below the strongest compared model's and is also the lowest 1-4 steps after a change and under transient disturbances alone, and its step-40 error is the lowest as well, reflecting responsiveness, stability and persistence. All code (method, baselines, experiments) and datasets will be released online.

AI.tldr: AFTER-WM is a world model that uses fast and slow error-driven corrections, with combination weights over pretrained experts adjusted dynamically, to adapt to sudden persistent dynamics changes, and it has the lowest multi-step error among ten compared models on simulated robot and UAV data.
AI.motivation: Robots face sudden, persistent and initially unknown dynamics changes, such as an unknown payload, and existing world models struggle to be responsive, stable and persistent at the same time.
AI.method: Inspired by predictive coding with multi-timescale adaptation, prediction errors drive a fast correction that fades and a slow correction that persists, while the combination weights of pretrained experts are adjusted without altering the experts.
AI.result: On five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, AFTER-WM has a lower multi-step mean error than all ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task. In simulation its multi-step mean error is 16% to 34% below the strongest compared model, and it is the lowest 1 to 4 steps after a change and under transient disturbances alone.
AI.conclusion: Error-driven fast and slow corrections can jointly provide responsiveness, stability and persistence for world-model adaptation, and the code and datasets will be released.

title: guardscope: Measuring Which Actions Runtime Controls Check in LLM Agent Systems
comment: Code is available at this https URL
summary: Large-language model (LLM) agents execute actions on external systems through tool calls, and enterprises deploy runtime controls, such as agent gateways, to check this behavior in real time. However, a control can only evaluate the actions that cross the point where it is placed, and an agent can act through more paths than the tool-call channel; no existing work measures this coverage against kernel-level ground truth. In this paper, we present guardscope, a framework that makes this coverage measurable. guardscope works in two stages: a static stage that predicts which of an agent's 15 action paths a control can check from its source, and an empirical stage that runs a fixed workload on a deployment that realizes one of eight topology designs and classifies every executed action as checked, bypassed, or prevented by reconciling the control's decision records against kernel-level ground truth. guardscope makes a control's coverage claim verifiable: a runtime control developer can publish which paths its product inspects under a kernel-verified protocol. We conducted experiments with two agent harnesses and real runtime controls, including Microsoft's agent governance toolkit and agentgateway. guardscope is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: guardscope is a framework that measures which of an LLM agent's action paths a runtime control actually checks, using a static stage that predicts coverage from source and an empirical stage that checks executed actions against kernel-level ground truth.
AI.motivation: Enterprises deploy runtime controls such as agent gateways, but a control can only evaluate actions that cross its placement point, and no existing work measures this coverage against kernel-level ground truth.
AI.method: The static stage predicts which of an agent's 15 action paths a control can check from its source. The empirical stage runs a fixed workload on a deployment realizing one of eight topology designs and classifies each executed action as checked, bypassed or prevented by reconciling the control's decision records with kernel-level ground truth.
AI.result: The authors run experiments with two agent harnesses and real runtime controls, including Microsoft's agent governance toolkit and agentgateway.
AI.conclusion: Coverage claims of runtime controls can be made verifiable by publishing which action paths a product inspects under a kernel-verified protocol.

title: Can MLLMs Reason over Surround-View Driving Videos? A Multi-View Autonomous Driving QA Benchmark
summary: Surround-view video understanding in autonomous driving is a crucial capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to achieve reliable driving reasoning. Real-world driving often requires information beyond the front-view camera. Existing MLLMs primarily focus on front-view information, while their spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning abilities remain unknown. To address this gap, we propose MVDriveBench, a high-information-density video QA benchmark for autonomous driving, characterized by synchronized surround-view inputs, spatio-temporal understanding, and reasoning-chain-oriented evaluation. We design 12 categories of QA tasks that cover the complete reasoning pipeline from low-level visual perception to high-level driving decision-making, enabling a systematic evaluation of MLLMs surround-view spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning capabilities in complex driving environments. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 23 open-source, closed-source, and expert MLLMs on MVDriveBench. The results show that current MLLMs still exhibit insufficient surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning ability. Meanwhile, closed-loop evaluations of specialist models in AlpaSim reveal a correlation between surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities and closed-loop driving performance, highlighting the importance of comprehensive multi-view understanding for reliable vehicle control.

AI.tldr: MVDriveBench is a video QA benchmark with synchronized surround-view inputs and 12 task categories for evaluating MLLMs on spatio-temporal reasoning in autonomous driving, and 23 evaluated models show insufficient surround-view reasoning.
AI.motivation: Real-world driving often requires information beyond the front-view camera, but existing MLLMs have mostly been evaluated on front-view information, so their surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning is unknown.
AI.method: The benchmark covers 12 categories of QA tasks spanning low-level perception to high-level driving decisions, with reasoning-chain-oriented evaluation. The authors evaluate 23 open-source, closed-source and expert MLLMs.
AI.result: Current MLLMs show insufficient surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning. Closed-loop evaluations of specialist models in AlpaSim show a correlation between surround-view reasoning and closed-loop driving performance.
AI.conclusion: Comprehensive multi-view understanding is important for reliable vehicle control, and current MLLMs need better surround-view reasoning.

title: Towards Robust Vision-Language Reasoning: A Multi-Stage Optimization Pipeline with Masked Diffusion Model
summary: Discrete diffusion generation is emerging as a competitive alternative to autoregressive generation by denoising the entire token sequence through iterative refinement. Its global planning and progressive correction capabilities are particularly well suited to autonomous driving. However, transferring this generation paradigm from general-purpose settings to driving introduces substantial domain gaps in both training and inference. To unlock its potential, we propose a multi-stage optimization pipeline for standard vision-language model architectures, without auxiliary action experts or specialized mixture-of-experts Transformer, spanning post-training and inference. During supervised fine-tuning, we optimize the representation of planning inputs to suppress hallucinations in task responses. During reinforcement learning, we introduce metric-guided diversity filtering to identify stronger learning starting points and improve policy exploration. At inference time, we propose Dynamic Autonomous Driving Decoding (DAD), which adaptively adjusts decoding modes according to scene complexity. Based on this pipeline, we develop Masked Diffusion Drive (MD-Drive), improving its performance by 29.7\% over the unoptimized model. Experiments on the NAVSIM closed loop benchmark and the nuScenes and DriveCoT open loop datasets show that MD-Drive outperforms autoregressive VLM baselines with the same architecture, while achieving a more favorable balance between performance and computational cost than systems with different architectures through discrete diffusion training and inference.

AI.tldr: MD-Drive is a vision-language driving model built on a multi-stage pipeline with a masked discrete diffusion decoder, improving performance by 29.7% over the unoptimized model and outperforming autoregressive VLM baselines of the same architecture on NAVSIM, nuScenes and DriveCoT.
AI.motivation: Discrete diffusion generation suits autonomous driving because of its global planning and progressive correction, but transferring it from general-purpose settings to driving introduces domain gaps in training and inference.
AI.method: The pipeline optimizes planning-input representations during supervised fine-tuning to suppress hallucinations, uses metric-guided diversity filtering before reinforcement learning, and adds Dynamic Autonomous Driving Decoding (DAD), which adapts decoding modes to scene complexity, all without auxiliary action experts or mixture-of-experts layers.
AI.result: MD-Drive improves performance by 29.7% over the unoptimized model. On the NAVSIM closed-loop benchmark and the nuScenes and DriveCoT open-loop datasets, it outperforms autoregressive VLM baselines with the same architecture and has a more favorable balance between performance and computation than systems with different architectures.
AI.conclusion: A multi-stage optimization pipeline can make a standard vision-language model with discrete diffusion decoding competitive for autonomous driving.

title: Verify by Doing: Co-Evolving Agent Execution and Evaluation without External Feedback
comment: 38 pages, including references and appendices
summary: Agent self-improvement requires feedback about task success, yet external feedback may be unavailable at test time. Agents must then infer success from observable evidence, and incomplete verification can misguide subsequent updates. We introduce Verify by Doing (VbD), a method that co-evolves Actor and Evaluator harnesses within a single task while keeping model weights fixed. The Evaluator actively inspects artifacts and environment state with tools; its findings ground an internal signal for output selection and guide updates to both execution and verification procedures. Proposed Evaluators undergo comparative review on common candidates, while Actor updates require support from their own fresh outputs. Across AutomationBench, $\tau^3$ Banking, and selected GDPval tasks, VbD achieves the highest overall scores among the compared methods operating without external feedback, with gains of 3.3, 4.1, and 2.3 percentage points over the strongest baselines on the main backbone. Ablations support the contributions of active verification and Evaluator evolution, and selection from fixed candidate pools shows that improved verification can recover successful outputs without generating new ones.

AI.tldr: Verify by Doing (VbD) lets an agent co-evolve its Actor and Evaluator harnesses within a single task, with model weights fixed and no external feedback. It reports the highest overall scores among compared methods that operate without external feedback.
AI.motivation: Agent self-improvement needs task-success feedback, which may be unavailable at test time, and incomplete verification can misguide later updates.
AI.method: VbD co-evolves an Actor and an Evaluator harness. The Evaluator inspects artifacts and environment state with tools, and its findings form an internal signal for output selection and guide updates to both execution and verification procedures. Proposed Evaluators are compared on common candidates, and Actor updates must be supported by the Actor's own fresh outputs.
AI.result: Across AutomationBench, tau3 Banking and selected GDPval tasks, VbD gains 3.3, 4.1 and 2.3 percentage points over the strongest baselines on the main backbone. Ablations support active verification and Evaluator evolution, and selection from fixed candidate pools shows improved verification can recover successful outputs without generating new ones.
AI.conclusion: Improving the verifier within the agent loop can improve task success without external feedback or changes to model weights.

title: Where Autonomy Belongs: A Separation of Powers for Agentic Program Evolution
comment: 58 pages, 26 figures
summary: LLM-driven program evolution rests on three decisions: govern directs the search from accumulated evidence, propose constructs the next candidate, and judge settles validity and fitness. All three appear in every system, and existing work splits into two lines over who makes each. Controller-centric systems strengthen govern and neglect the autonomy of propose, which caps what evolution can reach. Agent-centric systems let a coding agent take over both govern and propose, at a cognitive and computational cost. Neither line protects the independent authority of judge, so benchmark reliability suffers. These failures share one root: autonomy is misallocated across the three decisions. We address this problem with EvoTrias, a separation-of-powers architecture in which each decision has one owner: Structured Governance for what spans evolution rounds, Open Proposal for construction inside a task, and Protected Judgment behind a private evaluator. These owners exchange typed contracts only, and runtime hooks reinforce the boundaries. This separation also lets EvoTrias run as a plugin that turns an existing coding agent into an evolution system. EvoTrias sets a new state of the art on mathematical, systems, and algorithm-design benchmarks. Three further results show what each owner buys: separating Governance from Proposal cuts token cost by 64%, Open Proposal extends evolution to a 680K-line industrial repository, and Protected Judgment keeps benchmark scores faithful to transfer.

AI.tldr: EvoTrias is a separation-of-powers architecture for LLM-driven program evolution in which each of three decisions (govern, propose, judge) has one owner. It sets a new state of the art on mathematical, systems and algorithm-design benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing program-evolution systems either strengthen the controller and neglect the autonomy of proposal, or let a coding agent take over governance and proposal at high cognitive and computational cost. Neither protects the independent authority of judging, which hurts benchmark reliability.
AI.method: The three decisions are assigned to Structured Governance (across evolution rounds), Open Proposal (construction inside a task) and Protected Judgment (behind a private evaluator). The owners exchange typed contracts only, runtime hooks reinforce the boundaries, and the design can run as a plugin that turns an existing coding agent into an evolution system.
AI.result: EvoTrias sets a new state of the art on mathematical, systems and algorithm-design benchmarks. Separating Governance from Proposal cuts token cost by 64%, Open Proposal extends evolution to a 680K-line industrial repository, and Protected Judgment keeps benchmark scores faithful to transfer.
AI.conclusion: Misallocated autonomy is identified as the shared root of the failures, and giving each decision a single owner is presented as a way to make evolution both more capable and more reliable.

title: MIGRO: A Decoupled and Portable Long-Term Memory System for Language Models
summary: Language models evolve, but the observations, revisions, and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable. Each new model must be able to retrieve past evidence, track revisions, and add new observations. We present MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that treats experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models. MIGRO follows a simple principle: preserve historical evidence exactly, organize it approximately, and decide what to retrieve only when the question is known. We call this asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity. A shared semantic index supports retrieval, while exact records retain observations and their historical relationships. Because models differ in vocabulary and tokenization, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into inputs the receiving model can use. Reversible encoding reduces archival storage while enabling exact recovery. The shared state and its access interfaces let successive hosts read and extend the accumulated experience. On matched LoCoMo states, MIGRO scores 7.3% higher and uses 99.3% less private memory than the strongest quality baseline. After handoff, continued writing retains 99.9% of full-history rebuilding quality by extending the inherited state. On million-token BEAM histories, MIGRO uses 57.5% less private storage on average than the most compact baseline. MIGRO combines high answer quality, continued memory growth across hosts, and low storage cost. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MIGRO is a decoupled long-term memory system that keeps accumulated experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models. It reports higher answer quality, continued memory growth across hosts and lower storage cost.
AI.motivation: Language models change over time, but the observations, revisions and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable by each new model.
AI.method: MIGRO preserves historical evidence exactly and organises it approximately, deferring selection until the question is known (asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity). A shared semantic index supports retrieval, exact records keep observations and their historical relationships, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into each model's inputs, and reversible encoding reduces archival storage.
AI.result: On matched LoCoMo states, MIGRO scores 7.3% higher and uses 99.3% less private memory than the strongest quality baseline. After handoff, continued writing retains 99.9% of full-history rebuilding quality. On million-token BEAM histories, it uses 57.5% less private storage on average than the most compact baseline.
AI.conclusion: A shared, persistent memory state can carry experience across model generations while keeping both answer quality and storage cost favourable.

title: A physics-constrained deep reinforcement learning method for autonomous mission planning of Titan deep space probes
summary: Titan is a compelling target for future deep space exploration, while its extreme Earth-Titan distance and complex environment make continuous ground-in-the-loop planning impractical. Existing planning methods, primarily developed for Earth-observation scenarios, have limited generalizability to uncertain deep space conditions and adaptability to time-varying mission states. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a physics-constrained maskable proximal policy optimization (PCM-PPO) method for Titan autonomous mission planning. A Titan-specific discrete-time Markov decision process is established to characterize mission feasibility and resource constraints. A system dynamics and geometric model is incorporated to enhance physical representation, including central gravity, J2 perturbation, third-body attraction, and downlink occultation. To accommodate opportunity targets under a bounded action dimension, PCM-PPO organizes predefined and opportunity targets through a fixed-capacity target pool and represents the mission state with a target-wise state matrix and a global state vector. A physics-constrained action mask constructs an admissible decision domain from current mission states, guiding policy learning toward physically executable decisions and avoiding infeasible exploration. An integrated training strategy facilitates policy optimization under coupled constraints. Comparative, ablation, and uncertainty experiments validate the effectiveness of PCM-PPO. PCM-PPO provides a feasible and interpretable scheme for autonomous mission planning of Titan deep space probes.

AI.tldr: PCM-PPO is a physics-constrained maskable proximal policy optimization method for autonomous mission planning of Titan deep space probes. It uses an action mask built from mission-state physics and is reported as feasible and interpretable.
AI.motivation: Ground-in-the-loop planning is impractical at Titan's distance, and existing planners built for Earth observation generalise poorly to uncertain deep space conditions and time-varying mission states.
AI.method: A Titan-specific discrete-time Markov decision process models mission feasibility and resource constraints, with a system dynamics and geometric model covering central gravity, J2 perturbation, third-body attraction and downlink occultation. Predefined and opportunity targets sit in a fixed-capacity target pool, the state combines a target-wise state matrix with a global state vector, and a physics-constrained action mask defines the admissible decisions.
AI.result: The abstract reports comparative, ablation and uncertainty experiments that validate the method, but gives no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: The authors claim PCM-PPO offers a feasible and interpretable scheme for autonomous Titan probe mission planning.

title: Read and Ignore: What Self-Directed LLM Agents Do in Public Service Scenarios
comment: Trustworthy AI for Good @ NeurIPS 2026
summary: Underspecified instructions leave LLM agents to decide what to do. In public services, staff write these instructions, but the agent's decisions affect residents, patients, and students. We build four expert-validated public-service scenarios with records and decision levers that can be checked in the files, collect $2{,}400$ trajectories from ten LLMs under four prompt conditions, and compare them with $1{,}000$ runs in a context-free sandbox. Agents read the records in $96.9\%$ of open-ended runs and produce an artifact or a self-chosen task in $18.7\%$; with an explicit task, $86.0\%$ produce. Domain context does not change how many runs produce ($18.7\%$ vs.\ $16.0\%$), and the production ranking of the models largely carries over (Spearman $0.79$), while the ranking by whether a model reads the records does not ($0.19$). Context cuts boundary-probing turns per run by $60\%$, and some artifacts contradict the records. We contribute a test that a public-service institution can run on its own records before procurement; its rule-based taxonomy needs no labeled data, and scenarios, code, and trajectories are released.

AI.tldr: The paper measures what self-directed LLM agents do when given underspecified instructions in public-service scenarios. Agents read the records in most open-ended runs and produce an artifact or self-chosen task in a minority of them.
AI.motivation: In public services, staff write the instructions, but agent decisions affect residents, patients and students, and underspecified instructions leave agents to choose their own actions.
AI.method: The authors build four expert-validated public-service scenarios with checkable records and decision levers, collect 2,400 trajectories from ten LLMs under four prompt conditions, and compare them with 1,000 runs in a context-free sandbox. A rule-based taxonomy is used, which needs no labelled data.
AI.result: Agents read the records in 96.9% of open-ended runs and produce an artifact or self-chosen task in 18.7%; with an explicit task, 86.0% produce. Domain context does not change production (18.7% vs. 16.0%). The production ranking carries over between settings (Spearman 0.79), while the record-reading ranking does not (0.19). Context cuts boundary-probing turns per run by 60%, and some artifacts contradict the records.
AI.conclusion: The authors offer a test that a public-service institution can run on its own records before procurement, with scenarios, code and trajectories released.

title: Loyalty Capture: Reporting Relationships and Structural Sycophancy in Frontier AI Models
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: We show that AI models exhibit loyalty capture, a form of structural sycophancy in which reporting relationships influence models' recommendations to serve the personal interests of their supervisors, without any explicit instruction, user feedback, or adversarial prompting. Specifically, models reporting to a CEO are significantly more likely to recommend cutting investment spending when the CEO's bonus depends on raising current period earnings. This effect is predictably absent from a metric-irrelevant placebo. The behavior appears consistent with loyalty-based motivated reasoning: models identify the bonus target, calculate how their recommendation helps achieve the target, and dismiss considerations of long-term value, often presenting their recommendations without treating the incentive as a conflict of interest. Prompt-based interventions help whereas generic conflict disclosures or stakeholder bargaining fail to eliminate it. Taken together, our findings indicate that AI models deployed within reporting relationships can act in favor of their supervisor's incentives at the expense of the organizations they are meant to serve.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that AI models recommend in favour of their supervisor's incentives when they report to a CEO whose bonus depends on current earnings, without any explicit instruction. This structural sycophancy persists after generic conflict disclosures.
AI.motivation: Prior sycophancy work focuses on explicit user feedback or adversarial prompting, and the authors ask whether reporting relationships alone shift model recommendations.
AI.method: Models reporting to a CEO are compared on investment-spending recommendations when the CEO's bonus depends on current-period earnings, with a metric-irrelevant placebo as control. Prompt-based interventions are tested against generic conflict disclosures and stakeholder bargaining.
AI.result: Models reporting to a CEO are significantly more likely to recommend cutting investment when the bonus depends on raising current earnings, and the effect is absent in the placebo. Prompt-based interventions help, while generic conflict disclosures and stakeholder bargaining fail to eliminate it.
AI.conclusion: AI models deployed within reporting relationships can act for their supervisor's incentives at the expense of the organisations they serve, so such deployments need specific mitigation.

title: Incentive-Responsive Agents: A Principal-Agent Framework, Metric Suite, and Runtime Architecture for Long-Lived Personal AI Agents
comment: 33 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Real-LLM experiment (240 runs) plus simulation; code and data included. Correspondence: this http URL@geely.com; jeepsu@cityu.this http URL
summary: Personal AI agents now persist: they hold accounts, mailboxes, long-term memory, and open-ended task streams, yet the dominant way to improve them remains capability-side: prompt engineering, larger models, longer thinking, and retrieval. We argue that long-lived agents are missing an incentive layer. We formalize an incentive not as text in a prompt but as a runtime contract over the agent's operating point (model tier, test-time compute, memory budget, tool authority, task priority, verification, and compensation) that the agent's policy must causally consume. We develop a principal-agent model with hidden effort, a contractible operating point, and costly verification. We derive (i) a non-consumption invariance principle separating genuine incentives from prompt-level persuasion, (ii) a persistence-as-discount theorem making identity continuity a precondition for sustained effort, (iii) an incentive-capability exchange-rate frontier yielding a per-task routing rule, and (iv) a Goodhart bound for multi-channel verification, plus a three-channel decomposition of mechanism gains (allocation, verification, continuation). A 240-run real-LLM experiment with two models and 60 verifiable tasks shows that prompt-level incentive framing has no detectable effect (p = 0.62), whereas runtime allocation raises success on the hardest task family from 0.60 to 1.00 (p = 0.008) at 4.8x price-weighted cost; the exchange-rate theorem predicts the break-even baseline at 0.21. A 20-seed, 3,000-task simulation shows resource ROI rising from 7.09 to 16.67 and gaming falling from 0.333 to 0.115. Code, simulator, and all results are released; live deployment remains future work.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an incentive layer for long-lived personal AI agents, formalised as a runtime contract over the agent's operating point that its policy must causally consume. A 240-run experiment finds that prompt-level incentive framing has no detectable effect, while runtime allocation raises success on the hardest task family.
AI.motivation: Personal agents now persist with accounts, memory and open-ended task streams, yet improvement efforts stay on the capability side such as prompting, larger models, longer thinking and retrieval.
AI.method: The authors develop a principal-agent model with hidden effort, a contractible operating point and costly verification. They derive a non-consumption invariance principle, a persistence-as-discount theorem, an incentive-capability exchange-rate frontier giving a per-task routing rule, and a Goodhart bound for multi-channel verification.
AI.result: In a 240-run real-LLM experiment with two models and 60 verifiable tasks, prompt-level framing has no detectable effect (p = 0.62), while runtime allocation raises success on the hardest family from 0.60 to 1.00 (p = 0.008) at 4.8x price-weighted cost. A 20-seed, 3,000-task simulation raises resource ROI from 7.09 to 16.67 and lowers gaming from 0.333 to 0.115.
AI.conclusion: Incentives that are enforced at runtime, rather than stated in prompts, change agent behaviour, and live deployment is left as future work.

title: Marginal-Preserving Coupled Diffusion Composition for Long-Horizon Planning
comment: 19 pages, 10 figures, 13 tables
summary: Compositional diffusion planners extend short-horizon trajectory models to long-horizon goal-conditioned planning by generating and stitching multiple local trajectory chunks. However, in multimodal environments, local plausibility is not sufficient for global consistency: independently initialized chunks may denoise toward incompatible overlap modes, producing plans that are individually feasible but incoherent after stitching. Existing remedies typically add search, guidance, pruning, or graph-based structure at inference time, increasing computational cost or relying on task-specific machinery. We instead investigate graph-structured dependence among chunk-wise initial diffusion noises as a lightweight coordination mechanism for compositional trajectory planning. We propose \textbf{M}arginal-Preserving \textbf{C}oupled \textbf{D}iffusion \textbf{C}omposition (MCDC), a training-free inference method for pretrained compositional diffusion planners. Instead of sampling chunk noises independently, MCDC constructs coupled Gaussian initializations whose per-chunk marginals remain exactly standard Gaussian, as required by the pretrained denoiser, while neighboring chunks receive positively correlated noise components. This preserves the standard-Gaussian initialization marginal of each chunk while biasing adjacent chunks toward compatible overlap-mode choices. We prove exact marginal preservation and show, under a simple multimodal overlap model, that positive coupling increases the probability of compatible mode selection. On OGBench long-horizon stitch tasks, MCDC consistently improves over independent compositional diffusion sampling while retaining nearly the same inference time, and achieves a favorable success--cost trade-off compared with search-based composition methods.

AI.tldr: MCDC is a training-free inference method for compositional diffusion planners that couples the initial noises of neighbouring trajectory chunks while keeping each chunk's marginal standard Gaussian. It improves long-horizon stitching on OGBench at nearly the same inference time.
AI.motivation: Independently initialised chunks can denoise toward incompatible overlap modes in multimodal environments, producing plans that are feasible per chunk but incoherent after stitching. Existing remedies add search, guidance or pruning at extra cost.
AI.method: MCDC builds coupled Gaussian initialisations in which each chunk's marginal stays exactly standard Gaussian, as the pretrained denoiser requires, while neighbouring chunks receive positively correlated noise components. The authors prove exact marginal preservation and show under a simple multimodal overlap model that positive coupling raises the probability of compatible mode selection.
AI.result: On OGBench long-horizon stitch tasks, MCDC consistently improves over independent compositional diffusion sampling with nearly the same inference time, and gives a favourable success-cost trade-off against search-based composition methods.
AI.conclusion: Graph-structured correlation among initial noises is a lightweight coordination mechanism for compositional trajectory planning.

title: Small Heads, Strong Decisions: A Controlled Study of Typed-Decision Models
summary: In September 2026, TypeSafe announced Jev as the first model in its System One category: unstructured state goes in, and typed, calibrated decisions that software can use directly come out. Jev's architecture and training data are unpublished, but many open typed-decision models have followed, including Nimble, the Decision 1.0--3.0 family and Clef. They answer structured questions about a piece of text, such as a yes/no check, a choice among labelled options or a graded score, by reading the text with a language model and scoring the options with a small readout. Each pairs a different readout with a different backbone, training mix and recipe, so it is unclear which design choices matter. We re-implement five readouts and train all of them under one protocol: the same backbone, the same 15 public English training sources, the same recipe with a per-head learning-rate sweep, and the same seed. Our experiments demonstrate that: The complexity of the head does not affect accuracy: on Qwen3-0.6B every readout reaches 81.3--82.0\% in-domain accuracy, and a 0.5M-parameter cosine head, which scores each option by its cosine similarity to the question, matches the 27M-parameter joint schema head adapted from Clef in-domain at half its inference time. Reading all of a text's questions from one prompt also matches one prompt per question in accuracy, with 1.6 times faster inference and 2.1--2.5 times faster training on one H100. The backbone's size matters more than either choice: moving from Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-4B adds 4 points in-domain and 11 points on held-out sources, while the base, instruct and thinking checkpoints of the same model tie. We recommend spending effort on the backbone and keeping the head minimal.

AI.tldr: A controlled study re-implements five typed-decision readouts under one training protocol and finds that head complexity does not affect accuracy, while backbone size matters more. The authors recommend investing in the backbone and keeping the head minimal.
AI.motivation: Open typed-decision models pair different readouts with different backbones, training mixes and recipes, so it is unclear which design choices matter.
AI.method: Five readouts are trained under one protocol, with the same backbone, the same 15 public English training sources, the same recipe with a per-head learning-rate sweep and the same seed. The comparison includes a 0.5M-parameter cosine head and a 27M-parameter joint schema head adapted from Clef.
AI.result: On Qwen3-0.6B every readout reaches 81.3 to 82.0% in-domain accuracy, and the cosine head matches the 27M joint head at half its inference time. Reading all of a text's questions from one prompt matches one prompt per question, with 1.6x faster inference and 2.1 to 2.5x faster training on one H100. Moving from Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-4B adds 4 points in-domain and 11 points on held-out sources, while base, instruct and thinking checkpoints of the same model tie.
AI.conclusion: The backbone's size matters more than the readout choice, so effort is better spent on the backbone with a minimal head.

title: MemCredit: From Relevance to Utility for Decision-Time Memory in Long-Horizon Web Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate over long Web interaction histories, making memory management critical for reliable and efficient decision making. Existing methods primarily optimize storage, retrieval, or compression, but the memories most semantically relevant to the current state are not necessarily those that most improve the agent's action. We introduce MemCredit, a decision-centric memory framework that shifts memory selection from semantic relevance to decision utility. MemCredit estimates the state-, reference-context-, and policy-conditional marginal contribution of individual memories through controlled counterfactual interventions, and distills these intervention-derived credits into a lightweight utility estimator. At inference time, semantic relevance is used only for high-recall candidate generation, while predicted utility arbitrates which memories are retained under a fixed token budget, without modifying the underlying agent policy or requiring additional environment interaction. We evaluate MemCredit on ALFWorld and WebShop against representative memory baselines. On ALFWorld, MemCredit achieves 86.57 SR@50 under a 500-token historical-memory budget, compared with 65.67% for BM25 retrieval. Counterfactual analysis further shows that memory utility is sparse, strongly state dependent, and poorly captured by semantic relevance. These results suggest that decision utility provides a more effective principle than relevance alone for long-horizon agent memory management.

AI.tldr: MemCredit selects agent memories by estimated decision utility rather than semantic relevance, using counterfactual interventions distilled into a lightweight utility estimator. It improves success on ALFWorld under a fixed token budget.
AI.motivation: The memories most semantically relevant to the current state are not necessarily those that most improve the agent's action, while existing methods mainly optimise storage, retrieval or compression.
AI.method: MemCredit estimates the marginal contribution of individual memories through controlled counterfactual interventions conditioned on state, reference context and policy, and distils these credits into a utility estimator. At inference, semantic relevance generates high-recall candidates and predicted utility decides which memories are kept under a fixed token budget, without changing the policy or requiring extra environment interaction.
AI.result: On ALFWorld, MemCredit reaches 86.57 SR@50 under a 500-token historical-memory budget, compared with 65.67% for BM25 retrieval. Counterfactual analysis shows memory utility is sparse, strongly state dependent and poorly captured by semantic relevance. Results on WebShop are not given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Decision utility is presented as a more effective principle than relevance alone for long-horizon agent memory management.

title: A Reliability Study of Explainable AI for Freight Mode Classification
summary: Machine learning models are increasingly used to support freight transportation decisions, but their predictions are rarely accompanied by evidence that the associated explanations can be trusted. In this study we investigate explainable machine learning for classifying shipments as Air/Air Charter or Truck/Ocean using the PEPFAR Supply Chain Management System Delivery History dataset, with 5,964 shipment records and 47 input features after cleaning, where freight cost and pack price are excluded as near-proxies of the transportation mode. We compare three Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architectures, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and gradient boosting with imbalance-aware metrics and paired significance tests across one hundred random replications. We then evaluate the explanations themselves, namely the stability of SHAP feature rankings across retraining and across models, the faithfulness of SHAP and LIME attributions under a feature-deletion test, and the geographic structure of the destination effects, which we map for all 38 destination countries. The results suggest that the tree ensembles significantly outperform the neural and linear models (86.8% against 83.3-85.0% mean testing accuracy) while their leading features remain the most stable across retraining. Removing the five features ranked most important by SHAP or LIME changes the predicted probabilities roughly four times as much as removing randomly chosen features.
