The destination effects form a coherent geographic pattern that simple port access does not explain. However, models with similar accuracy disagree substantially on which features matter most, and thus explanation stability and faithfulness should be assessed before such explanations are used to support freight transport decisions.

AI.tldr: The study tests whether explanations for an ML freight-mode classifier can be trusted, comparing SHAP and LIME faithfulness and stability. Tree ensembles are the most accurate models, but models with similar accuracy disagree on which features matter.
AI.motivation: Freight decisions rely on ML predictions that are rarely accompanied by evidence that the explanations can be trusted.
AI.method: The authors classify shipments as Air/Air Charter or Truck/Ocean using 5,964 PEPFAR shipment records with 47 features. They compare three MLP architectures, Logistic Regression, Random Forest and gradient boosting over 100 random replications with paired significance tests, and assess SHAP stability across retraining and models, SHAP and LIME faithfulness under feature deletion, and the geography of destination effects across 38 countries.
AI.result: Tree ensembles outperform neural and linear models (86.8% against 83.3 to 85.0% mean test accuracy), and their leading features are the most stable across retraining. Removing the top five SHAP or LIME features changes predicted probabilities about four times as much as removing random features. Destination effects form a coherent geographic pattern that simple port access does not explain. Similar-accuracy models disagree substantially on feature importance.
AI.conclusion: Explanation stability and faithfulness should be checked before explanations are used to support freight transport decisions.

title: DISCERN: Preserve at Write, Resolve at Read for Persistent LLM-Agent Memory
summary: Enterprise agents accumulate memory across dozens of sessions in which facts contradict, get superseded, and blur as similarly named entities collide in embedding space. The field treats this as a retrieval problem; we show it is not. On ENT-310, a synthetic enterprise sales-agent memory benchmark of 310 queries (210 answerable, 100 unanswerable), a vanilla Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) reader over a memory store already matches strong memory systems on the recall pillars. Retention and currency are near-saturated, roughly 0.93 to 0.98 for every competent system, so recall is essentially solved. What remains unsolved is resolution: which entity a query refers to, which time-state is current, and whether to commit an answer at all or decline when evidence is insufficient. We propose DISCERN (DISambiguation and Cross-session Episodic memoRy Navigation), an agent-memory framework built on a single rule: preserve at write, resolve at read. At write time DISCERN builds a strictly additive bi-temporal provenance graph that never merges confusable entities and never drops superseded values. At read time a zero-LLM tool surface drives an agentic loop that navigates this graph and commits exactly one of four gated terminal actions. A four-judge LLM-as-a-Judge council scores two axes: answer correctness on answerable questions, and the answer-versus-abstain decision as a classification problem. On ENT-310, DISCERN is the best-calibrated system on abstention (F1 0.924 versus at most 0.802 across eight baselines) and leads macro answer correctness under equal pillar weighting (0.861 versus 0.806 for the strongest baseline), a lead driven by entity resolution (0.800, where no baseline exceeds 0.40). Applied with zero tuning to the full LoCoMo corpus, the same pipeline again leads macro answer correctness (0.663 versus 0.638) and stays among the best-calibrated on false-premise abstention.

AI.tldr: DISCERN is an agent-memory framework built on the rule preserve at write, resolve at read. It reports the best-calibrated abstention and the strongest macro answer correctness on ENT-310, a synthetic enterprise memory benchmark.
AI.motivation: Enterprise agent memory fails through contradictions, superseded facts and confusable entity names rather than recall. The authors argue that resolution, not retrieval, is the unsolved problem.
AI.method: At write time DISCERN builds an additive bi-temporal provenance graph that never merges confusable entities and never drops superseded values. At read time a zero-LLM tool surface drives an agentic loop over this graph that commits one of four gated terminal actions. A four-judge LLM-as-a-Judge council scores answer correctness and the answer-versus-abstain decision.
AI.result: On ENT-310 (310 queries, 210 answerable), DISCERN has abstention F1 of 0.924 against at most 0.802 for eight baselines, and macro answer correctness of 0.861 against 0.806 for the strongest baseline, led by entity resolution (0.800, where no baseline exceeds 0.40). On the full LoCoMo corpus with no tuning it reaches 0.663 against 0.638.
AI.conclusion: Resolution rather than recall is the bottleneck for persistent agent memory, and the write-then-resolve design addresses it.

title: NIBench: benchmarking autonomous AI agents for execution, skill evolution and scientific judgment in neuroimaging
summary: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly used to automate biomedical research, creating a growing need to benchmark their capabilities on real scientific data and workflows. Their reliability in neuroimaging remains insufficiently characterized, where plausible analytical outputs can conceal errors that affect scientific conclusions. Existing studies have advanced scientific question answering and tool-based automation, but provide limited evidence on workflow reconstruction, acquisition of procedural expertise and evidence-based scientific judgment. Here we present NIBench, a neuroimaging benchmark comprising three complementary evaluations of autonomous agents. First, we benchmark execution and workflow reconstruction using 56 tasks across seven tool ecosystems, covering structural, diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography and multimodal analyses. Second, we examine whether agents can evolve their procedural skills through distillation of execution trajectories, evaluating the resulting skills on previously encountered tasks, unseen tasks and other models. Third, we assess scientific judgment using 36 claims from published Alzheimer's disease studies, requiring agents to analyse raw cohort data and provide reproducible evidence. We evaluate 19 language models within a shared agent framework, with selected models undergoing skill distillation and claim evaluation. Leading agents execute supplied analysis protocols nearly perfectly, whereas withholding procedural guidance widens performance differences. Distilled skills improve performance on acquisition tasks and transfer between models, but benefits on unseen tasks are inconsistent. Agents reproduce their reported results yet sometimes reach conclusions inconsistent with expert-derived answers, and access to data does not always improve judgment.

AI.tldr: NIBench is a benchmark of three evaluations of autonomous agents in neuroimaging, covering execution, skill evolution and scientific judgment. Leading agents execute supplied protocols nearly perfectly, but judgment and skill transfer are less reliable.
AI.motivation: Neuroimaging analyses can produce plausible outputs that hide errors affecting scientific conclusions, and existing studies give limited evidence on workflow reconstruction, procedural expertise and evidence-based judgment.
AI.method: The benchmark has three parts: 56 execution and workflow tasks across seven tool ecosystems, a skill-distillation test of procedures learned from execution trajectories evaluated on seen tasks, unseen tasks and other models, and 36 claims from published Alzheimer's disease studies that agents must check against raw cohort data. Nineteen language models are evaluated in a shared agent framework.
AI.result: Leading agents execute supplied protocols nearly perfectly, and withholding procedural guidance widens performance differences. Distilled skills improve acquisition tasks and transfer between models, but benefits on unseen tasks are inconsistent. Agents reproduce their reported results yet sometimes reach conclusions inconsistent with expert answers, and data access does not always improve judgment.
AI.conclusion: Reproducing a workflow is not the same as judging a scientific claim, so agent evaluation in neuroimaging needs to test judgment separately.

title: Controlling the Probability of Unknown Unknowns in Pre-Deployment Testing of AI Systems
comment: 62 pages, 10 figures
summary: In pre-deployment testing of AI systems such as AI agents, a developer can often deal with known failure modes (e.g., leaking API keys, deleting important databases, or installing a malicious package) by implementing fixes or making contingency plans for when the same issue might occur again. What is more challenging are the unknown unknowns: the unseen failure modes that haven't surfaced during testing. The decision to stop testing and deploy therefore faces an inherent tradeoff: continue testing to observe more behaviors, at the cost of time and resources, or stop testing and deploy, at the risk of failure modes remaining undiscovered. How then does the developer decide when they have tested enough? To answer this, we develop an algorithm that certifies when the probability of observing an unseen failure mode is sufficiently small. The algorithm constructs an anytime-valid upper confidence sequence on this quantity, so the developer can repeatedly test a system, inspect the bound, and decide to stop when it falls below a chosen threshold without invalidating the statistical guarantee. Our problem can be interpreted as a sequential variant of the missing-mass estimation problem which gave rise to the classic Good-Turing estimator (Good, 1953). On SWE-Chat, a dataset of real-world coding agent traces (Baumann et al., 2026), we implement our procedure and show that it achieves tighter upper bounds than a simple multiple-testing corrected Good-Turing baseline, and even dominates a fixed-horizon (non-multiple-testing-corrected) Good-Turing upper confidence bound, which is not anytime valid. Additionally, to better match realistic evaluation pipelines, we extend our method to handle sampling from a different task distribution and imperfect automated failure labeling.

AI.tldr: The paper gives an algorithm that certifies when the probability of an unseen failure mode in pre-deployment testing is small, using an anytime-valid upper confidence sequence. A developer can keep testing and stop once the bound falls below a chosen threshold.
AI.motivation: Known failure modes can be fixed, but unknown unknowns are unseen during testing, and the developer needs a principled rule for when to stop testing and deploy.
AI.method: The problem is framed as a sequential variant of missing-mass estimation, which underlies the Good-Turing estimator. The algorithm builds an anytime-valid upper confidence sequence on the probability of observing an unseen failure mode. It is extended to sampling from a different task distribution and to imperfect automated failure labelling.
AI.result: On SWE-Chat, a dataset of real coding agent traces, the procedure gives tighter upper bounds than a multiple-testing-corrected Good-Turing baseline and dominates a fixed-horizon Good-Turing bound, which is not anytime valid. No numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Stopping rules for deployment can be certified with statistical guarantees that hold under repeated inspection of the bound.

title: Before AI Agents Negotiate for Us: A Competitive Tournament of Rule-Based, Search, Optimization, Learned, and Language-Model Negotiators Under Scarcity
comment: 28 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Code, data and trained models: this https URL (archived at doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24122038)
summary: Automated bilateral negotiation underlies two-sided matching markets such as freight brokering, where many shippers and carriers negotiate price before a matching mechanism decides who is paired with whom. Prior strategy comparisons typically use isolated one-on-one duels or a single fixed market, so they cannot show how a strategy behaves against several live rivals under a changing balance of supply and demand. We built nine negotiation architectures spanning rule-based, search-based, optimization-based, imitation-learning, and reinforcement-learning families, and ran all nine simultaneously on both sides of a Gale-Shapley matching market under a balanced condition and two scarcity conditions rotated across all 36 exclusion pairs. In the balanced carrier market, an imitation-learned engine (ML2), a reinforcement-learning policy trained only on isolated negotiations (RL), and an expected-utility optimization engine (OPT) formed a statistically tied top group, and no architecture led in every condition and role. RL beat all eight carrier rivals when carriers were scarce, but its match rate collapsed from 62% to 16% when shippers were scarce and it had to compete with the other carrier agents for demand. A second reinforcement-learning policy trained against rival agents (RL2) kept its match rate above 91% in every condition, yet lost on realized payoff to all eight shipper-side rivals in two of the three conditions, traced to a confirmed train/deployment feature mismatch. We also tested nine large language models (LLMs), from 1 to 72 billion parameters, under the same protocol: they lost significantly to the two strongest engines (OPT2 and ML2) in 32 of 36 comparisons and won none. These results show that isolated or single-condition evaluation can hide failure modes that a many-sided, scarcity-varying, statistically corrected tournament exposes directly.

AI.tldr: A tournament of nine negotiation architectures in a two-sided Gale-Shapley market finds that no architecture leads in every condition and role. Language models lose to the strongest engines in most comparisons.
AI.motivation: Prior strategy comparisons use one-on-one duels or a single fixed market, so they cannot show how a strategy performs against several live rivals as supply and demand change.
AI.method: Nine architectures from rule-based, search-based, optimisation, imitation-learning and reinforcement-learning families run simultaneously on both sides of a Gale-Shapley matching market, under a balanced condition and two scarcity conditions rotated across 36 exclusion pairs. Nine LLMs from 1 to 72 billion parameters are tested under the same protocol.
AI.result: In the balanced carrier market, the imitation-learned ML2, the reinforcement-learning policy RL and the optimisation engine OPT form a statistically tied top group. RL beats all eight carrier rivals when carriers are scarce but its match rate falls from 62% to 16% when shippers are scarce. RL2 keeps its match rate above 91% but loses on payoff in two of three conditions, traced to a train/deployment feature mismatch. The LLMs lose significantly to OPT2 and ML2 in 32 of 36 comparisons and win none.
AI.conclusion: Isolated or single-condition evaluation can hide failure modes that a many-sided, scarcity-varying, statistically corrected tournament reveals.

title: Food Critic: An Agentic Visualization System for Auditable Restaurant-Safety Reasoning
summary: Generative AI agents are increasingly being embedded into visualization systems that can search data, invoke tools, summarize evidence, and produce recommendations. However, when agents rely solely on their own knowledge, the visualization problem is not only whether the agent provides a useful answer, but also whether users can inspect how that answer is grounded. We present Food Critic, an agentic visualization system for diners' restaurant decision support that integrates public health inspection records with crowd review data. The system grounds agents under three conditions: a database-only ReAct agent, a retrieval- augmented agent with access to food-safety regulations, and an ontology-guided agent that produces structured hypotheses and typed evidence. Food Critic externalizes the agent's reasoning within these groundings as inspectable visual evidence. We evaluate LLM models with several use cases under each grounding of our agentic system. Our work positions restaurant choice as a concrete case for studying human-agent collaboration, visual provenance of agent reasoning, and the design of visual interfaces for grounded GenAI decision support.

AI.tldr: Food Critic is an agentic visualization system for restaurant choice that combines public health inspection records with crowd reviews. It externalises the agent's reasoning as inspectable visual evidence under three grounding conditions.
AI.motivation: When agents rely only on their own knowledge, users cannot inspect how an answer is grounded, so the visualisation problem includes whether the grounding can be seen.
AI.method: The system integrates inspection records and crowd review data and compares three agent conditions: a database-only ReAct agent, a retrieval-augmented agent with food-safety regulations, and an ontology-guided agent that produces structured hypotheses and typed evidence. LLMs are evaluated on several use cases under each grounding.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results and describes the system and its evaluation design only.
AI.conclusion: Restaurant choice is positioned as a concrete case for studying human-agent collaboration, visual provenance of agent reasoning and interfaces for grounded GenAI decision support.

title: Reward-Driven Collider Physics Challenges for Self-Improving Agentic AI via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Recent advances in agentic AI have demonstrated the potential to automate complex high-energy physics (HEP) workflows. We focus on the regime of HEP tasks where frontier models still struggle to provide correct and complete solutions, and introduce an open-ended optimization task format with continuous, automatically evaluated rewards. Unlike conventional benchmarks focused on task completion, these tasks target reinforcement learning (RL) environments to generate agentic improvement on state- of-the-art HEP challenges. We benchmark frontier reasoning models on several HEP tasks and demonstrate an initial proof of concept in which a small language model improves through RL using automated feedback without human intervention. By connecting challenging HEP problems with verifiable scientific rewards and RL, we aim to advance agentic AI from reproducing established workflows to autonomously discovering better scientific solutions, paving the way toward self-improving scientific agents.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes open-ended high-energy physics optimisation tasks with continuous, automatically evaluated rewards for reinforcement learning of agents. A small language model improves through RL with automated feedback in a proof of concept.
AI.motivation: Frontier models still struggle with some HEP tasks, and existing benchmarks focus on task completion rather than improvement on hard scientific problems.
AI.method: The authors introduce an open-ended optimisation task format with continuous, automatically evaluated rewards, benchmark frontier reasoning models on several HEP tasks, and run an RL proof of concept in which a small language model improves using automated feedback without human intervention.
AI.result: The abstract reports a benchmark of frontier models and an initial proof of concept of RL improvement, but gives no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: The authors aim to move agentic AI from reproducing established HEP workflows toward autonomously finding better scientific solutions.

title: Between Niti and Nyaya: A Society-Centered Framework for AI Governance
summary: Governments are making decisions about AI before they can measure its public effects, and those decisions determine whether a person can learn that AI influenced an outcome, challenge it, and see it corrected. Research has documented what AI governance produces: principles, strategies, registers, and audits. However, we lack shared language for understanding AI policy while it is still being made. We introduce the Society-Centered AI Governance Framework, which gives policymakers, researchers, and the public a way to assess instruments in any jurisdiction by whether a person can get notice, challenge a decision, and see it corrected. It reads a jurisdiction's instruments together by date and binding status, separates an agency duty from a right a person can invoke, and traces which later instrument must enforce each commitment. We evaluated it in North Carolina using interviews with nine AI Leadership Council members, conducted before and after the state's 2026 AI roadmap, and a provision-level reading, with human-reviewed model-assisted coding, of 49 AI governance documents from 19 states. For the state's own AI systems, we find visibility-first governance: visibility duties are in effect, notice exists as an agency duty with no right a person can invoke, and AI-specific challenge and correction remain advisory. The roadmap assigns owners and dates to the missing protections, so the gaps are documented but not yet closed. Recent federal preemption proposals focus on AI development, so recourse for a state's own systems is likely to remain a state decision. We identify "legitimacy before protection" as a testable risk of visibility-first governance and name the milestones that would test it. More broadly, judging AI policy by who can act on what it makes visible lets the field assess recourse while policy is still forming, before harm occurs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Society-Centred AI Governance Framework that judges instruments by whether a person can get notice, challenge a decision and see it corrected. Applied to North Carolina, it finds visibility-first governance with recourse still advisory.
AI.motivation: Governments set AI policy before its public effects can be measured, and existing work documents what governance produces, such as principles and audits, but lacks shared language for policy as it is being made.
AI.method: The framework reads a jurisdiction's instruments together by date and binding status, separates an agency duty from a right a person can invoke, and traces which later instrument must enforce each commitment. It is applied through interviews with nine AI Leadership Council members before and after the 2026 AI roadmap, and a provision-level reading of 49 documents from 19 states, using human-reviewed model-assisted coding.
AI.result: For the state's own AI systems, visibility duties are in effect, notice exists as an agency duty with no right a person can invoke, and challenge and correction remain advisory. The roadmap assigns owners and dates to the missing protections.
AI.conclusion: The authors name legitimacy before protection as a testable risk of visibility-first governance, and propose judging AI policy by who can act on what it makes visible.

title: Stack more levels: how to get general and human-like Mario playing
summary: Super Mario Bros. is widely used in game AI and procedural content generation (PCG), yet it remains unclear whether a model-free agent can reliably win unseen levels. To address this question, we train Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agents on increasingly large sets of PCG-generated Mario levels and evaluate their generalization on 1000 held-out test levels. We then shape competent PPO policies into three gameplay archetypes---runner, killer, and collector. Finally, we fine-tune these PPO policies using Diffusion-Reward Adversarial Imitation Learning (DRAIL) with human gameplay demonstrations. We find that increasing the number of distinct PCG-generated training levels generally improves unseen-level performance, and that fine-tuning PPO policies with DRAIL increases action-level human-likeness while preserving much of the persona induced by PPO pretraining.

AI.tldr: The paper trains PPO agents on increasing numbers of procedurally generated Mario levels and shapes them into gameplay archetypes. Fine-tuning with DRAIL on human demonstrations increases action-level human-likeness while keeping much of the persona.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether a model-free agent can reliably win unseen Super Mario Bros. levels, which matters for game AI and procedural content generation.
AI.method: PPO agents are trained on growing sets of PCG-generated levels and tested on 1,000 held-out levels. Competent policies are shaped into runner, killer and collector archetypes, then fine-tuned with Diffusion-Reward Adversarial Imitation Learning (DRAIL) using human gameplay demonstrations.
AI.result: More distinct PCG training levels generally improve performance on unseen levels. DRAIL fine-tuning increases action-level human-likeness while preserving much of the persona induced by PPO pretraining. No numerical results are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Training on more varied procedural levels aids generalisation, and adversarial imitation can make persona-shaped agents more human-like without discarding their archetype.

title: Turning Multi-Agent Communication into Token-Level Credit with On Policy Self Distillation
comment: 14pages,4 figures
summary: Reinforcement learning improves problem solving in large language model multi-agent systems. Existing approaches overlook communication knowledge or compress it into scalar rewards, leaving coarse credit with little guidance on which decisions each agent should reinforce or revise. OPSD4MAS converts future communication into fine-grained token-level credit through On Policy Self Distillation (OPSD). An external model extracts facts and assesses their trajectory relations for coarse-grained filtering, followed by fine-grained leave-one-out filtering of target-token influence against agent-wise outcome advantages. The fact-conditioned policy supplies token-level credit, combined with GRPO through a linearly annealed joint objective. Our method improves mathematical pass@4 over GRPO by up to 20.00 percentage points. Ablations support complete filtering, while frozen-history injection diagnostics support fact utility. Together, these results support combining agent-level outcome guidance with communication-derived token-level credit. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: OPSD4MAS converts future communication among LLM agents into token-level credit using On Policy Self Distillation, and combines it with GRPO. It improves mathematical pass@4 over GRPO by up to 20.00 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent RL either ignores communication knowledge or compresses it into scalar rewards, which gives coarse credit with little guidance on which decisions each agent should reinforce or revise.
AI.method: An external model extracts facts and assesses their trajectory relations for coarse filtering, followed by fine-grained leave-one-out filtering of target-token influence against agent-wise outcome advantages. A fact-conditioned policy supplies token-level credit, combined with GRPO through a linearly annealed joint objective.
AI.result: The method improves mathematical pass@4 over GRPO by up to 20.00 percentage points. Ablations support complete filtering, and frozen-history injection diagnostics support the utility of the facts.
AI.conclusion: Agent-level outcome guidance and communication-derived token-level credit are complementary in multi-agent LLM reinforcement learning.

title: One Fuzzer, Many Reasoners: Adaptive Neuro-Symbolic Fuzzing with Reliability-Calibrated and Context-Gated Guidance
summary: Neural-symbolic AI (NSAI) combines learned perception with programs, constraints, and compositional reasoning, but remains difficult to test because small semantics-preserving changes can alter grounded symbols and trigger discontinuous reasoning failures. Existing neural fuzzers mainly rely on neural coverage or representation-space feedback and do not provide a common testing interface for heterogeneous NSAI systems. We introduce NSAI-Fuzz, a unified semantics-aware fuzzing framework that separates task-specific valid mutation from architecture-neutral guided search and represents each candidate using five availability-aware, rank-normalized risk signals: boundary pressure, grounding uncertainty, representation drift, constraint violation, and archive novelty. We further propose Reliability-Calibrated Weighting (RCW), which learns dataset-model-level signal allocations from calibrated reliability, and Contextual Signal Gating (CSG), which adapts signal weights to the current candidate pool. We evaluate four NSAI systems across four reasoning tasks, nine compatible dataset-model cells, 20 policies, and 1,800 on-policy runs. Fixed five-signal guidance outperforms Random and Uniform in every cell, while RCW and CSG further improve over Fixed in all nine cells. Under matched mutation and query budgets, RCW and CSG achieve 16.17% and 16.06% aggregate failure discovery, compared with 6.06% for the strongest neural-fuzzing baseline. Wall-clock evaluation further shows that TensorFuzz requires 1.11x the runtime of RCW while achieving only 0.45x its failure throughput. These results show that effective and efficient fuzzing of heterogeneous NSAI systems benefits from a common neural-symbolic risk interface with adaptive signal allocation.

AI.tldr: NSAI-Fuzz is a semantics-aware fuzzing framework for heterogeneous neural-symbolic AI systems, using five risk signals with adaptive weighting. It finds about 16% failures under matched budgets, against 6.06% for the strongest neural-fuzzing baseline.
AI.motivation: Neural-symbolic systems fail discontinuously under small semantics-preserving changes, and existing neural fuzzers rely on neural coverage or representation-space feedback without a common interface for heterogeneous systems.
AI.method: The framework separates task-specific valid mutation from architecture-neutral guided search and represents each candidate with five rank-normalised risk signals: boundary pressure, grounding uncertainty, representation drift, constraint violation and archive novelty. Reliability-Calibrated Weighting (RCW) learns signal allocations from calibrated reliability, and Contextual Signal Gating (CSG) adapts weights to the candidate pool.
AI.result: Across four systems, four reasoning tasks, nine dataset-model cells and 1,800 on-policy runs, fixed five-signal guidance beats Random and Uniform in every cell, and RCW and CSG beat Fixed in all nine cells. RCW and CSG reach 16.17% and 16.06% aggregate failure discovery against 6.06% for the strongest neural baseline. TensorFuzz needs 1.11x the runtime of RCW for 0.45x its failure throughput.
AI.conclusion: Effective fuzzing of heterogeneous neural-symbolic systems benefits from a common risk interface with adaptive signal allocation.

title: Causals: An Open Knowledge Graph for Research on Causal Reasoning
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures. Project website: this https URL
summary: Applying causal knowledge to a new event requires connecting the event to relevant entities and the relationships through which its consequences may unfold. We present Causals, an open knowledge graph for research on this form of reasoning. Its initial release, constructed from news reports, contains 369,184 nodes and 1,272,418 edges linking reported events, organizations, commodities, financial instruments, and other entities. Structural relationships, observations, and attributed causal claims retain distinct semantics and links to source records. We describe the construction and representation of the resource and characterize its connectivity and multi-hop retrieval properties. Causals provides shared relational knowledge for studying how language models retrieve relevant context and apply mechanisms to particular events. The dataset is available under CC BY 4.0 at this https URL, and we invite contributions to its ontology, records, and evidence.

AI.tldr: Causals is an open knowledge graph for causal reasoning, built from news reports, with 369,184 nodes and 1,272,418 edges. It keeps structural relations, observations and attributed causal claims distinct and linked to their sources.
AI.motivation: Applying causal knowledge to a new event requires connecting it to relevant entities and to the relations through which its consequences may unfold, and shared resources for studying this are needed.
AI.method: The authors construct the initial release from news reports, linking events, organisations, commodities, financial instruments and other entities. They describe the construction and representation, and characterise connectivity and multi-hop retrieval properties.
AI.result: The release has 369,184 nodes and 1,272,418 edges. The abstract reports connectivity and multi-hop retrieval characteristics but gives no further numerical results.
AI.conclusion: The graph provides shared relational knowledge for studying how language models retrieve context and apply mechanisms to events, released under CC BY 4.0.

title: SAGE-QA: Semantic-Aware, Grounded Evaluation for Closed-Context Question Answering on SQuAD 2.0
summary: Closed-context question answering (QA) requires a system to generate an answer strictly supported by a supplied passage, or to abstain when the passage lacks adequate evidence. SQuAD 2.0 is a widely used benchmark for this setting, scored by Exact Match (EM) i.e., character-level agreement with human reference spans after lexical normalization. For generative large language models (LLMs), however, an EM failure may reflect a valid paraphrase or an alternative passage-supported answer rather than a hallucination. The best prior leaderboard EM is approximately 91%, but evaluating generative models requires separating lexical divergence from factual error. We introduce SAGE-QA (Semantic-Aware, Grounded Evaluation for Question Answering), a multi-tiered framework combining reference-based Semantic Equivalence Scoring (SES) and passage-based Re-Validation Scoring (RVS). On a fixed set of 10,000 SQuAD 2.0 validation examples, we compute EM and decision-matrix F1 from TP, TN, FP, and FN counts for zero-shot closed-weight frontier models and for open-weight models, untuned and fine-tuned. Zero-shot, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro reach 85.21 and 86.66 EM, outperforming untuned Llama 3 8B (56.88), gpt-oss-20b (66.28), and Llama 3.3 70B (71.39). Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adds 21.19 to 34.06 EM points, raising these models to 90.94, 87.47, and 94.24 EM, respectively. Auditing the frontier models with SAGE-QA and an external LLM judge yields dataset-wide SES scores of 92.81 for Claude Opus 4.6 and 91.67 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and hybrid RVS scores, which combine benchmark credit with passage-based judge assessments, of 97.96 and 98.02. Fine-tuned open-weight models perform best, with fine-tuned Llama 3.3 70B surpassing the previous best known EM.

AI.tldr: SAGE-QA is an evaluation framework for closed-context question answering on SQuAD 2.0 that separates lexical divergence from factual error using semantic and passage-based scoring. Fine-tuned open-weight models perform best, with fine-tuned Llama 3.3 70B surpassing the previous best known EM.
AI.motivation: Exact Match penalises valid paraphrases and alternative passage-supported answers in generative LLM outputs, so it can misread them as hallucinations.
AI.method: SAGE-QA combines reference-based Semantic Equivalence Scoring (SES) with passage-based Re-Validation Scoring (RVS). EM and decision-matrix F1 are computed on 10,000 SQuAD 2.0 validation examples for zero-shot closed and open-weight models, and for untuned and parameter-efficiently fine-tuned open-weight models.
AI.result: Zero-shot, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro reach 85.21 and 86.66 EM. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning raises the open models to 90.94, 87.47 and 94.24 EM. Dataset-wide SES reaches 92.81 and 91.67 for the two frontier models, and hybrid RVS reaches 97.96 and 98.02.
AI.conclusion: Semantic and passage-based scoring shows that many EM failures on generative models are not hallucinations, and fine-tuned open-weight models lead on this benchmark.

title: Benchmarking AI risk behaviors
summary: We evaluate LLM risk propensities across a range of contexts and task demands. We evaluate models for how risk averse or risk tolerant they are in various conditions, as well as how stable and consistent their behavior is across conditions. We present a toolkit for developing model risk profiles that can be used to predict model behavior and which can be adapted to include new evaluations of risk propensities. We also examine how these properties have changed across model generations and families. We observe that 2026 state-of-the-art models tend to be more stable, more consistent, and more risk neutral than older models. These trends appear to be related; newer models are more stable and consistent because they are more likely to use expected value maximization as a decision procedure.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates LLM risk propensities across contexts and task demands, and presents a toolkit for building model risk profiles. It finds that 2026 state-of-the-art models are more stable, consistent and risk-neutral than older models.
AI.motivation: Models differ in how risk averse or tolerant they are, and it matters how stable and consistent this behaviour is across conditions.
AI.method: The authors measure risk aversion and tolerance across conditions and examine how these properties change across model generations and families. They present a toolkit for risk profiles that can be extended with new evaluations.
AI.result: Newer models are more stable and consistent, and the authors attribute this to a greater tendency to use expected value maximisation as a decision procedure. No numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Risk profiles can predict model behaviour, and the observed trends suggest newer models decide more by expected value.

title: From More to Better: Causal Inference and Digital Experimentation in the Age of AI
comment: 17 pages, 1 table. Perspective based on the 2026 Causal Inference and Digital Experimentation Roundtable (CIDER)
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is quickly expanding the capacity of organizations to produce and analyze data. We argue that this expansion shifts the leverage of data scientists from performing individual analyses to assessing the credibility and importance of findings and determining when evidence generalizes across contexts. Drawing on a roundtable of academic researchers and industry practitioners, we examine three ways in which data scientists who work on causal inference and experimentation can help organizations turn more analytical capacity into better decisions: preserving and accumulating the learning value of experimentation beyond individual tests; choosing and combining experimental, observational, and synthetic evidence; and ensuring evaluation keeps pace with AI as its capabilities and uses evolve. In each area, we distinguish established practice from open questions. We conclude with implications for the training and practice of data science and for organizations.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI shifts data scientists' leverage from running individual analyses to assessing the credibility of findings and whether they generalise. It draws on a roundtable of academic and industry researchers.
AI.motivation: AI expands organisations' capacity to produce and analyse data, so the bottleneck moves to judging which results are credible and when evidence generalises across contexts.
AI.method: Drawing on a roundtable, the authors examine three areas: preserving and accumulating the learning value of experiments, choosing and combining experimental, observational and synthetic evidence, and keeping evaluation in step with AI capabilities. In each area they separate established practice from open questions.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results; it gives a discussion of practice and open questions.
AI.conclusion: The authors draw implications for the training and practice of data scientists and for organisations that want better decisions from more analytical capacity.

title: DIAGNO: Diagonal Spherical Neural Operators for Heterogeneous Earth Dynamics Modeling
comment: 35 pages, 13 figures, 8 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Main Track, Oral)
summary: Accurate forecasting of Earth's dynamic systems is vital in geophysics, where neural operators offer a powerful data-driven paradigm. Standard operators often treat the Earth as a flat Euclidean plane, introducing geometric artifacts. In contrast, Spherical Neural Operators (SNOs) resolve this mismatch by operating within the spherical spectral space, naturally adapting to spherical geometries. However, for computational efficiency, existing SNOs typically rely on the rotation equivariance assumption. This assumption simplifies the transitions of physical states into isolated spectral modal evolutions, thereby over-idealizing the Earth as a homogeneous system. To solve this problem, we no longer rely on the rotation equivariance assumption that isolates spectral modal evolution, but directly derive an explicit modal interaction kernel and propose Diagonal Spherical Neural Operators named DIAGNO. DIAGNO explicitly parameterizes cross-modal interactions through spectral modal decomposition, thereby preserving the inherent heterogeneity of Earth dynamics. Furthermore, leveraging the unique diagonal structure of the spherical spectrum, we design inter- and intra-diagonal interaction mechanisms to natively capture essential zonal and meridional dynamics, respecting intrinsic geophysical regularities. Extensive experiments across simulated fluid dynamics and real-world Earth system reanalysis (including atmosphere and ocean) datasets demonstrate DIAGNO's superior capability, consistently achieving state-of-the-art performance in multi-step forecasting. Beyond this, we validate DIAGNO's practical analytical value in professional geophysical domains by assessing its fidelity in capturing climatological anomalies and maintaining physical consistency.

AI.tldr: DIAGNO is a spherical neural operator that drops the rotation equivariance assumption and explicitly models cross-modal spectral interactions for Earth system forecasting. It reports state-of-the-art multi-step forecasting on fluid dynamics and reanalysis datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing spherical neural operators rely on rotation equivariance for efficiency, which isolates spectral modes and treats the Earth as a homogeneous system.
AI.method: DIAGNO derives an explicit modal interaction kernel and parameterises cross-modal interactions through spectral modal decomposition. It uses inter- and intra-diagonal interaction mechanisms on the diagonal structure of the spherical spectrum to capture zonal and meridional dynamics.
AI.result: DIAGNO achieves state-of-the-art multi-step forecasting across simulated fluid dynamics and real atmosphere and ocean reanalysis datasets, and captures climatological anomalies while keeping physical consistency. No numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Explicit cross-modal interactions preserve the heterogeneity of Earth dynamics that equivariant spectral operators idealise away.

title: Evidence-Governed Adoption of Self-Generated Updates in Autonomous AI Agents
summary: Autonomous agents modify prompts, memories, tools, workflows, and policies using interaction histories. Yet a plausible modification is not necessarily suitable for persistent adoption: candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect, and local gains can hide degradation against an earlier baseline. We introduce Evidence-Governed Evolution (EGE), a framework for governing adoption of self-generated agent modifications. EGE separates candidate generation from confirmatory adoption, evaluates frozen candidates on fresh paired audits, requires meaningful improvement on a prespecified primary objective, protects declared capabilities through reference-relative non-inferiority tests, and applies governance constraints before bounded canary deployment. We establish an evaluator-calibrated simultaneous lower-bound construction for a countable sequence of adaptively generated candidates. It combines candidate-wise Hoeffding bounds with independent calibration samples comparing the operational evaluator with a prespecified reference procedure. We also formalise reference replacement through bridge tests, derive a cumulative degradation bound along a versioned reference lineage, and provide an audit-planning condition relating effect-size margin, sample sizes, and acceptance probability. A Monte Carlo stress test illustrates calibration under candidate-dependent evaluator optimism; it is a stylised statistical experiment, not an evaluation of a deployed agent. The guarantees are conditional on bounded paired scores, fresh sampling, a valid reference-evaluation construct, and declared evaluation distributions; they do not establish universal agent safety or robustness to arbitrary distribution shift.

AI.tldr: EGE is a framework for governing whether self-generated modifications of autonomous agents are adopted, using fresh paired audits, non-inferiority tests and bounded canary deployment. The guarantees are stated as conditional and the Monte Carlo study is stylised.
AI.motivation: A plausible agent modification is not necessarily fit for persistent adoption, because candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect and local gains can hide degradation against an earlier baseline.
AI.method: EGE separates candidate generation from confirmatory adoption, evaluates frozen candidates on fresh paired audits and requires improvement on a prespecified primary objective. Declared capabilities are protected by reference-relative non-inferiority tests, and governance constraints are applied before bounded canary deployment. The authors give an evaluator-calibrated simultaneous lower-bound construction and a cumulative degradation bound along a versioned reference lineage.
AI.result: A Monte Carlo stress test illustrates calibration under candidate-dependent evaluator optimism. The abstract explicitly says this is a stylised statistical experiment and not an evaluation of a deployed agent.
AI.conclusion: The guarantees hold under bounded paired scores, fresh sampling, a valid reference construct and declared distributions, and do not establish universal agent safety or robustness to arbitrary distribution shift.

title: Small Language Models for Inference-Capability Routing: Effects of Model Capacity and Prompt Optimization on Downstream Quality and Efficiency
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures
summary: Optional reasoning, retrieval, web search, and tool use can improve large language model responses but incur unnecessary computation when activated indiscriminately. This study investigates whether prompt optimization can compensate for limited router capacity and whether classification gains translate into downstream efficiency. The proposed framework uses prompt-driven small language models to make four independent capability decisions, allowing multiple capabilities to be selected per query. Qwen2.5 routers ranging from 1.5B to 14B parameters are compared across five prompting strategies, followed by an evaluation of capability-specific optimized configurations using a fixed GPT-OSS-120B downstream model on 127 questions. Under minimal prompting, increasing router capacity does not consistently improve classification performance. Prompt optimization narrows the capacity gap for reasoning and calculator routing, whereas RAG and web search retain larger benefits from higher capacity. Similar classification F1 scores do not necessarily imply equivalent downstream behavior: false-positive activations increase unnecessary computation, while missed capabilities can reduce answer quality. The 14B router achieves a mean BERTScore F1 of 0.8408, compared with 0.8418 when all capabilities are enabled, while reducing average downstream token consumption by 68.7\% (8,837 to 2,764 tokens) and median downstream latency by 80.5\% (9.79 to 1.91 seconds). These savings exclude router overhead, which is measured separately in a different inference environment and increases with router capacity. The findings demonstrate that the relationship between router capacity, prompt design, and downstream efficiency is capability-dependent. Consequently, router selection must consider error profiles and routing overhead alongside classification performance.

AI.tldr: The paper studies prompt-driven small language models that decide which capabilities (reasoning, calculator, RAG, web search) to activate for a query. A 14B router cuts downstream token use by 68.7% with almost no BERTScore loss.
AI.motivation: Optional capabilities improve LLM responses but waste computation when switched on indiscriminately, and it is unclear whether classification gains translate into downstream efficiency.
AI.method: Qwen2.5 routers from 1.5B to 14B parameters are compared under five prompting strategies, each making four independent capability decisions. Capability-specific optimised configurations are then evaluated with a fixed GPT-OSS-120B downstream model on 127 questions.
AI.result: The 14B router reaches a mean BERTScore F1 of 0.8408 against 0.8418 with all capabilities enabled, while cutting average downstream tokens from 8,837 to 2,764 (68.7%) and median downstream latency from 9.79 to 1.91 seconds (80.5%). Prompt optimisation narrows the capacity gap for reasoning and calculator routing, whereas RAG and web search keep larger benefits from capacity. Router overhead is measured separately and is excluded from these savings.
AI.conclusion: The relation between router capacity, prompt design and efficiency is capability-dependent, so router selection must account for error profiles and routing overhead as well as classification scores.

title: FPSRG: Heterogeneous User Simulation First-Person Post-Training and Multidimensional Semantic Response Grids
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures
summary: Simulating heterogeneous individuals with large language models is an active research direction, and heterogeneous user simulation requires models with different characteristics. We study profile construction: given dimensions, items, and scoring rules, build model configurations that can be retrieved by multidimensional target scores. We introduce First-Person Semantic Response Grids (FPSRG). Shared post-training first teaches the model to judge and answer as the participant; self-report and behavioral targets then refine dimension-specific control vectors. With the model frozen, we measure joint scores for vector-coefficient combinations, filter inadmissible configurations, and store the results in a searchable catalog. Per-token configuration routing, continuous batching, and isolated caches support parallel measurement of different profiles. Non-thinking five- and ten-dimensional Qwen instances and a thinking-mode six-dimensional instance following full-parameter post-training of Huihui demonstrate the complete workflow. With matched data, layers, and norms, refinement increases mean five-axis composite control span from 30.75 to 40.45. Within the five-dimensional 25-75 target region, the qualified five-level vector catalog covers 92.2% of fixed targets under per-axis error at most 20 and total error at most 60; combining it with the prompt catalog increases coverage to 98.7%. At a fixed coefficient range, three-, five-, and nine-level catalogs achieve 71.2%, 92.2%, and 94.6% coverage, demonstrating the gains from denser measurement. These results describe measured reachable regions under a fixed assessment protocol. Through shared adaptation, a small set of learned directions, and reusable joint measurements, FPSRG constructs heterogeneous individual configurations without retraining a model for every profile.

AI.tldr: FPSRG constructs heterogeneous simulated user profiles by post-training models to answer as the participant and storing a searchable catalog of measured trait combinations. Its five-dimensional catalog covers 92.2% of fixed targets within the stated error bounds.
AI.motivation: Simulating heterogeneous individuals with LLMs needs model configurations that can be retrieved by multidimensional target scores.
AI.method: Shared first-person post-training is followed by dimension-specific control vectors refined with self-report and behavioural targets. With the model frozen, joint scores are measured for vector-coefficient combinations, inadmissible configurations are filtered and the results are stored in a catalog. Per-token configuration routing and isolated caches allow parallel measurement of profiles.
AI.result: Refinement raises the mean five-axis composite control span from 30.75 to 40.45. The qualified five-level vector catalog covers 92.2% of fixed targets under per-axis error of at most 20 and total error of at most 60, and 98.7% when combined with the prompt catalog. Three-, five- and nine-level catalogs reach 71.2%, 92.2% and 94.6% coverage.
AI.conclusion: Reachable regions of trait configurations can be mapped with reusable measurements and a small set of learned directions, without retraining for every profile.

title: Rational Alignments of Superintelligences via Debates
summary: Artificial superintelligences (ASI) is artificial intelligences with greater capability. However, as human principal has to use it, we have to ensure that the agent will perform in the interest of the human. We investigate the framework of ASI-assisted question answering where ASI agents know the correct answer but the human does not. We provide some example of mechanism for rational alignment, where the agent utility is unchanged, but the interaction between the agent and the human principal is controlled to be in a certain fashion. We show specifically that a debate framework where the agents can further reason and behave in a subgame perfect equilibrium manner will lead to a more predictable result, and in some case will be favorable.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that a superintelligent agent can be aligned by a debate protocol in which the agent's utility is unchanged but its interaction with the human principal is structured. It claims the subgame-perfect debate outcome is more predictable and sometimes favourable.
AI.motivation: A human principal relying on an ASI that knows the correct answer, but cannot verify it, needs a way to keep the agent's behaviour in the principal's interest.
AI.method: The authors study ASI-assisted question answering and give examples of mechanisms for rational alignment in which the interaction, not the agent's utility, is controlled. They analyse a debate framework in which agents reason and behave in a subgame-perfect equilibrium manner.
AI.result: The abstract reports theoretical claims that the debate framework leads to a more predictable result, which is favourable in some cases. No numerical results are given.
AI.conclusion: Structuring the interaction through debate offers a route to rational alignment of superintelligent agents without changing their utility.

title: Fine-Tuned Small Language Model for Synthetic Clinical Data Generation and Predictive Healthcare Analytics
summary: The reduced availability of medical datasets represents an important challenge in the development of predictive models for remote healthcare solutions, especially when the available data are imbalanced or difficult to extend through traditional methods. Small Language Models (SLMs) have become a promising alternative to Large Language Models (LLMs) for addressing these limitations due to their lower computational requirements and adaptability to specialized tasks. However, their performance remains highly dependent on the quality and representativeness of the available training data. In this paper, we propose a method for clinical data augmentation based on a fine-tuned Microsoft Phi-2 model that is used to generate synthetic instances, with the purpose of improving deep learning-based model for predicting remotely monitored vital signs. The Phi-2 model was adapted to the medical domain through supervised fine-tuning on the MedQuad dataset, through a Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA)-based method and by applying few-shot prompting techniques. The resulting model was used afterwards in the augmentation of a small-sized dataset, composed of vital sign values and labels associated with pathological and physiological states. The experimental results demonstrate that fine-tuned SLMs improved the performance on medical domain, achieving higher scores for both lexical (ROUGE) and semantic (BERTScore) evaluation metrics compared to the pretrained model. Moreover, the fine-tuned SLM is effective for generating structured synthetic clinical data. When used for data augmentation, the generated dataset improved the performance of a LSTM predictive model, increasing the classification accuracy from 89.0% to 93.7% and showing consistent improvements in precision, recall, and F1-score.

AI.tldr: The paper fine-tunes a Phi-2 small language model with QLoRA on MedQuAD to generate synthetic vital-sign data. Augmenting a small dataset with it raises an LSTM's classification accuracy from 89.0% to 93.7%.
AI.motivation: Medical datasets for remote healthcare are scarce and imbalanced, and existing augmentation methods are hard to extend to this setting.
AI.method: Phi-2 is adapted to the medical domain by supervised fine-tuning on MedQuAD with QLoRA and few-shot prompting. The fine-tuned model generates synthetic vital-sign records with labels for pathological and physiological states, which augment a small dataset used to train an LSTM predictor.
AI.result: The fine-tuned SLM scores higher than the pretrained model on ROUGE and BERTScore. The augmented data raises LSTM classification accuracy from 89.0% to 93.7% and improves precision, recall and F1-score.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuned small language models can generate useful structured synthetic clinical data for augmenting predictive healthcare models.

title: One Model, Two Precisions: Does Disagreement Between Quantized Copies Tell You When a Small Model Is Wrong?
summary: Local language models often exist at several precisions, and quantization is known to change individual answers. This study asks whether the disagreement between two precisions of the same weights, an 8-bit copy that answers and a lower-precision copy that reads the same prompt, works as a per-question error score for abstention, escalation and re-asking. The cost is one extra forward pass over fewer bytes, with no sampling and no training. We simulate round-to-nearest quantization with per-group scales (3 to 6 bits, groups of 32 to 256) on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B and score 8,398 multiple-choice questions from ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU and HellaSwag subsets. Error detection is measured by AUROC, risk-coverage curves and ECE on a held-out half, with paired bootstrap intervals over questions. For Qwen3-0.6B, the entropy of the 8-bit answer reaches AUROC 0.682; the best disagreement score, selected on a development half, reaches 0.684 (+0.001 [-0.009, +0.011]), and combining it with the confidence features adds +0.009 [+0.002, +0.015], mostly on ARC. On Qwen3-1.7B the selected score is -0.001 [-0.009, +0.006] from entropy and the combination +0.003 [-0.001, +0.006] on the test half. Gaussian weight noise at matched error energy is about as informative as rounding (0.6B only), so we find no evidence that the signal is specific to quantization, and shuffling the features within task and entropy cells removes the gain. One extra 8-bit pass that shifts the option order does better (+0.049 [+0.031, +0.067] over entropy) at about a third more weight traffic; routing to a larger model on free entropy beats both extra-pass scores at equal total traffic. After logistic recalibration the 0.6B confidences are calibrated within a few points of ECE. A deployment recipe and the cases where the method does not help are given.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether disagreement between an 8-bit and a lower-precision copy of the same model signals per-question errors. The disagreement score adds little beyond entropy, and the authors report where the method does not help.
AI.motivation: Local models often exist at several precisions and quantisation changes individual answers, so it is worth asking whether the disagreement works as a cheap error score for abstention, escalation or re-asking.
AI.method: Round-to-nearest quantisation with per-group scales (3 to 6 bits, groups of 32 to 256) is simulated on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, scoring 8,398 multiple-choice questions from ARC, MMLU and HellaSwag subsets. Error detection is measured by AUROC, risk-coverage curves and ECE on a held-out half, with paired bootstrap intervals.
AI.result: For Qwen3-0.6B, 8-bit answer entropy reaches AUROC 0.682 and the best disagreement score reaches 0.684 (+0.001, interval [-0.009, +0.011]). On Qwen3-1.7B the selected score is -0.001 relative to entropy. Gaussian weight noise is about as informative as rounding, and an extra 8-bit pass that shifts option order gives +0.049 over entropy at about a third more weight traffic.
AI.conclusion: The quantisation-disagreement signal is not specific to quantisation and gives little gain over entropy on these models, while an option-order pass is more useful at higher cost.

title: Contain, Conform, Compare (Extended Version): A Red-Teamed Evaluation Kit for Small Coding Agents and the Full Record of Its Experiments
comment: 52 pages, 15 figures, 37 tables. Code: this https URL (tag v0.4.0). Data and analysis scripts are included as ancillary files
summary: A hosted score in the Gemma 4 Developer Agent competition is one noisy number, so development needs a local evaluator that is fast, safe for agent-written code, and matching the hosted scorer's prompts. drydock-eval evaluates a small coding agent (Gemma 4 E4B) at about 250 runs per hour on one RTX 5090. Contain runs each job in a fresh container without network and passed 200 scripted escape tests; conform provides eight checks that compare a local stack's requests with the scorer's configuration, down to rendered tokens; compare provides paired statistics that respect repository clusters. AI agents built and attacked the kit; a human owner approved machine use and release. This extended version repeats the short paper and adds the full record of the experiments made with and around the kit: 9,660 rows of agent runs, 2,494 grading controls and 72 serving measurements, all released. On four L4 GPUs the 31B model decodes 38.1 tokens per second in one stream and E4B 105.8. Six configurations of a 31B agent solved between 37 and 44 of 70 development tasks, and no pairwise difference was detected. A pre-registered five-arm experiment (231 tasks, 4,620 jobs) measured four prompt divergences: no E4B solve-rate change was detected (largest estimate -2.1 points, 95% interval -4.4 to +0.4). Three changes of the E4B agent led their screens by +1.0 to +6.2 points; each was then tested once on new tasks under a frozen pass rule, and none was confirmed (gains -0.35, -0.39 and +4.10 points). The unchanged baseline, run again on the same 128 tasks, moved by 1.17 points, and 65% of these tasks were solved in none of eight runs. Prompts and agent bundles are withheld; every run-level result is public.

AI.tldr: drydock-eval is a local, container-isolated evaluator for a small coding agent (Gemma 4 E4B) that reproduces the hosted scorer's prompts, and the paper reports its experiments. Pre-registered prompt and agent changes did not produce confirmed gains.
AI.motivation: A hosted competition score is one noisy number, so development needs a fast local evaluator that is safe for agent-written code and matches the hosted scorer.
AI.method: Contain runs each job in a fresh container without network and passed 200 scripted escape tests. Conform provides eight checks comparing a local stack's requests with the scorer's configuration. Compare gives paired statistics that respect repository clusters. The extended version releases the full record of runs and grading controls.
AI.result: The evaluator runs about 250 runs per hour on one RTX 5090. A pre-registered five-arm experiment (231 tasks, 4,620 jobs) detects no E4B solve-rate change (largest estimate -2.1 points, 95% interval -4.4 to +0.4). Three changes that led their screens by +1.0 to +6.2 points were not confirmed on new tasks (gains -0.35, -0.39 and +4.10 points). The unchanged baseline moved by 1.17 points on re-run.
AI.conclusion: Single-screen gains on a small task set can be noise, so changes need frozen confirmation on new tasks before they are trusted. Prompts and agent bundles are withheld.

title: HeMeR: Heterogeneous Memory Reconciliation for Embodied Agents via Structured KV Reuse
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Oral)
summary: Embodied agents make decisions by combining information from heterogeneous memory modules, including declarative memory for explicit knowledge, procedural memory for learned routines, and working memory for current observations. During interaction, the memory contents required for decision making change with the agent's state, goal, and task progress, while many contents remain shared across consecutive decisions. However, existing memory modules are typically accessed through separate interfaces, so each updated memory context is often processed as a new input to the foundation model. This prevents selective key-value (KV) cache reuse for unchanged memory contents and forces full KV cache recomputation even when much of the memory context remains valid. We introduce HeMeR, an inference framework that performs KV reconciliation between dynamically updated memory contexts and reusable KV states. HeMeR tracks declarative, procedural, and working memory contents across action decisions, preserves KV states for unchanged contents, and reconciles only the KV states affected by memory-content updates. This enables efficient and stable inference as memory contents evolve during interaction. We evaluate HeMeR on ALFWorld, Habitat, and real-world robotic deployments requiring coordinated use of heterogeneous memory contents. In the real-world setting, HeMeR achieves 83.20% task success and reduces per-step inference time from 2.94 to 1.87 seconds compared with MemRL, while preserving compatible KV states as task progress updates the memory context.

AI.tldr: HeMeR is an inference framework for embodied agents that reconciles KV caches across heterogeneous memory modules, reusing states for unchanged memory and recomputing only the affected ones. It reports 83.20% real-world task success and lower per-step inference time than MemRL.
AI.motivation: Each updated memory context is usually processed as a new input, which blocks selective KV cache reuse and forces full recomputation even when much of the memory is unchanged.
AI.method: HeMeR tracks declarative, procedural and working memory across action decisions, preserves KV states for unchanged contents, and reconciles only the states affected by memory updates.
AI.result: In real-world robotic deployment, HeMeR achieves 83.20% task success and reduces per-step inference time from 2.94 to 1.87 seconds compared with MemRL. It is also evaluated on ALFWorld and Habitat.
AI.conclusion: Structured KV reconciliation allows efficient and stable inference as heterogeneous memory evolves during interaction.

title: Time and Space: A Dual-Axis, Evidence-Grounded Context Substrate for Personal Agents
summary: We argue that a binding constraint for personal agents is not model capacity but the form in which context is represented: the agent does not know which entity a phrase denotes, when a fact held, or which source record licenses a claim. We call the missing representation spatio-temporal context (STC) and define it on two axes. The temporal axis carries event time, validity intervals and ingestion time. The spatial axis is a relational space in which entities are points, typed relations are edges, and distance is semantic rather than geographic; physical places are one entity type among many. Every relation is anchored to immutable source records, and every answer must be closed over those records. We formalise the substrate and six invariants, a context operator that composes temporal intersection with relational expansion, an ambiguity-preserving resolution state machine, a conflict detector that converts mutually exclusive facts into user adjudication rather than silent overwrite, and a four-regime consumption taxonomy spanning query, insight, triage and proactive reminder. We describe a local-first prototype of the retrieval layer built on SQLite with on-device embeddings and hybrid lexical-dense recall, report measurements from a deployed store of 341 documents, 340,079 chunks and 190,271 embedded vectors, and specify, but do not yet implement, the analytic layer on which the framework depends. We close with an evaluation protocol with per-invariant metrics for evidence coverage, temporal correctness, conflict precision and interruption cost. The proposal targets the representation of context rather than the volume of it.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes spatio-temporal context (STC), a representation with temporal and relational axes, as the binding constraint for personal agents, and describes a local-first retrieval prototype. The analytic layer is specified but not implemented.
AI.motivation: Personal agents fail less from limited model capacity than from how context is represented, since they do not know which entity a phrase denotes, when a fact held, or which source supports a claim.
AI.method: The temporal axis carries event time, validity intervals and ingestion time. The spatial axis is a relational space where entities are points, typed relations are edges and distance is semantic. Each relation is anchored to immutable source records. The authors formalise six invariants, a context operator, an ambiguity-preserving resolution state machine, a conflict detector that routes conflicts to user adjudication, and a four-regime consumption taxonomy. A SQLite-based prototype uses hybrid lexical-dense recall.
AI.result: The deployed store has 341 documents, 340,079 chunks and 190,271 embedded vectors. The abstract reports no retrieval accuracy numbers, and the analytic layer is specified but not yet implemented.
AI.conclusion: The proposal targets how context is represented rather than how much of it there is, and an evaluation protocol with per-invariant metrics is specified.

title: ReA-Bench: Benchmarking Responsible Agent Auditing
summary: As agents perform tasks autonomously in local and cloud environments, auditing their execution trajectories can help service providers identify risks and improve agent harnesses and foundation models. Our analysis of production and red-team trajectories shows that some risks are repeatedly missed across auditing configurations. Overall recall obscures which risks are missed and whether higher recall comes with more false positives on legitimate behavior. Existing benchmarks offer limited insight into these failures. Generated trajectories can contain inconsistent tool calls and responses, conspicuous risky actions, or repetitive attack patterns. Grouping results by risk type also makes it difficult to tell whether auditors overlooked evidence, accepted an unsupported conclusion, or lacked information needed to make a judgment. We introduce ReA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark for auditing responsible agent behavior. It organizes auditing challenges into six tiers: internal safety knowledge, contradictions within trajectories, evidence retrieval in long contexts, verification of sources and reasoning, indirect steering, and missing information. It includes challenging benign cases in which actions resemble risky ones but are consistent with the task and its authorization. It also provides paired trajectory versions to test whether auditors detect the same risks more reliably when the trajectory is shortened or missing information is supplied. Most samples are drawn from real production trajectories, with scenarios manually selected and adapted to preserve realistic tasks and risks that could plausibly arise during execution.

AI.tldr: ReA-Bench is a diagnostic benchmark for auditing whether agents' execution trajectories show responsible behaviour, organised into six tiers of auditing challenges. It includes benign cases that resemble risky actions and paired trajectory versions.
AI.motivation: Overall recall hides which risks auditors miss and whether higher recall brings more false positives on legitimate behaviour, and existing benchmarks offer limited insight into these failures.
AI.method: Auditing challenges are organised into six tiers: internal safety knowledge, contradictions within trajectories, evidence retrieval in long contexts, verification of sources and reasoning, indirect steering and missing information. The benchmark includes benign cases that are consistent with authorisation and paired trajectory versions that are shortened or supplied with missing information. Most samples come from real production trajectories.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results, and describes the benchmark's design only.
AI.conclusion: Per-tier diagnostics can show why an auditor misses a risk, which aggregate recall cannot.

title: How many LLM-labelled rows does a decision encoder need, and how wrong can the labels be?
comment: 24 pages, 20 figures, 15 tables
summary: A decision encoder such as Laya reads a question with named options (for example, which department should handle a ticket) and a text, and picks an option. It reads both in one forward pass and returns a probability for every option, without writing any text. We ask how many LLM-written training rows such an encoder needs and how wrong those labels may be. We ran 19 fine-tunes of Laya (ModernBERT-large) on nested subsets of a 2,818-row pool and scored them on 1,065 held-out items from the same generator, so every test item is in-distribution and no out-of-family test was run. Accuracy rises from 69.4% before fine-tuning to 74.3% with 5% of the rows, 84.8% with 50% and 86.9% with all rows. The curve flattens, and a saturating fit with bootstrap intervals cannot pin down its plateau. Seed spread at 20% of the rows (s.d. 1.6 points) exceeds some of the steps between sizes. Giving small subsets as many updates as the full pool gains 1.9 points at 5% and 1.9 points at 20% of the rows (one seed; p=0.14 and 0.13), and at 20% that is below the 2.3-point difference between two ordinary seeds. A single run with 10% symmetric label noise shows no detectable change (-0.2 points, 95% interval -1.7 to +1.4); 20% costs 3.4 points and 40% costs 8.7 points. Confusable-pair noise at 20% costs 7.4 points, and under noise the model moves from over-confident to under-confident. An independent labeller disagrees with the gold labels on 3.5% of held-out items, and about half of its choice disagreements (16 of 33, leaving each item out of the partner map) name the partner option that the confusable-pair noise uses. Laya is +0.9 points ahead of a TF-IDF classifier trained on the same rows at full size (the interval includes zero) and +21.1 points ahead at 5% of the rows. Everything is synthetic, LLM-labelled and from one backbone, one trainer and mostly one seed.

AI.tldr: The paper measures how many LLM-labelled training rows a decision encoder (Laya, ModernBERT-large) needs and how much label noise it tolerates. Accuracy rises with data and flattens, and 20% symmetric label noise costs 3.4 points.
AI.motivation: Decision encoders pick an option for a question and text in one forward pass, and training data is written by an LLM, so the required row count and tolerable label error are open questions.
AI.method: Nineteen fine-tunes of Laya are run on nested subsets of a 2,818-row pool and scored on 1,065 held-out items from the same generator. Noise is injected as symmetric and confusable-pair label noise, and Laya is compared with a TF-IDF classifier. Results are largely from one backbone, one trainer and mostly one seed.
AI.result: Accuracy rises from 69.4% before fine-tuning to 74.3% with 5% of rows, 84.8% with 50% and 86.9% with all rows. 10% symmetric noise shows no detectable change (-0.2 points), while 20% costs 3.4 points and 40% costs 8.7 points. Confusable-pair noise at 20% costs 7.4 points. Laya is 0.9 points ahead of TF-IDF at full size, the interval including zero, and 21.1 points ahead at 5% of rows.
AI.conclusion: Modest label noise is tolerable for this task, but the results are synthetic, LLM-labelled and from a single setup, so they do not generalise yet.

title: Recalibrating a Typed-Decision Model in an Afternoon: A Hands-On Recipe for Laya's Confidence Scores
comment: 25 pages, 21 figures, 16 tables
summary: A typed-decision model such as Laya reads a text and a list of options that the caller defines, for example ticket categories, and returns a probability for each option. Code around it compares the top probability with a threshold to answer, abstain or escalate to a person. Earlier work reports, for a Turkish model, that temperature scaling can raise held-out calibration error (ECE). This tutorial gives a five-step recipe (measure, diagnose, fit, validate, deploy) in 130 lines of numpy with standard methods, none new. On 1,065 synthetic, LLM-labelled items the released Laya checkpoint has a pooled ECE of 0.073 but a bucket-macro ECE of 0.143 (0.127-0.184), the mean over buckets (questions grouped by type and option count): the 12-option bucket is over-confident by +0.22, the three-to-five-option bucket under-confident by 0.05, and they cancel. One global temperature makes pooled ECE worse (0.173); a cross-fitted temperature per bucket brings macro-ECE to 0.073 (0.078 over 10 fold assignments) and reaches 0.089 with 10 labelled items per bucket, but holding out one of seven evaluation sets gives 0.099. After the refit, a gate aimed at 10% error answers 46.3% of items (10.5% wrong) against 6.9% on the published confidences, but one cut-off per bucket on the published confidences answers 45.4%, so most of the gain comes from separating buckets. Confidence-only maps (Platt, histogram, isotonic) need 20 or more labelled items per bucket to approach the temperature; with 320 per bucket the lowest macro-ECE belongs to Platt. In these files the retrained checkpoints store no per-bucket table and the stored 12-option value 0.1006 is clamped to 0.5 at runtime; the refit helps 31 of 33 checkpoints on random folds and 21 with a set held out. Fit and test share one generator and LLM labels, so these are findings about these checkpoints and this data.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a five-step, 130-line numpy recipe for recalibrating a typed-decision model (Laya) by bucket-wise temperature scaling. The pooled calibration error is 0.073, while bucket-macro error is 0.143 before refitting and 0.073 after.
AI.motivation: Earlier work reports that temperature scaling can raise calibration error for a Turkish model, and the Laya confidences are used to decide between answer, abstain and escalate.
AI.method: The five steps are measure, diagnose, fit, validate and deploy, using standard methods.
