A cross-fitted temperature is fitted per bucket of questions grouped by type and option count, and compared with a global temperature and with confidence-only maps such as Platt, histogram and isotonic.
AI.result: Before refitting the bucket-macro ECE is 0.143, with the 12-option bucket over-confident by +0.22 and the three-to-five-option bucket under-confident by 0.05. A global temperature worsens pooled ECE to 0.173, and per-bucket cross-fitted temperatures bring macro-ECE to 0.073. After the refit a gate answers 46.3% of items (10.5% wrong) against 6.9% before, but most of this gain comes from separating buckets. The refit helps 31 of 33 checkpoints on random folds.
AI.conclusion: Per-bucket recalibration of this model's confidences is a practical fix, with the findings limited to these checkpoints and this synthetic, LLM-labelled data.

title: SignRot: LLM Quantization with Massive Outlier-Aware Sign-Adjusted Rotation
comment: 23 pages, 4 figures, 19 tables. Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: While quantization compresses LLMs and accelerates inference, outlier activations impede efficient low-bit representation. In particular, massive outliers cause substantial performance degradation. Although rotation-based methods that rely on randomized Hadamard transforms for online inference aim to mitigate this, they can produce fragmented distributions with empty bins when a massive outlier dominates a token's activation. This fragmentation severely undermines uniform quantization performance. Moreover, massive outliers concentrate in the down-projection input, where the preceding nonlinearity requires the rotation to be applied at inference time. This constraint prevents training-based approaches such as SpinQuant from learning the online rotation at this position, as a learned dense matrix cannot use the Fast Walsh-Hadamard Transform and would require a full matrix multiplication during inference. To address this, we propose SignRot (Sign-adjusted Rotation), which identifies massive outlier channels and constructs a sign adjustment vector that unifies the signs of the corresponding Hadamard row, collapsing the bimodal distribution into a unimodal profile amenable to quantization. Since the aligned outlier shifts the activation mean away from zero, we pair SignRot with asymmetric activation quantization, whose zero-point absorbs this shift. As a lightweight, drop-in improvement compatible with any Hadamard-based quantization method, SignRot requires only a single calibration forward pass and adds only element-wise sign flips at inference, without an additional matrix multiplication. Applying SignRot to QuaRot achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 5.88 and an average zero-shot reasoning accuracy of 72.73, surpassing SpinQuant on the LLaMA3-70B model. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: SignRot is a drop-in improvement to Hadamard-based LLM quantisation that adds sign flips to align massive outlier channels, collapsing bimodal activations into a unimodal profile. Applied to QuaRot, it reaches a WikiText2 perplexity of 5.88 and surpasses SpinQuant on LLaMA3-70B.
AI.motivation: Massive outliers degrade low-bit quantisation, and randomised Hadamard rotation can leave fragmented distributions with empty bins when one outlier dominates a token's activation.
AI.method: SignRot identifies massive outlier channels and builds a sign-adjustment vector that aligns the signs of the corresponding Hadamard row. Because the aligned outlier shifts the mean away from zero, it is paired with asymmetric activation quantisation. It needs one calibration forward pass and only element-wise sign flips at inference.
AI.result: Applied to QuaRot, SignRot achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 5.88 and average zero-shot reasoning accuracy of 72.73, surpassing SpinQuant on LLaMA3-70B.
AI.conclusion: Sign alignment of massive outlier channels is a lightweight way to improve Hadamard-based quantisation without extra matrix multiplications.

title: AI has its own style in mathematical proving
summary: As large language models increasingly generate mathematical proofs, whether they develop a proving style distinct from that of human mathematicians remains an open question. This question is particularly pressing as mathematicians increasingly voice concerns that proofs generated by large language models are difficult to interpret. Here we ask three large language models to independently reprove all 465 propositions of Euclid's \textit{Elements} and compare their citation choices against the human-proof baseline through Jaccard similarity and complex network analysis. We find that AI-generated proofs differ from human proofs, and this difference is stable and reproducible: mean pairwise Jaccard similarity among AI runs (~0.68) is nearly twice that between AI and human proofs (~0.37), and cross-run classification consistency is also high. By examining citation structure in detail, we identify the concrete signature of this difference: approximately 40% of AI citations point to foundational elements (definitions, common notions, and postulates), compared with only 13\% in human proofs; even among theorem-to-theorem citations, AI tends to cite more distant results. Roughly half of AI's extra citations trace to the upstream dependencies of the human proof. Together, these findings suggest that the AI proving style is a tendency to construct arguments on its own from foundational elements rather than directly citing later, more established results, which we term "building from the ground up". Our findings offer a new perspective on how AI systems organise and invoke mathematical knowledge, with implications for understanding the interpretability of AI-generated proofs.

AI.tldr: The paper compares citation choices of three LLMs reproving all 465 propositions of Euclid's Elements with those of human proofs. AI proofs build from foundational elements more often and cite distant results, and this style is stable across runs.
AI.motivation: Mathematicians report that LLM-generated proofs are hard to interpret, and it is open whether models develop a proving style distinct from human mathematicians.
AI.method: Three LLMs independently reprove all 465 propositions of Euclid's Elements. Their citation choices are compared with the human-proof baseline using Jaccard similarity and complex network analysis, and cross-run classification consistency is assessed.
AI.result: Mean pairwise Jaccard similarity among AI runs is about 0.68, nearly twice the roughly 0.37 between AI and human proofs. About 40% of AI citations point to foundational elements (definitions, common notions and postulates), against 13% in human proofs. Roughly half of AI's extra citations trace to upstream dependencies of the human proof.
AI.conclusion: The AI proving style is a tendency to build arguments from foundational elements rather than citing later, more established results, which the authors call building from the ground up.

title: SPARC: Accurate Photonic Matrix Multiplication via Representative Vectors
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables
summary: Photonic neural network accelerators have emerged as a promising solution for reducing the power consumption of deep neural network (DNN) inference by executing matrix multiplication on analog photonic hardware. However, their inference accuracy is limited by low-bit quantization required for photonic processing and by analog photonic noise. This paper proposes an approach for improving inference accuracy by exploiting the high similarity among activation vectors in DNNs. Specifically, our approach constructs a representative vector for each group of similar activation vectors, computes its inner product digitally with high precision, and offloads the residual inner products to the photonic accelerator. Since the activation vectors within each group are highly similar, the residual vectors have much smaller norms, thereby reducing the effects of quantization errors and analog photonic noise. Furthermore, our approach preserves the photonic inner-product computation pipeline, allowing seamless integration into existing and future photonic accelerators without hardware modification. Experimental results on six representative DNN models demonstrate that the proposed approach can improve inference accuracy across diverse network architectures and application domains.

AI.tldr: SPARC improves the inference accuracy of photonic neural network accelerators by computing a representative vector for each group of similar activations digitally at high precision and offloading only the residual inner products to the photonic hardware.
AI.motivation: Photonic accelerators are limited in inference accuracy by the low-bit quantization they require and by analog photonic noise.
AI.method: Similar activation vectors are grouped and each group gets a representative vector whose inner product is computed digitally; the residual inner products run on the photonic accelerator, which keeps its existing inner-product pipeline without hardware modification.
AI.result: Because vectors within a group are highly similar, the residuals have much smaller norms, which reduces the effects of quantization error and photonic noise; accuracy improves across six representative DNN models and diverse architectures and domains.
AI.conclusion: The approach raises photonic inference accuracy without hardware changes, so it can be integrated into existing and future photonic accelerators.

title: Large Language Models as Digital Twins: a Distribution-Aware Questionnaire-Based Evaluation
comment: This work was partially funded by the European Union within the National Programme 'Research, Innovation and Competitiveness' 2021-2027, project SINTESI (Nr. MI_0000962). F. Di Cursi's, C. Boldrini's, A. Passarella's, and M. Conti's work was also partly funded by the PNRR - M4C2 - Investimento 1.3, Partenariato Esteso PE00000013 - "FAIR"
summary: This paper investigates whether Large Language Models can answer a personality questionnaire as a specific individual would. Given a user's social-media posts, the model completes the BFI-2-60 Big Five questionnaire as that user. The predicted responses are converted into trait scores and compared with the user's actual scores. We evaluate GPT-4, Gemma, Llama 3.1, and Mistral on the MyPersonality dataset. To determine whether predictions reflect information from the user's writing, we compare them with answers produced without user text and with values derived from general population tendencies. We measure prediction error across all users and separately for individuals with low, intermediate, and high trait scores. We also test whether an LLM can express an explicit personality profile when given only the target Big Five scores, without user text, and examine how predictions change as more text is provided. The results show that user text does not consistently improve performance. Models perform better near the middle of the trait distribution, while at the lower and upper ends they often remain close to central values or perform well at one end but poorly at the other. When given an explicit profile, GPT-4 most clearly translates trait information into consistent questionnaire responses, particularly for Extraversion and Neuroticism. Increasing context does not systematically reduce error: open-source models fluctuate more, whereas GPT-4 remains comparatively stable. Overall, the evaluated models do not consistently reproduce the questionnaire behavior of specific individuals.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether LLMs (GPT-4, Gemma, Llama 3.1, Mistral) can complete the BFI-2-60 Big Five questionnaire as a specific user from that user's social-media posts, and finds they do not consistently reproduce individuals' questionnaire behaviour.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether LLMs can answer a personality questionnaire as a specific individual would, and whether predictions reflect information in the user's writing rather than general tendencies.
AI.method: Each model completes BFI-2-60 as a user on the MyPersonality dataset; predicted responses are converted to trait scores and compared with actual scores, overall and for low, intermediate and high trait levels, against answers without user text and against population tendencies; the paper also tests explicit Big Five profiles and increasing amounts of text.
AI.result: User text does not consistently improve performance; models do best near the middle of the trait distribution and often stay near central values at the extremes. With an explicit profile GPT-4 most clearly maps trait information to consistent answers, especially for Extraversion and Neuroticism; more context does not systematically reduce error, and open-source models fluctuate more than GPT-4.
AI.conclusion: The evaluated models do not consistently reproduce the questionnaire behaviour of specific individuals, so they are not reliable as individual-level digital twins in this setting.

title: AstroMemBench: A Benchmark for Memory Systems in Embodied Spacecraft Agents
comment: 31 pages, 4 figures, 19 tables. Includes Appendices A-E
summary: Long-term spacecraft autonomy requires embodied agents to use operational history under communication delays, time-critical operations, environmental uncertainty, complex physical interactions, power and computational constraints, and safety and reliability requirements. We introduce AstroMemBench and a Scenario-Challenge-Capability design method that maps these requirements to executable memory tests. The benchmark covers 16 memory subchallenges through 140 templates and 2240 instances across nine tasks in planetary surface operations, on-orbit servicing, and deep-space exploration. A deterministic environment scores actions for task completion, state changes, safety, and resource use. Ablations under nine conditions show that the benchmark is sensitive to how accurately agents recover and use historical information and to differences in memory-system design. Main experiments compare six configurations. Mem0, Chain-of-Memory, LightMem, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improve same-session mean scores over native Pi Agent, with no clear advantage of the three memory systems over RAG. After a session restart, Mem0 outperforms RAG by 12.25 points. Benefits favor instruction retention and result reuse over ongoing state tracking and energy reservation. AstroMemBench supports the design, development, and selection of memory systems for embodied spacecraft agents. AstroMemBench 1.0 and its evaluation code are publicly available: this https URL.

AI.tldr: AstroMemBench is a benchmark of 2,240 instances across nine tasks for testing memory systems in embodied spacecraft agents, and in its main experiments Mem0 outperforms RAG by 12.25 points after a session restart.
AI.motivation: Long-term spacecraft autonomy requires agents to use operational history under communication delays, time-critical operations, uncertainty, power limits and safety requirements, which existing evaluations do not cover.
AI.method: A Scenario-Challenge-Capability design method maps these requirements to executable memory tests; the benchmark has 16 memory subchallenges built from 140 templates across planetary surface operations, on-orbit servicing and deep-space exploration, and a deterministic environment scores task completion, state changes, safety and resource use.
AI.result: Ablations under nine conditions show sensitivity to how accurately agents recover historical information and to memory-system design. Across six configurations, Mem0, Chain-of-Memory, LightMem and RAG improve same-session mean scores over native Pi Agent with no clear advantage of the memory systems over RAG; after a restart Mem0 beats RAG by 12.25 points; gains favour instruction retention and result reuse over ongoing state tracking and energy reservation.
AI.conclusion: AstroMemBench supports the design, development and selection of memory systems for embodied spacecraft agents; version 1.0 and its evaluation code are publicly released.

title: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?
summary: Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. We introduce Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark for autonomous AI development with six end-to-end tasks spanning pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness, and cluster orchestration. Each task requires agents to implement core systems from a minimal starting point and evaluates them against mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware. Additionally, through extensive red-teaming covering 9 of the 10 categories in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, we expose reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the conventional Harbor framework and develop Breakwater, an extension of Harbor that blocks all attacks tested in our study. Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, suggesting it may have the skills needed to reach the singularity. The remaining agents average only 0.58. Our vision is for Singularity-Bench to track how much of AI development agents can already automate and when they may transition from assisting to taking end-to-end responsibility for building stronger successors.

AI.tldr: Singularity-Bench is an open-ended benchmark of six end-to-end AI development tasks in which the top agent, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code, matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six, while the other agents average a Singularity-Index of 0.58.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks restrict agents to narrow action spaces, simplified environments, or verification methods that are unreliable for arbitrary agent-built systems.
AI.method: Agents implement core systems from a minimal starting point for pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness and cluster orchestration, and are compared with mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware; red-teaming covering 9 of the 10 OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications exposed reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the Harbor framework, leading to Breakwater, an extension that blocks all tested attacks.
AI.result: Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, and the remaining agents average 0.58.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose the benchmark as a way to track how much AI development agents can already automate and when they may take end-to-end responsibility for building stronger successors.

title: A Dual-Branch Graph and Convolutional Network for Interpretable Movement EEG Classification
summary: Decoding upper-limb movements from scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is an important problem for brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), but many deep learning models provide limited insight into the brain regions underlying their predictions. We propose a two-branch architecture that combines an LGGNet-inspired local-global graph branch with an EEGNet-style convolutional branch for movement-versus-rest classification. The graph branch groups 61 EEG electrodes into anatomically informed regions and learns their spatial relationships, providing a direct representation of the regions emphasized by the model. We evaluate the proposed architecture using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation on the Ofner upper-limb movement dataset. The model achieves a mean F1-score of 0.74 +/- 0.06 across subjects. Beyond classification performance, we analyze the learned graph structure to identify the regions with the strongest connectivity. Across all held-out subjects, the highest connectivity is consistently observed in the Parietal Left Low region, corresponding to electrodes P1 and P3. This region is opposite to the performed right-arm movements and lies within the posterior parietal area previously associated with upper-limb movement processing. These results show that incorporating a region-based graph into the decoder can provide an anatomically interpretable representation while maintaining effective movement classification, offering a practical approach toward more transparent EEG-based BCIs.

AI.tldr: A two-branch graph and convolutional network classifies movement versus rest from EEG and exposes which brain regions it relies on, reaching a mean F1 of 0.74 +/- 0.06 under leave-one-subject-out evaluation.
AI.motivation: Deep learning decoders for upper-limb movement from scalp EEG give limited insight into the brain regions behind their predictions, which matters for BCIs.
AI.method: An LGGNet-inspired local-global graph branch groups 61 EEG electrodes into anatomically informed regions and learns their spatial relationships, and is combined with an EEGNet-style convolutional branch; the model is evaluated with leave-one-subject-out cross-validation on the Ofner upper-limb movement dataset.
AI.result: The model achieves a mean F1 of 0.74 +/- 0.06 across subjects; the learned graph shows the strongest connectivity consistently in the Parietal Left Low region (electrodes P1 and P3), which lies opposite the performed right-arm movements and in posterior parietal cortex.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating a region-based graph gives an anatomically interpretable representation while keeping effective movement classification, a practical step toward more transparent EEG-based BCIs.

title: Studies on Sign Language Retrieval in Low-Resource Dictionary Settings
summary: Most sign languages have no annotated corpus, only small dictionaries with one or a few example videos per sign. This study examines how well a pose encoder trained on a single sign language serves such languages without any target-language training. An encoder trained with metric learning on American Sign Language (ASL-Citizen) is evaluated frozen on six datasets of Turkish, Russian, Indian, Argentinian, Pakistani and Sri Lankan sign languages, with one or four clips per sign enrolled and, where signer identities are available, the query's signer excluded from the gallery. With one enrolled clip, the encoder retrieves the correct sign first in 36.4-80.7 % of queries, against 16.0-69.6 % for the best learning-free method (angle-based dynamic time warping) and a six-target mean of 39.3 % for an ASL-trained OpenHands graph network. In a crossed ablation of the encoder (embedding geometry, aggregation of body and hand embeddings, training objective, and attention between articulators), two choices matter: a per-pair InfoNCE objective outperforms supervised contrastive and cross-entropy training, and blocking attention between body, left hand and right hand inside the encoder raises accuracy by up to 5.1 points. The best configuration reaches 68.0 % one-shot accuracy (59.0 % for the reference encoder). On CISLR, an Indian Sign Language dictionary of 4,765 words with one video per word, the encoders find the correct word first for 17.3-19.0 % of queries, above the 16.8 % of the original RGB baseline. Over eight seeds with the joint encoder, spherical, Euclidean and hyperbolic embedding spaces differ by at most 1.6 points, except the hyperbolic token-attention head trained with InfoNCE, which is 1.4-2.0 points worse, so the geometry is a minor factor.

AI.tldr: A pose encoder trained on ASL-Citizen is evaluated frozen on six other sign languages and retrieves the correct sign with one enrolled clip in 36.4-80.7% of queries, with the best configuration reaching 68.0% one-shot accuracy.
AI.motivation: Most sign languages have no annotated corpus, only small dictionaries with one or a few example videos per sign, so they cannot be trained on directly.
AI.method: A metric-learning encoder trained on American Sign Language is used frozen on six datasets (Turkish, Russian, Indian, Argentinian, Pakistani and Sri Lankan sign languages) with one or four enrolled clips per sign and the query signer excluded from the gallery where identities are available; a crossed ablation varies embedding geometry, body and hand aggregation, training objective and attention between articulators.
AI.result: With one enrolled clip the encoder ranks the correct sign first in 36.4-80.7% of queries, against 16.0-69.6% for angle-based dynamic time warping and a six-target mean of 39.3% for an ASL-trained OpenHands graph network; per-pair InfoNCE outperforms supervised contrastive and cross-entropy training, and blocking attention between body, left hand and right hand raises accuracy by up to 5.1 points, giving 68.0% one-shot accuracy versus 59.0% for the reference encoder. On CISLR (4,765 Indian Sign Language words) the encoders reach 17.3-19.0% versus 16.8% for the RGB baseline, and over eight seeds the embedding spaces differ by at most 1.6 points apart from one hyperbolic variant.
AI.conclusion: Transfer from ASL to other sign languages works for dictionary retrieval; the training objective and articulator attention matter, while embedding geometry is a minor factor.

title: Folio: Recoverable Multi-Resolution Context Folding for Long-Horizon Language Agents
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables
summary: Long-horizon language agents accumulate tool results and replies until the history no longer fits the context window. Current agents shrink this history by having a model summarize it, so each compaction rereads and rewrites the history it replaces, and cache-aware triggers decide when to compact while taking the size of the result as given. We present Folio, a context manager that records, folds, and recovers history through one set of handles. While the agent runs, Folio records three linked levels: a short turn note the model writes as part of its ordinary reply (L1), an event manifest of every call written by the runtime (L2), and the captured source records (L3). Because these views already exist, the runtime folds the context programmatically, selecting coarser views for older turns. The fold prints the handles that index L2 and L3, so recovery tools that read bounded pages, compute over full text in files, and keep findings in a persistent dossier reach the evidence the agent needs with little added input. The fold trigger prices an explicit landing point that includes the retained budget. On 75 LOCA-bench tasks with DeepSeek-V4-Pro behind every system, Folio solves 66 tasks against 54 for the same runtime with model-written compaction and 49-59 for Claude Code, Codex, and SoL-Pi, in about half their working time, at 2.4 times lower cost than that runtime; each fold takes a median of 0.6 seconds.

AI.tldr: Folio is a context manager for long-horizon language agents that folds history programmatically over three linked, recoverable levels instead of having a model rewrite it, solving 66 of 75 LOCA-bench tasks against 54 for the same runtime with model-written compaction.
AI.motivation: Agents shrink long histories by having a model summarize them, so each compaction rereads and rewrites the history, and cache-aware triggers take the size of the result as given.
AI.method: While the agent runs, Folio records a short turn note written by the model as part of its reply (L1), an event manifest of every call written by the runtime (L2), and the captured source records (L3); the runtime folds the context by selecting coarser views for older turns, the fold prints handles that index L2 and L3, and recovery tools read bounded pages, compute over full text in files and keep findings in a persistent dossier; the fold trigger prices an explicit landing point that includes the retained budget.
AI.result: On 75 LOCA-bench tasks with DeepSeek-V4-Pro behind every system, Folio solves 66 tasks against 54 for the same runtime with model-written compaction and 49-59 for Claude Code, Codex and SoL-Pi, in about half their working time and at 2.4 times lower cost than that runtime; each fold takes a median of 0.6 seconds.
AI.conclusion: Because the views already exist, context can be folded cheaply and recovered on demand, so the agent keeps access to evidence with little added input.

title: InertiaMPDD: Multimodal Personalized Depression Detection via Emotional Inertia-Inspired Dynamics Modeling
summary: Multimodal depression screening estimates risk from speech, visual behavior and language. Current methods mainly predict labels, with limited evidence of departures from a non-depressed reference. Recording-level supervision also leaves fine-grained emotional dynamics unannotated. Motivated by emotional inertia, the persistence of affect, InertiaMPDD learns healthy next-state patterns using a world-model-inspired latent predictor. Using pretrained multimodal representations, it predicts from observed history and context. Reference deviation, residual decay rate and a Jacobian spectral descriptor form reference-derived emotional dynamics descriptors, evaluated as candidate proxy biomarkers for standalone screening and personalized decision correction. Across five cohorts from four datasets, fusion reaches 98.41% F1 on D-Vlog and 84.98% on LMVD. Standalone descriptors outperform fixed additive fusion on MPDD but discriminate weakly on AVEC2014. These findings distinguish reference informativeness from fusion benefit and reveal context-dependent utility.

AI.tldr: InertiaMPDD detects depression from speech, visual behaviour and language by modelling emotional inertia, reaching 98.41% F1 on D-Vlog and 84.98% on LMVD with fusion.
AI.motivation: Multimodal depression screening mostly predicts labels, with limited evidence of departure from a non-depressed reference, and recording-level supervision leaves fine-grained emotional dynamics unannotated.
AI.method: A world-model-inspired latent predictor trained to learn healthy next-state patterns from pretrained multimodal representations predicts the next state from observed history and context; reference deviation, residual decay rate and a Jacobian spectral descriptor form reference-derived emotional dynamics descriptors, evaluated as candidate proxy biomarkers for standalone screening and personalized decision correction.
AI.result: Fusion reaches 98.41% F1 on D-Vlog and 84.98% on LMVD across five cohorts from four datasets; standalone descriptors outperform fixed additive fusion on MPDD but discriminate weakly on AVEC2014.
AI.conclusion: Reference informativeness and fusion benefit are distinct, and the utility of the descriptors depends on context.

title: Natural Gradient Learning in Predictive Coding through Lateral Circuits
summary: Predictive coding (PC) trains neural networks through local energy-minimization dynamics without depending on a global error signal that backpropagation (BP) requires. Although PC is a promising alternative algorithm for efficient learning, the computational cost of inference dynamics currently outweighs the resulting learning benefits in practice. In this work, we take inspiration from optimization theory to extract more learning benefit from each inference phase. We introduce Natural PC, which augments standard PC with a lateral circuit, enabling exact and efficient natural gradient learning locally in space and time. Our lateral circuit learns the activity correlations that determine the Fisher information matrix and implicitly computes its inverse, avoiding expensive matrix inversion. Across all tested image reconstruction benchmarks, Natural PC achieves state of the art in terms of sample and compute efficiency compared to existing PC approaches. Most notably, Natural PC scales to ImageNet and matches the performance of BP trained with AdamW and various second-order optimizers at an order of magnitude lower computational cost while also using two orders of magnitude fewer training samples. Our results demonstrate that local natural gradient learning makes PC competitive with BP in both sample efficiency and computational cost in reconstruction tasks.

AI.tldr: Natural PC adds a lateral circuit to predictive coding that learns the activity correlations needed for exact local natural gradient learning, and on ImageNet it matches backpropagation with AdamW and second-order optimizers at roughly an order of magnitude lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Predictive coding trains networks with local energy-minimization dynamics instead of a global error signal, but its inference dynamics currently cost more than the learning benefit they bring.
AI.method: The lateral circuit learns the activity correlations that determine the Fisher information matrix and implicitly computes its inverse, avoiding explicit matrix inversion, so each inference phase yields more learning benefit.
AI.result: Natural PC achieves state-of-the-art sample and compute efficiency among predictive coding approaches on all tested image reconstruction benchmarks; it scales to ImageNet and matches backpropagation with AdamW and various second-order optimizers at an order of magnitude lower computational cost and with two orders of magnitude fewer training samples.
AI.conclusion: Local natural gradient learning makes predictive coding competitive with backpropagation in sample efficiency and computational cost for reconstruction tasks.

title: Acoustic Respiratory Phase Detection on Mobile Devices
summary: Breathing monitoring is important for well-being, stress regulation, and guided breathing exercises, yet existing approaches often rely on contact-based sensors or controlled environments. This paper presents a non-invasive framework for respiratory phase detection using acoustic signals recorded on commodity smartphones. The proposed hybrid CNN-Transformer architecture combines local spectral feature extraction with long-range temporal modeling to capture the cyclic structure of breathing. The model is evaluated using a Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) protocol on the Foundation Dataset and on an independent unseen test set comprising over 1300 breathing cycles and 2 hours of continuous recordings. The proposed 3-class formulation achieves 72.85% frame-level accuracy and 96.6% cycle-level exhalation detection efficiency in the LOSO evaluation, while achieving 76.94% frame-level accuracy, a Cohen's Kappa score of 0.65, and 99.2% cycle-level exhalation detection efficiency on the unseen test set. Results suggest that accurate respiratory monitoring may be achievable under data-constrained conditions, indicating that appropriate temporal modeling can learn transferable respiratory representations and generalize to previously unseen participants. An end-to-end ONNX deployment pipeline enables privacy-preserving on-device inference with latency below 20 ms, supporting real-time monitoring on mobile and wearable devices.

AI.tldr: A hybrid CNN-Transformer runs on commodity smartphone audio to detect respiratory phases, reaching 76.94% frame-level accuracy and 99.2% cycle-level exhalation detection efficiency on an unseen test set, with on-device inference below 20 ms.
AI.motivation: Breathing monitoring is useful for well-being and guided breathing, but existing approaches often need contact sensors or controlled settings.
AI.method: A non-invasive framework uses acoustic signals recorded on smartphones; a hybrid CNN-Transformer combines local spectral feature extraction with long-range temporal modelling, evaluated with leave-one-subject-out on the Foundation Dataset and on an independent unseen test set of over 1,300 breathing cycles and 2 hours of continuous recordings; an end-to-end ONNX pipeline enables on-device inference.
AI.result: The 3-class formulation achieves 72.85% frame-level accuracy and 96.6% cycle-level exhalation detection efficiency under leave-one-subject-out, and 76.94% frame-level accuracy, a Cohen's Kappa of 0.65 and 99.2% cycle-level exhalation detection efficiency on the unseen test set, with latency below 20 ms.
AI.conclusion: Accurate respiratory monitoring appears achievable with limited data, and temporal modelling can learn transferable respiratory representations that generalize to unseen participants, supporting real-time privacy-preserving monitoring on mobile and wearable devices.

title: Mind the Accuracy-Approval Gap: How Users Evaluate Sycophantic AI in Everyday Tasks
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy, a tendency to agree with users, flatter or affirm them, and preserve their face, even when independent judgment or critical feedback would be more useful. Prior work has largely evaluated sycophancy through benchmark evaluations, but less is known about how users perceive and respond to sycophantic AI in everyday tasks. We combine benchmark evaluations with two large-scale user studies. We study four personas defined through system prompts: objective (instructed to prioritize accuracy over agreement), soft-sycophantic, hard-sycophantic, and baseline (no persona-specific system prompt). Benchmarks show that even baseline exhibits substantial sycophancy, agreeing with users' stated views 71.7% of the time on NLP Survey, compared with 54.8% for objective and 89.5% for hard-sycophantic. Under conversational pressure on TruthfulQA, accuracy ranged from 81.9% for objective to 59.6% for baseline and 8.7% for hard-sycophantic. Participants were assigned to one of the four personas, and either discussed contested policy topics or collaborated with AI on email writing. Despite its higher accuracy under pressure, objective AI was rated significantly less respectful and satisfying than the other personas, and less trustworthy than baseline. Baseline and sycophantic personas did not differ significantly. Persona did not significantly affect how often participants changed their opinions, although participants who discussed with objective AI had greater odds of reduced confidence. Objective AI prompted greater writing expansion than soft-sycophantic AI, but final writing quality did not differ significantly across personas. These findings highlight a tension between accuracy and user approval: personas with substantially lower accuracy under conversational pressure received more favorable ratings for respect and satisfaction than objective AI.

AI.tldr: Across benchmarks and two user studies, LLM personas that are more accurate under pressure are rated less respectful and less satisfying by users, revealing a tension between accuracy and user approval.
AI.motivation: Sycophancy is usually measured with benchmarks, but little is known about how users perceive and respond to sycophantic AI in everyday tasks.
AI.method: Four system-prompt personas (objective, soft-sycophantic, hard-sycophantic and baseline) are evaluated on benchmarks, including NLP Survey agreement and TruthfulQA accuracy under conversational pressure; participants were assigned a persona and either discussed contested policy topics or collaborated on email writing.
AI.result: Baseline agrees with users' stated views 71.7% of the time on NLP Survey, versus 54.8% for objective and 89.5% for hard-sycophantic; under pressure on TruthfulQA accuracy is 81.9% for objective, 59.6% for baseline and 8.7% for hard-sycophantic. Objective AI is rated significantly less respectful, satisfying and trustworthy (versus baseline) than the other personas; persona did not significantly change how often participants changed opinions, though objective AI was associated with greater odds of reduced confidence; final writing quality did not differ significantly.
AI.conclusion: Higher accuracy under pressure does not translate into user approval, so designers face a tension between accuracy and user satisfaction.

title: Scale-Induced Semantic Shift in Visual Prompt Injection Against VLMs and Web Agents
comment: 14 pages, 10 figures, including supplementary material
summary: Visual content in multimedia systems may be resized, compressed, or re-rendered before it is interpreted by a vision-language model. We study a security failure mode in which these transformations change the machine-readable semantics of an image: a textual instruction is not recovered at a $512\times512$ presentation resolution under our evaluation protocol but becomes recoverable after aggressive downsampling. We formulate this behavior as Scale-Induced Semantic Shift (SISS) and develop a closed-loop black-box framework that combines dual-scale verification, selective self-hardening, shallow-layer low-rank adaptation, and pixel-space noise regularization. On a fixed 300-case benchmark, the third SISS refinement round obtains a $58.75\%$ average attack success rate across four closed-source vision-language models, compared with $41.08\%$ for the strongest generation baseline. A controlled sweep bounds the effect to aggressive compression: average success decreases to $17.68\%$, $6.85\%$, and $5.60\%$ at $128\times128$, $224\times224$, and $336\times336$, respectively. In a downstream web-agent study, the generated images increase hidden-instruction perception, but absolute behavioral compromise remains about $4\%$. Generic input transformations provide little protection in a separate defense protocol, whereas the proposed ScaleGuard consistency detector reduces non-adaptive success from $61.4\%$ to $24.3\%$ and one-round defense-aware success from $42.5\%$ to $15.0\%$, with no observed rejection among matched clean controls. The results characterize a bounded but reproducible semantic inconsistency in multimedia preprocessing and motivate scale-consistent visual-language inference.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that resizing or compressing an image can make a hidden text instruction recoverable by a vision-language model, and proposes a black-box attack framework and a ScaleGuard detector that cuts non-adaptive attack success from 61.4% to 24.3%.
AI.motivation: Visual content is often resized, compressed or re-rendered before a VLM reads it, so the machine-readable semantics of an image can change; this security failure mode is not well characterized.
AI.method: The authors formulate Scale-Induced Semantic Shift (SISS) and build a closed-loop black-box framework combining dual-scale verification, selective self-hardening, shallow-layer low-rank adaptation and pixel-space noise regularization; ScaleGuard is a consistency detector that compares behaviour across scales.
AI.result: On a fixed 300-case benchmark, the third refinement round reaches 58.75% average attack success across four closed-source VLMs versus 41.08% for the strongest generation baseline; a controlled sweep shows success falls to 17.68%, 6.85% and 5.60% at 128x128, 224x224 and 336x336; in a web-agent study absolute behavioural compromise stays near 4%; ScaleGuard reduces non-adaptive success from 61.4% to 24.3% and one-round defense-aware success from 42.5% to 15.0%, with no rejection of matched clean controls.
AI.conclusion: The effect is bounded to aggressive compression but reproducible, and it motivates scale-consistent visual-language inference in multimedia preprocessing.

title: A Modular Framework for ESG Prediction through Domain-Specific Language Modeling and Graph Learning
summary: Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) scores are increasingly used to evaluate corporate sustainability, supporting investment decisions, ensuring regulatory compliance and assessing risk. However, current ESG evaluations largely rely on proprietary methodologies that often produce inconsistent ratings. This motivates the development of data-driven prediction frameworks. In this paper, we present ESGPred, a modular framework for predicting ESG scores by combining domain-specific language modeling with graph-based learning over a network that models the relationships among the companies being evaluated. In addition to presenting the rationale behind ESGPred and detailing its ESG score prediction process, we show that ESGPred can effectively predict both overall ESG ratings and their individual Environmental, Social, and Governance components. We evaluated ESGPred using a dataset of 5,266 sustainability reports published by 2,134 publicly listed companies between 2020 and 2023. In this evaluation, we used ESG ratings provided by LSEG Data & Analytics as ground truth. Our experimental results demonstrated that integrating graph-based relational learning improves prediction performance over purely text-based baselines.

AI.tldr: ESGPred predicts overall and component ESG scores by combining domain-specific language modelling of sustainability reports with graph learning over company relationships, and the graph component improves over purely text-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Current ESG ratings rely on proprietary, inconsistent methodologies, which motivates data-driven prediction frameworks.
AI.method: ESGPred is a modular framework that combines domain-specific language modelling with graph-based learning over a network modelling relationships among the evaluated companies, and predicts overall ESG ratings and their Environmental, Social and Governance components.
AI.result: On 5,266 sustainability reports from 2,134 listed companies (2020-2023), with LSEG Data & Analytics ratings as ground truth, integrating graph-based relational learning improves prediction performance over purely text-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: Relational information among companies is useful for ESG score prediction alongside text, supporting a modular, data-driven alternative to proprietary ratings.

title: CADET: Construction of PCB Routing Instances with Executable Demonstrations
comment: 28 pages, 10 figures, 15 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Printed circuit board (PCB) routing is the stage of physical layout that finds paths connecting the placed pads of each net. Public datasets in this domain are few, and most contain only the final states of routed boards, not demonstrations of the electronic design automation (EDA) engine actions that produce them. To close this gap, we propose CADET (Constructing executAble Demonstrations for Engine-grounded Training), which jointly generates synthetic boards and demonstrations built from EDA engine actions. The resulting RouteDemos provides 100,000 synthetic boards routed with zero design rule violations (DRVs), together with their demonstrations. Their distributions over 17 statistics resemble those of 142 real reference boards. CADET trains a routing policy on these demonstrations with behavior cloning and fine-tunes it with reinforcement learning (RL). On real test boards, the policy raised the rate of complete DRV-free routing from 38.0% to 67.2% over an RL-only baseline. This rate was comparable to that of the open-source autorouter FreeRouting and exceeded those of the other baselines, including GPT-6 Astra. We release the dataset and its generation code as open source at this https URL.

AI.tldr: CADET jointly generates synthetic PCB boards and executable routing demonstrations from EDA engine actions, and its behaviour-cloned and RL-fine-tuned policy raises complete DRV-free routing on real test boards from 38.0% to 67.2% over an RL-only baseline.
AI.motivation: Public PCB routing datasets are few and mostly contain final routed states rather than the EDA engine actions that produced them.
AI.method: CADET (Constructing executAble Demonstrations for Engine-grounded Training) generates synthetic boards and demonstrations built from EDA engine actions; the resulting RouteDemos contains 100,000 synthetic boards routed with zero design rule violations and their demonstrations; a routing policy is trained with behaviour cloning and then fine-tuned with reinforcement learning.
AI.result: The synthetic boards resemble 142 real reference boards on 17 statistics; on real test boards the policy raises complete DRV-free routing from 38.0% to 67.2% over an RL-only baseline, comparable to the open-source autorouter FreeRouting and above the other baselines, including GPT-6 Astra.
AI.conclusion: The dataset and generation code are released as open source, and demonstrations from engine actions give a useful training signal for routing policies.

title: Universal Infectious Disease Forecasting with Mantis 2
summary: Public health agencies need to anticipate how outbreaks will unfold, when they will peak, and how long demand on health services will remain elevated. We previously developed a foundation model, Mantis, which was trained entirely on simulated outbreaks---enabling us to generate the diversity and scale of training data needed to support forecasting across diseases. However, our previous work left unresolved when simulation improves predictions and how it should complement observational data. Here, we varied the balance of simulated and observed training data while holding forecasting tasks fixed and varying the available surveillance history. We found that simulation-rich training was particularly valuable with limited local history, and its relative advantage diminished as more observations became available. We also found that simulation-based training reduced exceptionally large forecast errors, suggesting that mechanistic knowledge can help compensate for limited local evidence. Building on these findings, we developed Mantis 2, which combines simulated and observational training to jointly forecast up to six variables sixteen weeks ahead. Across 30 forecasting tasks, Mantis 2 achieved the best aggregate probabilistic accuracy over short, medium, and long horizons among the machine learning, statistical, and baseline models evaluated. It missed roughly 30\% fewer outbreak peaks than the strongest comparison model, with successfully anticipated peaks identified more than six weeks in advance on average. We publicly release Mantis 2, enabling public health agencies and researchers to forecast disease outcomes without developing a separate model for each disease or location.

AI.tldr: Mantis 2 is a foundation model for infectious disease forecasting that jointly predicts up to six variables sixteen weeks ahead, achieving the best aggregate probabilistic accuracy across 30 tasks and missing about 30% fewer outbreak peaks than the strongest comparison model.
AI.motivation: Public health agencies need to anticipate outbreak trajectories and peaks, and it was unclear when simulated training data helps and how it should complement observed surveillance data.
AI.method: The authors vary the balance of simulated and observed training data for the earlier Mantis model while holding forecasting tasks fixed and varying the available surveillance history; they then build Mantis 2, which combines simulated and observational training.
AI.result: Simulation-rich training is particularly valuable with limited local history, and its advantage shrinks as observations accumulate; simulation-based training reduces exceptionally large forecast errors. Across 30 forecasting tasks Mantis 2 achieves the best aggregate probabilistic accuracy over short, medium and long horizons among the machine learning, statistical and baseline models, missing roughly 30% fewer outbreak peaks than the strongest comparison and anticipating successful peaks more than six weeks ahead on average.
AI.conclusion: Mantis 2 is publicly released so agencies and researchers can forecast disease outcomes without building a separate model for each disease or location.

title: S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models
comment: none
summary: Typed System-1 (S1) decision models are increasingly deployed in LLM agents for routing, moderation, and authorization to cut inference cost, yet untrusted context can still manipulate typed outputs and alter execution branches. Unlike autoregressive System-2 (S2) models, S1 interfaces score dynamic rules and options without token-by-token decoding, mismatching attacks targeting text continuation or explicit override commands. We propose S1-Evo, a self-evolving framework tailored to S1's contract-based option competition and margin feedback. S1-Evo perturbs untrusted fields via contract-aware evidence channels to induce \emph{evidence competition} with original task evidence while preserving fact invariance. Offline on seed tasks, it optimizes candidates via feedback search guided by directional margins and re-verification, distilling verified flips into experience cards. At test time, S1-Evo retrieves relevant cards to construct perturbations for unseen tasks. Across four benchmarks and three S1 models, S1-Evo reaches 71.99\% mean ASR and 57.47\% high-confidence ASR on \texttt{jev-1.14}, and causes up to 24.00\% E2E agent violations.

AI.tldr: S1-Evo is a self-evolving attack framework against typed System-1 decision models in LLM agents, reaching 71.99% mean attack success rate on jev-1.14 and causing up to 24.00% end-to-end agent violations.
AI.motivation: Typed S1 models route, moderate and authorize inside LLM agents to save inference cost, but untrusted context can still manipulate their typed outputs, and attacks designed for autoregressive S2 models do not match how S1 models score options.
AI.method: S1-Evo perturbs untrusted fields through contract-aware evidence channels to induce evidence competition with the original task evidence while preserving fact invariance; offline, it optimizes candidates by feedback search guided by directional margins and re-verification and distils verified flips into experience cards, which are retrieved at test time to build perturbations for unseen tasks.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks and three S1 models, S1-Evo reaches 71.99% mean attack success rate and 57.47% high-confidence attack success on jev-1.14, and causes up to 24.00% end-to-end agent violations.
AI.conclusion: S1 decision interfaces are vulnerable to contract-aware evidence competition, so typed routing and authorization components in agents need defences that account for margin-based feedback.

title: The Value of Thinking: Learning When to Reason in Hybrid Decision Models
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures
summary: Existing adaptive-reasoning methods shorten the explicit reasoning a model writes, or skip it by switching modes; either way the answer is still written out token by token. \emph{Rather than deciding how much to think}, we explore a different paradigm, \emph{zero-or-$T$ thinking}: a single model either answers from the implicit thinking inside one forward pass, generating no token, or performs full autoregressive reasoning at a cost of $T$ tokens when that is worth paying. We realise it in a \emph{hybrid decision model} (HDM), where one frozen backbone serves both modes and a lightweight \emph{self-routing block} chooses between them. The block estimates the \emph{value of thinking}, the utility the slow mode is expected to add over the fast one, from what that implicit thinking has already produced, and the slow mode runs only where that value exceeds a price $\lambda$ set per request. Where no per-decision label exists, as in episodic agentic tasks, we introduce \emph{Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation} (CDPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that trains the block from episode-level returns. We evaluate HDM on MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, GPQA-Diamond, JevBench, BANKING77 and MiniWoB. Specifically, on JevBench HDM-4B scores $0.857$ against Jev's $0.851$ ($+0.7\%$) at a median $0.179$\,s against $0.652$ ($-72.5\%$). On the agentic venue MiniWoB HDM-27B cuts token cost by $80.1\%$.

AI.tldr: Hybrid decision models choose per request between answering from one forward pass and full reasoning at a cost of T tokens, and on JevBench the 4B model matches the reasoning baseline's accuracy at 72.5% lower median latency.
AI.motivation: Adaptive reasoning methods shorten or skip written reasoning, but the answer is still produced token by token; the paper instead asks whether to think at all.
AI.method: A hybrid decision model (HDM) uses one frozen backbone for both a fast implicit mode with no generated tokens and a slow autoregressive mode; a lightweight self-routing block estimates the value of thinking from what the implicit pass has produced and runs the slow mode only when that value exceeds a per-request price; where no per-decision label exists, Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation (CDPO) trains the block from episode-level returns with reinforcement learning.
AI.result: On JevBench HDM-4B scores 0.857 against 0.851 for Jev (+0.7%) at a median 0.179 s against 0.652 s (-72.5%); on MiniWoB HDM-27B cuts token cost by 80.1%; the paper also evaluates MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, GPQA-Diamond and BANKING77.
AI.conclusion: Deciding whether to think, rather than how much, can preserve accuracy while greatly reducing the cost of reasoning.

title: Compiling Known Rules into Compact Neural Agents: Weight-Space Programming on Unseen Games
comment: 32 pages, 4 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Weight-space programming (WSP) uses language models to construct neural network weights without training. We test whether known game mechanics can be compiled into compact agents that generalise to held-out levels, renderings and start states within a game family. Writers receive simulator source with held-out level data removed for 20 privately authored, unpublished ARC-AGI-3-style game families. With a fixed 57k-parameter recurrent architecture, the strongest writer reaches 56% held-out-level success with feedback, while the four main writers' Python players reach 97-100%. An exploratory free-architecture condition reaches 68-90%. Learning from support-level examples transfers much less well, but these learners lack the source information given to writers. Written networks have a program-like structure: 93% of parameters are zero, and 90% of the rest are small integers or powers of two. NumPy players under comparable computation caps reach 91%, versus the networks' 79%. Training the strongest writer's architectures from scratch yields about 1% success within our budget. Written fixed-network weights are fragile, and standard PPO removes most of their success. Prompts for noise robustness increase tolerance by about four orders of magnitude for two of three writers, but PPO makes larger updates and still removes most success. These results demonstrate rule-to-network compilation in this setting, while showing limited benefits over Python programs and no successful combination with the tested PPO fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: Weight-space programming compiles known game rules into a compact 57k-parameter recurrent network that reaches 56% held-out-level success, but Python players reach 97-100% and standard PPO removes most of the written networks' success.
AI.motivation: The authors test whether known game mechanics can be compiled by language models into compact neural agents that generalize to held-out levels, renderings and start states within a game family.
AI.method: Writers receive simulator source with held-out level data removed for 20 privately authored ARC-AGI-3-style game families and write weights for a fixed 57k-parameter recurrent architecture (with an exploratory free-architecture condition); written networks are compared with Python players, NumPy players under comparable computation caps, learners trained from support-level examples, and PPO fine-tuning.
AI.result: The strongest writer reaches 56% held-out-level success with feedback, the four main writers' Python players reach 97-100%, and the free-architecture condition reaches 68-90%; written networks are 93% zero-valued and 90% of the rest are small integers or powers of two; NumPy players reach 91% versus 79% for the networks; training the strongest writer's architecture from scratch yields about 1% success; PPO removes most success.
AI.conclusion: Rule-to-network compilation works in this setting but offers limited benefit over Python programs, and it did not combine successfully with the tested PPO fine-tuning.

title: Primer: An AI Framework for Instructor-Centered Educational Simulation Creation
summary: Educational simulations are a well-established pedagogical technique that gives learners opportunities to apply knowledge, respond to challenges, and reflect on their performance. High-quality simulations, however, are difficult to build, requiring instructor input, scenario design, character development, scaffolding, technical implementation, and repeated revision. This paper presents Primer, an open-source, LLM-agnostic AI-supported system that helps educators create adaptive educational simulations. Educators contribute their knowledge of the subject, lesson, and students, while generative AI produces responsive variations of practice for students. Primer uses a multi-agent system centered around executing educator's instructional intent through the entire learning experience. We hope that by releasing Primer as an open-source system, including its prompts and GitHub repository, we provide a foundation for development and research on educator-in-the-loop AI authoring, multi-agent educational workflows, and simulation-based pedagogy. Further, by allowing the use of various AI models, including local and open source models, we provide the opportunity for implementation under varied governance regimes. Primer points toward a model of educational AI in which instructors can create locally grounded practice opportunities based on their own materials, goals, examples, and knowledge of students.

AI.tldr: Primer is an open-source, LLM-agnostic multi-agent system that helps educators build adaptive educational simulations from their own materials and instructional intent.
AI.motivation: High-quality educational simulations are hard to build, requiring scenario design, character development, scaffolding, technical implementation and repeated revision.
AI.method: Educators contribute their subject knowledge, lesson and student knowledge, and a multi-agent system executes the educator's instructional intent through the learning experience while generative AI produces responsive practice variations; the system supports various AI models, including local and open-source ones.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative evaluation; the system, its prompts and its GitHub repository are released as open source.
AI.conclusion: Primer offers a foundation for educator-in-the-loop AI authoring and multi-agent educational workflows, allowing implementation under varied governance regimes.

title: AnalogLayoutWorld: An Open Benchmark for Agentic Analog Layout Design
summary: Coding agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in software development, yet their ability to tackle long-horizon engineering tasks governed by physical constraints remains less understood. We study this question through analog circuit layout, which demands domain knowledge, geometric reasoning, and iterative interaction with design and verification tools. We introduce \textbf{AnalogLayoutWorld}, an open-source agent benchmark with 40 expert-reviewed tasks for end-to-end layout generation from fixed transistor-level netlists. It combines an integrated design environment with independent physical and post-layout electrical verification, as well as objective layout quality metrics co-designed with analog layout experts. Across 13 model--harness configurations, 91.1\% of attempts produce GDS layouts, but only 23.0\% satisfy the benchmark's acceptance criteria. We also evaluate Novara, an internally developed agent system, which achieves the highest reported aggregate score. Our analysis links performance differences to test-time scaling under fixed budgets, suggesting that reasoning efficiency and effective use of verification feedback help sustain design quality as task complexity grows.

AI.tldr: AnalogLayoutWorld is an open benchmark of 40 expert-reviewed tasks for agentic analog circuit layout, in which 91.1% of attempts produce GDS layouts but only 23.0% satisfy the acceptance criteria.
AI.motivation: Coding agents are strong at software tasks, but their ability on long-horizon engineering tasks governed by physical constraints, such as analog layout, is less understood.
AI.method: The benchmark asks agents to generate end-to-end layouts from fixed transistor-level netlists in an integrated design environment, with independent physical and post-layout electrical verification and objective layout quality metrics co-designed with analog layout experts; the Novara agent system is also evaluated.
AI.result: Across 13 model-harness configurations, 91.1% of attempts produce GDS layouts but only 23.0% satisfy the acceptance criteria; Novara achieves the highest reported aggregate score; performance differences are linked to test-time scaling under fixed budgets.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning efficiency and effective use of verification feedback help sustain design quality as task complexity grows.

title: Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents use external skills to reuse task procedures and experience with tools. General-purpose skills describe shared execution procedures, while specific tool choices, operating practices, and output requirements vary across users. In long-horizon tasks, subgoals, available inputs, and environmental states change as execution progresses. Agents must select currently applicable skills from an expanding skill pool and prepare candidates for subsequent steps. We propose Skill Adapter, which enables personalized modification and online routing of general-purpose skills. The system distills local adjustments from user requirements and execution feedback and stores them as Adapters linked to general-purpose skills. The routing agent selects general-purpose skills and applicable Adapters based on the current subtask, execution progress, and environmental feedback, incrementally maintaining a task-level online skill library that the main LLM reads on demand. The system preloads candidates for subsequent nodes and rechecks their applicability once actual inputs are determined. Reinforcement learning optimizes the two types of decisions using modification gains and routing outcomes, respectively. We evaluate Skill Adapter on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SkillsBench. Compared with SkillRL, it improves task success rates by an average of 11.43 percentage points and reduces mean execution time on all three benchmarks. Skill Adapter retains its performance advantage when the skill pool grows to 1,000 skills.

AI.tldr: Skill Adapter personalizes general-purpose LLM agent skills with user-specific Adapters and routes them online, improving task success over SkillRL by 11.43 percentage points on average across ALFWorld, WebShop and SkillsBench.
AI.motivation: General-purpose skills are shared procedures, but tool choices, operating practices and output requirements vary across users, and agents must pick applicable skills from a growing pool as subgoals and environment states change.
AI.method: The system distils local adjustments from user requirements and execution feedback into Adapters linked to general-purpose skills; a routing agent selects skills and Adapters from the current subtask and feedback, maintains a task-level online skill library, preloads candidates for later nodes and rechecks applicability once inputs are known; reinforcement learning optimizes modification and routing decisions using modification gains and routing outcomes.
AI.result: Compared with SkillRL, task success improves by an average of 11.43 percentage points and mean execution time falls on all three benchmarks; the advantage holds when the skill pool grows to 1,000 skills.
AI.conclusion: Personalized modification and online routing of skills can help LLM agents reuse procedures across users in long-horizon tasks while keeping performance as the skill pool grows.

title: Your Vision Foundation Model Is Secretly an EEG Foundation Model
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models are pretrained on thousands of hours of recordings, yet their frozen features transfer poorly to downstream tasks, and this transfer does not consistently improve with larger models or more pretraining data. We show that a vision foundation model that has never seen EEG is a stronger frozen EEG encoder than these specialized models, once the signals are rendered as images that a vision transformer can read. Our method, SeeEEG, keeps the vision backbone frozen and learns only how EEG is displayed to it. Each channel occupies a dedicated row of patches and is drawn either as a waveform at a fixed gain or as a scalogram whose frequency range spans the patch height, so that task-relevant patterns fall within individual tokens. The montage, filtering, and contrast parameters of this display are initialized from a standard clinical montage and optimized with the task loss through the frozen backbone, which amounts to at most 1,113 trainable parameters per view. We compare SeeEEG with seven EEG foundation models on eight clinical, sleep, affective, and brain-computer interface datasets, with every encoder frozen and paired with identical readout heads. With a frozen DINOv3 ViT-B, SeeEEG outperforms every EEG foundation model in balanced accuracy on all eight datasets and reaches a mean rank of 1.3 in Cohen kappa or AUROC, compared with 2.9 for the strongest baseline, REVE. The learned displays transfer without further optimization to the video encoder V-JEPA 2.1, which outperforms every EEG foundation model on both metrics on six of the eight datasets. Replacing DINOv3 with a randomly initialized ViT-B lowers the score by 15.2 points on average, so the ability to read rendered EEG comes from visual pretraining.

AI.tldr: SeeEEG renders EEG as images read by a frozen vision transformer, and with a frozen DINOv3 ViT-B it outperforms seven EEG foundation models in balanced accuracy on all eight datasets.
AI.motivation: EEG foundation models pretrained on thousands of hours of recordings transfer poorly to downstream tasks, and transfer does not reliably improve with model size or pretraining data.
AI.method: The vision backbone stays frozen and only the display of EEG is learned: each channel occupies a row of patches drawn as a waveform at a fixed gain or as a scalogram, with montage, filtering and contrast parameters initialized from a clinical montage and optimized through the frozen backbone using at most 1,113 trainable parameters per view; all encoders are paired with identical readout heads on eight clinical, sleep, affective and BCI datasets.
AI.result: With frozen DINOv3 ViT-B, SeeEEG outperforms every EEG foundation model in balanced accuracy on all eight datasets and has a mean rank of 1.3 in Cohen kappa or AUROC, versus 2.9 for the strongest baseline REVE; the learned displays transfer to V-JEPA 2.1 and beat every EEG foundation model on six of eight datasets; a randomly initialized ViT-B lowers the score by 15.2 points on average.
AI.conclusion: The ability to read rendered EEG comes from visual pretraining, so a vision foundation model can serve as a strong frozen EEG encoder.

title: Speed-to-Power Dominates Energy Costs for AI Data Centers: Technoeconomic Analysis of Powering AI in the Continental United States
comment: 80 pages incl. SI
summary: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence is driving demand for new data centers at large scale and on short deployment timelines. To power them, firms connect to the commercial grid or contract generation directly, but interconnection and gas-turbine delays now incentivize on-site generation. We compare grid-connected and off-grid data center energy infrastructure (AC- and DC-coupled solar-plus-storage, islanded natural gas, and grid interconnection) across the continental U.S. Using an open-source technoeconomic framework built on empirically calibrated AI training loads, climate-driven cooling, stage-by-stage power conversion, and physics-based battery degradation, we model designs providing equivalent energy services. Our central contribution is a speed-adjusted cost of energy that values the compute unlocked by faster construction, making options with different deployment timelines directly comparable on one physically consistent basis. We find DC coupling reduces lifetime energy costs by 18% ($0.09/ kWh) on average versus AC counterparts by eliminating inverters and improving efficiency. Though rarely cheapest on unadjusted energy cost, DC-coupled microgrids' faster deployment makes them the lowest-cost modeled option in 85% of U.S. locations once foregone compute is valued, or 55% under accelerated natural gas timelines. For AI infrastructure, deployment speed rather than unit energy cost determines the economically preferred path to power.

AI.tldr: A technoeconomic analysis finds that DC-coupled solar-plus-storage microgrids are the lowest-cost option in 85% of US locations once speed-adjusted cost values the compute unlocked by faster deployment, so deployment speed matters more than unit energy cost.
AI.motivation: Data centers need power on short timelines, and gas-turbine and interconnection delays push firms toward on-site generation, but the comparison of options is not on a common basis.
AI.method: The authors compare grid-connected and off-grid designs (AC- and DC-coupled solar-plus-storage, islanded natural gas and grid interconnection) across the continental US, using an open-source framework with empirically calibrated AI training loads, climate-driven cooling, stage-by-stage power conversion and physics-based battery degradation; a speed-adjusted cost of energy values the compute unlocked by faster construction.
AI.result: DC coupling reduces lifetime energy costs by 18% ($0.09/kWh) on average versus AC counterparts; DC-coupled microgrids are rarely cheapest on unadjusted energy cost but are the lowest-cost modelled option in 85% of US locations once foregone compute is valued, or 55% under accelerated natural gas timelines.
AI.conclusion: For AI infrastructure, deployment speed rather than unit energy cost determines the economically preferred path to power.

title: Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation systems attach citations to attribute claims to their sources. These citations frequently misstate provenance, and standard verification cannot detect this. We measure provenance by counterfactual value substitution: a fact in the retrieved passages is replaced with a false variant and the model re-queried. We find that across five sizes of one model family and a second comparator family, 1.2% to 15.7% of citable claims derive from parametric memory rather than the retrieved context. At the most conservative substitution distance these figures are 4.6% and 8.5% on the two models we tested at it, with the rate rising with model size within a family. We further find that natural language inference verification, the standard approach, gives results indistinguishable from chance across models, even when restricted to the cited passage. We determine that the cause is structural: a model answering from memory selects a citation that agrees with its output. Comparing ten attribution methods on identical claims, the contrast between the model's distribution with and without context best separates provenance. Acting on that signal does not improve provenance honesty at these base rates. The resulting detector is hence still not accurate enough to act on: it measures what the model knew rather than what it used, and separating those remains the open problem.

AI.tldr: Counterfactual value substitution shows that 1.2% to 15.7% of citable claims in retrieval-augmented generation come from parametric memory rather than the retrieved context, and standard NLI verification cannot detect this.
AI.motivation: RAG citations often misstate provenance, and standard verification cannot detect this misattribution.
AI.method: Provenance is measured by replacing a fact in the retrieved passages with a false variant and re-querying the model; five sizes of one model family and a second comparator family are tested, ten attribution methods are compared on identical claims, and natural language inference verification is evaluated on its own.
AI.result: Across models, 1.2% to 15.7% of citable claims derive from parametric memory; at the most conservative substitution distance the rates are 4.6% and 8.5% on the two models tested at it, rising with model size within a family; NLI verification is indistinguishable from chance even when restricted to the cited passage; the contrast between the model's distributions with and without context best separates provenance, but acting on that signal does not improve provenance honesty at these base rates.
AI.conclusion: The detector is not yet accurate enough to act on, because it measures what the model knew rather than what it used, and separating those remains the open problem.

title: Cortex-FL: Agent-Mediated Collaboration for Federated Learning
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables independent data owners to train models collaboratively without centralizing raw data. However, identifying collaborators, preparing training tasks, and coordinating execution and incentives hinder its practical adoption by organizations without specialized expertise. We present Cortex-FL, an agent-native FL system that enables users to express learning objectives in natural language and delegate the collaboration required to train a model. Agents translate these objectives into shared tasks, discover collaborators, and negotiate participation agreements, connecting collaboration formation with distributed training and incentive management. The architecture separates agent coordination from local execution authority, allowing owners to delegate coordination while retaining control over their data, computation, and financial commitments. We demonstrate the complete workflow on a four-node deployment, in which a model requested in natural language proceeds through collaboration formation, contract-governed training, verified model delivery, and x402 settlement on a blockchain testnet.

AI.tldr: Cortex-FL is an agent-native federated learning system in which agents turn natural-language learning objectives into shared tasks, find collaborators, negotiate agreements and coordinate contract-governed training.
AI.motivation: Federated learning is hard for organizations without specialized expertise because identifying collaborators, preparing tasks and coordinating execution and incentives are difficult.
AI.method: Agents translate objectives into tasks, discover collaborators and negotiate participation agreements, linking collaboration formation with distributed training and incentive management; the architecture separates agent coordination from local execution authority so owners keep control of their data, computation and financial commitments.
AI.result: The complete workflow is demonstrated on a four-node deployment, from a natural-language model request through collaboration formation, contract-governed training and verified model delivery to x402 settlement on a blockchain testnet.
AI.conclusion: Owners can delegate coordination to agents while retaining control over their data, computation and payments.

title: Al-Ghasali: A Computational Framework for Simulating Islamic Jurisprudential Rulings via Finite State Automata and Large Language Models
comment: 18 pages, 1 figure
