summary: This paper presents Al Ghasali, a computational framework designed to formalize and simulate Islamic jurisprudential (Fiqh) rulings. Building upon recent set theoretic formalizations of al sabr wa al Taqsim that extract minimal operational rules as simple Horn clause logical programs, this work proves that the semantics of closed Fiqh chapters collapse completely to deterministic Finite State Automata (FSA). We establish a formal computational hierarchy, demonstrating that restricting formalization to finite propositional Horn theories guarantees decidability and constant time (O(1)) verdict extraction after offline compilation. The framework formally proves that hierarchical compositions of sub-chapter FSAs preserve this O(1) complexity, and that temporal juristic requirements, such as Tartib (order), are deterministically flattened into static ontological states, preserving the memoryless property of the automaton. To generate human-readable juristic summaries, Al Ghasali incorporates Large Language Models (LLMs) via an architecture where the deterministic FSA strictly controls the probabilistic LLM. Crucially, the paper formulates sufficient design safety conditions for this FSA LLM integration, ensuring strict adherence to the epistemological boundaries of Usul al Fiqh. To neutralize the risk of LLM hallucination, the system employs a Grammar Guided Constrained Decoding mechanism. We formally define the mapping function that dynamically constructs unambiguous right linear grammars from the FSA execution history. The paper mathematically proves that this architecture, augmented by a Bounded Neutral Lexicon and Valence Locking, guarantees the absolute absence of Decisional Hallucination, Juristic Factual Hallucination, and Semantic Inversion reducing the LLM to a pure linguistic transformer of deterministic juristic facts

AI.tldr: Al-Ghasali formalizes Islamic jurisprudential (Fiqh) rulings as deterministic finite state automata, so that verdicts are extracted in O(1) time, and uses grammar-constrained decoding to let an LLM only verbalize those facts.
AI.motivation: Computational simulation of Fiqh rulings needs a formal, decidable basis, and LLM-generated juristic summaries carry a risk of hallucination.
AI.method: Building on set-theoretic formalizations of al sabr wa al Taqsim expressed as Horn clause programs, the paper proves that closed Fiqh chapters collapse to deterministic FSAs, that hierarchical compositions preserve O(1) verdict extraction, and that temporal requirements such as Tartib are flattened into static states; the FSA controls the LLM, which is constrained by a grammar built from the FSA execution history, together with a Bounded Neutral Lexicon and Valence Locking.
AI.result: The paper claims mathematical proofs that this architecture guarantees the absence of Decisional Hallucination, Juristic Factual Hallucination and Semantic Inversion; no experimental evaluation is reported in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The LLM is reduced to a pure linguistic transformer of deterministic juristic facts, under the stated design safety conditions.

title: Ballad: Bandit-Based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery
summary: Modern automated heuristic discovery (AHD) systems increasingly rival hand-crafted heuristics by leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively mutate and refine solutions. A natural assumption is that more powerful and more expensive models consistently yield better heuristics. We challenge this empirically: across multiple NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, we find no consistent advantage for larger, costlier models. This raises a deeper question: given a pool of LLMs spanning frontier and freely hosted or open-weight models, how should one adaptively select which model to invoke at each step of the search? The challenge is non-trivial. The optimal LLM may shift over the course of a run, and because one LLM's output seeds the context for subsequent calls, each model's reward signal is non-stationary and entangled across the heuristic population, thus violating the independence assumptions of classical online decision-making settings. We address this through Ballad (Bandit-based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery), an online bandit algorithm that learns to orchestrate a pool of LLMs into an ensemble that matches or exceeds what any soloist LLM achieves alone. This orchestration is powered by an LLM selection policy that favors rare, high-scoring heuristics over stable averages, a DAG-based credit propagation mechanism through the genealogy of the heuristic population, and discounting of stale observations to remain attuned to each model's current utility. Across five NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems and a pool of four models of varying capability and cost, Ballad not only matches the best individual LLM in hindsight but, in several cases, surpasses every individual model while reducing API cost by up to 65.6% relative to always using the strongest model.

AI.tldr: Ballad is an online bandit router that chooses among a pool of LLMs at each step of automated heuristic discovery, matching the best single model in hindsight and cutting API cost by up to 65.6% versus always using the strongest model.
AI.motivation: Larger, costlier LLMs do not consistently yield better heuristics, and the best model may shift over a run, while rewards are non-stationary and entangled across the heuristic population, which violates the independence assumptions of classical bandits.
AI.method: Ballad (Bandit-based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery) combines an LLM selection policy that favours rare, high-scoring heuristics over stable averages, DAG-based credit propagation through the heuristic genealogy, and discounting of stale observations.
AI.result: Across five NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems and a pool of four models of varying capability and cost, Ballad matches the best individual LLM in hindsight and in several cases surpasses every individual model, while reducing API cost by up to 65.6% relative to always using the strongest model.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive ensemble routing can match or exceed any single LLM in automated heuristic discovery at lower cost.

title: LiveGeo: Benchmarking Geographic Agents in Continuously Evolving Worlds
summary: We introduce GeoWorld, a controllable and continuously evolving geographic environment platform for LLM agents, and LiveGeo, a benchmark for evaluating reliable decision-making in real-world geographic environments using GeoWorld. Unlike existing evaluations that largely reason and plan over fixed geographic states, GeoWorld is grounded in real-world geographic structure and allows external world states to evolve along their own temporal processes while preserving verifiable state histories. LiveGeo places geographic tasks within this evolving environment, requiring agents to actively acquire task-relevant information, verify whether the evidence supporting prior decisions remains valid, and revise their plans when necessary. Our results reveal that even frontier LLMs struggle with static tasks, with no model consistently excelling across tasks, while strong static performance does not ensure dynamic reliability. Further analysis identifies a key bottleneck: agents struggle to acquire and translate relevant evidence into valid decisions and maintain their correctness as the world evolves. By releasing LiveGeo together with its GeoWorld platform, we aim to provide the community with a flexible and extensible infrastructure for studying the next generation of agents capable of reliable action in evolving geographic worlds.

AI.tldr: LiveGeo is a benchmark for LLM agents in GeoWorld, a continuously evolving geographic environment, and finds that even frontier models struggle, with strong static performance not ensuring dynamic reliability.
AI.motivation: Existing geographic agent evaluations reason and plan over fixed geographic states, which does not test reliable decision-making as the real world changes.
AI.method: GeoWorld is a controllable platform grounded in real-world geographic structure in which external world states evolve along their own temporal processes while verifiable state histories are preserved; LiveGeo places tasks in this environment, requiring agents to acquire evidence, check whether supporting evidence remains valid and revise plans.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs struggle even on static tasks, with no model consistently excelling across tasks, and strong static performance does not ensure dynamic reliability; the key bottleneck is acquiring and translating relevant evidence into valid decisions and keeping them correct as the world evolves.
AI.conclusion: GeoWorld and LiveGeo are released as infrastructure for studying agents that act reliably in evolving geographic worlds.

title: Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000x Faster than Looped Models
summary: Looped models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for reasoning, with successes on simple reasoning puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique. However, these models can be unstable, slow to train, and use many parameters and FLOPs to solve simple puzzles. Descent on an energy not only mitigates these issues but also offers advantages: built-in early stopping, compute that adapts to problem difficulty, fast training without differentiating through a solver, and interpretable weights that learn the constraints of the puzzle. Here we demonstrate this with a learned version of Hopfield & Tank's energy from the 80s, which we term CRAM, solves 99.996% of Sudoku-Extreme and 100% of Maze-Unique test puzzles after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one GPU, at least 1,000x faster than looped models on these tasks. CRAM also matches baseline looped models at their highest accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme using at least 282x fewer inference FLOPs. Our work suggests two things. First, that energies are an extremely promising direction for training reasoning from data. Second, a caution against using trivially solvable benchmarks like Sudoku and Maze to test the scalability of looped reasoning techniques.

AI.tldr: CRAM, a learned version of the Hopfield and Tank energy, solves 99.996% of Sudoku-Extreme and 100% of Maze-Unique test puzzles at least 1,000 times faster than looped models, training in tens to hundreds of milliseconds on one GPU.
AI.motivation: Looped reasoning models are unstable, slow to train and parameter- and FLOP-hungry on simple puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique.
AI.method: Descent on a learned energy function, which gives built-in early stopping, compute that adapts to problem difficulty, training without differentiating through a solver, and interpretable weights that learn the puzzle constraints.
AI.result: CRAM solves 99.996% of Sudoku-Extreme and 100% of Maze-Unique test puzzles after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one GPU, at least 1,000 times faster than looped models on these tasks; it matches baseline looped models at their highest Sudoku-Extreme accuracy with at least 282 times fewer inference FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: Energies are a promising direction for learning reasoning from data, and trivially solvable benchmarks such as Sudoku and Maze are a weak test of the scalability of looped reasoning.

title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
comment: NeurIPS 2026. Project Website: this https URL
summary: Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent's feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.

AI.tldr: AgentSSL shows that MLE agents can write semi-supervised learning programs that beat the strongest human baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to 21.8%, but program selection is a major bottleneck.
AI.motivation: MLE agents have been studied almost only in fully supervised settings, although many real domains have scarce labels and abundant unlabeled data.
AI.method: The authors frame SSL as program search, and introduce ProgramSelectBench, a benchmark of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, to evaluate unsupervised and active program selection methods; AgentSSL is also evaluated on real-world ecology detection tasks.
AI.result: Even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents synthesize code combining and adapting established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%; performance drops by as much as 47% when programs are selected by the agent's own feedback metric.
AI.conclusion: Program selection is a critical bottleneck, and transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks brings both opportunities and challenges.

title: Care, Human Enfeeblement, and the Existential Implications of AGI
comment: 8 pages
summary: Stuart Russell has named "human enfeeblement" as a long-term societal risk of advanced AI. This paper gives a new interpretation of the enfeeblement danger by interpreting it in light of recent work by Brian Christian, Alison Gopnik, and David Spivak on care and caregiving, and connecting it with the ontological design tradition of Terry Winograd and Fernando Flores. The enfeeblement that threatens is not merely a matter of cognitive off-loading and loss of knowledge, but a form of disengagement with the world which I explain in terms of an erosion of our capacities to care. This paper articulates a conception of care as a constellation of cultivable skills that involve us in the world and with each other, while making life worth living. Designing AI to support our capacities to care addresses the worry recently raised by Demis Hassabis and others regarding the questions of "meaning and purpose" that are looming in a post-AGI world.

AI.tldr: The paper reinterprets Russell's concept of human enfeeblement as an erosion of the capacity to care, drawing on work on care and ontological design, and argues AI should be designed to support those capacities.
AI.motivation: Enfeeblement is usually framed as cognitive off-loading and loss of knowledge, but the author argues it is a deeper disengagement from the world, and the risk relates to questions of meaning and purpose in a post-AGI world.
AI.method: The paper conceptualizes care as a constellation of cultivable skills that involve people in the world and with one another, drawing on Christian, Gopnik and Spivak on care and caregiving and on the ontological design tradition of Winograd and Flores.
AI.result: The paper is conceptual and reports no empirical results.
AI.conclusion: Designing AI to support human capacities to care addresses concerns about meaning and purpose and makes life worth living.

title: EasyFoam: Skill-Oriented OpenFOAM Agents with Evidence-Driven Evolution
comment: 26 pages, 3 figures
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of automating end-to-end OpenFOAM workflows for computational fluid dynamics (CFD). However, current progress is bottlenecked by two critical limitations. First, existing evaluations are dominated by tutorial-level cases and execution-oriented metrics, masking a substantial executability--acceptability gap: successfully executed simulations often fail to satisfy prescribed numerical or quantity-of-interest (QoI) criteria. Second, domain expertise in existing systems is tightly coupled with bespoke agent architectures, limiting its reuse and continual refinement across agent implementations. To address these challenges, we introduce ExtFoamBench, a challenging benchmark for OpenFOAM agents that spans five axes of workflow variation, and separately assesses execution completion, numerical soundness, and QoI satisfaction. Complementing this, we propose EasyFoam, an agent framework that decouples CFD expertise into modular, externalized skills driven by a dual-loop mechanism. An execution loop constructs workflows from explicit task requirements and uses structured simulation evidence to diagnose failures and guide targeted repairs. Meanwhile, an evolution loop distills task experience into reusable skill updates selected through paired evaluation. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that EasyFoam achieves substantially higher task acceptance rates than baseline agents, establishing this work as a starting point for future research toward self-improving CFD agents.

AI.tldr: EasyFoam is an OpenFOAM agent framework that externalizes CFD expertise into skills and improves itself through execution and evolution loops, with a new benchmark, ExtFoamBench, that separately tests execution, numerical soundness and quantity-of-interest satisfaction.
AI.motivation: LLM agents for OpenFOAM are judged mostly on tutorial-level cases and execution metrics, which hides a gap between executable simulations and acceptable ones, and domain expertise is tightly bound to individual agent architectures.
AI.method: ExtFoamBench spans five axes of workflow variation and assesses execution completion, numerical soundness and QoI satisfaction; EasyFoam decouples CFD expertise into modular externalized skills, with an execution loop that builds workflows from task requirements and uses simulation evidence for targeted repairs, and an evolution loop that distils task experience into skill updates chosen through paired evaluation.
AI.result: EasyFoam achieves substantially higher task acceptance rates than baseline agents, according to the abstract's empirical evaluations.
AI.conclusion: The work is presented as a starting point for self-improving CFD agents.

title: Gaussian processes for real-time urban traffic estimation using a fleet of drones
summary: Real-time urban traffic monitoring is essential for modern city management, yet conventional static sensors provide only limited spatial coverage. Autonomous drone fleets can complement this infrastructure by offering flexible, high-resolution mobile sensing across different parts of the network. This paper introduces a spatio-temporal Gaussian process (GP) framework for reconstructing network-wide traffic states from partial aerial observations. The model accounts for the physical structure of the road network through a graph Matérn kernel, which embeds network topology into the spatial covariance structure, and captures temporal dependencies through an exponential temporal kernel. Within this framework, historical loop detector data provide an informative prior mean that is updated in real time using incoming drone observations, yielding network-wide point estimates together with predictive uncertainty. We validate our framework in two distinct case studies: a microscopic simulation of Barcelona and real-world drone data from Athens. The results demonstrate that our approach outperforms historical baselines in estimating and predicting Vehicle Hours Traveled (VHT), notably reducing the required fleet size. Furthermore, leveraging the model's predictive uncertainty to guide drone movements yields additional performance gains, highlighting the potential for future uncertainty-aware fleet routing algorithms.

AI.tldr: A spatio-temporal Gaussian process fuses historical loop-detector data with drone observations to estimate network-wide urban traffic, outperforming historical baselines on Vehicle Hours Traveled while reducing the required fleet size.
AI.motivation: Static traffic sensors give limited spatial coverage, and drone fleets can add flexible high-resolution sensing, but their observations must be combined into network-wide estimates with uncertainty.
AI.method: A graph Matern kernel embeds road network topology into the spatial covariance, an exponential temporal kernel captures temporal dependence, and historical loop-detector data give a prior mean that is updated in real time with incoming drone observations, yielding point estimates and predictive uncertainty.
AI.result: The approach outperforms historical baselines in estimating and predicting Vehicle Hours Traveled in a microscopic simulation of Barcelona and in real drone data from Athens, notably reducing the required fleet size; using predictive uncertainty to guide drone movement yields additional gains.
AI.conclusion: The results point to future uncertainty-aware fleet routing algorithms for urban traffic monitoring.

title: metalSPARSE: A 2:4 Semi-Structured Sparse GEMV Kernel for Apple Silicon GPUs
summary: Autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) generate text one token at a time, and each token reads every weight from memory, so on edge devices, decoding is limited by memory bandwidth. 2:4 semi-structured sparsity keeps two of every four weights, but Apple-silicon GPUs have no sparse matrix hardware, so pruning helps only if a kernel actually reads fewer bytes. We present metalSPARSE, to our knowledge the first 2:4 sparse kernels for Apple GPUs, together with a fused decoder written in Metal. The kernels stream weights in compressed form and expand them in registers. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with 2:4 sparsity on every decoder linear layer, decoding runs 3.6x faster than HuggingFace Transformers on PyTorch-MPS on an 8 GB M2 MacBook Air and 1.52x faster than MLX on a 16 GB M4. The same engine on dense weights matches MLX, so the gain comes from the compressed weights, and sparsity delivers 97% of the speedup its byte reduction allows. Prompt processing, which is compute-bound, does not speed up. To preserve quality, we combine a Wanda mask with block-wise reconstruction and low-rank adapters trained jointly with the surviving weights and quantized to 4 bits. On WikiText-2 this brings perplexity from 3.01x dense after one-shot pruning (Wanda with a closed-form refit) to 1.34x, and the whole pipeline runs on the same laptop/hardware.

AI.tldr: metalSPARSE provides 2:4 semi-structured sparse GEMV kernels and a fused Metal decoder for Apple silicon GPUs, decoding Qwen2.5-1.5B 3.6x faster than PyTorch-MPS on an 8 GB M2 and 1.52x faster than MLX on a 16 GB M4.
AI.motivation: Edge LLM decoding is limited by memory bandwidth, and 2:4 sparsity halves the weights read, but Apple GPUs have no sparse matrix hardware, so pruning helps only if the kernel reads fewer bytes.
AI.method: The kernels stream weights in compressed form and expand them in registers; the decoder is fused in Metal; quality is preserved with a Wanda mask, block-wise reconstruction and low-rank adapters trained jointly with the surviving weights and quantized to 4 bits.
AI.result: With 2:4 sparsity on every decoder linear layer, decoding runs 3.6x faster than HuggingFace Transformers on PyTorch-MPS on an 8 GB M2 MacBook Air and 1.52x faster than MLX on a 16 GB M4; the same engine on dense weights matches MLX; sparsity delivers 97% of the speedup its byte reduction allows; prompt processing does not speed up; on WikiText-2 perplexity falls from 3.01x dense to 1.34x.
AI.conclusion: Compressed weights, not the engine alone, give the decoding gain on Apple GPUs, and the pipeline runs on the same laptop hardware.

title: SideTaskBench: Measuring Unauthorized Side-Task Delivery in Coding Agents
summary: Can a coding agent fix a user's repository while also completing and delivering work the user never requested? In this paper, we introduce SideTaskBench to measure this failure where third-party technical references induce agents to produce independent side-task artifacts during an authorized repair. Repair success alone misses this behavior. Our key measurement contribution is to pair each repair with a self-contained side task and verify side tasks' delivery success rate along with the repair success rate. The benchmark contains 25 Python repairs and 190 side-task units. Its four-level similarity index defines 300 executable repair--side-task pairs. The experiments show roughly 40% valid delivery under wrapped requests for two models, alongside repair success close to their clean baselines. The completed v10 similarity run uses DeepSeek-V4-Flash on all 300 pairs, with eight repetitions per pair (2,400 runs). Conditional delivery ranges from 20.48% for L0 unrelated tasks to 57.44% for L3 mechanism-overlapping tasks, while the L1-L0 difference is 5.37 percentage points and remains sensitive to task composition. The central insight is that technical relevance may blur the authorization boundary for an agent, such that an agent can solve the requested problem and still deliver unauthorized work. SideTaskBench emphasizes this potential weakness of existing agents and provides a testbed for defenses that preserve repair capability while preventing unauthorized delivery. The code is available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: SideTaskBench measures whether coding agents deliver unrequested side-task work while completing a legitimate repair, finding roughly 40% valid delivery under wrapped requests for two models with repair success close to clean baselines.
AI.motivation: Repair success alone misses the behaviour in which third-party technical references lead agents to produce independent side-task artifacts during an authorized repair.
AI.method: The benchmark pairs 25 Python repairs with 190 self-contained side-task units, defines a four-level similarity index giving 300 executable repair-side-task pairs, and verifies side-task delivery and repair success; the completed v10 run uses DeepSeek-V4-Flash on all 300 pairs with eight repetitions per pair, 2,400 runs in total.
AI.result: Repair success stays close to clean baselines while roughly 40% of wrapped requests produce valid delivery for two models; conditional delivery ranges from 20.48% for L0 unrelated tasks to 57.44% for L3 mechanism-overlapping tasks, and the L1-L0 difference is 5.37 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Technical relevance can blur the authorization boundary, so an agent can solve the requested problem and still deliver unauthorized work; the benchmark is a testbed for defences that keep repair capability while blocking such delivery.

title: AVA: Agentic Variant Adjudication for Automated, Auditable Read-Level Review in Cancer Diagnostic Sequencing
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at ML4H (Machine Learning for Health) 2026 Findings Track
summary: Identifying a tumor's DNA mutations is central to cancer diagnosis and treatment, but distinguishing genuine mutations from sequencing artifacts is error-prone. In practice, genuine mutations are identified using fixed variant-allele-frequency (VAF) and depth thresholds which cannot separate artifacts from genuine mutations in the borderline low-VAF zone where they overlap. A laboratory specialist must manually inspect the read-level sequencing data, a slow step that has high inter-rater variability and causes diagnosis delays. We present AVA: Agentic Variant Adjudication; an agentic framework that automates this read-level inspection with subagents that reason over evidence, generate investigative code, and return a real-or-artifact adjudications with an auditable reasoning trace all without training on existing data. On both the SEQC2 DNA-seq benchmark and patient RNA-seq data, restricted to a subsample of borderline variants where thresholds fail, both closed-source (Claude Sonnet 5) and open-weight (GLM 5.3 Flash and Gemma 4 31b) agents outperform the best achievable VAF/depth thresholds. Ultimately, AVA is suited for privacy-constrained clinical deployment, since the framework can run on locally deployed open-weight models with descriptive reasoning traces to keep specialists in the loop.

AI.tldr: AVA uses subagents that reason over read-level sequencing evidence and write investigative code to adjudicate borderline low-VAF variants as real or artifact, and outperforms the best achievable VAF and depth thresholds with closed-source and open-weight models.
AI.motivation: Fixed VAF and depth thresholds cannot separate artifacts from genuine mutations in the borderline low-VAF zone, and manual read-level review is slow, variable between raters and delays diagnosis.
AI.method: An agentic framework of subagents reasons over evidence, generates investigative code and returns a real-or-artifact adjudication with an auditable reasoning trace, without training on existing data.
AI.result: On the SEQC2 DNA-seq benchmark and patient RNA-seq data, restricted to borderline variants where thresholds fail, closed-source Claude Sonnet 5 and open-weight GLM 5.3 Flash and Gemma 4 31b agents all outperform the best achievable VAF and depth thresholds.
AI.conclusion: Because it can run on locally deployed open-weight models with descriptive reasoning traces, AVA suits privacy-constrained clinical deployment and keeps specialists in the loop.

title: Deep learning-guided discovery reveals the diversity and mutational potential of environmental beta-lactamases
summary: Beta-lactamases are a major mechanism of bacterial resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics; however, their functional diversity and mutational potential in environmental microbial communities remain partially understood. This study aimed to characterize environmental beta-lactamase diversity and investigate how sequence variation influences antibiotic resistance. By integrating protein language model (PLMs) with ensemble learning, we identified more than 46,000 putative beta-lactamases across all four Ambler classes from environmental metagenomes, widely distributed across diverse habitats, with distinct habitat-associated class compositions. The candidates sharing approximately 30% sequence identity with known beta-lactamases conferred resistance to multiple beta-lactam antibiotics when expressed in Escherichia coli. Combining inverse folding model with PLMs further identified mutations that altered resistance profiles, including substitutions that increased resistance to carbapenems. Predicted high-fitness sites exhibited greater natural sequence variability overall, with higher variability in wastewater-derived than ocean-derived enzymes. These findings reveal undercharacterized beta-lactamase diversity and substantial mutational flexibility in environmental microbiomes, providing a basis for investigating their potential contribution to the diversification of antibiotic resistance.

AI.tldr: A protein language model and ensemble learning pipeline finds more than 46,000 putative beta-lactamases across all four Ambler classes in environmental metagenomes, and several candidates confer resistance to multiple beta-lactams in E. coli.
AI.motivation: Environmental beta-lactamase diversity and how sequence variation affects resistance are only partly understood.
AI.method: Protein language models are integrated with ensemble learning to identify candidates from environmental metagenomes; an inverse folding model combined with protein language models then proposes mutations that alter resistance profiles.
AI.result: More than 46,000 putative beta-lactamases were identified across habitats with distinct habitat-associated class compositions; candidates sharing about 30% sequence identity with known enzymes conferred resistance to several beta-lactams in E. coli; some substitutions increased carbapenem resistance; predicted high-fitness sites show greater natural variability, more so in wastewater-derived than ocean-derived enzymes.
AI.conclusion: Environmental microbiomes harbour undercharacterized beta-lactamase diversity and substantial mutational flexibility, which may contribute to the diversification of antibiotic resistance.

title: MechFoundry: An agentic loop that poses and performs engineering analyses and optimization of real-world objects
summary: AI agents can automate software engineering because a compiler or a test suite checks that the code does what the user or the agent intended. In engineering analysis, however, the steps that precede the computation have few easily verifiable checks: modeling a design or an object, deciding how it is used, where supports and loads are applied, and what material each part is made of. A human expert therefore makes these decisions, carries out the steps, and judges the result, one object at a time. We present MechFoundry, an agentic loop coupled with bespoke software that automates structural analyses of real-world objects without a human in the loop. From an object's lexical description, it generates a shape, poses a loading case relevant to how the object is used, assigns a material to each part, solves the nonlinear structural response, and improves the design against the loads it carries. A differentiable GPU solver built on an adaptive octree that need not conform to the surface enables the transition from shape generation to simulation and optimization. Across 50 everyday and engineering objects, the agent posed and solved a loading case in 6.5 minutes and for US$1.3 per object on average. Without a test suite to check against, we had language-model reviewers grade each session, as a first indication of where the agent's engineering judgment holds and where it fails.

AI.tldr: MechFoundry is an agentic loop that turns a lexical description of a real object into a shape, a loading case, material assignments and a nonlinear structural analysis with design optimization, solving 50 everyday and engineering objects at about US$1.3 per object.
AI.motivation: Software agents can be checked by compilers and tests, but the modelling decisions in engineering analysis, such as the object's use, supports, loads and materials, have few verifiable checks and are usually made by human experts.
AI.method: The agentic loop, coupled with bespoke software, generates a shape from the object's description, poses a loading case relevant to its use, assigns a material to each part, solves the nonlinear structural response and improves the design; a differentiable GPU solver on an adaptive octree that need not conform to the surface links shape generation to simulation and optimization.
AI.result: Across 50 everyday and engineering objects the agent posed and solved a loading case in 6.5 minutes and for US$1.3 per object on average; without a test suite, language-model reviewers graded each session as a first indication of where the agent's engineering judgment holds and where it fails.
AI.conclusion: The approach is a first step toward automating structural analysis of real objects without a human in the loop, and its judgment still needs independent checks.

title: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench
comment: 38 pages, 3 figures, 11 tables. Submitted to Empirical Software Engineering. Replication package: this https URL. Supplementary material (Online Resource 1) is included as an ancillary file
summary: Agentic workflows, in which a large language model (LLM) calls tools to read and write data, are evaluated in two ways. Benchmarks compare the final state against a gold answer. Deployed services have none; an LLM judge reads the transcript and decides. Practice treats the two as interchangeable. This paper measures whether they are. We ran 2,160 episodes in tau2-bench's airline and retail domains and recorded every database write. We scored each episode four ways: native scoring against gold state, an LLM judge, that judge given the policy document, and the boundary evaluator, a minimal rule-based check of whether a write was expected against whether one occurred in the trace. Two annotators independently labeled 120 episodes for task correctness, policy compliance, and commitment correctness. The judge repeated its verdict 98.2% of the time but agreed with native scoring on 56.2%. In 11 episodes the agent executed a forbidden write. The judge passed 10 to 11, with or without the policy or transcript. A stronger judge still passed 6. The boundary evaluator, with no model call, caught all 11; no judge significantly exceeded it on human labels. Forbidden writes occurred in 11.1% of episodes without gates. Verification, correction, and safe-termination gates did not reduce them significantly. The traces show a candidate cause: the gates' evidence digest dropped the order status and customer authentication, so valid requests were rejected. The choice of evaluator decides the conclusion; the minimal check exposes failures the judges miss. Traces, code, prompts, and labels are released.

AI.tldr: On tau2-bench, an LLM judge agrees with native gold-state scoring on only 56.2% of episodes and passes 10 to 11 of 11 forbidden-write episodes, while a minimal rule-based boundary check catches all 11.
AI.motivation: Agentic workflows are evaluated either by comparing final state to a gold answer or, in deployed services with no gold answer, by an LLM judge reading the transcript; practice treats the two as interchangeable, and the paper tests this.
AI.method: The authors ran 2,160 episodes in the airline and retail domains of tau2-bench, recorded every database write, and scored each episode four ways: native scoring, an LLM judge, the judge given the policy document, and a boundary evaluator comparing expected and occurring writes; two annotators labelled 120 episodes for task correctness, policy compliance and commitment correctness.
AI.result: The judge repeated its verdict 98.2% of the time but agreed with native scoring on 56.2%; in 11 episodes the agent executed a forbidden write, and the judge passed 10 to 11 with or without policy or transcript, with a stronger judge still passing 6; the boundary evaluator, with no model call, caught all 11, and no judge significantly exceeded it on human labels; forbidden writes occurred in 11.1% of episodes without gates, and verification, correction and safe-termination gates did not reduce them significantly.
AI.conclusion: The choice of evaluator determines the conclusion, and the minimal check exposes failures that the judges miss; traces, code, prompts and labels are released.

title: CAFIN: CUDA-accelerated Adaptive Fisher Information Matrix Network Optimization via GPU-Native Kernel Fusion
summary: Second-order optimizers improve deep neural network training using curvature information, but their practical efficiency is limited by GPU execution overhead. AdaFisher reduces Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) approximation costs through diagonal Kronecker structures and exponential moving averages, yet its PyTorch implementation requires sequential CUDA kernel launches, intermediate tensor allocations, and repeated memory accesses. We introduce CAFIN, a GPU-native CUDA kernel fusion framework that improves AdaFisher execution efficiency without changing its optimization formulation. The proposed approach progressively integrates FIM preconditioner construction, exponential moving average updates, gradient preconditioning, momentum accumulation, weight decay, and parameter updates into fused CUDA kernels. Shared-memory reuse, register-resident computation, and in-place operations further reduce memory traffic and intermediate allocations. Experiments using ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet across NVIDIA GTX 1660 Ti and RTX 3060 Laptop GPUs demonstrate up to 78.4% lower isolated FIM construction latency and 2.1-26.9% lower optimizer-step latency. The implementation also eliminates approximately 18.91 MB of intermediate GPU memory allocations per optimizer step. Numerical validation confirms consistency within the predefined FP32 tolerance, while convergence accuracy remains comparable across evaluated datasets and random seeds. These findings demonstrate that CUDA kernel fusion can substantially accelerate second-order optimization while preserving AdaFisher's underlying mathematical formulation and learning behavior.

AI.tldr: CAFIN fuses the steps of the AdaFisher second-order optimizer into GPU-native CUDA kernels, reducing isolated FIM construction latency by up to 78.4% and optimizer-step latency by 2.1-26.9% without changing the optimization formulation.
AI.motivation: AdaFisher reduces Fisher information matrix costs with diagonal Kronecker structure and moving averages, but its PyTorch implementation launches many sequential kernels, allocates intermediate tensors and repeatedly accesses memory.
AI.method: CAFIN progressively integrates FIM preconditioner construction, moving-average updates, gradient preconditioning, momentum, weight decay and parameter updates into fused CUDA kernels, using shared-memory reuse, register-resident computation and in-place operations.
AI.result: Using ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet on an NVIDIA GTX 1660 Ti and an RTX 3060 Laptop GPU, isolated FIM construction latency falls by up to 78.4% and optimizer-step latency by 2.1-26.9%; about 18.91 MB of intermediate GPU allocations per step is eliminated; numerical results match within the FP32 tolerance and convergence is comparable across datasets and seeds.
AI.conclusion: Kernel fusion can substantially speed up second-order optimization while preserving AdaFisher's mathematical formulation and learning behaviour.

title: Multi-Step Underwater Acoustic Channel Prediction via Dual-Domain Structure Preservation and Pretrained Transformer
summary: Accurate future channel state information (CSI) is essential for underwater acoustic (UWA) communication because delays associated with signal propagation, feedback, scheduling, and transceiver reconfiguration can render currently available CSI outdated. However, most existing predictors estimate only the next channel state and obtain multi-step forecasts through recursive rollout, which causes prediction errors to accumulate as the multipath structure evolves. The scarcity of sea-trial measurements further limits reliable model training. To address these challenges, we propose LLM4UACP, a dual-domain, structure-preserving framework that adapts a pretrained Transformer for few-shot multi-step UWA channel prediction. LLM4UACP extracts complementary features from the channel impulse response (CIR) and channel frequency response (CFR), aligns them through Fourier-consistent fusion, and encodes the fused representation as delay-time tokens. A pretrained Transformer with a frozen backbone is adapted through Butterfly Orthogonal Fine-tuning to jointly predict multiple future CIRs in a single forward pass, thereby avoiding the error accumulation associated with recursive prediction. Experiments on the measured SO-06 and SO-07 channels show that LLM4UACP achieves normalized mean squared error (NMSE) values of 0.0411 and 0.0399, corresponding to reductions of 88.53% and 85.15%, respectively, relative to the most recent baseline. With only 0.11M trainable parameters, LLM4UACP maintains robust performance across varying prediction horizons and observation-window lengths, limited-data settings, and cross-dataset transfer scenarios.

AI.tldr: LLM4UACP adapts a pretrained Transformer with a frozen backbone to predict multiple future underwater acoustic channel impulse responses in one forward pass, using dual-domain (CIR and CFR) features. It reaches NMSE of 0.0411 and 0.0399 on measured SO-06 and SO-07 channels.
AI.motivation: Recursive multi-step channel prediction accumulates errors as the multipath structure evolves, and sea-trial measurements are scarce, which limits reliable model training.
AI.method: Complementary CIR and CFR features are fused with Fourier-consistent fusion and encoded as delay-time tokens. A frozen pretrained Transformer is adapted with Butterfly Orthogonal Fine-tuning to jointly predict several future CIRs in a single pass, avoiding recursive rollout.
AI.result: On the measured SO-06 and SO-07 channels the NMSE is 0.0411 and 0.0399, a reduction of 88.53% and 85.15% relative to the most recent baseline. The model has 0.11M trainable parameters and stays robust across prediction horizons, observation windows, limited-data settings and cross-dataset transfer.
AI.conclusion: Adapting a pretrained Transformer with few trainable parameters enables accurate few-shot multi-step underwater acoustic channel prediction without error accumulation from recursion.

title: KernelMosaic: An Open Dataset and Agentic Framework for CUDA Kernel Generation
summary: Training large language models to generate efficient CUDA kernels requires supervision spanning diverse computational requirements and iterative code optimization. Constructing this supervision is challenging because of heterogeneous specifications, and useful implementations emerge through iterative complicated testing and refinement. We introduce KernelMosaic, an open dataset pairing diverse CUDA tasks with verified solutions and trajectories. Human-guided review and diversity-aware selection curate tasks expressed as natural-language descriptions, reference programs, mathematical specifications, and their intersections. To build the solutions and trajectories, our agentic framework guides a strong LLM through implementation, correctness repair, and performance optimization with reusable CUDA guidance and execution feedback. Supervised fine-tuning of a small open-source model on KernelMosaic raises correctness from 4%, 0%, and 0% to 88%, 82%, and 16% on KernelBench L1, L2, and L3, respectively, while increasing the fraction of tasks with kernels faster than PyTorch eager at every level. Further training experiments show that supervision from the curated trajectories substantially outperforms direct responses and promotes sustained testing and revision. These results demonstrate that KernelMosaic enables a general-purpose model to achieve substantial gains in CUDA kernel generation.

AI.tldr: KernelMosaic is an open dataset of CUDA tasks paired with verified solutions and trajectories, together with an agentic framework that generates them. Supervised fine-tuning of a small open-source model on it raises KernelBench correctness substantially.
AI.motivation: Training LLMs to generate efficient CUDA kernels needs supervision that covers diverse computational requirements and iterative optimization, but such supervision is hard to construct from heterogeneous specifications and iterative testing.
AI.method: Human-guided review and diversity-aware selection curate tasks given as natural-language descriptions, reference programs, mathematical specifications, and their intersections. A agentic framework guides a strong LLM through implementation, correctness repair and performance optimization using reusable CUDA guidance and execution feedback.
AI.result: Fine-tuning a small open-source model on KernelMosaic raises correctness on KernelBench L1, L2 and L3 from 4%, 0% and 0% to 88%, 82% and 16%. The fraction of tasks with kernels faster than PyTorch eager also increases at every level, and curated trajectories outperform direct responses.
AI.conclusion: The dataset and framework let a general-purpose model achieve substantial gains in CUDA kernel generation, and the trajectories promote sustained testing and revision.

title: Evaluating AI Musical Creativity: Towards a Quantitative Multi-Dimensional Framework Based on Value, Novelty, and Surprise
summary: Despite the increasing sophistication of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI), research on the evaluation of AI-generated musical creativity remains limited. To address this gap, this paper proposes a quantitative framework for the formalization and evaluation of AI musical creativity. Building on Margaret Boden's theory, which conceptualizes creativity in terms of value, novelty, and surprise, the framework adapts and operationalizes these three dimensions for the musical domain. On the hypothesis that certain aspects of musical creativity can be assessed with a degree of objectivity, a domain-specific set of quantitative metrics for evaluating the creativity of AI-generated music is introduced. Rather than reducing musical creativity to a single unifying measure, this article proposes an ensemble of complementary metrics that capture its different dimensions, recognizing the complexity of musical artifacts and the difficulty of defining meaningful multi-objective compositional criteria. The framework has two implications. First, it gives researchers and developers a principled methodology and quantitative tools for empirically evaluating creative outputs, enabling more informed model development and reducing unnecessary computational costs. Second, it lays the groundwork for future generative models to optimize directly for creativity by adopting these metrics as learning objectives.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantitative multi-dimensional framework for evaluating the creativity of AI-generated music, built on Boden's value, novelty and surprise dimensions. It uses an ensemble of complementary metrics rather than a single score.
AI.motivation: Research on evaluating AI musical creativity is limited, and existing treatments do not provide a principled, quantitative way to assess creativity in musical artifacts.
AI.method: Boden's theory of creativity is adapted and operationalized for music along value, novelty and surprise. A domain-specific set of quantitative metrics is introduced, based on the hypothesis that some aspects of musical creativity can be assessed objectively.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experimental results; the contribution is the framework and its set of metrics.
AI.conclusion: The framework gives researchers a principled methodology and tools for empirical evaluation, and it lays groundwork for generative models to use these metrics as learning objectives.

title: Multiple-Choice Secretary Problem with Predictions
summary: We study the multiple-choice secretary problem, in which candidates arrive in uniformly random order and the goal is to select at most $k$ candidates to maximize their total value. We consider a setting where predictions of individual candidate values are available before any candidate arrives. Fujii and Yoshida's Learned Kleinberg algorithm achieves competitive loss $O(\min\{\log k/\sqrt{k},\eps\})$, where $k$ is the selection capacity and $\eps$ is the maximum multiplicative prediction error. We remove the logarithmic factor through a sharper analysis of the same switching algorithm with a retuned threshold. The resulting competitive ratio is at least $\max\{0,1-\min\{32/\sqrt{k},4\eps\}\}$. In particular, exact predictions ($\eps=0$) achieve the offline optimum on every arrival order.

AI.tldr: The paper removes a logarithmic factor from the competitive loss of the Learned Kleinberg algorithm for the multiple-choice secretary problem with predictions, using a sharper analysis and a retuned threshold. Exact predictions achieve the offline optimum on every arrival order.
AI.motivation: The previous Learned Kleinberg algorithm of Fujii and Yoshida has competitive loss O(min{log k / sqrt(k), eps}), where k is the selection capacity and eps the maximum multiplicative prediction error, and the logarithmic factor was not removed.
AI.method: The same switching algorithm is analyzed more sharply, with its threshold retuned, to remove the logarithmic factor. Predictions of individual candidate values are assumed available before any candidate arrives.
AI.result: The competitive ratio is at least max{0, 1 - min{32/sqrt(k), 4 eps}}. With exact predictions (eps = 0) the algorithm achieves the offline optimum on every arrival order.
AI.conclusion: A sharper analysis of the existing switching algorithm gives a tighter guarantee for learning-augmented multiple-choice secretary selection.

title: Outcome Over Learning? Evidence from Student Use of AI Code Assistants for Unit Test Writing
comment: 8 pages
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) code assistants are rapidly being adopted in programming education, yet little is known about how students naturally use these tools when given unrestricted access. In a user study investigating AI-assisted unit test writing, we observed that a majority of students adopted a one-shot interaction strategy, asking the AI to generate a complete unit test directly from the initial requirements. While this approach is capable of efficiently producing a solution, it shifts students' focus from learning how to write effective unit tests to simply completing the task. Moreover, because students rarely engaged in critically evaluating, refining, or iterating on AI-generated output, they may be missing opportunities to develop the critical thinking skills that are essential for effective and responsible use of AI. In an effort to shift student focus from outcome to learning we also discuss how training, accountability and improved learning task design can better support a more learning-centric responsible use of AI.

AI.tldr: In a user study of unrestricted AI code assistant use for unit test writing, most students used a one-shot strategy, asking the AI to generate a complete test from the requirements. The authors argue this shifts focus from learning to completing the task.
AI.motivation: Little is known about how students naturally use AI code assistants in programming education when they have unrestricted access.
AI.method: A user study observed students writing unit tests with an AI code assistant and characterized their interaction strategies. The paper also discusses training, accountability and learning-task design.
AI.result: A majority of students adopted a one-shot interaction strategy. Students rarely critically evaluated, refined or iterated on the AI-generated output.
AI.conclusion: Unrestricted AI use can trade learning for outcomes, so training, accountability and improved task design are needed to support learning-centric responsible use.

title: Where Should the Code Go? Locating Foundation-Model Errors in Bitemporal Inventory Simulation
comment: 22 pages. Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Foundation Models for Temporal Systems (FMTS). Code and data: this https URL
summary: Operational reports carry two clocks: when an event happened and when its report arrived; later reports can revise earlier ones. A foundation-model component that maintains the state supported by the reports visible at a cutoff, then rolls a supplied scenario forward, can be helped by exact code before it, after it or inside the call, or asked to reason harder. We ask which remedy removes which error, for which models, on an exactly solvable lost-sales inventory environment: 36,672 independently rescored requests over twelve configurations of closed and open-weight models, with a forced-answer-call interface as a control and protocols frozen before the calls. Weak models fail in separable ways. Canonical input removes report-selection error, exact continuation removes rollout error, neither repairs the other, and which error dominates differs by model; strong models are at ceiling on raw reports. Asking for more reasoning is no substitute and can depend on the interface: under a forced answer call high effort collapses GPT-5.4 mini and DeepSeek V4 Pro, which gain or hold under automatic choice; on its provider the forced call disables reasoning for DeepSeek V4 Flash; and at high effort gpt-oss exhausts its output budget. The contribution is a controlled component diagnostic, released with every request, and evidence that for some model and provider pairs the tool-calling interface confounds reasoning evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper diagnoses which remedy removes which error when a foundation model maintains bitemporal inventory state and rolls scenarios forward. Exact code placed before, after or inside the model call fixes different error types, and more reasoning does not uniformly help.
AI.motivation: Operational reports carry an event time and an arrival time, and later reports revise earlier ones, so a foundation-model state tracker can fail in several ways. It is unclear which remedy, exact code or more reasoning, targets which error.
AI.method: On an exactly solvable lost-sales inventory environment, 36,672 independently rescored requests were run over twelve configurations of closed and open-weight models. A forced-answer-call interface served as a control, and protocols were frozen before the calls.
AI.result: Weak models fail in separable ways: canonical input removes report-selection error and exact continuation removes rollout error, and neither repairs the other. Strong models are at ceiling on raw reports. Under a forced answer call, high effort collapses GPT-5.4 mini and DeepSeek V4 Pro, and gpt-oss exhausts its output budget at high effort.
AI.conclusion: The work contributes a controlled component diagnostic and shows that the tool-calling interface can confound reasoning evaluation for some model and provider pairs.

title: Risk-Aware Joint Inference and Resource Control for Physical AI in 6G Networks
comment: Submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: Wireless edge inference enables Physical-AI devices to execute edge-inferred actions using transmitted sensory inputs. Since the risk of incorrect actions vary across observations and tasks, the associated uplink transmission of sensory inputs requires different levels of wireless reliability. For instance, applying a fixed signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) requirement can overprovision low-risk tasks while underprovisioning high-risk ones. Therefore, we propose risk-aware control for edge inference (RACE), which maps predicted action-failure probability and task criticality to adaptive SINR targets and combines them with deadline-derived SINR requirements. A slow-timescale large language model (LLM) proposes task requirements for deterministic validation, while a fast hybrid actor selects inference configurations and transmit power levels, complemented by analytical receive beamforming and finite power restoration. Simulations show $11\%$ improvement in the average accuracy-latency-energy objective over fixed-high-SINR control, with near-zero constraint outage.

AI.tldr: RACE is a risk-aware control scheme for wireless edge inference in 6G Physical-AI systems. It maps predicted action-failure probability and task criticality to adaptive SINR targets, and it reports gains over fixed high-SINR control.
AI.motivation: A fixed SINR requirement overprovisions low-risk tasks and underprovisions high-risk ones, because the risk of incorrect actions varies across observations and tasks.
AI.method: Predicted action-failure probability and task criticality map to adaptive SINR targets, which are combined with deadline-derived SINR requirements. A slow-timescale LLM proposes task requirements that are deterministically validated, and a fast hybrid actor selects inference configurations and transmit power, with analytical receive beamforming and finite power restoration.
AI.result: Simulations show an 11% improvement in the average accuracy-latency-energy objective over fixed-high-SINR control, with near-zero constraint outage.
AI.conclusion: Risk-aware reliability allocation with LLM-proposed, validated requirements can improve the joint objective of edge inference in wireless Physical-AI systems.

title: The Rebundling of Freelance Work in the AI Age
summary: This paper examines how freelance work is changing in the AI era. We compare the activities people undertake in ChatGPT with the work clients request on Upwork, an online freelance platform, and examine how clients combine tasks into projects. We find that activities more prevalent in ChatGPT tend to lose marketplace share on Upwork, while those less prevalent tend to gain share. Within AI-related work, demand is becoming more diverse, and job postings combine tasks that were rarely requested together before the generative AI era. AI-related postings also have substantially larger project budgets and involve more hours of work, while differences in hourly rates are small. Together, these findings suggest that AI is reshaping not only which tasks clients outsource, but also how they combine tasks into larger, higher-value projects.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that generative AI is changing freelance work by shifting which tasks clients outsource and how they bundle them into projects. Activities more common in ChatGPT lose share on Upwork, and AI-related projects are larger.
AI.motivation: The authors examine how freelance work changes in the AI era by comparing activities people carry out in ChatGPT with the work clients request on Upwork.
AI.method: The study compares ChatGPT activity distributions with Upwork job requests and examines how clients combine tasks into projects, including demand diversity and co-requested task combinations.
AI.result: Activities more prevalent in ChatGPT tend to lose marketplace share on Upwork, and less prevalent ones gain share. AI-related postings have substantially larger budgets and more hours, while hourly rates differ little. Demand within AI-related work is more diverse, and some task combinations were rarely requested before generative AI.
AI.conclusion: AI reshapes not only which tasks clients outsource but also how they combine them into larger, higher-value projects.

title: From Nodes to Pixels: Topological and Structural Two-View Graph Imaging
comment: 22 pages
summary: Graph learning still lacks a broadly reusable input interface comparable to patches in vision or tokens in language. Unlike images or text, graphs are irregular, vary in size and density, and are invariant under many equivalent node labelings, making it difficult to standardize inputs across tasks and architectures. We introduce G2Image, a fixed-budget graph imaging framework that converts each graph into two complementary image-like views. TopoGrid provides a stable topological view by encoding an intrinsic bifiltration as a compact multipersistence surface grid, while GraphGrid provides a higher-bandwidth structural view by aggregating edge densities between groups defined by intrinsic node scores. Both views are permutation-invariant and come with resolution-controlled stability guarantees. Because the resulting representations are fixed-size tensors, they can be processed by lightweight 2D encoders and aligned through a supervised cross-view contrastive objective. Across graph classification and molecular prediction benchmarks, G2Image achieves strong average performance among the compared methods, improves over single-view and standard fusion variants, and extends to attribute-rich molecular graphs without changing the overall architecture. These results suggest that fixed-budget graph images offer a practical and reusable interface for graph representation learning.

AI.tldr: G2Image converts each graph into two fixed-size, image-like views, a topological view and a structural view, so that lightweight 2D encoders can process graphs. It reports strong average performance on graph classification and molecular prediction benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Graph learning lacks a reusable input interface comparable to patches in vision or tokens in language, because graphs are irregular, vary in size and density, and are invariant to node relabeling.
AI.method: TopoGrid encodes an intrinsic bifiltration as a compact multipersistence surface grid, and GraphGrid aggregates edge densities between groups defined by intrinsic node scores. Both views are permutation-invariant with resolution-controlled stability guarantees, and they are aligned by a supervised cross-view contrastive objective.
AI.result: Across graph classification and molecular prediction benchmarks, G2Image achieves strong average performance among compared methods. It improves over single-view and standard fusion variants and extends to attribute-rich molecular graphs without changing the architecture.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-budget graph images offer a practical and reusable interface for graph representation learning.

title: Graph Label Alignment: A Diagnostic Atlas for Graph Classification
comment: 40 pages
summary: Graph classification benchmarks vary widely in difficulty: some are solved by simple pooled baselines, while others remain challenging for GNNs and graph transformers. We take a data-centric view and ask whether benchmark success is driven by genuine structure--feature reasoning or by label signal already accessible from restricted marginal views. We introduce graph label alignment, a lightweight diagnostic that measures label accessibility through two supervised probes computed without training a graph encoder: structural label alignment (SLA), based on permutation-invariant topological and spectral summaries, and feature label alignment (FLA), based on pooled node features with edges removed. Across real graph classification benchmarks and multiple pooled backbones, the resulting SLA--FLA plane strongly organizes test accuracy, with low-alignment datasets forming a consistent regime where standard pooled pipelines struggle. To probe what lies beyond marginal accessibility, we introduce controlled interaction-dominated stress tests, including heterophilic ego-graphs and synthetic Twins tasks whose structural and feature marginals are matched across classes but whose role--feature couplings differ. These results show that high alignment explains much of easy benchmark performance, while low alignment reveals regimes where success requires preserving structure--feature correspondence beyond standard pooled representations.

AI.tldr: Graph label alignment is a lightweight diagnostic that measures how accessible the label signal is in a graph classification benchmark, using two supervised probes. The SLA-FLA plane organizes test accuracy and identifies regimes where standard pooled pipelines struggle.
AI.motivation: Graph classification benchmarks differ widely in difficulty, and it is unclear whether success reflects genuine structure-feature reasoning or label signal already accessible from restricted marginal views.
AI.method: Structural label alignment (SLA) uses permutation-invariant topological and spectral summaries, and feature label alignment (FLA) uses pooled node features with edges removed. Both are computed without training a graph encoder. Controlled stress tests include heterophilic ego-graphs and synthetic Twins tasks whose marginals are matched across classes.
AI.result: Across real benchmarks and multiple pooled backbones, the SLA-FLA plane strongly organizes test accuracy, and low-alignment datasets form a consistent regime where pooled pipelines struggle. High alignment explains much of the easy benchmark performance.
AI.conclusion: Low-alignment regimes reveal settings where success requires preserving structure-feature correspondence beyond standard pooled representations.

title: Mach2: Scientific Discovery Platform with Deterministic Execution Constraints
summary: Language-model agents can formulate workflows and invoke specialized tools, yet compliance with natural-language operating rules is not guaranteed by prompting alone. Mach2 addresses this limitation by coupling Eigen orchestration to deterministic, lint-like checks of tool requests, source changes, acceptance tests, and artifact contracts. Domain requirements are represented as executable predicates: mandatory failures prevent advancement of the checked operation, while diagnostic findings are retained for correction or review. User-specified test-driven development (TDD), CodeGrapher's abstract-syntax-tree analysis, and history-guided evolutionary search provide complementary verification and optimization mechanisms. Mach2 also generates task-specific agent packages for execution through independently selected endpoints. The originating harness validates returned artifacts against declared interfaces and evidence requirements without assuming continuous supervision of the remote run. Model-internal-knowledge (MIK) dependencies are recorded separately from source-grounded and test-supported findings. This paper formalizes the rule-gated execution model and the agent-package lifecycle, and proposes measurable criteria for evaluating rule compliance, engineering validity, and cross-endpoint task continuity.

AI.tldr: Mach2 is a scientific discovery platform that couples agent orchestration with deterministic, lint-like checks, so that mandatory rule failures block progress. The paper formalizes the rule-gated execution model and the agent-package lifecycle, and it proposes criteria for evaluating them.
AI.motivation: Language-model agents do not reliably comply with natural-language operating rules when relying on prompting alone.
AI.method: Domain requirements are encoded as executable predicates. Checks cover tool requests, source changes, acceptance tests and artifact contracts, and mandatory failures prevent advancement while diagnostic findings are retained. TDD, AST analysis via CodeGrapher and history-guided evolutionary search supply complementary verification. Task-specific agent packages run on independently selected endpoints, and their returned artifacts are validated against declared interfaces.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experimental results; it proposes measurable criteria for rule compliance, engineering validity and cross-endpoint task continuity.
AI.conclusion: Rule-gated execution with recorded model-internal-knowledge dependencies is proposed as a basis for verifiable agent-driven scientific workflows.

title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. In this paper, we present OverServe, a multi-agent framework for constructing such attacks against SaaS agents. OverServe co-designs Model Context Protocol (MCP) status tools and completion-confirmation prompts for the attacker. Each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, yet the agent may repeatedly check an unfinished condition to satisfy the prompt. This consumes the SaaS provider's resources even after the original business task is completed. OverServe constructs service-specific tool--prompt pairs and uses separate tool and prompt reviews to guide candidate pair selection. Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. We evaluate Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks. All OverServe runs pass the original task checks. OverServe can reach a maximal amplification of API requests by $93.88\times$ while preserving the original task goal and collateral checks.

AI.tldr: OverServe is a multi-agent framework that builds resource amplification attacks on SaaS agents by pairing MCP status tools with completion-confirmation prompts. The attack makes the agent repeatedly check an unfinished condition, which consumes provider resources after the task is done.
AI.motivation: In subscription SaaS deployments, model and tool calls cost the provider without extra customer payment, and an agent that decides when to stop can be exploited to extend execution.
AI.method: OverServe co-designs MCP status tools and completion-confirmation prompts for the attacker. It builds service-specific tool-prompt pairs and uses separate tool and prompt reviews to select candidate pairs. The tool outputs are accurate and terminate normally.
AI.result: Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek and Sonnet were evaluated on selected tasks from nine benchmarks, all runs pass the original task checks, and API request amplification reaches up to 93.88 times.
AI.conclusion: Agent completion decisions are an attack surface for resource exhaustion in SaaS, and existing MCP scanners do not detect these tool-prompt pairs.

title: When Safety Becomes an Attack Surface: Manipulating Abstention in Tool-Using AI Agents
summary: An AI agent's decision not to act can itself become an attack surface. We study warning-induced over-abstention, an availability attack in which adversaries place fabricated risk warnings in low-trust content to prevent legitimate task completion. Our central premise is that safe abstention requires evaluating both the claimed risk and the authority of the evidence supporting it. We develop controlled counterfactual task variants that vary risk content, source provenance, and warning wording, and evaluate a Verify-Before-Abstain protocol that corroborates warnings against authoritative records or the underlying content. Across three model families and 51 injectable AgentAbstain task pairs, caution-first prompting amplifies the attack. For Gemini, induced over-abstention rises from $9.8\%$ to $86.3\%$, despite unchanged clean-task completion. Matched wording comparisons further reveal sensitivity to warning language, with substantial variation across models and environments. Provenance-aware verification improves legitimate completion, while forgery and sensitive-content controls expose its dependence on authoritative evidence and its limitations in preserving confidentiality. These results motivate evaluating agent safety through the justification for restraint, alongside the safety of actions taken.

AI.tldr: The paper studies warning-induced over-abstention, an availability attack in which fabricated risk warnings in low-trust content cause tool-using agents to refuse legitimate tasks. It proposes Verify-Before-Abstain, which corroborates warnings against authoritative records.
AI.motivation: An agent's decision not to act can itself be attacked, and safe abstention requires evaluating both the claimed risk and the authority of the evidence supporting it.
AI.method: Controlled counterfactual task variants vary risk content, source provenance and warning wording. A Verify-Before-Abstain protocol corroborates warnings against authoritative records or the underlying content. The evaluation covers three model families and 51 injectable AgentAbstain task pairs.
AI.result: Caution-first prompting amplifies the attack. For Gemini, induced over-abstention rises from 9.8% to 86.3% with unchanged clean-task completion. Provenance-aware verification improves legitimate completion, but forgery and sensitive-content controls show its dependence on authoritative evidence and limits on confidentiality.
AI.conclusion: Agent safety should be evaluated through the justification for restraint as well as the safety of actions taken.

title: MLIRBench - A Benchmark and Dataset for Compiler and Hardware-Aware Reasoning
comment: Accepted at the 2027 IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Code Generation and Optimization (CGO 2027)
summary: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly popular in software engineering and have performed well on different programming tasks. However, it is still difficult to know whether these models truly understand program behavior or whether they mainly rely on patterns learned from their training data. This distinction is particularly important for intermediate representations (IRs), where operations, dataflow, and execution semantics are explicitly represented. In this paper, we introduce MLIRBench, a benchmark for evaluating how LLMs reason about MLIR programs. MLIRBench uses a multi-agent pipeline to generate program mutations, validate their behavior through execution, and construct reasoning tasks from torch and linalg program pairs. The dataset contains 1,768 validated pairs, including 888 linalg pairs and 880 torch pairs, labeled as EQUIV, DIVERGE, or ERROR. We evaluated nine models, including five open-weight and four proprietary models. Gemini 3.1 Pro achieved the highest hard-label accuracy of 92.65% across all 1,768 pairs, counting unsuccessful predictions as incorrect. Across its 1,768 scored predictions, it achieved an aggregate score of 74.18 and a judge-assigned result-behavior score of 5.04/10. These results show that strong semantic classification does not necessarily imply accurate prediction of detailed execution behavior, highlighting a gap in current LLM reasoning over compiler IRs. By exposing this gap through execution-validated program pairs, MLIRBench provides a reproducible foundation for studying semantic reasoning over compiler IRs and related tasks such as program repair and semantic classification.

AI.tldr: MLIRBench is a benchmark and dataset of 1,768 execution-validated MLIR program pairs for testing whether LLMs reason about compiler IR behavior. The best model classifies pairs well but predicts detailed execution behavior poorly.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether LLMs truly understand program behavior or rely on training patterns, which matters especially for intermediate representations where operations, dataflow and execution semantics are explicit.
AI.method: A multi-agent pipeline generates program mutations, validates their behavior through execution, and builds reasoning tasks from torch and linalg program pairs. Pairs are labeled EQUIV, DIVERGE or ERROR, and nine models were evaluated, five open-weight and four proprietary.
AI.result: Gemini 3.1 Pro achieves the highest hard-label accuracy, 92.65% across all 1,768 pairs, with unsuccessful predictions counted as incorrect. Over its 1,768 scored predictions it gets an aggregate score of 74.18 and a judge-assigned result-behavior score of 5.04/10.
AI.conclusion: Strong semantic classification does not imply accurate prediction of detailed execution behavior, which exposes a gap in LLM reasoning over compiler IRs.

title: Understanding the Effects of Multi-Agent Deliberation for Human-AI Decision-Making
summary: Multi-agent deliberation (MAD), where multiple LLMs engage in structured discussion, improves AI performance on many benchmarks, but whether it helps humans make better decisions remains untested. We conduct two user studies on LLM-response-verification and fact-checking. We first compare MAD against common AI decision-support methods that isolate its two defining dimensions --- multiple AIs and multi-round interaction. We find MAD outperformed single-round AI assistance on both tasks; multi-round interaction was the main driver of this benefit, while a second AI added value when the single AI had room to improve.
