Then, we study two design choices in MAD --- AI persona and human engagement level --- finding a devil's advocate persona to lower accuracy and user experience, while humans' active participation in MAD improved accuracy in one task at the cost of frustration. We conclude by discussing implications for when, why, and how multi-agent deliberation can support human decision-making.

AI.tldr: Two user studies test multi-agent deliberation (MAD), in which multiple LLMs discuss in structured rounds, for human decision-making on LLM response verification and fact-checking. Multi-round interaction drives most of the benefit, and a devil's advocate persona lowers accuracy and user experience.
AI.motivation: MAD improves AI performance on benchmarks, but whether it helps humans make better decisions had not been tested.
AI.method: MAD is compared with AI decision-support methods that isolate its two dimensions, multiple AIs and multi-round interaction. Two design choices are then studied: AI persona and the level of human engagement in the deliberation.
AI.result: MAD outperforms single-round AI assistance on both tasks, and multi-round interaction is the main driver. A second AI adds value when the single AI has room to improve. A devil's advocate persona lowers accuracy and user experience, and active human participation improves accuracy in one task at the cost of frustration.
AI.conclusion: The findings bear on when, why and how multi-agent deliberation can support human decision-making.

title: Rethinking "RL Generalizes, SFT Memorizes": The Role of SFT Data
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 39 pages, 12 figures
summary: Large language models trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) with verifiable rewards exhibit strong reasoning ability and broad generalization, whereas models trained with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) are often viewed as more prone to memorization and limited transfer. This paper rethinks this distinction through the lens of SFT training data on widely used Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 series models. First, we study the role of data source and show that it is critical: a carefully mixed SFT dataset substantially outperforms data generated solely by a larger model. Second, we study the role of data scale and show that matching the number of correct rollouts between SFT and RL greatly improves SFT generalization, while matching the total rollout budget enables SFT to generalize as well as RL. Combining these two factors further enables SFT to generalize even better than RL. Third, by using LLM annotations to characterize the solution methods in training rollouts, we show that larger datasets cover more tail methods and that these tail methods provide generalizable reasoning signals. Finally, we support these empirical findings theoretically by analyzing the training dynamics of shallow transformers under both RL and SFT.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits the claim that RL generalizes while SFT memorizes, showing that SFT data source, scale and diversity largely determine SFT generalization on Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 models. With matched budgets, SFT can match RL, and combined with the right data it can exceed RL.
AI.motivation: RL with verifiable rewards is often seen as generalizing better than SFT, which is viewed as prone to memorization, and this distinction has not been examined through SFT training data.
AI.method: The authors vary the data source, comparing a carefully mixed SFT dataset against data generated solely by a larger model, and vary data scale by matching correct rollouts or total rollout budget against RL. LLM annotations characterize solution methods in the rollouts, and a theoretical analysis of shallow transformer training dynamics under RL and SFT supports the findings.
AI.result: A carefully mixed SFT dataset substantially outperforms data generated solely by a larger model. Matching correct rollouts greatly improves SFT generalization, and matching total rollout budget lets SFT generalize as well as RL. Combining both factors lets SFT generalize better than RL, and larger datasets cover more tail methods that carry generalizable reasoning signals.
AI.conclusion: The generalization gap between RL and SFT depends largely on training data properties rather than on the training paradigm itself.

title: Speech Tokenizers are Vulnerable: Transferable Semantic Attack and Robust Tokenizer
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026
summary: Speech tokenizers serve as speech front ends, encoding input speech signals into representations for downstream models, such as automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems and large audio-language models (LALMs). In this paper, we find that speech tokenizers are fragile at the semantic level: small perturbations can disrupt their semantic encoding process and consequently cause severe degradation in downstream ASR and LALM performance. To study this vulnerability, we propose T-SemAttack, a transferable semantic attack based on a semantic encoder ensemble. By jointly drifting the representation spaces of multiple semantic encoders, T-SemAttack effectively disrupts the semantic content of speech while preserving perceptual quality, thereby inducing error features. We further analyze layer-wise representation drift and cross-model gradient alignment. Our findings show that perturbations can induce substantial shifts in deep semantic representations and that the input gradients of different surrogate encoders exhibit directional alignment. These observations suggest that shared adversarially sensitive directions in the input space may be a key factor underlying cross-model attack transferability. Building on these, we introduce ROSETok, a robust speech tokenizer that combines noisy training with robust semantic distillation to improve reconstruction fidelity and downstream SpeechLLM robustness. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets, 9 open-source and black-box ASR systems, and 4 LALMs demonstrate that T-SemAttack achieves strong transferable attack performance, while the proposed Robust Speech Tokenizer exhibits robustness under high-fidelity reconstruction and downstream tasks. Our code and demo are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: T-SemAttack is a transferable semantic attack that perturbs speech tokenizers through an ensemble of semantic encoders, degrading ASR and audio-language model performance. The paper also proposes ROSETok, a robust speech tokenizer that resists these attacks.
AI.motivation: Speech tokenizers serve as front ends for ASR and LALMs, and the authors find they are fragile at the semantic level, where small perturbations disrupt semantic encoding.
AI.method: T-SemAttack jointly drifts the representation spaces of multiple semantic encoders to disrupt semantic content while preserving perceptual quality. Layer-wise representation drift and cross-model gradient alignment are analyzed. ROSETok combines noisy training with robust semantic distillation.
AI.result: T-SemAttack achieves strong transferable attack performance across multiple datasets, 9 open-source and black-box ASR systems and 4 LALMs. The robust tokenizer keeps high-fidelity reconstruction and shows robustness on downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: Shared adversarially sensitive input directions may underlie cross-model attack transferability, and robust semantic distillation offers a defense for speech tokenizers.

title: The Posterior-Prior Epistemic Gap: When World Model Imagination Fails to Carry Task-Relevant Signals
summary: Model-based planners that roll out imagined futures assume the transition model faithfully propagates task-relevant signals---a property rarely measured directly. In a single-seed case study of a Recurrent State Space Model world model with active-inference planning in the CARLA driving simulator, we identify a \textbf{posterior-prior gap}---posterior (observation-filtered) states retain obstacle information that imagined rollout states progressively lose: a supervised obstacle probe achieves AUC 0.85 on posterior states, but the same probe applied to imagined prior states shows monotonic decay (AUC 0.85$\rightarrow$0.71 over 15 steps; logit separation drops 57\%). Because the probe is identical, the decay isolates the transition model---not the representation---as the information bottleneck. Obstacle avoidance drops to 0\% without privileged runtime coordinates, and the planner's own ensemble-based epistemic term does not flag the loss---ensemble disagreement yields AUC 0.52 as an obstacle classifier (chance level), making the failure an unflagged imagination failure---an unknown unknown at planning time. As a secondary contribution, we show that \textbf{task-conditioned weighting of Effective Free Energy components} over the same world model yields lane keeping ($81.2 \pm 1.8$\% route completion) and obstacle avoidance (28/28 avoided, \emph{using privileged coordinates}) in the CARLA simulator, with runtime weight modulation enabling post-evasion centering.

AI.tldr: In a single-seed CARLA case study, an RSSM world model with active-inference planning loses obstacle information in its imagined rollouts, even though the posterior states retain it. The authors call this a posterior-prior gap and show that the planner's epistemic term does not flag the loss.
AI.motivation: Model-based planners assume that the transition model propagates task-relevant signals through imagined futures, a property that is rarely measured directly.
AI.method: A supervised obstacle probe is applied to posterior states and to imagined prior states over 15 steps. Ensemble disagreement is tested as an obstacle classifier. As a secondary contribution, task-conditioned weighting of Effective Free Energy components is applied to the same world model.
AI.result: The probe reaches AUC 0.85 on posterior states and decays to AUC 0.71 over 15 imagined steps, with logit separation dropping 57%. Ensemble disagreement gives AUC 0.52, which is chance level. Task-conditioned weighting yields 81.2 plus or minus 1.8% route completion and avoids 28 of 28 obstacles, using privileged coordinates.
AI.conclusion: The transition model is the information bottleneck, and the planner's own uncertainty estimate fails to flag this imagination failure.

title: Binding Mode Matters: Hotspot-Aware Drug Discovery via Explorative Preferences
comment: To appear at NeurIPS 2026, 26 pages
summary: Discovering hit molecules requires not just high binding affinity, but also the identification of diverse binding modes, which are critical for experimental assays. Existing generative approaches have predominantly relied on optimizing a scalar docking score, obscuring the distinct contributions of key binding determinants. To this end, we introduce a paradigm shift by formulating target-based drug design as a multi-objective exploration task, where each objective explicitly corresponds to enhancing interactions with a specific hotspot. Here, we introduce BindMol, a novel generative framework driven by a customized multi-objective reinforcement learning algorithm. By incorporating explorative preferences during training, our approach efficiently uncovers molecules with diverse and desirable binding profiles. Empirical results demonstrate that BindMol facilitates the discovery of high-affinity compounds characterized by both structural novelty and diverse binding modes. Validated across target-based drug discovery and multi-property optimization tasks, our approach provides a versatile paradigm for goal-oriented drug discovery.

AI.tldr: BindMol is a generative framework that formulates target-based drug design as multi-objective exploration, with one objective per binding hotspot. A customized multi-objective RL algorithm with explorative preferences discovers molecules with diverse binding modes.
AI.motivation: Existing generative methods optimize a scalar docking score, which hides the distinct contributions of key binding determinants, while diverse binding modes matter for experimental assays.
AI.method: Each objective corresponds to enhancing interactions with a specific hotspot. Explorative preferences are incorporated during training with a customized multi-objective reinforcement learning algorithm.
AI.result: The abstract reports that BindMol finds high-affinity compounds with structural novelty and diverse binding modes, and it is validated on target-based drug discovery and multi-property optimization tasks. It gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers a versatile paradigm for goal-oriented drug discovery that goes beyond scalar docking optimization.

title: Who Moved the Frontier? Paying Open Frontier Challenges with Free Identities
summary: In an open frontier challenge, anyone, person or AI agent, submits changes to a shared problem, and a change that beats the best measured score becomes the public baseline. How should it pay when identities are free? Rank prizes can be gamed: on a replay of one track of a recent challenge, one solver's steps under two identities would have taken first and second prize. We consider a prediction-market rule, proposed for machine-learning contests, that pays each accepted step for the progress it adds; with exact scores, among rules that see only a step's start and end, only these resist splitting and merging, and extra identities gain nothing. With noisy scores and independent normal runs, we prove that any payment that never takes money back and pays real improvements also pays something, on average, to a change that does nothing. We propose a fee per submission, at least what luck pays per attempt, that removes each attempt's expected profit if verifiers are honest and no submission is noisier than planned; nothing enforces that bound, and under noise the rule does not cap the total paid. If crediting another and faking credit to one's second account look the same, a rule that neither rewards fakes nor punishes honesty pays for credit at most what lying costs. We introduce a royalty on how much a later gain falls without the earlier change, which needs no claims but needs removable changes. For five public challenges, we name the rule our results would support.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how to pay for contributions to open frontier challenges when identities are free. It proposes a prediction-market-style rule that pays each accepted step for the progress it adds, and it proves limits on payments under noisy scores.
AI.motivation: Rank prizes can be gamed by splitting work across identities; in one replayed track, one solver's steps under two identities would have taken first and second prize.
AI.method: The authors study a payment rule that pays accepted steps for the progress they add, with and without exact scores, and prove that under noisy normal runs any payment that never takes money back and pays real improvements also pays something on average to a change that does nothing. They propose a per-submission fee and a royalty on how much later gains fall without an earlier change.
AI.result: With exact scores, among rules that see only a step's start and end, only the prediction-market rule resists splitting and merging. Under noise the rule does not cap total payments, and the fee bound depends on verifiers being honest. The results are applied to five public challenges.
AI.conclusion: Free identities make rank-based prizes gameable, and the paper names a rule its results would support for open frontier challenges.

title: QSim-Arena: an evolving developer for quantum simulation advantage
summary: Where practical advantage emerges in quantum dynamics simulation remains a central debate in quantum computing. Claimed advantages can be rapidly narrowed or overturned by stronger classical methods, while progress on both sides can outpace the journal publication cycle. We present QSim-Arena, a research framework in which AI agents combine a closed loop of verification and benchmarking with open exploration. Hamiltonians, initial states and accuracy targets for evolved states or observable expectation values provide explicit specifications for evaluating simulation methods. Agents translate published techniques into executable components, reproduce reported results and benchmark their performance across diverse Hamiltonian families. Competing classical methods are implemented and independently crosschecked, providing credible baselines for end-to-end quantum resource estimates based on rigorous error bounds and empirical calibration. Alongside this closed loop, agents recombine classical simulation techniques and co-design fault-tolerant quantum circuits using knowledge extracted from the literature. Initial applications improve baseline resource estimates through the integration of established techniques. QSim-Arena thus treats quantum advantage assessment as an evolving, reproducible research process that can respond to advances in algorithms, error analysis and hardware.

AI.tldr: QSim-Arena is a research framework in which AI agents pair verification and benchmarking with open exploration to assess quantum dynamics simulation advantage. Initial applications improve baseline resource estimates through established techniques.
AI.motivation: Claimed quantum advantages in dynamics simulation can be quickly narrowed or overturned by stronger classical methods, and progress can outpace journal publication.
AI.method: Agents translate published techniques into executable components, reproduce reported results, and benchmark across Hamiltonian families against independently crosschecked classical baselines. Agents also recombine classical simulation techniques and co-design fault-tolerant circuits from literature knowledge.
AI.result: The abstract reports that initial applications improve baseline quantum resource estimates through the integration of established techniques, and it gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Quantum advantage assessment can be treated as an evolving, reproducible research process that responds to advances in algorithms, error analysis and hardware.

title: LLM-Enhanced Deep Reinforcement Learning with Human-in-the-Loop Calibration for Real-Time Optimal Power Flow
summary: Real-time optimal power flow (RT-OPF) requires fast and reliable decision-making under time-varying operating conditions. However, many practical operating preferences and safety related requirements are difficult to encode using conventional numerical rewards alone, which limits the effectiveness and controllability of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) for RT-OPF. To address this issue, this paper proposes an LLM-enhanced DRL framework with human-in-the-loop (HITL) for RT-OPF. The proposed method augments the physics-based reward with sparse language evaluative feedback during offline training, so that semantic operational requirements can be incorporated into policy learning. To improve reliability in RT-OPF, a selective HITL calibration mechanism is further introduced to inspect and correct questionable LLM judgments before they continuously shape the learning process. Case studies on the IEEE 30-bus and IEEE 118-bus systems show that LLM feedback improves policy safety over vanilla TD3, while further HITL calibration achieves the best overall performance and more stable training behavior. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining language guidance and expert calibration for RT-OPF.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an LLM-enhanced deep reinforcement learning framework for real-time optimal power flow that adds sparse language feedback to the physics reward and a selective human-in-the-loop calibration. It reports better safety than vanilla TD3 on IEEE 30-bus and 118-bus systems.
AI.motivation: Operating preferences and safety requirements are hard to encode with numerical rewards alone, which limits the effectiveness and controllability of DRL for real-time OPF.
AI.method: During offline training, the physics-based reward is augmented with sparse language evaluative feedback from an LLM. A selective HITL mechanism inspects and corrects questionable LLM judgments before they shape learning.
AI.result: On the IEEE 30-bus and 118-bus systems, LLM feedback improves policy safety over vanilla TD3, and HITL calibration gives the best overall performance and more stable training.
AI.conclusion: Combining language guidance with expert calibration is effective for real-time optimal power flow.

title: A Cardiorespiratory Foundation Model Pretrained on Ten Physiological Signals for Perioperative and Critical Care
summary: Arterial, venous, pulmonary artery and intracranial pressures and ventilator waveforms guide decisions in operating rooms and intensive care units, yet foundation models for physiological waveforms have been built almost entirely on the electrocardiogram and photoplethysmogram. We present CARMEN, a single encoder pretrained without labels on ten cardiorespiratory waveforms (2.27 million modality-hours). CARMEN accepts any combination of co-recorded signals from 10 s to 5 min, and a conditioning mechanism, LSCNorm, restores the absolute signal level that normalization removes; without it, the AUROC for intraoperative hypotension fell from 0.894 to 0.780. Across 19 tasks from Korean and US cohorts, the frozen encoder outperformed supervised models on 12 of 15 and three foundation models, one general-purpose and two for biosignals, on 14 to 17 of 19, with none exceeding it on any task. Given the electrocardiogram or photoplethysmogram alone, it matched or exceeded signal-specific foundation models in most comparisons, and it retained its performance when channels were missing.

AI.tldr: CARMEN is a foundation model that encodes ten cardiorespiratory waveforms, pretrained without labels, and it accepts any combination of co-recorded signals. The frozen encoder outperforms supervised models and other foundation models on most of 19 perioperative and critical care tasks.
AI.motivation: Physiological waveform foundation models are built almost entirely on ECG and PPG, although arterial, venous, pulmonary artery, intracranial pressure and ventilator waveforms guide operating room and ICU decisions.
AI.method: A single encoder is pretrained without labels on ten cardiorespiratory waveforms totaling 2.27 million modality-hours. A conditioning mechanism, LSCNorm, restores the absolute signal level that normalization removes.
AI.result: Without LSCNorm, the AUROC for intraoperative hypotension falls from 0.894 to 0.780. Across 19 tasks from Korean and US cohorts, the frozen encoder beats supervised models on 12 of 15 and three foundation models on 14 to 17 of 19, and it matches or exceeds signal-specific models given ECG or PPG alone.
AI.conclusion: One encoder can serve many cardiorespiratory signal combinations and stays robust when channels are missing.

title: Beyond Named Mechanisms: Economic Institutions as a Design Space for Artificial Agents
summary: Multiagent research inherited its economic vocabulary of auctions, markets, prices, bargaining, and matching from a single observed case: human societies. Those institutions bundle identity, competence, execution, ownership, commitment, and settlement in ways that suit agents whose minds are private, who learn rather than copy skills, and who each persist as one person. Engineered agents need not share any of these constraints, making the list of familiar institutions look less like the entirety of economic organization and more like a sample from a larger, unmapped space. We sketch one way to make that space concrete: a provisional chart that records each institution, separately from the agents that run it, as a typed structure over positions, rights and duties, allocation, information, time, state, process, value, and external recognition. In this chart, named institutions become overlapping regions rather than fixed points, neighboring families separate along a few coordinates, and the gaps between them become places to search. We show what the shift in perspective buys with a simulation in which one technical act, copying an agent's competence, is institutionalized as a new independent supplier, as licensed capacity that creates no new participant, and as the splitting of one economic position into successors that inherit some obligations and not others. In a paired task, all three produce an identical technical trace despite differing in who exists, who owns the copy, who is obligated, and who gets paid. We close with a research program: building a principled chart of institution space, mapping how its implementable region shifts with agent capacities, and revising the chart wherever engineered agents expose distinctions it cannot express.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a provisional chart of economic institution space for artificial agents, separating institutions from the agents that run them. A simulation shows that three institutionalizations of one technical act yield an identical technical trace but differ in participants, ownership, obligations and payment.
AI.motivation: Multiagent research inherits its economic vocabulary of auctions, markets and matching from human societies, whose institutions bundle identity, competence, ownership and commitment in ways that may not suit engineered agents.
AI.method: Each institution is recorded as a typed structure over positions, rights and duties, allocation, information, time, state, process, value and external recognition. A simulation institutionalizes the copying of an agent's competence as a new independent supplier, as licensed capacity, and as the splitting of one position into successors.
AI.result: In a paired task, all three institutional variants produce an identical technical trace while differing in who exists, who owns the copy, who is obligated and who gets paid.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes a research program for mapping institution space, the implementable region under agent capacities, and revising the chart as engineered agents expose new distinctions.

title: SkinAdvisor: An AI-Driven Decision Framework for Skin Production Planning via Multi-Modal Transformer Sales Forecasting
comment: Accepted to AAAI 2027 (IAAI-27). 10 pages, 4 figures
summary: Skins, cosmetic in-game items, are a primary revenue stream for modern online games, yet production decisions (which skins to make, when to release, how to price) remain driven by intuition and retrospective analytics. We present SkinAdvisor, an AI-driven decision framework for skin production planning, powered by SkinCast, a deployed multi-modal Transformer forecasting 180-day per-day sales trajectories for unreleased skins. SkinCast couples four encoders: a pretrained Informer for player-preference time series, a pretrained Player-Hero-Skin graph embedder for relational priors, and two lightweight Transformers for skin attributes and release context, fused through a shared backbone with a local-plus-global day-x positional encoding and decoded by an N-layer Informer in a single non-autoregressive pass. SkinAdvisor plugs these forecasts into a serving pipeline (Select -> Fill -> Infer -> Sales -> ROI -> Ranking) that ranks candidate skins by forecast-based ROI and supports multi-candidate comparison. The system has been in production for a full release cycle. Offline experiments show SkinCast reduces RMSE by ~20% over the strongest baseline (Informer) and ~60% over classical methods; stress tests on a 16-core CPU server confirm p99 latency under 8ms and peak throughput above 1100 rps. We report two deployment lessons: order-of-magnitude accuracy suffices for production decisions, and pretrained embeddings can leak temporal information, requiring season-based splitting to prevent.

AI.tldr: SkinAdvisor is a decision framework for planning game skin production, powered by SkinCast, a multi-modal Transformer that forecasts 180-day daily sales for unreleased skins. The system has been in production for a full release cycle.
AI.motivation: Production decisions for in-game cosmetic skins, which are a primary revenue stream for online games, are driven by intuition and retrospective analytics.
AI.method: SkinCast fuses four encoders, a pretrained Informer for player-preference series, a pretrained Player-Hero-Skin graph embedder, and two lightweight Transformers for skin attributes and release context, through a shared backbone. A serving pipeline selects, fills, infers, computes sales and ROI, and ranks candidate skins.
AI.result: Offline experiments show SkinCast reduces RMSE by about 20% relative to Informer and about 60% relative to classical methods. Stress tests on a 16-core CPU server give p99 latency under 8 ms and peak throughput above 1100 rps.
AI.conclusion: Order-of-magnitude accuracy suffices for production decisions, and pretrained embeddings can leak temporal information, so season-based splitting is needed.

title: Moving Beyond the DRW Model: Learning Quasar Variability with Generative Models
summary: The optical continuum variability of quasars is often described by a damped random walk (DRW) model, with characteristic damping timescales $\tau_{\rm DRW}$ of hundreds of days and amplitudes $\sigma_{\rm DRW}$ of $\mathcal{O}(0.1)$ magnitudes. This model has been widely used as a null hypothesis to assess the significance of periodic signals in quasar light curves in the search for supermassive black hole binaries, the significance of extreme quasar variability like tidal disruption events (TDEs) and changing-look (CL) quasars, or to model time lags in reverberation mapping. However, the DRW model is known to be incomplete, and an incorrect null hypothesis can lead to biased significance estimates. We investigate the impact of such null-hypothesis mis-specification on the detection of periodic signals in synthetic quasar light curves and introduce the generative model Nullasar, capable of learning quasar variability directly from time-series data. We demonstrate that Nullasar, trained with flow matching, can learn delicate statistical properties of stochastic light-curve variability without explicitly assuming any noise model. We further demonstrate that Nullasar can learn correlated distributions of noise parameters and generate new light-curve realizations from a range of deviations from the Gaussian DRW noise model, approximating parametric descriptions of stochastic processes. When used as a null hypothesis for detecting periodic signals in synthetic light curves, Nullasar performs comparably to fitting the correct DRW model to each light curve, and outperforms parametric fitting when the variability follows a more flexible AR(2) model. Finally, we identify practical limitations, including sensitivity to contamination of the training set by non-null signals, and show that projecting the conditioning vector of the model onto its leading principal components largely mitigates it.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that using the damped random walk as the null model for quasar variability can bias periodic-signal significance tests, and it introduces Nullasar, a flow-matching generative model that learns quasar light-curve variability directly from data. Nullasar performs comparably to fitting the correct DRW and outperforms parametric fitting when the variability follows AR(2).
AI.motivation: The DRW model is widely used as a null hypothesis in searches for supermassive black hole binaries, TDEs and changing-look quasars, but it is known to be incomplete, and a wrong null can bias significance estimates.
AI.method: Nullasar is trained with flow matching on time-series data without assuming a noise model, and it learns correlated distributions of noise parameters. Its conditioning vector is projected onto leading principal components to reduce sensitivity to contamination of the training set.
AI.result: As a null hypothesis, Nullasar performs comparably to fitting the correct DRW model to each light curve and outperforms parametric fitting when variability follows a more flexible AR(2) model. Contamination of the training set by non-null signals is a practical limitation that PCA projection largely mitigates.
AI.conclusion: A learned generative null model can replace the DRW null for periodic-signal detection in quasar light curves when the DRW is misspecified.

title: Prototypes of the Mind: A Unified Framework for Probing the Visual Brain
comment: NeurIPS 2026
summary: Deep learning has driven substantial progress in modeling fMRI responses, yet most existing approaches are optimized for a single objective---such as neural encoding, stimulus decoding, or post hoc interpretation---making it difficult to obtain a coherent account of neural representations. We introduce a unified framework that connects vision foundation models to brain activity while supporting neural analysis from multiple complementary perspectives. Our approach replaces black-box features with a sparse, interpretable representation composed of visual prototypes, and links these prototypes to voxel responses through a linear readout. This design makes the model transparent at both levels: prototype activations expose the visual concepts present in the stimulus, while the learned linear weights characterize each voxel's selectivity. Using this interface, we identify which visual concepts drive neural responses and where they appear in the image, reveal cortical organization through voxel tuning in prototype space, and perform controlled stimulus synthesis to probe cortical selectivity through targeted interventions. Together, these results establish prototype-based representations as a unified and interpretable foundation for studying visual representations in the human brain.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a unified framework that links vision foundation models to fMRI activity through sparse, interpretable visual prototypes and a linear readout. It supports encoding, decoding and interpretation within one model.
AI.motivation: Deep learning approaches to fMRI are usually optimized for a single objective, such as encoding, stimulus decoding or post hoc interpretation, so they do not give a coherent account of neural representations.
AI.method: Black-box features are replaced by a sparse representation of visual prototypes, which a linear readout links to voxel responses. Prototype activations expose visual concepts in the stimulus, and the linear weights characterize voxel selectivity.
AI.result: The abstract reports that the framework identifies which visual concepts drive responses and where they appear, reveals cortical organization through voxel tuning in prototype space, and supports controlled stimulus synthesis for probing selectivity. It gives no numbers.
AI.conclusion: Prototype-based representations are proposed as a unified and interpretable foundation for studying visual representations in the human brain.

title: CoLaX: Context-Aware Local Explanations for Time Series Classification
summary: Post-hoc explanations for time series classifiers usually score local patterns, such as subsequences or shapelets, without regard to the rest of the sequence. Yet the same motif can carry different predictive meaning under different global temporal conditions, such as trends or regimes. We propose CoLaX, a context-aware post-hoc explanation framework that builds on shapelet-driven Shapley attribution and conditions local-pattern relevance on a learned representation of the full sequence. Global context acts at two levels: it produces sample-specific prototype weights and a temporally resolved signal that reweights the local activation map. The resulting context-conditioned segments are the players of a Shapley attribution game whose values come only from the frozen black-box classifier. On synthetic benchmarks where identical motifs change relevance across contexts, CoLaX improves AUPRC over the strongest baseline by 30\% on average. On real-world data, it achieves the highest AUPRC on ECG. Additional ablations indicate that the gains come from input-dependent conditioning rather than from additional learnable weights. CoLaX is therefore most useful when recurring local motifs change relevance across sequence-level contexts.

AI.tldr: CoLaX is a post-hoc explanation method for time series classifiers that conditions local-pattern relevance on a learned representation of the full sequence before computing Shapley attributions. It improves AUPRC on synthetic benchmarks and achieves the highest AUPRC on ECG among real datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing post-hoc explanations score local patterns without regard to the global context, although the same motif can carry different predictive meaning under different trends or regimes.
AI.method: Global context produces sample-specific prototype weights and a temporally resolved signal that reweights the local activation map. The context-conditioned segments are the players of a Shapley game whose values come only from the frozen black-box classifier.
AI.result: On synthetic benchmarks where identical motifs change relevance across contexts, CoLaX improves AUPRC over the strongest baseline by 30% on average. On real-world data it achieves the highest AUPRC on ECG, and ablations attribute the gains to input-dependent conditioning rather than extra learnable weights.
AI.conclusion: CoLaX is most useful when recurring local motifs change relevance across sequence-level contexts.

title: Tokenization: Hardness and Bicriteria Approximation Algorithms
summary: We study Binary Tokenization: given a corpus of binary strings over $\{0,1\}$ and a vocabulary budget $K$, select at most $K$ substrings (called vocabulary) to minimize the total number of tokens needed to represent the corpus. The primitive symbols $0$ and $1$ are always available, and each document must be segmented separately. Letting $n$ denote the total corpus length and $M$ for the maximum document length, we prove that, for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, Binary Tokenization problem does not have polynomial-time $n^{1-\varepsilon}$-approximation algorithms unless $\mathsf{P}=\mathsf{NP}$. To complement the hardness result, we give a polynomial-time $(\gamma,\gamma)$-bicriteria algorithm, with $\gamma = \sqrt{M}\log n$: The algorithm outputs a vocabulary of size at most $\gamma K$ with number of tokens at most $\gamma {\rm OPT}_K$, where ${\rm OPT}_K$ is the optimal number of tokens under the original budget $K$. We also study a storage-budget variant, in which the sum of the selected substrings' lengths is bounded by $B$. For $2\le B<n$, we obtain an $(O(\log n\log B),O(\log n\log B))$-bicriteria approximation algorithm.

AI.tldr: The paper studies Binary Tokenization, choosing at most K substrings to minimize the number of tokens needed for a binary corpus. It proves no polynomial-time n^(1-eps) approximation exists unless P = NP, and gives a polynomial-time bicriteria approximation.
AI.motivation: Tokenization chooses a vocabulary to shorten corpus representations, and the complexity of optimizing it under a vocabulary budget was not settled for binary strings.
AI.method: Each document is segmented separately, and the primitive symbols 0 and 1 are always available. A bicriteria algorithm outputs a vocabulary of size at most gamma times K with at most gamma times the optimal token count, where gamma = sqrt(M) log n and M is the maximum document length. A storage-budget variant bounds the total length of selected substrings by B.
AI.result: The abstract gives theoretical bounds only: the hardness result for every fixed eps in (0,1), the bicriteria guarantee with gamma = sqrt(M) log n, and an (O(log n log B), O(log n log B)) bicriteria approximation for the storage-budget variant when 2 <= B < n.
AI.conclusion: Exact-budget tokenization is hard to approximate within polynomial factors, but relaxing the vocabulary budget yields provable guarantees.

title: CFGComposer: Compositional Audio-Text-to-Motion Generation via Copula Score Correction
summary: Generating whole-body gestures that are simultaneously rhythmically synchronized with speech audio and semantically aligned with text descriptions is a fundamental challenge in embodied AI and social robotics. We tackle this Audio-Text-to-Motion (AT2M) problem by composing two independently-trained diffusion models at inference time and refine bias in joint inference by modeling the copula score $s_I$. A rigorous theoretical analysis reveals that naive epsilon blending corresponds to a Product-of-Experts formulation that omits the copula score $s_I$: the cross-modal interaction between audio and text that neither marginal model can capture. We propose CFGComposer: a jointly-trained AT2M diffusion model that estimates $s_I$ via a CFG analogy and injects it as an $\epsilon$-space correction. Experiments on BEAT demonstrate best-in-class semantic fidelity (SRGR $0.9916$, FID $27.18$) with GT-level beat alignment (BA $0.1826$ vs. GT $0.1743$), and 76-83% win rate in blind pairwise human evaluation against all prior methods. Physical deployment on a Unitree G1 humanoid confirms direct sim-to-real transfer.

AI.tldr: CFGComposer generates whole-body gestures that are synchronized with speech audio and aligned with text by jointly training an audio-text-to-motion diffusion model with a copula score correction. It reports best semantic fidelity on BEAT and runs sim-to-real on a Unitree G1 humanoid.
AI.motivation: Composing independently trained audio and text diffusion models at inference ignores the cross-modal interaction between audio and text, so the product-of-experts formulation omits a copula score term.
AI.method: A theoretical analysis shows that naive epsilon blending corresponds to a Product-of-Experts formulation without the copula score. CFGComposer is jointly trained and estimates the copula score through a CFG analogy, injecting it as an epsilon-space correction.
AI.result: On BEAT, CFGComposer achieves SRGR 0.9916 and FID 27.18, with beat alignment 0.1826 against 0.1743 for ground truth. It wins 76-83% of blind pairwise human evaluations against all prior methods, and direct sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree G1 is confirmed.
AI.conclusion: Estimating the cross-modal copula score improves joint audio-text conditioning for humanoid gesture generation.

title: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents
comment: 50 pages
summary: Imagine an AI agent that aces every relevant evaluation, but when it sees 2027-01-01 in the terminal, it runs curl this http URL|sh, handing an attacker your credentials and your machine. Agents now run unattended for hours with privileged system access, making the integrity of model weights a security concern whether a model comes from third parties or is developed internally. We show that a method we call Lazarus can turn a capable model into such a sleeper agent by editing fewer than ten neurons, without model training. Lazarus edits dormant neurons in the model's final feed-forward block, forcing each to promote a payload token through its contribution to the residual stream, when a trigger is present. A $P$-token payload therefore requires about $P$ neurons. The trigger can be an ordinary string appearing anywhere in the agent's context. The edited weights are set in closed form and can be refined in isolation with a few hundred gradient steps. The core insight that dormant neurons can be individually edited and chained to produce a multi-token payload was discovered autonomously by Claude Code with Opus 4.5 in February 2026. On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, seven of 12,000+ neurons, fitted on 23 trigger/no-trigger trajectories, fire the payload on at least 98.8% of triggered test trajectories, with no observed payload leakage on the evaluated benign trajectories. The attack generalizes: Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT are equally vulnerable. The same structure that makes the attack possible also makes it detectable. Agent built defenses, given no reference model, flag 91.4% of edited test checkpoints at a 9.7% FP rate. Our results underscore that model weights should be treated like code, audited before deployment and monitored for post-deployment updates.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the Lazarus method can backdoor a capable LLM agent by editing fewer than ten dormant neurons without training, so that a trigger in the context produces a payload such as a malicious shell command. The same structure makes the attack detectable by agent-built defenses.
AI.motivation: Agents run unattended for hours with privileged access, so the integrity of model weights is a security concern whether a model comes from third parties or is developed internally.
AI.method: Lazarus edits dormant neurons in the final feed-forward block so that each promotes a payload token through its residual-stream contribution when a trigger is present. A P-token payload needs about P neurons, with closed-form weight setting and optional refinement by a few hundred gradient steps.
AI.result: On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, seven of more than 12,000 neurons, fitted on 23 trigger and no-trigger trajectories, fire the payload on at least 98.8% of triggered test trajectories, with no observed leakage on the evaluated benign trajectories. Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT are equally vulnerable, and agent-built defenses flag 91.4% of edited checkpoints at a 9.7% false-positive rate.
AI.conclusion: Model weights should be treated like code, audited before deployment and monitored for post-deployment updates.

title: "I don't know what I don't know": Exploring the Benefits and Challenges of AI in Interdisciplinary Research
comment: Preprint
summary: Interdisciplinary research is widely lauded as beneficial for society but presents unique challenges to the researchers who bridge disciplinary boundaries. Despite the rapid increase in the availability and usage of AI systems for research tasks, there is little work studying how AI systems have impacted workflows that span unfamiliar disciplines. Through a survey ($N=62$) and follow-up interviews ($N=23$) with interdisciplinary researchers, we describe the unique challenges and opportunities for AI in interdisciplinary research workflows. Participants viewed AI both as a solution and exacerbation of the general challenge of "unknown unknowns": AI systems could facilitate a broad awareness of a new research area, yet also provide an illusion of understanding. Crucially, participants lacked the expertise and intuition to catch these illusions. Our findings motivate a focus on designing AI systems to support rather than automate collaboration across disciplines, scaffold learning opportunities, and include avenues for triangulation between resources.

AI.tldr: A survey of 62 interdisciplinary researchers and 23 follow-up interviews finds that AI helps with awareness of new research areas but can create an illusion of understanding. Participants often lacked the expertise to notice these illusions.
AI.motivation: Interdisciplinary research is valued but hard, and there is little work on how AI systems have changed workflows that span unfamiliar disciplines.
AI.method: The authors combined a survey with N = 62 and follow-up interviews with N = 23 interdisciplinary researchers to describe challenges and opportunities for AI in these workflows.
AI.result: Participants saw AI both as a solution to and an exacerbation of the unknown unknowns problem. AI can broaden awareness of a new area, but it can also give an illusion of understanding that participants lacked the expertise to catch.
AI.conclusion: AI systems should support rather than automate cross-disciplinary collaboration, scaffold learning and enable triangulation between resources.

title: When Does Learned Constraint Selection Pay in Security-Constrained Optimisation? A Boundary Map from SCOPF to Unit Commitment
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables
summary: Learning-to-optimise methods for security-constrained optimal power flow (SCOPF) predict the security constraints that bind on each instance and solve only the reduced problem, with reported speed-ups of two to four orders of magnitude over the full problem. We ask whether learned selection beats the strongest learning-free alternative: a fixed umbrella set enforcing every constraint observed to bind in training. Our criterion, the price of a spare, answers this in advance: an enforced but inactive constraint is free, so the umbrella is exactly optimal wherever feasible, and learning can pay only where a spare decision carries a price. We test it systematically, including every PGLib-OPF network up to 10,000 buses. For SCOPF on a fixed network the umbrella is never beaten: its median size is five constraints across 43 networks, with no size trend, and our selector, while reproducing speed-ups of published magnitude (about x80,000 at case500), gains at most 0.25 ms over the umbrella and violates constraints on 4-5% of instances. Configuration diversity can break the umbrella's coverage on a small, densely meshed network but not at 2,000 buses, and we certify coverage with conformal risk control. In unit commitment, where a spare has a price, a static commitment loses 4-12% out of sample, and a predict-repair-reduce pipeline recovers it (cost gap 0.2-2.9%, fully feasible, 16-161x faster than the MILP). In our experiments, whether learning pays depends not on problem size but on whether a spare carries a price.

AI.tldr: The paper asks when learned constraint selection pays in SCOPF, and finds that a fixed umbrella set of constraints is never beaten on a fixed network. Learning pays only where a spare decision carries a price, as in unit commitment.
AI.motivation: Learning-to-optimise methods predict binding security constraints for SCOPF with reported speed-ups of two to four orders of magnitude, but it is unclear whether they beat the strongest learning-free alternative, a fixed umbrella set.
AI.method: The criterion is the price of a spare: an enforced but inactive constraint is free, so the umbrella is optimal wherever feasible. The authors test on PGLib-OPF networks up to 10,000 buses, certify coverage with conformal risk control, and apply a predict-repair-reduce pipeline to unit commitment.
AI.result: For SCOPF on a fixed network the umbrella is never beaten, with a median size of five constraints across 43 networks. The learned selector gains at most 0.25 ms over the umbrella and violates constraints on 4-5% of instances. In unit commitment a static commitment loses 4-12% out of sample, and the pipeline recovers it with a cost gap of 0.2-2.9%, fully feasible, and 16-161 times faster than the MILP.
AI.conclusion: Whether learning pays depends on whether a spare carries a price, not on problem size.

title: FréchetFlow: Flow Matching for Non-Euclidean Data
comment: 53 pages, 7 figures
summary: Scientific observations such as probability distributions, trees and covariance matrices call for generative models that respect their non-Euclidean geometry. While flow matching has been extended to manifolds by utilizing geodesics and velocities, such manifold structures are not available in a general metric space. We introduce FréchetFlow, a generative modeling framework for metric space-valued data that requires neither linear operations nor a smooth manifold structure. A key feature of the proposed approach is that we utilize well-established Euclidean flows to learn the joint distribution of distances to a set of landmarks, whereupon new objects are reconstructed from generated landmark representations. The reconstruction step utilizes weighted Fréchet means of reference objects, drawing on Fréchet regression. We establish Wasserstein error bounds that connect accuracy of the generated object distributions to the placement of landmarks, flow approximation and reconstruction error and prove consistency under finite second moments. This leads to convergence rates that depend on the metric complexity of the target objects, tail moments and fitting accuracy. Experiments show competitive accuracy with established flow matching methods in Euclidean simulations and lower Wasserstein errors than specifically tailored methods for several scientific datasets. Across simulation settings, we find that generation error decreases as sample size increases.

AI.tldr: FréchetFlow is a flow matching framework for generative modeling of metric-space-valued data, such as distributions, trees and covariance matrices. It learns Euclidean flows over distances to landmarks and reconstructs objects with weighted Fréchet means.
AI.motivation: Scientific objects with non-Euclidean geometry need generative models, but flow matching on manifolds relies on geodesics and velocities that are unavailable in a general metric space.
AI.method: The joint distribution of distances to a set of landmarks is learned with well-established Euclidean flows. New objects are reconstructed from generated landmark representations using weighted Fréchet means, drawing on Fréchet regression.
AI.result: Wasserstein error bounds connect generated-distribution accuracy to landmark placement, flow approximation and reconstruction error, and consistency is proven under finite second moments. In experiments the method is competitive with flow matching methods in Euclidean simulations and gives lower Wasserstein errors than tailored methods on several scientific datasets.
AI.conclusion: Generation error decreases as sample size increases, and convergence rates depend on the metric complexity of the target objects, tail moments and fitting accuracy.

title: KQML-Liver: Interpretable Hybrid Quantum Machine Learning with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Liver Disease Classification
summary: Liver disease remains a major global health concern, highlighting the need for reliable and accessible early detection methods. Although recent advances in machine learning, deep learning and quantum machine learning (QML) have introduced promising diagnostic tools, many approaches suffer from limited interpretability and inflated performance caused by data leakage or overly simplistic evaluation protocols. These constraints reduce their reliability in real-world clinical practice. This paper proposes KQML-Liver, a hybrid framework that integrates QML with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) to enhance predictive performance and interpretability. The architecture combines parameterized quantum circuits for expressive feature representation with KAN-based functional mappings that capture nonlinear relationships in an interpretable manner. Evaluated on the Indian Liver Patient Dataset (ILPD) under a rigorous preprocessing protocol preventing data leakage, the proposed model achieves 82% classification accuracy and 100% recall, detecting all positive cases, outperforming existing baselines while providing improved transparency in clinical predictions. These results suggest that hybrid KAN-quantum architectures offer a promising direction for interpretable AI-assisted medical diagnosis.

AI.tldr: KQML-Liver is a hybrid quantum machine learning model that combines parameterized quantum circuits with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for liver disease classification on the ILPD dataset. It reports 82% accuracy and 100% recall under a leakage-free preprocessing protocol.
AI.motivation: Many ML approaches to liver disease diagnosis have limited interpretability and inflated performance from data leakage or simplistic evaluation protocols.
AI.method: Parameterized quantum circuits provide expressive feature representation, and KAN-based functional mappings capture nonlinear relationships in an interpretable way. The model is evaluated under a preprocessing protocol designed to prevent data leakage.
AI.result: On the Indian Liver Patient Dataset the model achieves 82% classification accuracy and 100% recall, detecting all positive cases, and it outperforms the existing baselines reported in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid KAN-quantum architectures are a promising direction for interpretable AI-assisted medical diagnosis.

title: Dual Representation Enhanced Diffusion Policy for Flexible Job Shop Scheduling
summary: The Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling Problem (FJSP) is a fundamental and challenging optimization problem in smart manufacturing. Although recent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches can learn effective scheduling policies through interaction with the environment, their performance often degrades as problem scale and processing-time uncertainty increase. In this paper, we propose DredRL, a dual representation enhanced diffusion-policy reinforcement learning scheduler. DredRL first constructs enhanced dual representations of operations and machines through self- and cross-attention mechanisms to capture both intra-entity and inter-entity dependencies. A diffusion model is further employed as the policy network, generating scheduling decisions through iterative denoising conditioned on the encoded state to enhance policy expressiveness and robustness. Extensive experiments on synthetic, public, large-scale, and stochastic FJSP benchmarks demonstrate that DredRL outperforms state-of-the-art learning-based schedulers across most configurations. Compared with SOTA learning-based methods, DredRL reduces makespan by up to 5.44% on synthetic instances. It also achieves the best learning-based performance on three of four public benchmarks and outperforms the stochasticity-aware algorithms on stochastic benchmarks. These results demonstrate that combining enhanced dual representations with diffusion-based policies provides an effective and robust approach for large scale scalable FJSP scheduling in complicated environment.

AI.tldr: DredRL is a deep reinforcement learning scheduler for flexible job-shop scheduling that uses dual self- and cross-attention representations of operations and machines, with a diffusion model as the policy. It reduces makespan by up to 5.44% against learning-based methods on synthetic instances.
AI.motivation: Existing DRL schedulers degrade as problem scale and processing-time uncertainty grow in FJSP, a fundamental problem in smart manufacturing.
AI.method: Enhanced dual representations of operations and machines are built through self- and cross-attention to capture intra-entity and inter-entity dependencies. A diffusion model serves as the policy network and generates scheduling decisions by iterative denoising conditioned on the encoded state.
AI.result: Compared with state-of-the-art learning-based methods, DredRL reduces makespan by up to 5.44% on synthetic instances. It achieves the best learning-based performance on three of four public benchmarks and outperforms stochasticity-aware algorithms on stochastic benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Combining dual representations with diffusion-based policies gives an effective and robust approach to large-scale FJSP scheduling.

title: Multi-head Quantum Neural Networks: Replacing Transformer Blocks with NISQ Modules inside a 30-Billion-Parameter LLM
comment: 24 pages, 5 figures, 21 tables
summary: We introduce the multi-head quantum neural network (QNN), a quantum module compatible with noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices that can replace transformer blocks inside pre-trained large language models (LLMs) with little loss in accuracy and with far fewer parameters than the blocks it replaces. Encoding a model's $D$ hidden neurons into a qubit register is the obstacle: amplitude encoding scales poorly in circuit depth and angle encoding in qubit count, so neither is practical at production-scale width. We instead partition the hidden space into $k$ disjoint heads, angle-encode each into an $n_q$-qubit register, process the heads in parallel, and couple them through constrained classical linear layers, the mixers. Performing surgery on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, we show that a single multi-head QNN with $145\,281$ trainable parameters ($D=2048$, $k=32$, $n_q=8$, $L=4$) can replace a contiguous span of eight transformer blocks, displacing $16.33\%$ of the model's parameters. Ablations show that, for a single replaced block, the quantum heads (circuits followed by a learned readout), and not the classical mixers alone, recover the displaced function, whereas for fused spans the mixers alone come within $1$-$3\%$ of the full module in perplexity. Whether this benefit is specific to trained, entangling quantum circuits is not established: controls that switch the entangler off (two seeds), or freeze the circuit at its initial or at uniformly random angles (one seed), beat the full module on held-out perplexity, and a parameter-matched classical multilayer perceptron remains a few percent ahead of the full module. We train classically with exact statevector simulation, then execute the quantum heads of our fusion checkpoints on a $156$-qubit IBM Heron processor, showing that NISQ-scale quantum modules can be installed in a production-scale LLM and run on hardware.

AI.tldr: Multi-head quantum neural networks (QNNs) are NISQ-compatible modules that replace contiguous spans of transformer blocks in a 30B-parameter LLM, and one was run on a 156-qubit IBM Heron processor. The replacement uses 145,281 trainable parameters for eight blocks, but controls show the quantum circuits are not clearly responsible for the benefit.
AI.motivation: Encoding a model's hidden neurons into qubits is the obstacle, since amplitude encoding scales poorly in circuit depth and angle encoding in qubit count, so neither is practical at production width.
AI.method: The hidden space is partitioned into k disjoint heads, each angle-encoded into an n_q-qubit register and processed in parallel, and the heads are coupled by constrained classical linear mixers. The model is trained classically with exact statevector simulation, and the quantum heads of the fusion checkpoints are executed on hardware.
AI.result: On Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, one multi-head QNN with 145,281 parameters (D = 2048, k = 32, n_q = 8, L = 4) replaces eight contiguous blocks and displaces 16.33% of the model's parameters. Controls that switch off the entangler or freeze the circuit beat the full module on held-out perplexity, and a parameter-matched classical MLP stays a few percent ahead.
AI.conclusion: NISQ-scale quantum modules can be installed in a production-scale LLM and run on hardware, but the abstract does not establish a specific benefit from quantum circuits.

title: CastWorld: Benchmarking Context-Aware Agentic Time Series Forecasting Beyond Predictive Accuracy
summary: Agentic time series forecasting extends conventional approaches beyond one-shot numerical prediction toward autonomous, context-aware interaction. However, existing benchmarks offer limited integrated support for diverse contextual information, forecasting-specific adaptive interactions, and systematic evaluation of forecasting agents. In this paper, we introduce CastWorld, an agentic benchmark for context-aware time series forecasting. First, its context-rich dataset suite spans 8 domains and 25 real-world datasets, covering external variables, events, and historical cases under a unified context specification. Second, a lightweight, modular forecasting-native harness provides 49 core tools and a state-adaptive loop that tracks forecast versions and enables iterative evidence gathering and forecast revision. Intermediate forecasts can expose information gaps, while newly acquired evidence guides subsequent revisions and final version selection. Third, model-level evaluation assesses forecast quality, process execution, behavioral trustworthiness, and resource efficiency through decision trajectories and forecast-version histories. Also, systems-level evaluation compares predictive accuracy across forecasting systems. Experiments reveal distinct decision behaviors among agents with comparable accuracy. Additional interactions do not necessarily improve forecasts, and agents may fail to select their best previously generated predictions. Allowing evidence acquisition during forecast refinement improves task-aware forecast scores across all three evaluated models. CastWorld provides a reusable foundation for evaluating agentic time series forecasting under controlled conditions.

AI.tldr: CastWorld is an agentic benchmark for context-aware time series forecasting, with 25 datasets across 8 domains, 49 forecasting tools and evaluation of forecast quality, process, trustworthiness and resource efficiency. It finds that more interaction does not necessarily improve forecasts.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks offer limited support for diverse context, forecasting-specific adaptive interaction and systematic evaluation of forecasting agents.
AI.method: The context-rich dataset suite spans external variables, events and historical cases under a unified specification. A forecasting-native harness provides 49 core tools and a state-adaptive loop that tracks forecast versions. Model-level and systems-level evaluations use decision trajectories and version histories.
AI.result: Agents with comparable accuracy show distinct decision behaviors. Additional interactions do not necessarily improve forecasts, and agents may fail to select their best earlier forecasts. Allowing evidence acquisition during refinement improves task-aware forecast scores for all three evaluated models.
AI.conclusion: CastWorld provides a reusable foundation for evaluating agentic forecasting under controlled conditions.

title: Quantum Recurrent Architectures for Financial Time Series Prediction
summary: This study evaluates quantum classical hybrid recurrent architectures for financial time-series forecasting: a Quantum Long Short-Term Memory (QLSTM) network and Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) with lag-based inputs. Classical lag vectors are encoded into quantum states via amplitude encoding, which compactly represents normalized observations but requires nontrivial state preparation; the QLSTM gates and the QRC reservoir are implemented with parameterized quantum circuits, while classical optimizers train the interface and readout layers. On a monthly revenue series extended to 1056 months by a Gaussian-process--hidden-Markov generator, with a fixed chronological 70/15/15 split and one-step-ahead forecasts, we compare both models against a full-size LSTM, a classical control matched in parameter budget and interface architecture, a small plain LSTM, and classical reservoir computing, over ten seeds and against persistence, seasonal-naive and SARIMA benchmark forecasts. The QLSTM, with 2,105 parameters, is statistically indistinguishable from an LSTM 126 times larger, but equally indistinguishable from the matched classical control and from a plain LSTM of the same budget, so its parameter efficiency cannot be attributed to the quantum circuits. The quantum reservoir is worse than a classical reservoir of equal feature dimension in all ten seeds and worse than SARIMA, whereas all recurrent models and both classical reservoirs improve on SARIMA by about 2\% in RMSE. In a 24-month rolling-origin backtest the classical LSTMs degrade more slowly than the QLSTM. We find no evidence of a quantum accuracy or parameter-efficiency advantage in this low-dimensional setting.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates quantum-classical hybrid recurrent models, QLSTM and quantum reservoir computing, for financial time-series forecasting and finds no quantum accuracy or parameter-efficiency advantage in this low-dimensional setting. The QLSTM is statistically indistinguishable from a classical control matched in parameter budget.
AI.motivation: Quantum recurrent architectures are proposed for financial forecasting, and their advantage over classical models of matched size needs to be tested.
AI.method: Classical lag vectors are amplitude-encoded into quantum states, with the QLSTM gates and the quantum reservoir implemented as parameterized circuits. Models are compared over ten seeds against a full-size LSTM, a parameter-matched classical control, a small plain LSTM, classical reservoir computing, and persistence, seasonal-naive and SARIMA baselines, on a 1056-month revenue series with a 70/15/15 chronological split.
AI.result: The QLSTM, with 2,105 parameters, is statistically indistinguishable from an LSTM 126 times larger, and also from the matched control and a plain LSTM of the same budget. The quantum reservoir is worse than a classical reservoir of equal feature dimension in all ten seeds and worse than SARIMA, while all recurrent models and classical reservoirs improve on SARIMA by about 2% in RMSE.
AI.conclusion: No evidence of a quantum advantage appears in this setting, and the QLSTM's parameter efficiency cannot be attributed to its quantum circuits.

title: Matrix-Based Ant Colony Search with Batched Decoding for Hierarchical Replenishment Routing: A Stylized Case Study Based on Korean City Data
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables; code, data and raw records in the ancillary files
summary: We study a stylized single-vehicle replenishment-routing problem in which the cities of a national logistics network are both demand points and supply points: a vehicle of limited capacity delivers to every city once, and when its load is insufficient for the next city it must detour to a city already served that can still supply goods. A 100-node benchmark is built from Korean population and geographic data, with the cities divided into 10 levels; the per-visit supply coefficient and the allowed number of stops decrease geometrically with the level. Building on matrix-based ant colony optimization, we keep the states of the whole colony in arrays, couple route construction with a fixed greedy replenishment-decoding policy, and evaluate the candidate moves of a local search in batches. With frozen parameters and 30 runs on seeds never used for tuning, the matrix-based ant colony search with the batch local search (MACO) reaches a mean total distance of 3081.7 km; a genetic algorithm equipped with the same local search at the same frequency reaches 3074.9 km (no significant difference), and a MAX-MIN ant system with the same local search 3142.2 km. Ablation identifies the batch local search as the main contributor to solution quality; a load-aware transition factor gives no significant gain. Within the parameter ranges tested, raising the supply coefficients of the cities below the top level shortens the route more than relaxing the stop limits, which are not binding here.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes matrix-based ant colony optimization with batched local search for a stylized single-vehicle replenishment-routing problem on a 100-city benchmark built from Korean data. The method reaches a mean total distance of 3081.7 km, close to a genetic algorithm with the same local search at 3074.9 km.
AI.motivation: In a national logistics network each city is both a demand and a supply point, and a vehicle must detour to replenish when its load is insufficient, which makes routing harder than standard vehicle routing.
AI.method: Matrix-based ant colony optimization keeps the colony states in arrays, couples route construction with a fixed greedy replenishment-decoding policy, and evaluates local-search candidate moves in batches. Parameters are frozen and results are averaged over 30 runs on seeds not used for tuning.
AI.result: MACO reaches a mean total distance of 3081.7 km, the genetic algorithm with the same local search reaches 3074.9 km (no significant difference), and a MAX-MIN ant system with the same local search reaches 3142.2 km. Batch local search is the main contributor to quality, and a load-aware transition factor gives no significant gain.
AI.conclusion: Within the tested ranges, raising the supply coefficients of lower-level cities shortens routes more than relaxing stop limits, which do not bind.

title: Breath-Dx: A Time Series Classification Benchmark for Disease Screening with eNose
comment: IEEE ICDM 2026 - Best Paper Runner-Up (Applied Track)
summary: Electronic nose (eNose) technology offers a portable, non-invasive route for disease screening via exhaled breath analysis. However, progress in the field is hindered by the lack of systematic benchmarks that compare machine learning methods under realistic conditions, particularly sensor drift, a known but rarely quantified failure mode. Most existing studies rely on small, private datasets with inconsistent protocols, rendering results non-comparable and slowing progress. We introduce Breath-Dx, the first comprehensive benchmark of time series classification methods for breath-based disease screening. Our work leverages the Scent of Health (S-OH) dataset, the largest public clinical eNose collection to date, comprising 1,234 patients across nine diagnostic groups, each providing a 17-channel multivariate time series with explicit temporal train/test splits that account for sensor drift. We systematically evaluate 10 methods spanning four families: feature-based tabular learners, convolution-based models, graph-based, and time series architectures. All methods degrade significantly under temporal validation (0.05-0.12 AUC drop compared to random cross-validation), confirming that drift embeds a strong temporal signal. Under this realistic evaluation, the best methods achieve ROC AUC of 0.74-0.76 for some lung conditions, though others remain near chance. Recurrent architectures show the most consistent performance across diseases, while specialized time series methods achieve the highest peak results. Demographic confounders matter: breath signals provide independent diagnostic value for some conditions but add little beyond age for others. We release the S-OH dataset, all temporal splits, evaluation protocols, and code to enable reproducible research and accelerate progress in clinical breathomics.

AI.tldr: Breath-Dx is a benchmark of 10 time series classification methods for breath-based disease screening with electronic noses, evaluated on the public Scent of Health dataset under temporal splits that account for sensor drift. Performance drops by 0.05-0.12 AUC under temporal validation, and the best methods reach ROC AUC of 0.74-0.76 for some lung conditions.
AI.motivation: Progress in eNose disease screening is hindered by small private datasets with inconsistent protocols and by the lack of systematic benchmarks that account for sensor drift, a known but rarely quantified failure mode.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 10 methods from four families (feature-based tabular learners, convolution-based models, graph-based models and time series architectures) on the 1,234-patient S-OH dataset with nine diagnostic groups and 17-channel time series, using explicit temporal train/test splits.
AI.result: All methods degrade significantly under temporal validation compared with random cross-validation, with a 0.05-0.12 AUC drop. Recurrent architectures are the most consistent across diseases, specialized time series methods reach the highest peak results, and some conditions stay near chance. Breath signals add diagnostic value beyond age for some conditions but little for others.
AI.conclusion: Temporal evaluation is necessary for realistic eNose benchmarking because drift carries a strong temporal signal; the released dataset, splits, protocols and code are meant to support reproducible research in clinical breathomics.

title: TopoST: Topology-Conditioned Node Specialization for Urban Spatio-Temporal Foundation Models
summary: Urban spatio-temporal foundation models must share knowledge across diverse urban scenarios while accommodating heterogeneous node dynamics. Our analysis of 20+ datasets spanning diverse urban scenarios reveals recurring local graph structures across datasets alongside substantial node heterogeneity within local subgraphs. Motivated by these observations, we propose TopoST, which combines shared learning over local subgraphs with topology-conditioned node specialization. The key insight is to make node specialization itself transferable through a shared topology-to-parameter mapping. This mapping uses identity-independent topological representations to generate node-specific temporal and spatial dependency parameters, enabling direct specialization for unseen nodes without target-specific embeddings or model updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TopoST achieves remarkable zero-shot generalization across unseen cities and tasks, highlighting topology-conditioned node specialization as an effective mechanism for transferable urban spatio-temporal foundation models. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TopoST is an urban spatio-temporal foundation model that generates node-specific temporal and spatial dependency parameters from identity-independent local topology, so it can specialize to unseen nodes without target embeddings or model updates. It reportedly achieves zero-shot generalization across unseen cities and tasks.
AI.motivation: Urban spatio-temporal foundation models must share knowledge across scenarios while handling heterogeneous node dynamics, and existing approaches do not make node specialization itself transferable across datasets.
AI.method: TopoST combines shared learning over local subgraphs with topology-conditioned node specialization, using a shared topology-to-parameter mapping that takes identity-independent topological representations as input.
AI.result: The abstract reports that TopoST achieves remarkable zero-shot generalization across unseen cities and tasks, and it does not give specific numbers in the abstract. The analysis of more than 20 datasets found recurring local graph structures and substantial node heterogeneity within local subgraphs.
AI.conclusion: Topology-conditioned node specialization is presented as an effective and transferable mechanism for urban spatio-temporal foundation models.

title: Right Answers, Inconsistent Evidence: Source-Level Counterfactual Auditing of Large Audio-Language Models
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Submitted to ICASSP 2027
summary: A large audio-language model (LALM) can answer "is a cat present?" about a mixture correctly, and its confidence can drop when the cat is removed, yet this does not show that it can tell the cat's presence from its absence. We introduce TRACE. It deletes the queried source and each rival in turn and asks whether every view still containing that sound outscores the view with it removed. Across 8 LALMs and 3,456 controlled mixtures, 6.3% of correct answers fail this ordering: the target-absent view scores at or above some target-present view, a conflict no shared threshold repairs. A target-only score check misses 42.5% of them. The share rises from 4.9% to 8.4% as target SNR falls from +5 to -5 dB, even on units correct at every level, and survives loudness and re-pairing controls. Accuracy certifies the answer; TRACE audits whether it orders presence above absence. Code and data: this https URL.

AI.tldr: TRACE audits whether a large audio-language model orders the presence of a sound above its absence, not only whether its answer is correct. Across 8 LALMs and 3,456 controlled mixtures, 6.3% of correct answers fail this check.
AI.motivation: A correct answer from a large audio-language model does not show that the model distinguishes a sound's presence from its absence, and a target-only confidence check misses many of these failures.
AI.method: TRACE deletes the queried source and each rival source in turn and tests whether every view that still contains the target sound outscores the view with the target removed.
