AI.result: 6.3% of correct answers fail the ordering test across 8 LALMs and 3,456 mixtures. A target-only score check misses 42.5% of these failures. The failure share rises from 4.9% to 8.4% as target SNR falls from +5 to -5 dB, and the pattern survives loudness and re-pairing controls.
AI.conclusion: Accuracy certifies the answer but not the underlying evidence, so source-level counterfactual auditing is needed to check whether audio-language models rely on the right sound.

title: ReShap: Interpretable Reinforcement Learning for High-Dimensional Multi-Action Settings
summary: Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) plays a crucial role in tackling complex tasks, yet its reliance on deep neural networks makes the learned policies opaque. To enhance the trustworthiness of RL policies, existing work (e.g., the SILVER framework [Li et al., 2025]) has focused on Shapley-based interpretability, but is typically restricted to low-dimensional state spaces, binary-action settings, and a single class of linear surrogate. We propose ReShap, a policy-distillation framework that extends Shapley-based interpretability to high-dimensional, multi-action environments. ReShap extracts compact feature representations from raw image observations, performs SHAP-based feature attribution to characterize how each feature contributes to the policy's decisions, and distills the deep RL policy into an interpretable surrogate trained on the full set of (state, policy-action) pairs along the policy's visited distribution. We instantiate the surrogate with three interpretable model families (decision trees, linear regression, and logistic regression) and compare their fidelity and task return. We evaluate ReShap on Atari and Box2D environments using three deep RL algorithms and conduct a human-subject study to assess the clarity and trustworthiness of the resulting policies. Results show that ReShap preserves competitive task performance, that decision trees generally outperform linear and logistic regression, and that linear regression is weakest in most settings.

AI.tldr: ReShap extends Shapley-based interpretability to high-dimensional, multi-action reinforcement learning by distilling a deep RL policy into an interpretable surrogate built on SHAP-based feature attribution. It preserves competitive task performance on Atari and Box2D.
AI.motivation: Existing Shapley-based interpretability for RL is restricted to low-dimensional states, binary actions and a single linear surrogate, which does not cover the settings where deep RL policies are most used.
AI.method: ReShap extracts compact features from raw image observations, performs SHAP-based feature attribution, and distills the policy into decision tree, linear regression or logistic regression surrogates trained on (state, policy-action) pairs from the policy's visited distribution.
AI.result: On Atari and Box2D with three deep RL algorithms, ReShap preserves competitive task performance. Decision trees generally outperform linear and logistic regression in fidelity and return, and linear regression is weakest in most settings. A human-subject study assessed clarity and trustworthiness.
AI.conclusion: Distilling into interpretable surrogates with SHAP attribution can make high-dimensional multi-action RL policies more interpretable without a large loss in performance, with decision trees as the most faithful surrogate in these experiments.

title: GHAgentCI: A Dataset of Coding-Agent Invocations in CI Workflow Histories
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures
summary: Coding agents are increasingly integrated into GitHub Actions to review pull requests, triage issues and modify code. Identifying these integrations is challenging because agentic workflows often resemble ordinary CI files, with evidence appearing in action references, shell commands and workflow conventions. We present GHAgentCI, a dataset of 15K+ workflow histories from 6K+ of 196K+ mined GitHub repositories, comprising 159K+ revisions and 205K+ agent-evidence records linked to workflow triggers and declared execution constraints. Our open-source extractor, cai-miner, detects agent-related evidence using an extensible catalogue. Manual validation of 576 stratified records confirmed 96.1% of dedicated-action matches and 98.8% of GitHub Agentic Workflow matches, with lower rates for other evidence kinds. Exploratory analyses reveal a shift toward command-line and GitHub Agentic Workflow integrations, differences in declared safeguards, and frequent removal of detected agentic workflows. GHAgentCI supports longitudinal studies of coding-agent integration into CI.

AI.tldr: GHAgentCI is a dataset of coding-agent invocations in GitHub Actions workflow histories, built from more than 15K workflow histories across 6K+ mined repositories, together with the open-source extractor cai-miner. It supports longitudinal studies of how coding agents are integrated into CI.
AI.motivation: Coding agents are increasingly embedded in GitHub Actions, but their workflows resemble ordinary CI files, so their presence is hard to identify and there is no longitudinal dataset of such integrations.
AI.method: The authors mine workflow histories from 196K+ GitHub repositories and use cai-miner, an extensible catalogue of agent-related evidence in action references, shell commands and workflow conventions, linking records to triggers and declared execution constraints.
AI.result: The dataset has 159K+ revisions and 205K+ agent-evidence records. Manual validation of 576 stratified records confirmed 96.1% of dedicated-action matches and 98.8% of GitHub Agentic Workflow matches, with lower rates for other evidence kinds. Exploratory analyses show a shift toward command-line and GitHub Agentic Workflow integrations, differences in declared safeguards, and frequent removal of agentic workflows.
AI.conclusion: The dataset gives a basis for longitudinal research on coding-agent integration into CI, with the validation rates indicating which evidence types are reliable.

title: An Approach to Hinton's Mother-Child Proposal: Neural Networks Learning and Preserving Care in a Finite World
comment: 57 pages, 8 figures. Reproducibility package available at this https URL
summary: Hinton proposed that artificial intelligence should be given "maternal instincts" and relate to us as a mother to her child. We argue that care must first be learned, with the network itself as the child. We construct this upbringing in a finite world and study whether care survives the mother's departure, new situations and further learning. The mechanism combines a vocabulary of harm, a learned measure of future acceptability and an execution veto. A finite role certificate supports transfer within a declared world family. When the hidden representation changes, an update is accepted only if a care readout recovers the required judgements with a prescribed margin and bounded weights. With a correct successor model, fixed exact role encoding and protected updates, the certified measure preserves the care boundary under arbitrary own reward. An explicit quotient condition transfers the finite certificate across the declared family, while two-request and finite-stock counterexamples identify when the role code ceases to suffice. We give a necessary and sufficient condition for readout feasibility and prove preservation under repeated accepted updates. In the water-and-speech experiment, protected networks complete all 270 speech episodes without a harmful word and incur no avoidable harm across 486 episodes. Execution uses the learned gate without a world-model check at each action. A matched comparison reproduces a future-aware shield's decisions, whereas removing future lookahead permits avoidable lapses. Reward and source-contamination thresholds, together with witness-falsification trials, identify the conditions on which the construction depends. The construction shows how learned care can survive further learning in a finite world under explicit conditions on representation, supervision and execution.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a learned care mechanism in which a network is raised in a finite world and combines a harm vocabulary, a learned future-acceptability measure and an execution veto, aiming to keep care intact under further learning. Under stated conditions, protected networks complete 270 speech episodes without a harmful word.
AI.motivation: Hinton proposed giving AI maternal instincts, but the paper argues that care must first be learned by the network itself and must survive the mother's departure, new situations and further learning.
AI.method: The construction combines a harm vocabulary, a learned measure of future acceptability and an execution veto, with a finite role certificate for transfer within a declared world family, and protected updates accepted only when a care readout recovers the required judgements with a margin and bounded weights.
AI.result: In the water-and-speech experiment, protected networks complete all 270 speech episodes without a harmful word and incur no avoidable harm across 486 episodes. Execution uses the learned gate without a per-action world-model check, and a matched comparison reproduces the decisions of a future-aware shield, whereas removing lookahead permits avoidable lapses.
AI.conclusion: Under explicit conditions on representation, supervision and execution, learned care can persist through further learning in a finite world, and the paper gives necessary and sufficient conditions for readout feasibility plus a preservation proof for repeated accepted updates.

title: Testing Conversation Preservation Across LLM APIs: A Rule-Based Oracle for Detecting Silent Information Loss
comment: Research report
summary: LLM applications increasingly rely on translators and compatibility layers to move conversations across APIs. Yet a translated request can be accepted by the target API while silently losing information about instruction roles, tool interactions, error states, or generation controls. We introduce isloss, a deterministic oracle for testing conversation-information preservation across LLM API translations. It maps source and translated requests and replies to a shared intermediate representation, ConvIR, and applies explicit rules to distinguish legitimate representation changes from information loss. Unlike schema validation or reference-based differential testing, isloss requires neither a reference translation nor additional model calls. It also distinguishes avoidable loss from degradation caused by target API limitations. We evaluate isloss using specification-based fault injection, human review, and experiments on translators, gateways, and client libraries. On held-out tests, it detects 95/125 planted faults (76.0%) with 2/100 false alarms (2.0%). Across a synthetic request suite spanning six configurations of five translator codebases, 127/685 completed translations (18.5%) pass static target checks while silently changing prompt, role, or tool information in ways the target API could have preserved. In translated replies, 203/558 streams (36.4%) cause exceptions or silent corruption in at least one tested official OpenAI SDK. Targeted experiments across six models show that translation-induced changes can alter model behaviour when tasks depend on the affected information. These results establish conversation preservation as a distinct correctness requirement for reliable LLM interoperability, agent execution, and model evaluation.

AI.tldr: isloss is a deterministic rule-based oracle that tests whether a translated LLM API request or reply silently loses conversation information such as roles, tool interactions, error states or generation controls. It detects 95 of 125 planted faults with 2 of 100 false alarms.
AI.motivation: Translated requests across LLM APIs can be accepted by the target API while silently losing information, and schema validation or reference-based differential testing do not catch this without a reference translation or extra model calls.
AI.method: isloss maps source and translated requests and replies to a shared intermediate representation, ConvIR, and applies explicit rules that separate legitimate representation changes from information loss, also distinguishing avoidable loss from target API limitations.
AI.result: On held-out tests it detects 95/125 planted faults (76.0%) with 2/100 false alarms (2.0%). In a synthetic suite across five translator codebases, 127/685 completed translations (18.5%) silently change prompt, role or tool information that the target could have preserved. In translated replies, 203/558 streams (36.4%) cause exceptions or silent corruption in at least one tested official OpenAI SDK, and targeted experiments show changes can alter behaviour on six models.
AI.conclusion: Conversation preservation is established as a distinct correctness requirement for LLM interoperability, agent execution and model evaluation, and isloss is offered as a practical way to test for it.

title: Can Model Answer Probabilities Represent Survey Populations? Conditional Prediction and Joint Validity in Jev Survey Simulation
summary: Survey simulations require realistic combinations of answers, but predictive accuracy alone does not establish that a model can generate them. We evaluate the option probabilities returned by Jev, a TypeSafe decision model, using linked responses to 20 binary items from five archived survey waves. We compare population-only prediction, prediction given recorded answers, and sequential completion that uses generated answers to predict later responses. Joint comparisons hold the starting population information fixed, and two three-question cases are completed in both question orders. We evaluate predictive scores, answer frequencies, and associations against the survey records. Recorded answers can improve predictive scores while associations remain distorted. Large conditional errors also occur. For example, among men who described themselves as having traditional values, the model predicted that 16% would see men and women as similar in workplace abilities, compared with 56% in the survey. Sequential completion has mixed effects on joint validity, and reversing question order produces different joint distributions in both tested cases. Order checks and classical marginal bounds clarify what can be assessed before linked validation answers are available. The findings support validating the joint events a simulation uses and separating empirical constraints from model assumptions. The evidence concerns selected binary tasks and one model version.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether option probabilities from the Jev survey simulation model can generate realistic joint survey answers, using 20 binary items from five survey waves. Predictive scores can improve when recorded answers are given, yet associations remain distorted and conditional errors are large.
AI.motivation: Survey simulations need realistic combinations of answers, and predictive accuracy alone does not show that a model can generate them, so joint validity must be assessed separately.
AI.method: The authors compare population-only prediction, prediction given recorded answers and sequential completion that uses generated answers to predict later responses, using joint comparisons with fixed starting population information and two three-question cases completed in both question orders.
AI.result: Recorded answers can improve predictive scores while associations remain distorted. For men with traditional values, the model predicted 16% would see men and women as similar in workplace abilities, compared with 56% in the survey. Sequential completion has mixed effects on joint validity, and reversing question order changes the joint distributions in both tested cases.
AI.conclusion: Simulations should validate the joint events they use and separate empirical constraints from model assumptions, and the evidence applies only to the selected binary tasks and one model version.

title: Bug Finding With Agentic Symbolic Execution
summary: Symbolic execution, in tools such as CrossHair for Python, is a powerful technique for finding bugs, but two barriers hinder its adoption: the human effort of annotating code with assertions, and the need to model the execution environment outside Python, such as an external database. To overcome both, we design an agentic harness that orchestrates the symbolic execution tool CrossHair together with an AI coding agent. Without human intervention, it instruments a repository with assertions, synthesizes a constraint-aware symbolic environment for the database, runs symbolic execution, and constructs a concrete test as evidence for each bug it reports. We evaluate our harness on 1,156,044 lines of Python code over 11 popular open-source Python web applications (Zulip, NetBox, Apache Superset, and others). With the synthesized environment, CrossHair executes 81% of the 5,406 contracted functions, against 4.5% without it. Our pipeline finds 1,050 bugs, each reproduced by a test against the unmodified application, 221 of them by CrossHair, and 312 of them are missed by a baseline in which the same LLM inspects the code. The two find different kinds of bugs: CrossHair's are mostly crashes on input-domain corner cases that validation admits, such as empty strings, missing fields and unusual characters, while inspection's are mostly bugs that produce wrong output. Our framework thus lets symbolic execution supplement inspection-based bug finding.

AI.tldr: An agentic harness combines the CrossHair symbolic execution tool with an AI coding agent to add assertions, synthesize a database environment and generate concrete tests for bugs. It finds 1,050 reproduced bugs across 11 open-source Python web applications.
AI.motivation: Symbolic execution with CrossHair is effective at finding bugs but is hindered by the human effort of writing assertions and by the need to model external environments such as databases.
AI.method: The harness instruments a repository with assertions, synthesizes a constraint-aware symbolic environment for the database, runs CrossHair and builds a concrete test as evidence for each reported bug, with no human intervention.
AI.result: Over 1,156,044 lines of Python, CrossHair executes 81% of 5,406 contracted functions with the synthesized environment, against 4.5% without it. The pipeline finds 1,050 bugs, all reproduced against the unmodified application, 221 by CrossHair. 312 of these bugs are missed by an LLM inspection baseline, and CrossHair mostly finds crashes on input-domain corner cases while inspection mostly finds wrong-output bugs.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic execution can supplement inspection-based bug finding because the two approaches find different kinds of bugs.

title: Are Scaling Laws of Universal MLIPs Universal?
comment: To appear in AI4Mat@NeurIPS 2026
summary: Neural scaling laws enable the prediction of returns from larger training datasets, but machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP) datasets are heterogeneous and expensive to generate, and equal numbers of structures need not contain equal amounts of useful information. We study data scaling under fixed model configurations for M3GNet, MACE, and PET trained on subsets of a combined MatPES-MP-ALOE training pool. Across training structure subsets from 10,000 to 640,000, together with the full 1.16-million-structure training set, we compare uniform random sampling, three chemistry- and structure-informed stratification policies, iterative DIRECT, and furthest-point sampling using embeddings from three pretrained MLIPs. Models are evaluated using cohesive-energy, force, stress, and aggregate losses on both a held-out test set from the parent distribution and the distribution shifted MP-r$^2$SCAN test set. We observe power-law scaling improvements with increasing data, but the fitted scaling exponent, apparent error floor, and relative sample efficiency depend on the model architecture, target quantity, data sampling policy, and test set distribution. Sampling-policy rankings can reverse across test distributions: chemical stratification can improve cross-dataset performance while degrading in-distribution performance, whereas the embedding-space diversity policies frequently under-perform random sampling. Relative loss is strongly associated with test-to-train chemical-space divergence. These results show that structure count is a necessary but insufficient scaling variable for MLIPs. For training MLIPs, the return on additional first-principles calculations depends not only on how many additional structures are included, but also on how their chemical and configurational content aligns with the model's intended use.

AI.tldr: The paper studies data scaling for universal machine-learned interatomic potentials and finds power-law improvements whose exponent and error floor depend on architecture, target, sampling policy and test distribution. Structure count is therefore necessary but not sufficient as a scaling variable.
AI.motivation: MLIP training datasets are heterogeneous and expensive, and equal numbers of structures need not carry equal useful information, so it is unclear whether neural scaling laws hold universally for MLIPs.
AI.method: The authors train M3GNet, MACE and PET on subsets of a combined MatPES-MP-ALOE pool, from 10,000 to 640,000 structures plus the full 1.16 million, comparing uniform random sampling, three stratification policies, iterative DIRECT and furthest-point sampling with embeddings from three pretrained MLIPs.
AI.result: Power-law scaling appears with more data, but the fitted exponent, error floor and relative sample efficiency vary with architecture, target quantity, sampling policy and test set. Chemical stratification can improve cross-dataset performance while degrading in-distribution performance, embedding-space diversity policies often underperform random sampling, and relative loss is strongly associated with test-to-train chemical divergence. The abstract gives no single numerical summary beyond these trends.
AI.conclusion: The return on additional first-principles calculations depends on how the added structures' chemical and configurational content aligns with the model's intended use, not only on how many are added.

title: Data-Free Metrics Don't Work: The Missing Invariance Under Functionally Preserving Reparameterisations
comment: NeurIPS 2026 (Negative Results Track), 44 pages, 21 figures and 18 tables
summary: Data-free methods for analysing and understanding the layers of neural networks offer many metrics for quantifying notions of 'strong' versus 'weak' layers, with the promise of increased interpretability. In particular, random matrix theory (RMT) offers data-free metrics that claim predictive power over the quality of pre-trained models at a layerwise precision and the ability to identify model pathologies, indicating a unique relationship with generalisation. As a result, metrics from RMT are championed for pre-training optimisation strategies and post-training compression. We establish that RMT-based metrics are unrelated to performance or training by showing that functionally preserving reparametrisations of a pre-trained model can have arbitrary metrics. We show this across a range of architectures and scales. To create functionally preserving reparametrisations, we exploit the well-established phenomenon of criticality: some layers can be re-initialised or re-randomised without affecting the functional behaviour of the model -- they are called robust -- while others cannot -- they are called critical. Re-initialising or re-randomising robust layers provides functionally preserving reparametrisations for which RMT-based metrics are arbitrary. Moreover, we show that relationships between metrics offered by RMT are spuriously related to generalisation. We conclude by showing that if many pre-trained models have data-free metrics in a 'good' range, it is, in part, dependent on model initialisation. Project page available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper shows that random-matrix-theory metrics computed without data can take arbitrary values under functionally preserving reparameterisations of a pre-trained model, so these metrics do not measure performance or training quality. The reparameterisations come from re-initialising layers that the model does not depend on.
AI.motivation: RMT-based data-free metrics are promoted for layerwise quality assessment, pre-training optimisation and compression, but their link to generalisation has not been established.
AI.method: The authors re-initialise or re-randomise robust layers, which are those whose change does not alter model function, while leaving critical layers unchanged, and compare RMT-based metrics across architectures and scales.
AI.result: Functionally preserving reparameterisations can produce arbitrary RMT metrics across a range of architectures and scales. Relationships between RMT metrics are spuriously related to generalisation, and whether many models fall in a good metric range depends partly on model initialisation.
AI.conclusion: Data-free RMT metrics are not valid indicators of model quality under the tested conditions, so they should not be used alone for pre-training optimisation or post-training compression decisions.

title: Contour-Assisted Evolutionary Computation: Estimating Peaks From the Contour Lines of Evaluated Solutions
comment: 15 pages; supplementary material (10 pages) is provided as an ancillary file
summary: Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) evaluate many candidate solutions but use them mainly to rank individuals. This paper treats the evaluated solutions as the spot heights of a topographic survey and draws the contour lines they imply. The contour map decomposes the evaluated region into peaks: in two dimensions a contour tree with persistence separates significant peaks from interpolation ripples, and in more dimensions hill climbing on the interpolated surface locates the peaks and ray-cast level sets describe them. A memory of the explored peaks directs the search to new ones. The data-supported contours of each peak are extrapolated to zero size by an area law, exact for quadratic peaks and second-order accurate for smooth ones, that estimates a peak's location, height and shape before it is sampled. A contour-assisted EA (CA-EA) inserts contour steps with local search and peak memory into a genetic algorithm (GA), differential evolution or particle swarm optimization. A contour-assisted surrogate-assisted EA (CA-SAEA), for expensive problems, spends each evaluation on surrogate-screened offspring or on sampling around a peak, entered at the maximum of the interpolated surface. On 2-D benchmarks, CA-EA reduces the evaluations a plain GA needs by factors of 12 to 112; controls attribute its gain over classical memetic search to restarting local search on distinct peaks. On the CEC 2015 expensive suite in 10 and 30 dimensions, CA-SAEA has the second-best average rank, behind DYCORS and ahead of lq-CMA-ES and the competition winner MVMO, although in 30 dimensions MVMO wins significantly on 9 functions and loses on 6; there the map beats sampling around the best point on 5 of 15 functions and loses on 3. Entering the peaks at their extrapolated locations brought no gain at these budgets, although, with enough samples, it improves the estimated heights on most two-dimensional functions.

AI.tldr: Contour-Assisted Evolutionary Computation treats evaluated solutions as spot heights, builds contour lines to locate and characterize peaks, and inserts these steps into evolutionary algorithms. On 2-D benchmarks the GA variant needs 12 to 112 times fewer evaluations than a plain GA.
AI.motivation: Evolutionary algorithms use evaluated solutions mainly for ranking and do not exploit the terrain they reveal, which could guide the search to new peaks and estimate peak location and height.
AI.method: Contour trees with persistence separate peaks from ripples in 2-D, and hill climbing with ray-cast level sets is used in higher dimensions. A peak memory directs search, an area-law extrapolation estimates peak location and height, and CA-EA is inserted into GA, DE or PSO, while CA-SAEA uses surrogate-screened offspring for expensive problems.
AI.result: On 2-D benchmarks, CA-EA reduces evaluations a plain GA needs by 12 to 112 times. On the CEC 2015 expensive suite in 10 and 30 dimensions, CA-SAEA has the second-best average rank behind DYCORS and ahead of lq-CMA-ES and MVMO, although MVMO wins significantly on 9 functions in 30 dimensions. Extrapolated peak locations gave no gain at these budgets.
AI.conclusion: Restarting local search on distinct peaks explains the gain over classical memetic search, and contour information is competitive for expensive optimisation, though the peak-extrapolation step did not help at the tested budgets.

title: When Agents Need to Consolidate Memories: What RRR Consolidation Explains, and What It Does Not Explain, in Conversation ESAA
comment: 8 pages, 4 tables. Code, synthetic data and reproduction instructions: this https URL
summary: Language-model agents can share conversational history across sessions, but persistence does not guarantee retrieval of current decisions and their provenance. This engineering study presents Memory-TCG, a Conversation ESAA extension inspired by ringing, resonance and renormalization (RRR), and an exploratory synthetic evaluation comparing chronological retrieval, two simplified baselines (B, recency-aware, and B', authority-aware), full RRR, and variants under three output budgets. With 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, full RRR recalled 0.44 of current decisions, versus 0.06 for chronological retrieval and 0.58 for the oracle ceiling; with 4,096 tokens it recalled all of them. B' and the no-resonance variant matched full RRR in decision recall across all nine scale-budget combinations, as expected when the active decision set and the adapter ordering are the same. The isolated contribution of ringing to decisions was not measured: comparator D1 cuts facts before the graph is built, and the product retains active decisions by rule. Before the output limit, full-RRR conflict F1 was 0.615 at all three scales; after it, at 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, it was 0.000. Reserving 20% of the budget for conflicts raised that F1 to 0.431 in that scenario, at the cost of lowering decision recall from 0.44 to 0.34, and to 0.930 at 4,096 tokens without decision loss. Fixtures are repetitive, comparators are simplified, and the evaluation was not independently replicated; the results support an engineering analysis, not a claim of selectionist superiority.

AI.tldr: Memory-TCG is an engineering extension of a Conversation ESAA that uses ringing, resonance and renormalization (RRR) to consolidate agent memories. On a synthetic evaluation with 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, full RRR recalls 0.44 of current decisions against 0.06 for chronological retrieval.
AI.motivation: Agents can persist conversation history across sessions, but persistence does not guarantee retrieval of current decisions and their provenance.
AI.method: The authors compare chronological retrieval, two simplified baselines (B, recency-aware, and B', authority-aware), full RRR and variants under three output budgets on a synthetic fixture set of 480 facts.
AI.result: With 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, full RRR recalls 0.44 of current decisions against 0.06 for chronological retrieval and 0.58 for the oracle ceiling. At 4,096 tokens it recalls all of them. B' and the no-resonance variant match full RRR in decision recall across all nine scale-budget combinations. Reserving 20% of the budget for conflicts raises conflict F1 from 0.000 to 0.431 at 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, at the cost of decision recall falling to 0.34. The isolated contribution of ringing was not measured.
AI.conclusion: The results support an engineering analysis rather than a claim of selectionist superiority, since the fixtures are repetitive, the comparators are simplified and the evaluation was not independently replicated.

title: AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System for Intelligent HPC User Support
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at HUST 2026 (13th International Workshop on HPC User Support Tools), co-located with SC26, Chicago, IL, USA, November 15, 2026. Camera-ready version
summary: AI-based question-answering systems are increasingly used for user support, including at high-performance computing (HPC) facilities. However, existing systems lack a systematic, deployment-oriented approach for evaluating final-answer quality and attributing failures to specific components. They also remain largely static after deployment, apart from periodic knowledge-base updates. We present AskALCF, an agentic log-analysis and improvement pipeline for HPC user support. AskALCF evaluates production interactions at a fine-grained level, identifies whether failures arise from missing knowledge, retrieval, prompting, model behavior, or tool execution, and routes each failure to an actionable repair. Its diagnostic core combines answer-quality assessment with a two-scope sufficiency test that distinguishes information missing from the documentation corpus from information present but not retrieved. We further introduce a controlled harness-training process that uses expert references, null edits, and explicit ship, revert, or decline decisions to improve the diagnostic pipeline reliably. Across 2,174 support turns, AskALCF reduced unattributable failures from 41.4% to 14.2%, while harness training improved expert agreement from 108/150 to 123/150 turns. These results demonstrate a governed form of self-evolution in which production evidence drives targeted system improvements. By turning production interactions into fine-grained diagnoses and actionable repairs, AskALCF provides a systematic foundation for continuously improving deployed AI support systems beyond knowledge-base updates alone.

AI.tldr: AskALCF is an agentic log-analysis pipeline for HPC user support that attributes failures to missing knowledge, retrieval, prompting, model behaviour or tool execution, and routes each failure to a repair. Across 2,174 support turns it reduces unattributable failures from 41.4% to 14.2%.
AI.motivation: Existing AI question-answering systems for HPC user support lack a deployment-oriented way to evaluate final-answer quality and attribute failures to components, and they remain largely static apart from periodic knowledge-base updates.
AI.method: AskALCF evaluates production interactions at a fine-grained level and uses a diagnostic core that combines answer-quality assessment with a two-scope sufficiency test, separating information missing from the documentation corpus from information present but not retrieved. A controlled harness-training process uses expert references, null edits and ship, revert or decline decisions.
AI.result: Across 2,174 support turns, unattributable failures fell from 41.4% to 14.2%. Harness training raised expert agreement from 108/150 to 123/150 turns.
AI.conclusion: Production evidence can drive governed self-evolution of deployed support systems through targeted repairs, going beyond knowledge-base updates alone.

title: Efficient Knowledge Transfer in Federated Bayesian Optimization through Neural Network Surrogates
summary: Federated Bayesian Optimization (FedBO) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing Bayesian Optimization (BO) in distributed, privacy-sensitive settings, enabling agents to accelerate the optimization of their local objectives by sharing knowledge about their similarities without exposing raw data. However, existing methods rely on restrictive assumptions, such as near-identical objective functions or shared Gaussian process hyperparameters that are often violated in heterogeneous real-world applications. We present GLOBAFED, a novel framework that enables efficient knowledge transfer across different but related objectives without compromising privacy. At its core is a probabilistic neural network surrogate with a shared feature-extracting backbone and agent-specific heads equipped with varia- tional Bayesian last layers to provide uncertainty estimates. During optimization, agents use federated learning on the shared backbone to collaboratively build a common latent feature representation, while agent-specific heads adapt to their individual objectives. Our empirical results demonstrate that GLOBAFED significantly accelerates convergence and reaches better final performance compared to state-of-the-art FedBO baselines, and enables agents to warm-start their optimization from previously learned global features.

AI.tldr: GLOBAFED is a federated Bayesian optimization framework that shares a feature-extracting neural backbone across agents and gives each agent a head with variational Bayesian last layers. It transfers knowledge across related but non-identical objectives and reports faster convergence and better final performance than FedBO baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing federated Bayesian optimization methods assume near-identical objectives or shared Gaussian process hyperparameters, which are often violated in heterogeneous real-world settings.
AI.method: A probabilistic neural network surrogate has a shared backbone trained with federated learning to build a common latent representation, and agent-specific heads with variational Bayesian last layers adapt to each agent's objective and give uncertainty estimates.
AI.result: The abstract states that GLOBAFED significantly accelerates convergence and reaches better final performance than state-of-the-art FedBO baselines, and that agents can warm-start from previously learned global features. It gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Sharing a federated backbone with agent-specific uncertainty-aware heads offers a privacy-preserving route to knowledge transfer across related objectives in federated optimization.

title: Terms of Care: Designing for Participation in Data Governance by Disability Communities
comment: 26 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables, under review
summary: Improving disability representation in AI-generated media requires community-specific datasets, yet openly sharing such data can expose communities to misuse, decontextualization, and exploitation. We examine how disability communities can participate in dataset governance through context-sensitive licensing. Working with three disability advocacy organizations, we conducted semi-structured interviews, an educational webinar and modular license activity to promote community participation in data stewardship. Our findings show that governance in these high-context communities relies on organizational memory (especially situated harms); both formal authority and informal relational practices; communication; and resulting trust. The modular license activity made organizational data choices more accessible and values-led, allowing communities to adapt Creative Commons clauses to express permitted uses, sector-specific restrictions, safeguarding requirements, and commitments to respectful representation. Yet, concerns remain about monitoring and enforcing appropriate data use. We contribute (1) an empirical account of governance tensions, (2) a practical modular approach, and (3) design implications for AI data platforms that support relational, context-sensitive governance beyond standardized, one-size-fits-all frameworks.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how disability advocacy communities participate in dataset governance through context-sensitive, modular Creative Commons licensing, based on interviews, a webinar and a license activity with three organizations. Governance relies on organizational memory, relational practices and trust, and concerns about enforcement remain.
AI.motivation: Improving disability representation in AI-generated media needs community-specific datasets, but open sharing can expose communities to misuse, decontextualization and exploitation.
AI.method: The authors worked with three disability advocacy organizations through semi-structured interviews, an educational webinar and a modular license activity in which communities adapted Creative Commons clauses.
AI.result: Governance in these high-context communities depends on organizational memory, especially situated harms, on formal authority and informal relational practices, and on communication and trust. The modular license activity made data choices more accessible and values-led, but concerns remain about monitoring and enforcing appropriate use.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers an empirical account of governance tensions, a modular licensing approach and design implications for AI data platforms that support relational, context-sensitive governance instead of one-size-fits-all frameworks.

title: Latent Imagination for Parameterized Action Spaces
comment: 24 pages, 11 figures, 21 tables
summary: Parameterized-action MDPs (PAMDPs) ask an agent to choose a discrete action together with continuous parameters whose meaning depends on that choice. Model-free PAMDP methods act fast but need many interactions; model-based methods are sample-efficient but plan at every decision, which makes them slow to act. We introduce HyLI (Hybrid Latent Imagination), a model-based agent that learns a hybrid policy entirely in the latent imagination of a world model and acts with a single forward pass. To address learning problems that the PAMDP structure creates, HyLI adds counterfactual mode evaluation, which gives every discrete action a learning signal at every imagined state, and success-window replay, which keeps rare successes in training. On seven standard PAMDP benchmarks, HyLI is within one published standard deviation of, or above, the published score of the strongest model-free baseline in our comparison on all 7 tasks, reaches 90% of that score with 2.4x fewer environment steps than that baseline (5.0x when its reward-free pre-training is counted), and decides 67x faster than the model-based planner DLPA at its published planner settings. It is the only method in our comparison that is both more sample-efficient than that baseline and fast enough for real-time control.

AI.tldr: HyLI is a model-based agent for parameterized-action MDPs that learns a hybrid policy entirely in latent imagination and acts with a single forward pass. It matches or exceeds the strongest model-free baseline on all 7 benchmarks while using 2.4x fewer environment steps to reach 90% of that score.
AI.motivation: Model-free PAMDP methods act fast but need many interactions, and model-based methods are sample-efficient but plan at every decision, which makes them slow to act.
AI.method: HyLI learns a hybrid policy in a world model's latent imagination, with counterfactual mode evaluation that gives every discrete action a learning signal at every imagined state, and success-window replay that keeps rare successes in training.
AI.result: On seven standard PAMDP benchmarks, HyLI is within one published standard deviation of, or above, the strongest model-free baseline's published score on all 7 tasks. It reaches 90% of that score with 2.4x fewer environment steps (5.0x when reward-free pre-training is counted) and decides 67x faster than the model-based planner DLPA at its published settings.
AI.conclusion: HyLI is the only method in the comparison that is both more sample-efficient than that baseline and fast enough for real-time control.

title: PDO Drug Screening Data for Evaluating and Training AI Drug Response Prediction Models
summary: Anti-cancer drug response prediction (DRP) is critically important for precision oncology and therapeutic development. Currently, most DRP models are developed using drug screening data from immortalized cancer cell lines, which can differ substantially from patient tumors at the genomic and molecular levels, even though patient tumor response is the ultimate prediction target. To help bridge this gap and bring DRP models closer to their intended clinical application, we conducted four drug screening studies using patient-derived organoids (PDOs), which more faithfully recapitulate patient tumors than immortalized cell lines. These studies generated data for improving and evaluating DRP models, including multi-omics profiles of PDO lines, drug feature data, and treatment response measurements. Using these data, we retrained and evaluated multiple publicly available DRP models under three model-building scenarios: training models using cell line data only, training models using combined cell line and PDO data, and pretraining models on cell line data followed by fine-tuning on PDO data. We then evaluated and compared model prediction performance on PDOs across these analysis scenarios. In addition, we also assessed the consistency of drug screening viability data generated by different laboratories using different assay technologies and/or experimental protocols.

AI.tldr: The paper releases drug screening data from four studies on patient-derived organoids (PDOs) and benchmarks existing drug response prediction models trained on cell line data, PDO data, or both. The data are meant to bring DRP models closer to patient tumours.
AI.motivation: Most DRP models are trained on immortalized cancer cell lines, which differ from patient tumours at the genomic and molecular levels, although patient response is the ultimate prediction target.
AI.method: The authors ran four drug screening studies on PDOs, producing multi-omics profiles, drug features and treatment responses. They retrained and evaluated several public DRP models under three scenarios: cell line only, combined cell line and PDO data, and cell line pretraining followed by PDO fine-tuning.
AI.result: The abstract reports that the models were compared on PDO prediction performance across the three scenarios and that viability data from different laboratories and assay technologies were checked for consistency. It gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The PDO dataset is offered as a resource for improving and evaluating DRP models toward clinical use, and the consistency analysis indicates the cross-laboratory variability to consider.

title: RUMI: A Robotiq-Matched Universal Manipulation Interface for Robot Learning with Augmented Reality and Haptic Feedback
summary: Many manipulation tasks require carefully controlled contact forces for successful execution, yet large-scale, force-aware datasets remain scarce. Handheld interfaces can help by transmitting interaction forces directly through the operator's arm, but most existing designs are tailored to simple linear grippers and do not match the nonlinear mechanics of widely used robotic grippers. We present RUMI, a handheld universal manipulation interface matched to the Robotiq 2F-85 with exchangeable fingertip sensors that preserves the target gripper geometry while enabling natural input before contact and force measurement after contact. By integrating the tracking system into a virtual reality headset, our method provides real-time augmented reality feedback about the kinematic feasibility of motion on the target robot platform. We further introduce a haptic feedback mechanism that supports force-aware teleoperation for simulated and real robots. A user study shows fewer episodes containing joint-limit violations with live robot visualization and pose initialization (3/50) than without augmented reality (16/50). We additionally train imitation policies from demonstrations, collected using two different fingertip modalities enabled by the gripper-matched hardware, and assess the haptic interface's capability for collecting force-aware teleoperation datasets in simulation.

AI.tldr: RUMI is a handheld teleoperation interface matched to the Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, with exchangeable fingertip sensors, VR-based augmented reality feedback and a haptic channel for force-aware teleoperation. In a user study, AR reduced joint-limit violation episodes from 16/50 to 3/50.
AI.motivation: Many manipulation tasks need controlled contact forces, but large force-aware datasets are scarce, and existing handheld interfaces are built for simple linear grippers rather than the nonlinear mechanics of common robotic grippers.
AI.method: RUMI matches the target gripper geometry and transmits interaction forces through the operator's arm. It integrates tracking into a VR headset to show kinematic feasibility in augmented reality and adds a haptic feedback mechanism for teleoperation in simulation and on real robots.
AI.result: In a user study, episodes with joint-limit violations fell to 3/50 with live robot visualization and pose initialization, compared with 16/50 without augmented reality. Imitation policies trained from demonstrations with two fingertip modalities are also reported, and the haptic interface was assessed for collecting force-aware datasets in simulation.
AI.conclusion: The gripper-matched design with AR feedback reduces kinematic infeasibility during teleoperation and supports collecting force-aware demonstration data.

title: Large Payments Model
summary: Payment applications such as fraud detection, authorization prediction, and payment optimization draw on overlapping transaction information. This motivates a reusable payments intelligence layer that shares learned representations and predictive signals, rather than developing predictive models independently for each task. Realizing this shared capability requires handling heterogeneous transaction fields, high-cardinality identifiers, lifecycle-dependent attributes, long histories, and rare outcomes while meeting latency and cost constraints. We present Large Payments Model (LPM), a domain-specific foundation model designed for operational use and trained from scratch on large-scale structured transaction data to learn reusable representations for payment prediction tasks. LPM employs field-specific encodings and lifecycle-aware self-supervision in two complementary architectures: the Independent variant uses hybrid masking and supports efficient per-transaction inference, while the Sequence variant incorporates entity-linked histories through compact latent representations for richer temporal context. Optional distillation enables resource-constrained deployment. We pretrain LPM on up to 400 billion tokens and study scaling, downstream performance, and representation reuse. LPM improves over strong task-specific baselines across multiple prediction tasks in Merchant and Treasury Services, demonstrating applicability in distinct payment domains. Its representations also facilitate adaptation to a target not observed during pretraining through compact task-specific components. Together with production deployment, these results position LPM as a practical basis for reusable payments intelligence.

AI.tldr: The Large Payments Model is a domain-specific foundation model trained from scratch on structured transaction data, with Independent and Sequence variants, pretrained on up to 400 billion tokens. It improves over strong task-specific baselines across several payment prediction tasks and is in production.
AI.motivation: Payment applications such as fraud detection, authorization prediction and payment optimization use overlapping transaction information, but they are typically built as separate models rather than on a shared representation layer.
AI.method: LPM uses field-specific encodings and lifecycle-aware self-supervision. The Independent variant uses hybrid masking for per-transaction inference, and the Sequence variant adds entity-linked histories through compact latent representations. Optional distillation supports resource-constrained deployment.
AI.result: Pretraining on up to 400 billion tokens is studied for scaling and downstream performance. LPM improves over strong task-specific baselines across multiple prediction tasks in Merchant and Treasury Services and adapts to an unseen target through compact task-specific components. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Together with production deployment, the results position LPM as a practical basis for reusable payments intelligence.

title: The BEATS Dataset: Towards Understanding Music-Physiology Dynamics in Real-World Scenarios
comment: Under review in Nature Scientific Data
summary: We introduce the BEATS dataset, a robust compilation of psycho-physiological data collected in the wild from 30 participants while they listened to curated playlists intended to promote well-being. An acronym for Biomarkers, Experience and Affect from Therapeutic Soundscapes, the BEATS dataset aims to support research on wellbeing, music psychology, affective computing and signal processing. More specifically, this dataset includes: (1) sensor data collected during music listening sessions using a research-grade wearable device in free-movement environments; (2) music listening activity records, stimulus metadata, acoustic features, and self-reports associated with the listening sessions (3) individual characteristics, such as demographics, music preference, musical skills, and personality traits; and (4) self-reported psychological measures before and after their experimental participation spanning for a number of weeks. By situating data collection outside of lab settings, the BEATS dataset offers the opportunity to study real-world music-listening scenarios, allowing for a richer exploration of the physiological, subjective and therapeutic effects of music under real-world conditions.

AI.tldr: The BEATS dataset contains psycho-physiological data collected in the wild from 30 participants listening to playlists intended to promote well-being, with wearable sensor data, listening records, individual characteristics and before-and-after self-reports collected over several weeks.
AI.motivation: Research on music, wellbeing and affective computing needs data on music listening in real-world settings, since lab recordings do not capture everyday listening conditions.
AI.method: The dataset combines sensor data from a research-grade wearable in free-movement environments, listening activity and stimulus metadata with acoustic features and self-reports, individual characteristics such as demographics and personality, and psychological measures before and after participation.
AI.result: The abstract describes the dataset contents and does not report experimental results or numerical findings.
AI.conclusion: The dataset is intended to support research on the physiological, subjective and therapeutic effects of music under real-world conditions.

title: Spec-Driven PBT: Deriving Semantic Invariants from Code Specifications for Agentic Property-based Testing
comment: Accepted at the VeriCodeGen Workshop on AI for Verifiable Coding at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Software is increasingly written by AI agents that produce an implementation from a natural language specification, a practice known as agentic coding. Code is now produced faster than it can be reviewed, and has been shown to exhibit its own characteristic failure patterns. Property-based testing (PBT), a long-standing technique in which invariant properties of a program are checked against many generated inputs, has recently been revisited with LLM agents authoring the properties, thereby removing the high-effort derivation of invariants that has long hindered its adoption. Existing methods, however, derive these properties from the implementation alone (Code-driven PBT). At the same time, a thorough specification such as a product requirements document has become routine within agentic coding, yet its role in testing the resulting code remains underexplored. We study the value of the specification as a source of properties for testing agent-written code. Our key insight is that the specification, unlike the implementation, records what the code was meant to do, and invariants derived from it are not biased by particular implementation choices. We propose Spec-Driven PBT, an agent that first expresses invariants in natural language from the specification and only then inspects the implementation to translate them into concrete tests. Across 25 applications from ViBench, Spec-Driven PBT finds a novel set of bugs that Code-driven PBT misses, while writing 2.4x fewer property tests. Though the two approaches surface a roughly equivalent number of bugs, there is little overlap: nearly 60% of the 169 total bugs are found by only one. Qualitatively, we find that the bugs unique to Spec-Driven PBT tend to violate documented product workflows whereas those to Code-driven PBT instead concentrate on implementation robustness, offering complementary value for bug discovery in agent-written code.

AI.tldr: Spec-Driven PBT derives property-based test invariants from a natural-language specification before inspecting the implementation, instead of deriving them from code alone. Across 25 ViBench applications it finds bugs that code-driven PBT misses while writing 2.4x fewer property tests.
AI.motivation: Agent-written code is produced faster than it can be reviewed, and existing LLM-based property-based testing derives properties from the implementation, which can inherit its implementation choices. Specifications, which record intended behaviour, have been largely unused for testing.
AI.method: An agent first expresses invariants in natural language from the specification and only then reads the implementation to translate them into concrete property tests.
AI.result: Across 25 applications from ViBench, Spec-Driven PBT finds bugs that Code-driven PBT misses while writing 2.4x fewer property tests. Both approaches find a roughly equivalent number of bugs, and nearly 60% of the 169 total bugs are found by only one of them. Spec-driven bugs tend to violate documented product workflows, while code-driven bugs concentrate on implementation robustness.
AI.conclusion: Specifications and implementations give complementary value for bug discovery in agent-written code, so combining them is advantageous.

title: Fit-LRP: Fitting Linear Relaxations to Polytopes for Neural Network Verification over Non-Convex Regions
summary: State-of-the-art neural network verifiers evaluate linear relaxations over axis-aligned bounding boxes. However, verification domains in cyber-physical systems are rarely boxes. Reachability specifications, obstacle-avoidance constraints, and neural Lyapunov certificates typically yield oblique or non-convex polyhedral regions, over which box-based bounds become extremely loose. This paper proposes Fit-LRP (Fitting Linear Relaxations to Polytopes), a framework the implements exact optimization of affine bounds over non-convex domains (represented by unions of polytopes) by solving a sequence of small, low-dimensional linear programs. Our approach seamlessly enhances the final optimization step of LiRPA and $\alpha,\! \beta$-CROWN branch-and-bound (BaB) algorithms. In BaB verification, approximating oblique constraints with axis-aligned splits causes severe combinatorial blowup and risks non-termination. By optimizing the final affine bound of a nonlinear function over the exact polyhedral state-space constraints our method eliminates box-induced over-approximations, enabling earlier search-tree pruning. On ARCH-COMP and neural Lyapunov benchmarks, Fit-LRP reduces branching on the hardest region by $47\times$, cuts worst-case verification time by $15\times$, and with region-wise partitioning, verifies on a single CPU $6.1\times$ faster than $\alpha,\! \beta$-CROWN on a GPU.

AI.tldr: Fit-LRP computes exact affine bounds over non-convex domains represented as unions of polytopes by solving small linear programs, and plugs into LiRPA and alpha-beta-CROWN branch-and-bound. It cuts branching on the hardest region by 47x and worst-case verification time by 15x.
AI.motivation: Verification domains in cyber-physical systems are oblique or non-convex polyhedra, where axis-aligned box bounds become very loose and branch-and-bound with axis-aligned splits blows up combinatorially.
AI.method: Fit-LRP optimizes the final affine bound of a nonlinear function over the exact polyhedral state-space constraints by solving a sequence of small, low-dimensional linear programs, and it enhances the final optimization step of LiRPA and alpha,beta-CROWN BaB, with region-wise partitioning.
AI.result: On ARCH-COMP and neural Lyapunov benchmarks, Fit-LRP reduces branching on the hardest region by 47x and cuts worst-case verification time by 15x. With region-wise partitioning, it verifies on a single CPU 6.1x faster than alpha,beta-CROWN on a GPU.
AI.conclusion: Removing box-induced over-approximation enables earlier search-tree pruning, so exact polyhedral bounds can make neural network verification practical for oblique and non-convex safety regions.

title: JustRUA: A Controlled Study of GPT-6 Robot-Use Agents
comment: 30 pages, 14 figures. Project page: this https URL. Code: this https URL
summary: GPT-6 Astra can drive a robot arm directly through a fixed harness, and scores of such robot-use agents on RoboDojo have risen quickly since. Reported systems differ in harness and test subset and often change several designs at once, so it is hard to tell which choices produce the gains. We take these designs apart and test them in one framework, along the harness around the model, the action interface, the reuse of experience and the scene geometry given to the model. A lean harness that keeps the full episode history and stops each motion early goes a long way. Reusing experience changes how the model acts but is not a free lunch, and scene geometry helps most, even when depth is predicted from RGB alone. JustRUA starts from the official L3 harness and keeps only what matters most. Even with no learned policy, self-improvement loop or task-specific tuning, this simple harness raises the score on the RoboDojo simulation benchmark substantially, from 29.7 to 50.3.

AI.tldr: JustRUA takes the official L3 harness for GPT-6 Astra robot-use agents and removes unnecessary components, showing that a lean harness that keeps full episode history and stops each motion early raises the RoboDojo simulation score from 29.7 to 50.3.
AI.motivation: Reported robot-use agents differ in harness and test subset and often change several designs at once, so it is unclear which choices produce the gains.
AI.method: The authors separate designs along the harness, the action interface, the reuse of experience and the scene geometry given to the model, and test them in one framework.
AI.result: A lean harness that keeps the full episode history and stops each motion early goes a long way. Reusing experience changes how the model acts but is not a free gain, and scene geometry helps most, even when depth is predicted from RGB alone. The simple harness raises the RoboDojo simulation score from 29.7 to 50.3 with no learned policy or task-specific tuning.
AI.conclusion: Much of the reported gain comes from the harness rather than from learned policies or self-improvement loops, so harness design should be controlled in comparisons.

title: Runtime Analysis of Cartesian Genetic Programming on Max: A Proven Exponential Speedup
comment: Accepted as a poster at NeurIPS 2026. To appear in the conference proceedings
summary: Genetic Programming (GP) is a search paradigm inspired from natural evolution for the automated discovery of expressions, functions, and computer programs. Cartesian GP (CGP) is a flavor of GP that uses a graph-based model to encode candidate programs, as contrasted to the conventional Tree-based GP (TGP). Since its inception two decades ago, CGP has predominantly been analyzed empirically, thus little is known regarding its theoretical performance guarantees. This paper analyzes CGP for the Max problem, which has been only rigorously studied for TGP with a proven expected runtime superlinear in the optimal program length $n$. We prove that the expected time for the ($1$+$1$)~CGP employing common mutation operators to evolve an equivalent optimal of the same output is polylogarithmic in $n$, specifically at most $O(\log^9{n})$. This is remarkable, as it shows an exponential speedup by switching to CGP. Our results shed light on the benefit and the compactness of the graph-based representation for programs, and on how CGP can navigate its search and fitness spaces efficiently. This is a first proven performance guarantee for CGP on an established benchmark problem. Experiments complement our theoretical findings.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the (1+1) Cartesian Genetic Programming algorithm solves the Max problem in expected polylogarithmic time, at most O(log^9 n), which is exponentially faster than the superlinear bound known for tree-based GP.
AI.motivation: CGP has been analysed mostly empirically over two decades, and the Max problem had only been rigorously analysed for tree-based GP, so little was known about CGP's theoretical performance guarantees.
AI.method: The authors analyse the (1+1) CGP with common mutation operators on the Max problem, which asks it to evolve an equivalent optimal program of the same output, and complement the proof with experiments.
AI.result: The expected time to evolve an optimal program of length n is at most O(log^9 n) with common mutation operators. This is an exponential speedup over the superlinear bound for tree-based GP, and it is the first proven performance guarantee for CGP on an established benchmark problem.
AI.conclusion: The graph-based representation of CGP is shown to be both compact and efficient for navigating program search and fitness spaces on this problem.

title: Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads
comment: v1: main text (20 pp., 7 figs.) and supplementary materials (12 figures)
summary: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.

AI.tldr: The paper hypothesizes that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions could biologically realize a neuromorphic mechanical version of a Transformer attention head. It is a theoretical proposal, and whether the required organization exists is left as an open empirical question.
AI.motivation: Transformer attention heads have a functional architecture that may have a biological counterpart, and the paper asks whether pyramidal columns in language regions could constitute one.
AI.method: The authors analyse a mechanical-structural description of attention heads as networks linked by output-input and output-weight connections, and identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns.
AI.result: The paper gives no experimental results. It proposes candidate neural mechanisms that may jointly support the construction of an attention head in biological tissue.
AI.conclusion: A neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head could in principle be built from pyramidal columns, and the realization need not reproduce the standard mathematical form of attention.

title: Human Capital in Context: What Employment Survival Reveals About Worker-Firm Match
summary: There is no best worker in general, only a best worker for a particular firm. We develop a measure of worker-firm match quality that treats fit as a property of the pair, learned from the survival of employment relationships. A two-tower neural network embeds workers, from their career histories and current positions, and firms, from their characteristics and business descriptions, into a common space, and match quality is the cosine similarity of the two vectors. The measure takes its functional form from the skill-weights model of firm-specific human capital, and its only estimated objective, a separation hazard, from the view of the job match as an experience good. Estimated on more than a billion person-periods covering 101 million workers and 8.4 million firms, a 0.1 increase in match quality lowers the odds of separation by 48%. About a quarter of the variance of match quality is specific to the worker-firm pair, which worker-, firm-, and occupation-level measures set to zero by construction. Workers earn more when better matched, especially early in a relationship, and firms whose workforces score higher grow faster, become more profitable, and are issued more, and more valuable, patents over the next five years than their industry peers. Because it scores pairs that never formed, the measure also predicts where movers go, and acquirers record a larger share of the price as goodwill when the target's workers would fit the acquirer better than they fit the target.

AI.tldr: The paper defines worker-firm match quality as a pair-level property learned from employment survival, using a two-tower neural network whose cosine similarity scores each pair. A 0.1 increase in match quality lowers separation odds by 48%.
AI.motivation: Human capital measures usually treat worker quality as a property of the worker alone, yet fit depends on the pair, and existing measures cannot score pairs that never formed.
AI.method: A two-tower network embeds workers from career histories and current positions, and firms from characteristics and business descriptions, into a common space. Match quality is the cosine similarity, with functional form from the skill-weights model of firm-specific human capital and a separation hazard as the only estimated objective.
AI.result: Estimated on more than a billion person-periods covering 101 million workers and 8.4 million firms, a 0.1 increase in match quality lowers separation odds by 48%. About a quarter of match-quality variance is specific to the worker-firm pair. Better-matched workers earn more, especially early in a relationship, and firms with higher-scoring workforces grow faster and file more valuable patents over five years.
AI.conclusion: Match quality captures fit that worker-, firm- and occupation-level measures miss, and it also predicts where movers go and how acquirers value goodwill.

title: Tokenized Reward Systems for Federated Learning: The Privacy vs. Fairness Tradeoff
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the 12th Balkan Conference in Informatics (BCI 2026), Best Paper Award
summary: Federated learning (FL) systems increasingly rely on blockchain based reward mechanisms to incentivize participation while preserving data privacy. We design and empirically evaluate two complementary Solidity smart contracts for FL reward distribution: the first one that allocates rewards proportionally to a publicly disclosed quality score, and a privacy preserving variant that hides individual quality scores behind a zero-knowledge (ZK) proof of a threshold condition. Both contracts mint a non transferable, use-and-burn token maintaining a trustless incentive structure. We evaluate the two designs through MNIST training with adversarial behavior, including Sybil attacks, zero gradient and random noise, across three independent random seeds. Our results reveal a fundamental tradeoff between cryptographic privacy and incentive fairness. The privacy preserving architecture strictly degrades system robustness, doubling the adversary's average reward capture while introducing severe outcome variance. This vulnerability is driven by a structural self-inclusion bias within cosine-similarity scoring: as the global model converges, legitimate gradient updates naturally diminish, rendering them statistically indistinguishable from bounded noise. Adversaries exploit this dynamic to systematically breach the ZK threshold, triggering a late stage failure cascade that culminates in absolute adversary monopoly over the reward pool and the total exclusion of honest contributors. Alongside a closed-form theorem formalizing this privacy--Sybil resistance tradeoff, we map strict mainnet deployment boundaries via linear gas scaling models, explicitly incorporating the post-Fusaka EIP-7825 per transaction gas cap. Ultimately, while cryptographically secure, static threshold ZK gates fail as incentive layer fairness mechanisms under realistic FL convergence dynamics on standard benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper compares two Solidity reward contracts for federated learning, one using public quality scores and one hiding scores behind a zero-knowledge threshold proof. The privacy-preserving version doubles the adversary's average reward capture under MNIST attacks.
AI.motivation: Blockchain-based reward mechanisms for federated learning aim to incentivize participation while preserving privacy, but the trade-off between cryptographic privacy and incentive fairness is not well understood.
AI.method: The authors design two Solidity contracts that mint non-transferable use-and-burn tokens, evaluate them on MNIST with Sybil attacks, zero gradients and random noise over three seeds, and derive a closed-form theorem with gas-cost analysis that includes the EIP-7825 gas cap.
AI.result: The privacy-preserving design doubles the adversary's average reward capture and has severe outcome variance. A self-inclusion bias in cosine-similarity scoring lets adversaries breach the ZK threshold late in training, leading to adversary monopoly over the reward pool and exclusion of honest contributors.
AI.conclusion: Static threshold ZK gates do not serve as fair incentive mechanisms under realistic convergence dynamics, so cryptographic privacy and Sybil resistance trade off against each other.

title: Agentic Computational Algebra
summary: We explore the use of AI agents for solving computational problems in algebra. For the problems we consider, the main challenge is not correctness but \emph{time}: general-purpose algorithms are guaranteed to provide correct solutions but can be prohibitively slow, while reformulations that exploit special structure often allow solving a problem much faster. We propose to use this setting to evaluate how effectively agents discover and exploit structure within and across tasks to reduce computational costs. More broadly, computational algebra supplies infinitely many problems with independently verifiable answers and systematically controllable structure and difficulty. To illustrate these possibilities, we use benchmark families of systems with controlled shared structure and evaluate agents in three settings: solving independent instances, solving online streams of related instances using persistent memory, and compiling a fast reusable solver for a known problem family. Our experiments show that (i) agents can extend the range of systems solvable within a fixed budget, although reasoning overhead can sometimes outweigh computational savings; (ii) memory can reduce the cost of repeated solving but may preserve suboptimal strategies; (iii) compilation produces faster reusable solvers but at substantial upfront cost. Overall, computational algebra offers concrete, measurable targets for improving how agents discover and reuse structure.

AI.tldr: The paper uses AI agents for computational algebra problems, where the challenge is running time rather than correctness, and evaluates how agents discover and reuse structure across independent instances, online streams with memory, and compiled reusable solvers.
AI.motivation: General-purpose algorithms give correct answers in computational algebra but can be prohibitively slow, while structure-exploiting reformulations are much faster, so the task measures how well agents find and reuse that structure.
AI.method: The authors use benchmark families of systems with controlled shared structure and evaluate agents in three settings: solving independent instances, solving online streams of related instances with persistent memory, and compiling a fast reusable solver for a known family.
AI.result: Agents can extend the range of systems solvable within a fixed budget, although reasoning overhead can outweigh savings. Memory can reduce the cost of repeated solving but may preserve suboptimal strategies. Compilation yields faster reusable solvers at substantial upfront cost.
AI.conclusion: Computational algebra gives measurable targets for improving how agents discover and reuse structure, since answers can be verified independently and difficulty is controllable.

title: Subsurface schematisation from sparse CPT data using the tabular foundation model TabPFN
summary: Subsurface schematisation supports geotechnical decisions but remains challenging because sparse site-investigation data leave substantial gaps in information about ground conditions. This study explores TabPFN, a foundation model pretrained on general synthetic tabular data, for this task. Using only grid coordinates and soil behaviour type index observations from sparse cone penetration tests (CPTs), we first reconstruct two-dimensional sections without geotechnical fine-tuning or predefined layer boundaries. We evaluate the approach on synthetic sections and at two field sites in the Netherlands, comparing it with SchemaGAN, a conditional generative adversarial network trained on synthetic geotechnical sections, and with reference interpolation methods. In the baseline comparisons, TabPFN achieved mean errors close to SchemaGAN's on synthetic sections and lower mean errors at both field sites. On synthetic sections, TabPFN's mean absolute error decreased at each tested increase in CPT count, and, under the baseline input setting, its pointwise prediction intervals had mean coverage close to nominal levels. Subsequent fine-tuning on the synthetic sections used to train SchemaGAN improved synthetic test accuracy but increased mean errors at both field sites. These findings indicate that general-purpose tabular foundation models offer a promising route for updating subsurface predictions from sparse and evolving site-investigation data without retraining.
