AI.tldr: TabPFN, a tabular foundation model, reconstructs two-dimensional subsurface sections from sparse cone penetration test soil behaviour type index observations without geotechnical fine-tuning. It matches SchemaGAN on synthetic sections and has lower mean errors at two Dutch field sites.
AI.motivation: Subsurface schematisation supports geotechnical decisions, but sparse site-investigation data leave large information gaps about ground conditions.
AI.method: Using only grid coordinates and soil behaviour type index observations, TabPFN reconstructs sections with no predefined layer boundaries. It is compared with SchemaGAN, a conditional GAN trained on synthetic sections, and with reference interpolation methods, on synthetic sections and two field sites in the Netherlands.
AI.result: TabPFN's mean errors are close to SchemaGAN's on synthetic sections and lower at both field sites. Its mean absolute error falls with each tested increase in CPT count, and its prediction intervals have near-nominal mean coverage under the baseline input setting. Fine-tuning on the synthetic sections improves synthetic test accuracy but increases mean errors at both field sites.
AI.conclusion: General-purpose tabular foundation models offer a promising route for updating subsurface predictions from sparse and evolving site data without retraining, though fine-tuning did not help at the field sites.

title: Trained on What Screen Readers Cannot Read: Accessibility Debt in the GUI Corpora Behind Computer-Use Agents
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at the International Conference on Artificial Intelligence Centric Systems, Services, and Applications (AISSA 2026), San Antonio, TX, USA, December 8-10, 2026
summary: Computer-use agents learn to operate mobile interfaces from corpora of captured screens and accessibility trees. The same trees are what a screen reader consumes, so an agent trained on them inherits whatever labelling gaps the underlying applications carry. This paper measures one of those gaps, content-description coverage, in two Android corpora: Rico, collected in 2017, and AndroidControl, collected in 2024. Across 17,373,614 interface elements, 17.74% of the Rico elements that need a content description under our coding rule carry one, against 57.27% in AndroidControl. The difference of 39.5 percentage points holds under five alternative coding rules and when whole apps are resampled. It describes two datasets that also differ in app selection, capture method and platform version; it does not measure change over time. Input controls are the least labelled role in both corpora (2.20% and 27.21%, or 30.99% in AndroidControl if hint text counts as a name). Descriptions in the older corpus are also five times more likely to be placeholders (10.25% against 1.95%), so the difference is not an artefact of developers typing filler. Resolving 26,205 task actions to the elements they touched shows that, among tappable graphics with no text, demonstrations operate elements described 9.0 points more often than the others on the screens they visit, about 3.5 points of it from the choice of element within a screen. That is a selection effect inside the benchmark. A two-coder reliability check (kappa = 0.91 and 0.96) and the full pipeline accompany the paper.

AI.tldr: The paper measures content-description coverage in two Android GUI corpora, Rico from 2017 and AndroidControl from 2024, which train computer-use agents. Coverage is 17.74% in Rico and 57.27% in AndroidControl, so agents inherit labelling gaps from these corpora.
AI.motivation: Computer-use agents learn from accessibility trees, which are also what screen readers consume, so an agent trained on them inherits the labelling gaps of the underlying applications.
AI.method: Across 17,373,614 interface elements, the authors apply a coding rule for which elements need a content description and compare the two corpora, with five alternative coding rules, resampling of whole apps, and a two-coder reliability check (kappa 0.91 and 0.96). They also resolve 26,205 task actions to the elements they touched.
AI.result: 17.74% of the Rico elements that need a description carry one, against 57.27% in AndroidControl, a 39.5-point difference that holds under five alternative rules. Input controls are the least labelled role in both corpora (2.20% and 27.21%). Placeholder descriptions are 10.25% in Rico against 1.95% in AndroidControl. Among tappable graphics with no text, demonstrations operate elements described 9.0 points more often, about 3.5 points of it from choice within a screen.
AI.conclusion: The corpora differ in app selection, capture method and platform version, and the difference does not measure change over time, but the selection effect shows that benchmark demonstrations are biased toward better-labelled elements.

title: ADAPT: Agentic Diff-Aware Patch Testing for Pull Requests
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. Replication package: this https URL
summary: Modern software development relies on pull requests (PRs) that introduce small, targeted code changes. Once merged, these changes should be protected by focused tests that exercise the behavior the PR introduces, yet developers often submit PRs without such tests, leaving the new behavior unguarded against future regressions. Most test generation techniques target entire software units and optimize objectives such as code coverage rather than the behavior a change introduces, and prior diff-aware approaches have had limited success in capturing it. We propose ADAPT (Agentic Diff-Aware Patch Testing), a regression test generation approach that uses an autonomous coding agent to produce change-focused tests for PRs. Given a PR, the agent analyzes the diff between the base and head versions to identify the modified functions and their context, then plans and generates candidate unit tests. A dedicated fail-to-pass (F2P) verification tool runs each candidate on both versions and, after F2P success, reports which executable changed lines remain uncovered; guided by this feedback, the agent iteratively refines its tests. We evaluate ADAPT on the same 426 real-world PRs used by the prior state-of-the-art baseline, with GPT-4o and GPT-5-mini. ADAPT+GPT-4o reaches an F2P rate of 62.0% (264/426), compared with BLAST's reported 35.4% (151/426), while ADAPT+GPT-5-mini reaches 89.9% (383/426). On 137 PRs shared with Change And Cover (ChaCo), ADAPT achieves full patch coverage on 83.9% of PRs, compared with 79.6% for ChaCo, at considerably lower time and cost. A manual evaluation confirms that the F2P-valid tests target each PR's intended change, with mean scores of up to 4.54/5 for importance, 4.35/5 for assertion strength, and 4.49/5 for readability, often covering behavior beyond the developer-written tests.

AI.tldr: ADAPT uses an autonomous coding agent to generate change-focused regression tests for pull requests, using a fail-to-pass verifier and uncovered changed lines as feedback. With GPT-5-mini it reaches an F2P rate of 89.9% (383/426 PRs), against 35.4% reported for BLAST.
AI.motivation: Pull requests introduce small changes that often ship without tests, and existing test generation targets whole units and coverage rather than the behaviour a change introduces.
AI.method: Given a PR, the agent analyzes the diff between base and head, identifies the modified functions and their context, and plans and generates candidate unit tests. A dedicated fail-to-pass verifier runs each candidate on both versions and reports uncovered executable changed lines, which guide iterative refinement.
AI.result: On the same 426 real-world PRs used by BLAST, ADAPT+GPT-4o reaches an F2P rate of 62.0% (264/426) against BLAST's reported 35.4% (151/426), and ADAPT+GPT-5-mini reaches 89.9% (383/426). On 137 PRs shared with ChaCo, ADAPT achieves full patch coverage on 83.9% against 79.6% for ChaCo, at lower time and cost. Manual scores reach up to 4.54/5 for importance, 4.35/5 for assertion strength and 4.49/5 for readability.
AI.conclusion: Agentic, diff-aware test generation with feedback from a fail-to-pass verifier produces tests that target each PR's intended change more effectively than prior approaches in these experiments.

title: SwarmSafe-Delta: Isolating Message Effects on LLM Agent Safety
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables
summary: When a tool-using LLM agent team violates policy, aggregate outcomes do not reveal whether an upstream message changed the executor's action. We introduce SwarmSafe-Delta, a paired executable protocol that freezes upstream computation, varies real, hidden, and format-matched placebo delivery, and scores a single committed action against deterministic benign and risky policy states under preassigned budgets. Across four models and constructed optional tasks, real delivery at $N=4$ produces 21.4% risky-world violations, versus 5.0% with placebo and 1.0% with hidden delivery (paired differences +16.4 and +20.3 percentage points). Real delivery also improves benign task success, illustrating that suppressing communication sacrifices utility. In a second regime constructed to require an upstream lookup route, real delivery improves safe completion by 74.2 points relative to hidden delivery. These effects quantify message-delivery contrasts under specified information dependencies, not naturally occurring failure rates. Exploratory action-level analyses show that the effect depends strongly on whether the upstream message recommends a prerequisite check or direct execution; model differences also largely track these message compositions. The contribution is a controlled, execution-grounded measurement protocol rather than a general claim that agent communication is harmful or protective.

AI.tldr: SwarmSafe-Delta is a paired executable protocol that isolates how an upstream message changes a tool-using LLM agent team's actions, by varying real, hidden and placebo delivery while freezing upstream computation. Real delivery produces 21.4% risky-world violations, against 5.0% with placebo and 1.0% with hidden delivery.
AI.motivation: When a multi-agent team violates policy, aggregate outcomes do not show whether an upstream message changed the executor's action.
AI.method: The protocol freezes upstream computation and varies real, hidden and format-matched placebo delivery, then scores a single committed action against deterministic benign and risky policy states under preassigned budgets, across four models and constructed optional tasks.
AI.result: At N=4, real delivery produces 21.4% risky-world violations versus 5.0% with placebo and 1.0% with hidden delivery (paired differences +16.4 and +20.3 points). Real delivery also improves benign task success. In a second regime requiring an upstream lookup route, real delivery improves safe completion by 74.2 points relative to hidden delivery. The effect depends on whether the message recommends a prerequisite check or direct execution.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a controlled, execution-grounded measurement protocol for message-delivery effects under specified information dependencies, not a general claim that agent communication is harmful or protective.

title: Self-Supervised Attention-Based Virtual Metrology for CMP MRR Prediction
comment: Submitted to the IEEE International Symposium on Semiconductor Manufacturing (ISSM 2026)
summary: Chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) is a critical semiconductor manufacturing process where material removal rate (MRR) is a key metric for process monitoring and advanced process control (APC). Virtual metrology enables MRR estimation from process time series signals, supporting run-to-run(R2R) control and process optimization while reducing reliance on physical metrology. Existing approaches typically rely on simplified linear assumptions or require handcrafted feature engineering. In this paper, we propose Global Regression Pretraining(GREP), a self-supervised, attention-based framework for CMP MRR prediction. GREP learns temporal representations from unlabeled sensor signals through global proxy-target regression, followed by supervised fine-tuning for MRR estimation. The framework is evaluated against a feature-engineered supervised baseline under three conditions: limited labeled data, sensor noise, and temporal process drift. Experiments on the PHM 2016 CMP dataset demonstrate competitive performance under limited labeled-data conditions, with improvements in selected cases and performance largely comparable to the baseline across different labeled-data fractions. Both models exhibit relatively small changes in prediction error with increasing noise, while GREP achieves a 17.0% RMSE reduction in the final temporal interval.

AI.tldr: GREP is a self-supervised, attention-based framework that pretrains on unlabeled CMP sensor signals with global proxy-target regression and then fine-tunes to predict material removal rate. It is competitive with a feature-engineered baseline on the PHM 2016 CMP dataset and reduces RMSE by 17.0% in the final temporal interval.
AI.motivation: Virtual metrology for chemical mechanical planarization usually relies on simplified linear assumptions or handcrafted feature engineering, which limits MRR estimation from process time series.
AI.method: GREP learns temporal representations from unlabeled sensor signals through global proxy-target regression, followed by supervised fine-tuning for MRR estimation, and is evaluated against a feature-engineered supervised baseline under limited labels, sensor noise and temporal drift.
AI.result: On the PHM 2016 CMP dataset, GREP is competitive under limited labelled data, with improvements in selected cases and performance broadly comparable to the baseline across labelled fractions. Both models change little in error with increasing noise. GREP achieves a 17.0% RMSE reduction in the final temporal interval.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised attention pretraining is a viable route to virtual metrology for CMP, with gains concentrated in drift conditions and label-scarce cases rather than uniformly across settings.

title: Same-State Pairs Make One JEPA Proof of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis Vacuous
summary: In a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), the JEPA proof of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) assumes that every observation determines the world state and that a spectral gap makes minimizers unique up to rotation. Under the hard-whitening population objective, same-state positive pairs make the induced world kernel the identity: every centered whitened state function is a global minimizer, and, when $d_z-1\ge 2k$, two minimizers can have best-rotation squared residual $2k$. The uniqueness claim is conditional; for $k<d_z-1$, where $d_z$ is the number of world states, this limit makes its premise unsatisfiable, so the claim has no content there. The experiments that motivate it leave the assumption: a caption sees only part of an image, and the paper states no experiment meets its hypotheses exactly. The theorem does not reach those experiments, and for $k<d_z-1$ its idealized same-state limit is vacuous. One of the paper's four quantitative results survives: a gap-free lower bound. Its bound vanishes only at perfect scene-explained fraction; it bounds alignment error but cannot certify good-view alignment. A canonical frame is determined only up to a rotation and a latent permutation. Paired samples fix the relative frame at effective rank $k$; a global rotation remains. Component semantics fix the relative permutation only up to signs; value anchors fix it once the mixing frame is pinned. A resource--gauge ledger records which resource fixes which gauge.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that under a hard-whitening population objective, same-state positive pairs make the JEPA world kernel the identity, so the uniqueness claim in the JEPA proof of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis becomes vacuous for k below d_z minus 1. Only a gap-free lower bound survives.
AI.motivation: The JEPA proof of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis assumes that each observation determines the world state and that a spectral gap makes minimizers unique up to rotation, and the experiments motivating it do not meet these assumptions.
AI.method: The authors analyse the population objective under same-state positive pairs and derive the minimizer set, including the best-rotation squared residual, for different relations between k and the number of world states d_z. They also examine gauge freedoms of canonical frames and a resource-gauge ledger.
AI.result: Every centered whitened state function is a global minimizer, and when d_z minus 1 is at least 2k, two minimizers can have best-rotation squared residual 2k. For k below d_z minus 1 the uniqueness premise is unsatisfiable. One of four quantitative results survives: a gap-free lower bound that vanishes only at perfect scene-explained fraction.
AI.conclusion: The uniqueness claim does not reach the motivating experiments, and a canonical frame is fixed only up to rotation and latent permutation, so paired samples, component semantics or value anchors each fix different gauges.

title: When can an interpretability claim be trusted? Stability and certification of feature dimensionality, ridge leverage and the feature recovery rate
comment: 70 pages. Also archived at this https URL. The AI use statement is in the paper
summary: Interpretability tools increasingly support safety claims, such as that a sparse dictionary has recovered most of a model's features. Such claims rest on measurements with arbitrary thresholds, and small changes to the model weights, a different training seed or a different threshold can reverse them. We study two widely used measurements in toy models and synthetic dictionaries with known ground truth: the feature dimensionality of Elhage et al. and the feature recovery rate (FRR) with a cosine threshold. We characterize exactly where feature dimensionality is discontinuous and replace it with a regularized (ridge) version with sharp stability bounds: the ridge leverage score changes by at most $3\sqrt{3}/(8\sqrt{\lambda})$ times the operator-norm change of the weights, and this constant cannot be improved; for the regularized dimensionality the stability constant grows like $\rho/4$ in the scale $\rho=R/\sqrt{\lambda}$, with explicit upper and lower bounds. We also prove certificates stating when a claim "feature $i$ is recovered" must survive a given change of the dictionary. The certificates held in every test and are informative for small perturbations, but certify no feature non-trivially across independently trained dictionaries; at the standard threshold, whether a feature counts as recovered changed with the training seed for 55 percent of features. Experiments use toy models only. The proofs, code and text were drafted by AI agents directed by the authors and checked by an independent blind AI reviewer and by numerical tests; the authors take full responsibility for the content.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when interpretability claims about sparse dictionaries are stable, proposing a ridge-regularized feature dimensionality with sharp stability bounds and certificates for feature recovery. In toy models, the recovery status of 55% of features changes with the training seed at the standard threshold.
AI.motivation: Claims that a sparse dictionary has recovered most features rest on thresholds and measurements that are sensitive to small changes in weights, seeds or thresholds, and these claims can reverse under such changes.
AI.method: The authors analyse feature dimensionality of Elhage et al. and the feature recovery rate with a cosine threshold in toy models and synthetic dictionaries with known ground truth. They replace dimensionality with a ridge version, derive stability bounds on the ridge leverage score and dimensionality, and prove certificates for recovery claims.
AI.result: The ridge leverage score changes by at most 3*sqrt(3)/(8*sqrt(lambda)) times the operator-norm change of the weights, a constant the authors state cannot be improved. Certificates held in every test and are informative for small perturbations, but they certify no feature non-trivially across independently trained dictionaries. At the standard threshold, recovery status changed with the training seed for 55% of features.
AI.conclusion: Interpretability claims based on these measurements need stability conditions, and the certificates can bound change under small perturbations, though the experiments use toy models only.

title: Guided Generation of Linux Kernel Semantic Patches with Small Local Language Models
comment: 7 pages, 6 tables, 1 figure. Code, data, prompts and model responses: this https URL
summary: When a Linux kernel API changes, hundreds of drivers are converted by hand over months, and the earlier conversions are reviewed examples for the later ones. We ask whether small open language models running on a laptop can turn such examples into Coccinelle semantic patches, the rules kernel maintainers already use for tree-wide changes. We adapt guided code generation to this task: the training examples are decomposed by script into a tree of change variants, the model writes one small rule per variant under feedback from applying it to the examples, deterministic components repair SmPL syntax and generalise driver-specific names, rules are composed greedily, and a compile critic repairs or rejects a rule whose output does not build. We evaluate on a pre-registered test set of 7 migrations whose new APIs appeared after the training cutoffs of all three models (Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 4B), with 122 held-out driver conversions, counting a conversion as solved only if the rule's output matches the human fix and compiles. With the framework, Qwen2.5-Coder solves 35.3 conversions on average over three seeds (range 32-41), against 1.0 when prompted directly; Spinfer solves 41 and a frontier LLM agent 66. The local model solves fewer conversions than Spinfer but its rules are the most precise on the test set (0.74 of the files they change are solved, against 0.55 for Spinfer and 0.70 for the frontier agent), and the compile critic removes every output that matches the human fix but does not build. The two general-purpose models stay weak even with guidance (at most 12 solved). All code, prompts, model responses and results are released.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that small open language models on a laptop can generate Coccinelle semantic patches from examples of kernel API migrations, using a guided framework that decomposes examples into change variants. Qwen2.5-Coder 7B solves 35.3 conversions on average, against 1.0 when prompted directly.
AI.motivation: When a Linux kernel API changes, hundreds of drivers are converted by hand over months, and earlier conversions are reviewed examples that could guide the later ones through semantic patches.
AI.method: Training examples are decomposed by script into a tree of change variants, the model writes one small rule per variant under feedback from applying it to examples, deterministic components repair SmPL syntax and generalize driver-specific names, rules are composed greedily, and a compile critic repairs or rejects rules whose output does not build.
AI.result: On a pre-registered test set of 7 migrations with 122 held-out driver conversions, Qwen2.5-Coder solves 35.3 conversions on average over three seeds (range 32-41), against 1.0 when prompted directly. Spinfer solves 41 and a frontier LLM agent 66. The local model's rules are the most precise (0.74 of changed files solved, against 0.55 for Spinfer and 0.70 for the frontier agent). The two general-purpose models stay at most 12 solved.
AI.conclusion: Guided generation lets small local models produce precise semantic patches for kernel migrations, though they solve fewer conversions than Spinfer, and the compile critic is needed to reject outputs that match the human fix but do not build.

title: Rectified Looped Transformer
summary: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared block, offering a parameter-efficient approach to language modeling. However, most existing works directly reuse each loop's output as the next's input, which can lead to hidden-state scale growth and perturbation amplification as recurrence deepens. We propose Rectified Looped Transformer (RLT), which redesigns feedback between loops using an interpolation schedule inspired by flow-based modeling. At each loop, RLT forms the next input by linearly interpolating between the current state and its prediction. Such interpolation distributes state changes across loops, encouraging a smoother trajectory from the initial input to the final output. Theoretical analysis proves that, under appropriate assumptions, RLT keeps state magnitudes uniformly bounded across loops and reduces the worst-case perturbation amplification. We evaluate RLT on language modeling corpora and downstream benchmarks. At matched training and inference depths, RLT consistently achieves lower perplexity than a standard looped Transformer, while exhibiting greater robustness to input perturbations and variance in inference depth. Consistent with the theoretical results, latent trajectory analysis shows that RLT maintains more stable hidden-state norms across loops, which also facilitates extrapolation-based decoding strategies. Notably, RLT achieves these gains without requiring additional trainable parameters or extra recurrent block evaluations, thus providing a simple yet more stable feedback mechanism for looped Transformers.

AI.tldr: Rectified Looped Transformer redesigns feedback between loops by linearly interpolating between each loop's state and its prediction, inspired by flow-based modeling. It keeps hidden-state magnitudes bounded and gives lower perplexity than a standard looped Transformer at matched depths.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers reuse a shared block for parameter-efficient depth, but feeding each loop's output directly back as input can cause hidden-state scale growth and perturbation amplification as recurrence deepens.
AI.method: At each loop, RLT forms the next input as a linear interpolation between the current state and its prediction, which distributes state changes across loops and encourages a smoother trajectory from input to output. The method adds no trainable parameters or extra recurrent block evaluations.
AI.result: At matched training and inference depths, RLT consistently achieves lower perplexity than a standard looped Transformer, with greater robustness to input perturbations and to variance in inference depth. Latent trajectory analysis shows more stable hidden-state norms across loops, and the theory shows bounded state magnitudes and reduced worst-case perturbation amplification under stated assumptions.
AI.conclusion: RLT is a simple feedback mechanism that stabilizes looped Transformers without extra parameters, and its stable trajectories also facilitate extrapolation-based decoding strategies.

title: ORCHID-SAGE: Fully Reproducible CALPHAD Assessment from Evidence to Phase Diagram
comment: 24 pages, 19 figures. Code and data: this https URL (doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24045967%29%3B assessment record doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24045965
summary: Knowledge of phase stability is the first requirement for materials design, and predicting the conditions under which new materials can be synthesized has become a key capability of self-driving laboratories (SDLs). For inorganic materials, notably alloys, these predictions come from thermodynamic databases built with the CALPHAD method. Building a database, however, requires expert judgment at many steps, and because these decisions are rarely recorded, others can use a database but cannot regenerate or update it. Machines can already collect the data, build a first model with machine-learned interatomic potentials and refine it against experiments. The assessment itself, the sequence of judgments that turns these parts into a reliable database, is still carried out by human experts. We argue that it can be automated reproducibly only if the expert knowledge behind an assessment is encoded in formal protocols, so that an assessment delivers a record of its construction and not only its parameters. We introduce ORCHID-SAGE, a standard that organizes this record into reproducible and automatable protocols. In this first attempt, applied to Cr-Ni, the database was regenerated from its record by a script on a second machine, by an AI agent working only through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and by a refit from public sources only, with the same predictions. Recorded in this way, a database need no longer be fixed at publication but can be updated by AI agents as SDLs and other sources provide new evidence, while the judgment remains with people and on the record.

AI.tldr: ORCHID-SAGE is a standard that encodes CALPHAD assessment expertise in formal protocols so that a thermodynamic database can be regenerated, audited and updated from its recorded construction. In a first application to Cr-Ni, the database was regenerated from its record by a script, by an AI agent via MCP and by a refit from public sources, with the same predictions.
AI.motivation: CALPHAD thermodynamic databases encode many undocumented expert judgments, so others can use them but cannot regenerate or update them, which limits reproducibility and self-driving laboratory use.
AI.method: The authors introduce a standard that organizes the assessment record into reproducible, automatable protocols, and apply it to Cr-Ni, with machine-learned interatomic potentials and experiments as inputs.
AI.result: The Cr-Ni database was regenerated from its record by a script on a second machine, by an AI agent working only through the Model Context Protocol, and by a refit from public sources only, and all three gave the same predictions.
AI.conclusion: A database recorded in this way need not be fixed at publication, and AI agents can update it as new evidence arrives while the judgments remain with people and on the record.

title: Shared Item-Level Error Limits the Aggregation of Small Language Models in Fermi Estimation
comment: 21 pages, 2 figures, 17 tables
summary: Multi-agent systems of language models are often motivated by an averaging argument: if the agents' errors are unbiased and independent, the error of an aggregate of N answers falls as 1/sqrt(N). Fermi estimation, whose continuous answers are aggregated on the logarithmic scale, permits a direct test. We decompose the log10 error of each answer into the mean error of its model on the item, common to all its draws on the item, and a residual, and estimate both from 2.51M answers given before any communication by 15 open-weight models (3B-72B) on realFP, with replication under a single prompt pair on realFP, Science Olympiad Fermi questions and a guesstimation set. Given the item, teammates' errors are uncorrelated and teams behave as independent draws, but the item-level component accounts for a median 0.906 of the error variance over items. Teams of thirty therefore reduce a single agent's error by a median 1.7% (at most 5.4%), whereas draws that were also unbiased on each item would reduce it by 74-79%. All models compress their estimates toward about 10^6; this trend explains a median 17% of the item-level component, and a cross-validated linear recalibration on labelled items removes the overall bias but not that component. Three rounds of debate reduce within-team dispersion by 93% and leave the item-level component unchanged; revision without peers attains the same small gain. Mixing five models of similar accuracy reduces error by 6.6% relative to their own homogeneous teams, but no mixture improves on the most accurate model. Higher sampling temperature changes team error by about 1% at most, and contrastive activation steering not detectably; per-agent scaffold prompts (not significant after multiplicity correction) and skipping one layer in a single-model screen improve it. The results are conditional on the models, benchmarks, prompts and settings tested.

AI.tldr: Averaging across small language model teams in Fermi estimation reduces error only slightly, because a shared item-level error component accounts for a median 0.906 of error variance. Teams of thirty cut a single agent's error by a median of only 1.7%.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent language model systems are often motivated by an averaging argument in which the error of N answers falls as 1/sqrt(N) if errors are unbiased and independent, and Fermi estimation allows this to be tested directly.
AI.method: The log10 error of each answer is decomposed into the model's mean error on the item, shared across its draws, and a residual. Both are estimated from 2.51M pre-communication answers by 15 open-weight models (3B-72B) on realFP, with replication on Science Olympiad Fermi questions and a guesstimation set.
AI.result: Given the item, teammates' errors are uncorrelated, but the item-level component accounts for a median 0.906 of error variance over items. Teams of thirty reduce error by a median 1.7% (at most 5.4%), whereas unbiased per-item draws would reduce it by 74-79%. Three rounds of debate reduce within-team dispersion by 93% but leave the item-level component unchanged. Mixing five models reduces error by 6.6% relative to homogeneous teams, but no mixture beats the most accurate model.
AI.conclusion: Averaging helps little in these Fermi estimation settings because the shared item-level error dominates, and the results are conditional on the models, benchmarks, prompts and settings tested.

title: Wanda-Guided Sparse Perturbations for Efficient Zeroth-Order Optimization
summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models through forward-only evaluations, but high-dimensional random perturbations can limit optimization efficiency. Sparse perturbations reduce the search dimension, making the selection of informative coordinates critical. We propose Wanda-Importance Sparsity-MeZO (WIS-MeZO), which uses Wanda weight--activation saliency to construct task-conditioned sparse perturbation masks while keeping the pretrained model dense. We analyze support quality through gradient energy capture and relate it to gradient estimation and convergence. Across 16 benchmarks with LLaMA and Qwen models ranging from 3B to 32B parameters, WIS-MeZO achieves higher aggregate scores than MeZO and reaches comparable validation losses in fewer optimization steps. Comparisons with random and magnitude-based sparse perturbations further highlight the importance of informative support selection.

AI.tldr: WIS-MeZO builds task-conditioned sparse perturbation masks for zeroth-order LLM fine-tuning using Wanda weight-activation saliency, while keeping the pretrained model dense. It reaches higher aggregate scores than MeZO and comparable validation losses in fewer steps.
AI.motivation: Zeroth-order fine-tuning is memory-efficient but high-dimensional random perturbations limit its optimization efficiency, and selecting informative coordinates for sparse perturbations is critical.
AI.method: Wanda weight-activation saliency selects the coordinates of a sparse perturbation mask conditioned on the task. Support quality is analyzed through gradient energy capture and linked to gradient estimation and convergence.
AI.result: Across 16 benchmarks with LLaMA and Qwen models from 3B to 32B parameters, WIS-MeZO achieves higher aggregate scores than MeZO and reaches comparable validation losses in fewer optimization steps. Random and magnitude-based sparse perturbations are compared and perform worse, highlighting the value of informative support selection.
AI.conclusion: Informative support selection matters for sparse zeroth-order perturbations, and saliency-guided masks can make memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning faster to converge.

title: SUMNO: Spatially Unrolled Multigrid Neural Operator for Fluid Flow Surrogates
comment: 37 pages, 6 figures
summary: Data-driven surrogate modeling has emerged as a powerful paradigm for accelerating computational fluid dynamics, and hierarchical U-shaped networks, which resemble the structure of classical Geometric Multigrid (GMG) methods, have become prevalent designs. Modern surrogates built on these designs achieve competitive accuracy at a fraction of the cost of numerical solvers; however, accurate prediction of complex flows remains challenging, and no existing architecture leads across them. In such networks, the multigrid analogy mainly concerns the multi-resolution topology, while their components largely follow common vision practice. To address this, this study introduces SUMNO, a multigrid neural operator for fluid flow fields on regular grids that spatially unrolls a V-cycle into a feed-forward U-shaped network. Parameter-free down- and upsampling stand in for restriction and prolongation, and additive skip connections for coarse-grid correction, with normalization-free transfer and skip pathways. Within this macro-architecture, convolutions are used at the fine and intermediate resolutions and shifted-window attention at the coarsest, whose window partitioning is generalized to handle periodicity independently per axis. Evaluated on unseen test configurations across four unsteady and steady flow benchmarks against five representative baselines, SUMNO is best in 5 of 7 settings and ranks second in the remaining two. It reduces the 10-step rollout MSE by about 30% relative to the strongest baseline, and outperforms three baselines with over 130 million parameters using 9.4 million parameters.

AI.tldr: SUMNO is a multigrid neural operator for fluid flow surrogates that unrolls a V-cycle into a feed-forward U-shaped network. It is best in 5 of 7 settings against five baselines and cuts the 10-step rollout MSE by about 30% relative to the strongest baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing hierarchical U-shaped surrogates resemble geometric multigrid in their multi-resolution topology, but their components largely follow common vision practice, and no existing architecture leads across complex flows.
AI.method: The model spatially unrolls a V-cycle into a feed-forward network. It uses parameter-free down- and upsampling in place of restriction and prolongation, additive skip connections for coarse-grid correction, and normalization-free transfer and skip pathways. Convolutions are used at fine and intermediate resolutions and shifted-window attention at the coarsest, with window partitioning generalized to periodicity per axis.
AI.result: On unseen test configurations across four unsteady and steady flow benchmarks, SUMNO is best in 5 of 7 settings and second in the other two. It reduces the 10-step rollout MSE by about 30% relative to the strongest baseline and outperforms three baselines with over 130 million parameters while using 9.4 million parameters.
AI.conclusion: Building the full multigrid structure into the macro-architecture, rather than only the topology, yields a compact surrogate that is more accurate and far smaller than larger baselines.

title: DRAMA: Dissecting Attention Redundancy for Accelerating Multimodal Diffusion Large Language Models
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 27 pages, 19 figures
summary: Multimodal diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text through iterative masked denoising with bidirectional attention, offering a compelling alternative to autoregressive vision-language modeling. However, each denoising step requires a full forward pass over long multimodal sequences in which visual tokens dominate the sequence length, and a fixed step budget further compounds this quadratic per-step cost. Existing inference acceleration approaches for multimodal dLLMs characterize attention redundancy implicitly, motivating designs from isolated attention visualizations rather than from measurement. We close this gap with DRAMA, a training-free acceleration framework grounded in a systematic dissection of attention redundancy in multimodal dLLMs. By probing attention tensors along spatial and temporal axes, we reveal two persistent redundancy structures: (i) attention mass consistently concentrates on a sparse subset of visual tokens, and (ii) attention distributions rapidly stabilize across denoising steps after an initial formation phase. These findings motivate two complementary mechanisms: Spatial-Redundancy-Aware Visual Token Pruning (SVTP) and Sufficiency-Guided Adaptive Stopping (SGAS). Together, DRAMA achieves an average 18.67 times inference speedup across six vision-language benchmarks without training, architectural modification, or attention caching, while maintaining competitive accuracy. Our results establish a strong, measurement-grounded acceleration baseline for multimodal dLLM inference.

AI.tldr: DRAMA is a training-free acceleration framework for multimodal diffusion LLMs based on measured attention redundancy. It achieves an average 18.67 times inference speedup across six vision-language benchmarks while keeping competitive accuracy.
AI.motivation: Each denoising step of a multimodal diffusion LLM is a full forward pass over long sequences dominated by visual tokens, with a fixed step budget compounding the quadratic cost. Existing acceleration methods characterize attention redundancy implicitly, from isolated visualizations rather than measurement.
AI.method: The authors probe attention tensors along spatial and temporal axes and identify two redundancy structures: attention mass concentrates on a sparse subset of visual tokens, and attention distributions stabilize across denoising steps after an initial phase. These motivate Spatial-Redundancy-Aware Visual Token Pruning (SVTP) and Sufficiency-Guided Adaptive Stopping (SGAS).
AI.result: DRAMA achieves an average 18.67 times inference speedup across six vision-language benchmarks while maintaining competitive accuracy, without training, architectural modification, or attention caching.
AI.conclusion: A measurement-grounded acceleration baseline for multimodal diffusion LLM inference, derived from an explicit analysis of attention redundancy.

title: HyBridge: Bridge-Guided Self-Supervised Hyperbolic Hypergraph Representation Learning
summary: Hypergraphs capture groupwise relationships among multiple nodes and often exhibit tree-like structures. Although hyperbolic space is well suited for modeling such structures, simply extending existing hypergraph representation learning (HRL) methods to hyperbolic space does not consistently improve performance. In this paper, we investigate the relationship between node structural properties and hyperbolic embedding radii and find that bridge nodes tend to lie closer to the center in graphs, whereas this relationship is not consistently observed in hypergraphs. We further find that conventional bridge score estimation may fail to capture the groupwise connectivity of hypergraphs. Motivated by these findings, we propose HyBridge, a self-supervised hyperbolic HRL framework that (1) estimates node bridge scores by considering the external connectivity of individual hyperedges, (2) learns node and hyperedge embeddings through hyperbolic hypergraph encoding, (3) guides node radial positions according to their bridge scores, and (4) employs contrastive learning to preserve node discriminability. Extensive experiments on 10 real-world hypergraphs demonstrate that HyBridge outperforms 22 competing methods, achieving performance improvements of up to 9.82% in node classification. For reproducibility, we provide the code at this https URL.

AI.tldr: HyBridge is a self-supervised hyperbolic hypergraph representation learning framework that places nodes according to bridge scores computed from hyperedge external connectivity. It outperforms 22 competing methods on 10 real-world hypergraphs, with node classification gains of up to 9.82%.
AI.motivation: Simply extending hypergraph representation learning to hyperbolic space does not consistently help. Conventional bridge score estimation may miss the groupwise connectivity of hypergraphs, unlike the relation seen in ordinary graphs between bridge nodes and embedding radii.
AI.method: The framework estimates node bridge scores from the external connectivity of individual hyperedges, learns node and hyperedge embeddings through hyperbolic hypergraph encoding, sets node radial positions according to bridge scores, and uses contrastive learning to preserve node discriminability.
AI.result: On 10 real-world hypergraphs, HyBridge outperforms 22 competing methods, with performance improvements of up to 9.82% in node classification.
AI.conclusion: Guiding hyperbolic radial positions with hyperedge-aware bridge scores makes hyperbolic hypergraph embeddings more effective than naive extensions of existing methods.

title: SoScale: Second-Order Scale Search for FP4 Quantization
summary: Low-bit quantization reduces the memory footprint and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), yet accurate FP4 quantization remains challenging. Practical formats such as MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4 pair a 4-bit floating-point payload with block-wise or hierarchical scale codes, making accuracy highly sensitive to how each local distribution is scaled. Default maximum-absolute-value scaling preserves dynamic range, but can spend scarce FP4 levels on rarely occupied outlier regions and leave dense tensor values poorly resolved. Existing scale-search methods minimize local element-wise reconstruction error, optimizing tensor fidelity rather than layer-output fidelity. We propose SoScale, a second-order weight scale-code search method for hierarchical FP4 quantization. SoScale searches hardware-valid scale codes under a Hessian-aware layer reconstruction objective and couples this search with GPTQ-style error recovery, selecting scales by their impact on layer outputs. Across Qwen3 models, SoScale consistently reduces downstream quantization degradation under MXFP4, NVFP4, and HiF4.

AI.tldr: SoScale is a second-order weight scale-code search for hierarchical FP4 quantization that selects scales by their effect on layer outputs. Across Qwen3 models it consistently reduces downstream quantization degradation under MXFP4, NVFP4 and HiF4.
AI.motivation: Default max-absolute-value scaling can spend scarce FP4 levels on rare outliers and leave dense values poorly resolved. Existing scale-search methods minimize element-wise reconstruction error, which targets tensor fidelity rather than layer-output fidelity.
AI.method: SoScale searches hardware-valid scale codes under a Hessian-aware layer reconstruction objective and couples the search with GPTQ-style error recovery, selecting scales by their impact on layer outputs.
AI.result: Across Qwen3 models, SoScale consistently reduces downstream quantization degradation under MXFP4, NVFP4 and HiF4.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing scale codes for layer-output fidelity rather than local tensor reconstruction is an effective way to improve hierarchical FP4 quantization of LLMs.

title: Robots That Talk Too Much and Don't Listen Enough
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures, presented at EMF Workshop, HRI 2026, Edinburgh, Scotland
summary: Until recently, the biggest obstacles to natural spoken interaction with social robots were speech recognition errors and turn-taking failures. Advances in speech recognition have enabled much better spoken interaction, but turn-taking failures and other misunderstandings continue to be far too prevalent. This short paper looks back at earlier methods for improving speech recognition and turn-taking in interaction with social robots, and then looks at what can be done today, arguing that multimodal bidirectional streaming is needed to reduce the frequency of turn-taking failures.

AI.tldr: This short perspective argues that turn-taking failures remain the main obstacle to natural spoken interaction with social robots, even though speech recognition has improved. It argues that multimodal bidirectional streaming is needed to reduce these failures.
AI.motivation: Speech recognition has improved, but turn-taking failures and other misunderstandings in spoken interaction with social robots are still too frequent.
AI.method: The paper reviews earlier methods for improving speech recognition and turn-taking in social robot interaction and then discusses what can be done today. It does not describe an experimental method.
AI.result: The paper reports no experimental results; its findings are arguments based on the review of prior methods.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal bidirectional streaming is needed to reduce the frequency of turn-taking failures in social robot interaction.

title: PISim: A Unified Photonic Inference Simulator for Hardware-Aware Cross-Layer Design-Space Exploration
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures
summary: Photonic neural accelerators offer ultra-low latency linear algebra, yet their usable numerical precision, sustainable throughput, and application accuracy remain tightly bounded by surrounding electro-optical interfaces and physical non-idealities. Pre-fabrication design-space exploration (DSE) requires a cross-layer electronic design automation (EDA) framework capable of evaluating disparate optical topologies under identical neural workloads and physical assumptions. We present \textbf{PISim}, a unified Photonic Inference Simulator that couples pretrained deep neural network execution with physics-based models of six accelerator architecture families, six electro-optic modulator technologies, four optical source organizations, and direct or coherent readout schemes. PISim embeds stage-resolved impairment operators---covering control and analog-to-digital quantization, finite extinction ratio, shot noise, correlated relative-intensity noise (RIN), thermal drift, propagation loss, and channel crosstalk---alongside an analytical cycle-level interface timing model to expose electronic-optical bottlenecks. Using simulated MNIST multilayer perceptron (MLP) benchmarks, we demonstrate how PISim identifies optimal precision operating points under multi-impairment stress (peaking at 6 bits for Mach--Zehnder and microring modulators), quantifies a 52.5 percentage-point accuracy gap between VCSEL-array and parallel-fanout laser architectures arising, under the modeled conditions, from power partitioning and correlated source noise, and models interface-limited throughput scaling across emitter-array widths from 32 to 128 channels. This comprehensive framework establishes an extensible, reproducible foundation for accuracy-constrained Pareto optimization prior to photonic tape-out.

AI.tldr: PISim is a unified photonic inference simulator that couples pretrained DNN execution with physics-based models of accelerator architectures, electro-optic modulators, laser sources and readout schemes. It supports pre-fabrication design-space exploration, for example finding a 6-bit precision operating point for Mach-Zehnder and microring modulators on MNIST MLPs.
AI.motivation: Usable precision, throughput and application accuracy of photonic neural accelerators are bounded by electro-optical interfaces and physical non-idealities. Pre-fabrication design-space exploration requires a cross-layer framework that compares optical topologies under identical workloads and physical assumptions.
AI.method: PISim combines pretrained DNN execution with physics-based models of six accelerator architecture families, six electro-optic modulator technologies, four optical source organizations, and direct or coherent readout. It embeds stage-resolved impairment operators, including control and ADC quantization, finite extinction ratio, shot noise, correlated RIN, thermal drift, propagation loss and crosstalk, along with an analytical cycle-level interface timing model.
AI.result: On simulated MNIST MLP benchmarks under multi-impairment stress, precision peaks at 6 bits for Mach-Zehnder and microring modulators. The VCSEL-array and parallel-fanout laser architectures differ by a 52.5 percentage-point accuracy gap under the modeled conditions. Interface-limited throughput is modeled across emitter-array widths from 32 to 128 channels.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers an extensible and reproducible basis for accuracy-constrained Pareto optimization before photonic tape-out.

title: RESYNC: Residual Latent-State Synchronization for Deadline-Bound Streaming Inference
summary: Predicting every observation in a high-rate stream requires a model to finish before the next arrival. A large model may offer better predictions but miss that deadline. We propose RESYNC: the large model runs asynchronously, while a fast path updates its latest exact but stale latent state using the observations received since that state was computed and applies its unchanged prediction head. The updater learns from the frozen model's representations without task labels. Across one real and two synthetic streams and five architecture families, RESYNC beats the best compact or distilled alternative with a paired 95% interval above zero in all twelve dataset--architecture pairs with a material teacher advantage at anchor ages of 4--12 observations, and in eleven pairs at older tested ages up to 32. The share of the teacher's gain preserved remains complete on the real stream but is lower and generally declines with anchor age on the synthetic streams. In live replay with 1 ms arrivals, the synchronous large models cannot deliver any predictions on time while RESYNC serves at least 99.4% of arrivals within the interval, with 0.35--0.62 ms median latency on one CPU thread: around the same speed as or faster than the compact model, and 7.9--17.7$\times$ faster than synchronous large-model inference. RESYNC targets settings with background compute available but a strict per-observation response deadline.

AI.tldr: RESYNC runs a large model asynchronously and uses a fast path to update its latest stale latent state with newer observations, then applies the unchanged prediction head. It beats the best compact or distilled alternative in most tested settings and serves at least 99.4% of arrivals within the deadline.
AI.motivation: In high-rate streams, a large model may give better predictions but cannot finish before the next observation arrives, while compact models sacrifice accuracy.
AI.method: The large model runs asynchronously and produces an exact but stale latent state. A fast-path updater, trained on the frozen model's representations without task labels, advances this state using observations received since it was computed, and the unchanged prediction head makes the output.
AI.result: Across one real and two synthetic streams and five architecture families, RESYNC beats the best compact or distilled alternative in all twelve dataset-architecture pairs with a material teacher advantage at anchor ages of 4 to 12 observations, and in eleven pairs at older ages up to 32. In live replay with 1 ms arrivals, synchronous large models miss every deadline, while RESYNC serves at least 99.4% of arrivals with 0.35 to 0.62 ms median latency on one CPU thread, and is 7.9 to 17.7 times faster than synchronous large-model inference.
AI.conclusion: RESYNC suits settings with background compute and a strict per-observation response deadline, keeping much of the large model's gain while meeting latency bounds, although the preserved share of the gain is lower on synthetic streams and declines with anchor age.

title: A Joint LLM and Optimization Agent Solution for Drone Scheduling in Victim Search Missions
summary: Victim search in wilderness areas is time-critical. Drones enable rapid area search, but scheduling them is challenging because victims may continue moving, detection results are uncertain, and effective decisions must combine structured mission information with unstructured contextual clues and domain knowledge. To address this, we propose an agent-aided drone scheduling system. The system employs an agent at the ground control station (GCS) to coordinate multiple drones over successive search cycles. In each cycle, the agent applies a scheduling policy that combines a large language model (LLM) for reasoning about where to search with an optimizer for determining how to dispatch the drones under energy constraints. Simulation results show that the proposed system consistently completes the victim-search mission, whereas none of the six non-LLM baselines does so and direct LLM scheduling is considerably less reliable. The source code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an agent-aided drone scheduling system in which a ground-station LLM agent reasons about where to search and an optimizer decides how to dispatch drones under energy constraints. In simulation it completes victim-search missions where six non-LLM baselines fail and direct LLM scheduling is less reliable.
AI.motivation: Victim search in wilderness areas is time-critical, and scheduling drones is hard because victims move, detections are uncertain, and decisions must combine structured data with unstructured context.
AI.method: An agent at the ground control station coordinates multiple drones over successive search cycles. In each cycle it applies a policy that combines an LLM for reasoning about where to search with an optimizer for drone dispatch under energy constraints.
AI.result: In simulation, the proposed system consistently completes the victim-search mission, whereas none of six non-LLM baselines does, and direct LLM scheduling is considerably less reliable.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLM reasoning about search locations with constrained optimization can make drone scheduling for victim search reliable, and the source code is publicly available.

title: ZONOS3-Mini Technical Report
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Model weights: this https URL ; code: this https URL
summary: ZONOS3-Mini is an ultra-compact, ultra-fast, zero-shot voice-cloning TTS model. The model can run in real time on a laptop or smartphone. For its latency and size, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and cloning fidelity. To achieve this we propose a latent MoE backbone with only 886M parameters (100M active per token) and a new audio codec, Zyphra Audio Codec 1 (ZAC-1), which represents 44.1 kHz audio at a 15 Hz frame rate. On the new ZTTS2-Eval benchmark, ZONOS3-Mini reaches a 6.71% macro-average WER over 55 language sets (35 clean and 20 in the wild), which is competitive with larger and slower state-of-the-art models. We release the model weights, inference, and training code.

AI.tldr: ZONOS3-Mini is an 886M-parameter zero-shot voice-cloning TTS model with a latent MoE backbone and a new 15 Hz audio codec, ZAC-1. It runs in real time on a laptop or smartphone and reaches a 6.71% macro-average WER over 55 language sets on ZTTS2-Eval.
AI.motivation: The goal is a TTS model that is ultra-compact and fast enough for real-time use on consumer devices while remaining competitive in accuracy and cloning fidelity with larger, slower models.
AI.method: The model uses a latent MoE backbone with 886M total parameters, 100M active per token, and a new audio codec, Zyphra Audio Codec 1 (ZAC-1), which represents 44.1 kHz audio at a 15 Hz frame rate.
AI.result: On the new ZTTS2-Eval benchmark, ZONOS3-Mini reaches a 6.71% macro-average WER over 55 language sets (35 clean and 20 in the wild), which the abstract describes as competitive with larger and slower state-of-the-art models.
AI.conclusion: A small, fast zero-shot TTS model can be competitive with larger systems, and the authors release the weights, inference code and training code.

title: Reducing Batch Makespan for LLM Agent Workloads through Inference-Environment Coordination
comment: 26 pages, 12 figures. Technical report
summary: Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch. For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model guides GPU-memory allocation between key-value (KV) cache and recurrent state and provides a reference sample concurrency to exploit parallelism while limiting recomputation. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse while balancing worker load. Under constrained environment capacity, we decouple sample admission from environment execution and introduce Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS), which prioritizes long chains using observed progress to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay combines actual inference with recorded environment responses and durations for ablations of individual optimizations. Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on the BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas benchmarks demonstrate makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation scores remain aligned. Furthermore, these methods have been successfully applied to training and evaluation workflows for the Ling-3.x model series, accelerating the model-development cycle.

AI.tldr: The paper coordinates inference and environment execution for batched LLM agent workloads to reduce batch makespan. Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash show makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0% with aligned evaluation scores.
AI.motivation: Agent tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, so batch completion time depends on both, and efficient batch execution matters for benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation and RL rollouts.
AI.method: For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model allocates GPU memory between the KV cache and recurrent state. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse and balance worker load. Under constrained environment capacity, sample admission is decoupled from environment execution, and Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS) prioritizes long chains to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay mixes real inference with recorded environment responses for ablations.
AI.result: Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch and MCP-Atlas show makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation scores remain aligned.
AI.conclusion: The coordinated optimizations shorten batch makespan without hurting scores, and they have been applied to training and evaluation workflows for the Ling-3.x model series.

title: Edge-Gradient Augmentation under Reinforcement Learning for Temporal Graph
summary: Temporal link prediction is critical for understand- ing dynamic interactions in evolving networks, informing appli- cations ranging from social network analysis to recommendation systems. Existing methods typically rely on raw temporal graph data, often neglecting explicit edge-change information that can significantly improve predictive performance. To address this gap, we propose edge-gradient reinforced learning (EG-RL), a framework that explicitly encodes edge-gradient events (edge births and deaths) through dedicated node and link encoding modules. EG-RL uses a policy-driven reinforcement-learning mechanism to dynamically select and augment the most infor- mative edge snapshots, guided by critic-based feedback to opti- mize prediction accuracy. The model comprises distinct modules for node encoding, link encoding, token mixing, and channel mixing, integrated through global pooling and followed by a two-layer multilayer perceptron classifier. Extensive experiments on multiple dynamic graph datasets demonstrate substantial gains in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and average precision. Ablation studies further confirm the necessity of adaptive edge-gradient augmentation and validate the effectiveness of the proposed encoding and reinforcement- learning mechanisms.

AI.tldr: EG-RL is a temporal link prediction framework that explicitly encodes edge births and deaths as edge-gradient events and uses reinforcement learning to select and augment the most informative edge snapshots. Experiments on multiple dynamic graph datasets report substantial gains in AUC and average precision.
AI.motivation: Existing temporal link prediction methods mostly use raw temporal graph data and often ignore explicit edge-change information, which could improve prediction.
AI.method: Dedicated node and link encoding modules encode edge-gradient events. A policy-driven reinforcement learning mechanism, guided by critic feedback, selects and augments informative edge snapshots. The model adds token mixing and channel mixing, global pooling, and a two-layer MLP classifier.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple dynamic graph datasets show substantial gains in area under the ROC curve and average precision. Ablations confirm the need for adaptive edge-gradient augmentation and the effectiveness of the encoding and RL mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling edge-change events with adaptive augmentation improves temporal link prediction, according to the reported experiments.

title: MobileProbe: Adaptive Security Evaluation of Mobile Agents via Trajectory-Aware Injection
comment: Accepted at NDSS 2027
summary: Mobile GUI agents read the screen of a phone and operate apps on a user's behalf to complete multi-step tasks such as online shopping or messaging. Because the agent acts on whatever the screen shows, an attacker can embed malicious instructions into ordinary UI content and redirect its actions. We refer to this threat as environmental injection attack (EIA). Existing benchmarks measure this risk by pinning hand-crafted payloads to a fixed step of a fixed task. This approach faces two limitations. First, each payload is bound to one task in one app and does not transfer without manual redesign. Second, agents given the same task may follow different routes, so an agent that never reaches the injected page is recorded as safe without being tested. This insufficient test coverage can cause fixed-point benchmarks to underestimate the security risk of deployed mobile agents. In this work, we propose MobileProbe, a trajectory-aware red-teaming framework that evaluates mobile agents adaptively. MobileProbe discovers attacker-controllable content surfaces through automated pentesting, localizes vulnerable decision points along the agent's trajectory, and iteratively refines context-aware payloads through a surrogate-filtered evolutionary loop. We construct a benchmark of 83 long-horizon attack instances spanning 12 mobile applications. Each is annotated with a Confidentiality, Integrity, or Availability (CIA) attack goal to cover the principal categories of security threats facing mobile agents. On three representative agent architectures, MobileProbe attains higher attack success rates than human-written, zero-shot LLM, and prior automated red-teaming baselines adapted to the mobile domain. MobileProbe can serve as a pre-deployment auditing tool to systematically uncover vulnerabilities and inform security hardening of mobile agents.

AI.tldr: MobileProbe is a trajectory-aware red-teaming framework that adaptively evaluates the security of mobile GUI agents against environmental injection attacks. It attains higher attack success rates than human-written, zero-shot LLM and prior automated baselines on three agent architectures, using 83 attack instances across 12 apps.
AI.motivation: Fixed-point benchmarks pin hand-crafted payloads to one step of one task, so payloads do not transfer, and agents that never reach the injected page are scored as safe. Both can underestimate the security risk of deployed mobile agents.
AI.method: MobileProbe finds attacker-controllable content surfaces through automated pentesting, localizes vulnerable decision points along the agent's trajectory, and iteratively refines context-aware payloads with a surrogate-filtered evolutionary loop. The benchmark contains 83 long-horizon attack instances across 12 mobile applications, each labelled with a CIA attack goal.
AI.result: On three representative agent architectures, MobileProbe attains higher attack success rates than human-written, zero-shot LLM and prior automated red-teaming baselines adapted to the mobile domain.
AI.conclusion: MobileProbe is proposed as a pre-deployment auditing tool for uncovering vulnerabilities and informing security hardening of mobile agents.

title: MusicRWKV: A Multimodal RWKV Framework for Music Representation Learning
summary: Recent music foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in music representation learning, yet most existing approaches rely on Transformer architectures whose quadratic attention complexity introduces substantial computational and memory overhead when modeling long-duration music recordings. In this work, we propose MusicRWKV, a multimodal music representation learning framework built upon the RWKV architecture. MusicRWKV jointly models waveform, spectrogram, and metadata information within a unified self-supervised learning framework. To improve efficiency for long musical sequences, we introduce an invertible compression module that reduces sequence length while preserving reconstruction capability. A FiLM-based conditioning strategy is employed to facilitate modality-aware representation learning without introducing expensive cross-attention operations. We further investigate the integration of Soft ROSA as a differentiable retrieval mechanism for neural-symbolic interaction. Experimental evaluation across a diverse collection of Music Information Retrieval (MIR) benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed RWKV-based architecture can be effectively adapted to heterogeneous music understanding tasks. A controlled pretraining ablation shows that Soft ROSA improves validation performance, while layer-wise telemetry analysis reveals a progressive transition from distributed retrieval to selective retrieval in deeper network layers. These results suggest that RWKV provides a promising architectural alternative to Transformer-based models for multimodal music understanding.

AI.tldr: MusicRWKV is a multimodal music representation learning framework built on the RWKV architecture. It models waveform, spectrogram and metadata with an invertible compression module, and reports effective adaptation across MIR benchmarks without cross-attention.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based music foundation models have quadratic attention cost, which becomes expensive for long music recordings.
AI.method: The framework jointly models waveform, spectrogram and metadata in a self-supervised setup. An invertible compression module shortens sequences while preserving reconstruction, FiLM conditioning provides modality-aware learning without cross-attention, and Soft ROSA is examined as a differentiable retrieval mechanism.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse MIR benchmarks show the RWKV-based architecture adapts to heterogeneous music understanding tasks. A pretraining ablation shows Soft ROSA improves validation performance, and layer-wise analysis shows a shift from distributed to selective retrieval in deeper layers.
AI.conclusion: RWKV is presented as a promising alternative to Transformers for multimodal music understanding.

title: From Data to Wisdom: Rethinking AI Through an Epistemic Lens
comment: 23 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables
summary: This paper proposes the Data-to-Wisdom Epistemic Architecture for AI (EAAI), a conceptual framework treating Data, Information, Knowledge, Understanding and Wisdom as five distinct but recursively interacting epistemic functions: observation, contextual interpretation, modeling and prediction, critical evaluation and informed judgment. Two observations motivate it: sequential readings of the Knowledge Pyramid obscure how these functions interact, and a targeted review of ten Bayesian reference books finds that prior distributions are defined mathematically while "prior information" and "prior knowledge" are not consistently distinguished as epistemic categories. A Bayesian interpretation relates the likelihood, prior and posterior distributions, posterior prediction, model checking and decision analysis to the five functions, without limiting EAAI to Bayesian systems. Extending "prior" in an epistemic sense, the paper distinguishes five kinds of prior context that can shape the model, the likelihood, the prior, evaluation and action. Three worked applications -- quantitative financial risk, actuarial modeling in health insurance and agentic AI for medical reimbursement claims -- show how EAAI structures the analysis of model assumptions, evidence interpretation, validation, dependencies and decision consequences, separating the prediction of a risk, the appraisal of its reliability and the justification of action. It draws implications for AI and machine learning, including evaluation by function, treating intermediate model outputs as evidence open to challenge and separating generation from appraisal, and compares EAAI with work on DIKW, Bayesian workflow, AI evaluation and risk governance. Its contributions are an epistemic vocabulary with recursive relationships, a more accessible reading of Bayesian methodology, a typology of prior context and clearer methodological terminology.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Data-to-Wisdom Epistemic Architecture (EAAI), which treats Data, Information, Knowledge, Understanding and Wisdom as five recursively interacting epistemic functions. It is illustrated with three applications in financial risk, health-insurance actuarial modeling and medical reimbursement claims.
AI.motivation: The Knowledge Pyramid in sequential form obscures how its functions interact, and a review of ten Bayesian reference books finds that "prior information" and "prior knowledge" are not consistently distinguished as epistemic categories.
AI.method: A Bayesian interpretation relates likelihood, prior, posterior, posterior prediction, model checking and decision analysis to the five functions, without limiting the framework to Bayesian systems. The paper distinguishes five kinds of prior context that can shape the model, likelihood, prior, evaluation and action.
AI.result: Three worked applications show how EAAI structures analysis of model assumptions, evidence interpretation, validation, dependencies and decision consequences, separating risk prediction, reliability appraisal and the justification of action. The abstract reports no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: The contributions are an epistemic vocabulary with recursive relationships, a more accessible reading of Bayesian methodology, a typology of prior context and clearer methodological terminology, with implications such as evaluating by function and separating generation from appraisal.

title: EgoX: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Manipulation with Embodiment Dreaming
summary: Generalist manipulation policies can benefit from the complementary experience of humans, real robots, and simulated agents. However, differences in morphology, sensing, and control interfaces make it difficult to learn effectively from their combined demonstrations. We introduce EgoX, an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework that organizes heterogeneous demonstrations through semantically corresponding observation and action modalities. EgoX pretrains a Modularized Cross-Embodiment Transformer with Embodiment Dreaming (MXT+) on this mixture and fine-tunes it on target-embodiment demonstrations. Within each embodiment, MXT+ assigns a dedicated tokenizer to each observation modality and a dedicated expert to each action modality, with a Transformer trunk shared across embodiments. A training-only embodiment-dreaming objective predicts latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states, encouraging the shared trunk to model each embodiment's dynamics. Across 13 task-embodiment pairs spanning five tasks and six robot embodiments, including five physical robots and one simulated humanoid, cross-embodiment pretraining raises MXT+'s average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch. The gains are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Ablations demonstrate the benefits of broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces, and embodiment dreaming, with dreaming producing more similar latent geometry across embodiments. Project page: this http URL.

AI.tldr: EgoX is an egocentric cross-embodiment manipulation framework that pretrains a modular transformer with a training-only embodiment-dreaming objective on heterogeneous demonstrations. Across 13 task-embodiment pairs, cross-embodiment pretraining raises average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch.
AI.motivation: Humans, real robots and simulated agents provide complementary experience, but differences in morphology, sensing and control make it hard to learn from their combined demonstrations.
AI.method: EgoX organizes demonstrations through semantically corresponding observation and action modalities. Its MXT+ model uses a dedicated tokenizer per observation modality, a dedicated expert per action modality, and a Transformer trunk shared across embodiments. A training-only embodiment-dreaming objective predicts latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states.
AI.result: Across 13 task-embodiment pairs spanning five tasks and six robot embodiments, cross-embodiment pretraining raises average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over scratch training. Under out-of-distribution conditions the rise is from 0.53 to 0.77. Ablations show benefits from broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces and embodiment dreaming.
AI.conclusion: Cross-embodiment pretraining with embodiment dreaming improves manipulation policies, especially out of distribution, and dreaming produces more similar latent geometry across embodiments.

title: DPA: Decentralized Primal Averaging with Quasi-Global Momentum for Highly Heterogeneous Data
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 7 figures. Code available at this https URL
summary: Decentralized training of deep learning models keeps training data local and supports on-device learning over networks. In realistic scenarios, heterogeneity across agents' local data poses an optimization challenge and can severely degrade test accuracy, especially on sparse communication graphs. Building on recent advances in centralized primal averaging, we propose Decentralized Primal Averaging (DPA), a decentralized learning algorithm that combines primal averaging with a local quasi-global momentum buffer. DPA maintains three coupled sequences for optimization, gradient evaluation, and output averaging, while using consecutive mixed iterates to construct a network-aware momentum direction without transmitting an auxiliary tracking variable. For smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish a convergence bound for DPA and identify conditions for linear speedup in the number of agents for sufficiently many iterations. We also introduce DPA-1G, a variant that uses one communication round per iteration and matches the per-iteration communication cost of DSGD-style baselines.
