Experiments following the GUT decentralized image-classification benchmark show that DPA compares favorably with DSGD, gradient tracking, QG-DSGDm, momentum tracking, and QG-GUTm across datasets, architectures, topologies, and heterogeneity levels, with the largest gains under high heterogeneity on sparse rings. At the same total communication cost, both DPA variants achieve higher mean test accuracy than the best baseline on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-20. Our code is publicly available.

AI.tldr: DPA is a decentralized learning algorithm that combines primal averaging with a local quasi-global momentum buffer to handle highly heterogeneous data on sparse graphs. Its variant DPA-1G matches the per-iteration communication cost of DSGD-style baselines and reaches higher mean test accuracy than the best baseline on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-20.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous local data in decentralized training can severely degrade test accuracy, especially on sparse communication graphs, and existing methods face this optimization challenge.
AI.method: DPA maintains three coupled sequences for optimization, gradient evaluation and output averaging. It uses consecutive mixed iterates to form a network-aware momentum direction without transmitting an auxiliary tracking variable. DPA-1G uses one communication round per iteration.
AI.result: For smooth nonconvex objectives, the paper gives a convergence bound with conditions for linear speedup in the number of agents. Experiments following the GUT benchmark show DPA compares favorably with several baselines, with the largest gains under high heterogeneity on sparse rings. At the same total communication cost, both DPA variants achieve higher mean test accuracy than the best baseline on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-20.
AI.conclusion: DPA is a communication-efficient decentralized method that improves accuracy under heterogeneity, and the authors state that the code is publicly available.

title: Context Graph: Explainable Multi-Agent Decision Chains in AI-RAN
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: AI-RAN distributes network control across multiple autonomous agents, namely xApps and rApps operating over shared radio resources. When an alert or degradation appears, operators currently lack a structured way to trace which decision caused it, what context triggered that decision, and how other agents interacted. Existing explainability tools focus on single-model feature attribution or linear event logging, neither of which captures cross-agent decision chains. We propose the Context Graph, a heterogeneous directed graph that organizes policies, measurements, decisions, and alerts into a queryable explanation layer. Its foundational primitive is the Decision-Event node acting as a causal junction, where incoming edges capture triggering context and outgoing edges track downstream consequences that are progressively upgraded through counterfactual verification. Instantiated over existing E2, A1, and O1 data flows, our proof-of-concept demonstrates that compliance and diagnosis queries are resolved at sub-millisecond latency over graphs of tens of thousands of nodes, while reliably distinguishing true causal impacts from spurious correlations.

AI.tldr: Context Graph is a heterogeneous directed graph that records policies, measurements, decisions and alerts in AI-RAN, so operators can trace cross-agent decision chains. The proof-of-concept answers compliance and diagnosis queries at sub-millisecond latency over graphs of tens of thousands of nodes.
AI.motivation: In AI-RAN, xApps and rApps act as autonomous agents over shared radio resources, and existing explainability tools cover single-model attribution or linear event logs, not cross-agent decision chains.
AI.method: The graph has Decision-Event nodes as causal junctions. Incoming edges capture triggering context and outgoing edges track downstream consequences, which are upgraded through counterfactual verification. It is instantiated over existing E2, A1 and O1 data flows.
AI.result: The proof-of-concept resolves compliance and diagnosis queries at sub-millisecond latency over graphs of tens of thousands of nodes, and reliably distinguishes true causal impacts from spurious correlations.
AI.conclusion: A queryable explanation layer built on decision-event causal junctions can make multi-agent RAN control traceable, according to the proof-of-concept.

title: Protein Language Models Fail To Capture Contact Predictions Under Invariant Relabeling
comment: Accepted to the ICBINB - Failure Modes of AI in Biology Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. 15 pages, 6 figures
summary: Protein language models (pLMs) produce highly accurate contact maps from single-sequence inputs. People often take this accuracy as proof that these models implicitly learn invariant coevolutionary statistics, extracting the same signals as classical alignment-based methods like Potts. In this work, we introduce a diagnostic framework around a global bijective relabeling of the amino-acid alphabet. This transformation permutes residue letters while leaving all alignment-level information, column entropies, and pairwise edit distances unchanged. Pseudolikelihood Potts models and inverse-covariance estimators remain invariant under this transformation, but pLMs fail the test. Across multiple architectures (ESM-2, MSA Transformer, AMPLIFY) and model scales (8M to 3B parameters), pLM contact maps collapse under arbitrary relabeling. Using Hamming distance controls and biochemical grouping interventions, we attempt to isolate what likely causes this degradation and find that these models rely on explicit, canonical residue identities (``alphabet anchoring'') rather than pure coevolutionary statistics. Increasing scale makes models more responsive to biochemical classes, but their performance still degrades under relabeling. Our findings show a gap between how pLMs and classical coevolutionary models compute contacts. More broadly, our work shows how diagnostic perturbations that leave classical models provably unchanged can expose hidden representation biases and prevent over-reliance on neural black boxes in biological modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that protein language models lose their contact-prediction accuracy when the amino-acid alphabet is relabeled by a bijection, while Potts and inverse-covariance models are unchanged. The authors conclude that pLMs rely on canonical residue identities rather than coevolutionary statistics.
AI.motivation: Protein language models produce accurate contact maps from single sequences, and this is often taken as evidence that they learn invariant coevolutionary statistics like classical alignment-based methods do.
AI.method: A global bijective relabeling of the amino-acid alphabet is used as a diagnostic. It leaves alignment-level information, column entropies and pairwise edit distances unchanged, and classical Potts and inverse-covariance models are invariant under it. Hamming distance controls and biochemical grouping interventions are used to probe the cause.
AI.result: Across ESM-2, MSA Transformer and AMPLIFY at scales from 8M to 3B parameters, pLM contact maps collapse under arbitrary relabeling. The models rely on explicit canonical residue identities ("alphabet anchoring"). Scale makes models more responsive to biochemical classes, but performance still degrades under relabeling.
AI.conclusion: There is a gap between how pLMs and classical coevolutionary models compute contacts, and diagnostic perturbations can expose hidden representation biases in neural models of biology.

title: LLM-Assisted Verification in Dafny
comment: 16 pages (excluding references), 20 pages including references; 1 figure, 2 tables. Submitted to FSEN 2027
summary: Formal verification of complex algorithms requires expertise in program specification, invariant construction, mathematical proof, and the management of automated theorem provers. Although large language models (LLMs) can generate program code and proof fragments, reliably developing complete machine-checked verifications remains challenging: it requires an iterative process of constructing and validating specifications and invariants, building proofs, diagnosing solver failures, and optimizing verification performance. This paper presents a systematic ten-step workflow for LLM-assisted verification of scientific algorithms using the Dafny verification system. The workflow integrates algorithm formalization, contract development, empirical invariant validation, proof construction, bottleneck profiling, and resource-driven proof optimization. We applied the workflow using Antrhopic's Claude Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 models, combining LLM-driven development with automated testing and verification feedback, while retaining human oversight for correctness-critical decisions and strategic interventions. We evaluate the approach on 37 complex algorithms from graph theory and labelled transition systems. Notably, we verified the Hopfcroft-Tarjan triconnectivity test, demonstrating that even highly challenging algorithmic verification tasks can be carried out through a structured LLM-assisted workflow. Many of our machine-checked verifications were obtained within hours to a few days of interactive development. Our results suggest that LLM-assisted workflows can shift the role of the human verifier from detailed proof construction toward supervision, specification review, and strategic guidance.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a ten-step workflow for LLM-assisted formal verification of scientific algorithms in Dafny. Applied with Claude Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 to 37 algorithms, it verified the Hopcroft-Tarjan triconnectivity test, often within hours to a few days.
AI.motivation: Machine-checked verification of complex algorithms needs specification, invariant, proof and solver expertise, and LLMs can generate code and proof fragments but do not reliably complete verifications on their own.
AI.method: The workflow covers algorithm formalization, contract development, empirical invariant validation, proof construction, bottleneck profiling and resource-driven proof optimization, combined with automated testing, verifier feedback and human oversight for correctness-critical decisions.
AI.result: The approach is evaluated on 37 complex algorithms from graph theory and labelled transition systems. The Hopcroft-Tarjan triconnectivity test is verified, and many verifications were obtained within hours to a few days of interactive development.
AI.conclusion: LLM-assisted workflows can move the human verifier's role from detailed proof construction toward supervision, specification review and strategic guidance.

title: STEALTH: Steganographic Text Encoding Agnostic to Low-Level Tensor Hardware
summary: Provably secure linguistic steganography hides a message inside text sampled from a language model, so that without the key, a stegotext is computationally indistinguishable from an honest model sample. Nearly every such scheme assumes the receiver can recompute the sender's token probabilities exactly bit for bit. We show this assumption is fragile: across three model families, bit-exact schemes decode almost none of our messages once the receiver's floating-point precision, quantization, or GPU architecture differs from the sender's, or even when the receiver merely scores a text in parallel versus one token at a time, with the same model, precision, and hardware held fixed. We present STEALTH, a scheme built for exactly this setting. The sender draws each token with an exponential race driven by keyed pseudorandom noise, so a receiver's probability mismatch flips a token only when the race is close; a rateless spinal code, decoded by beam search, absorbs the resulting flips without the sender and receiver ever agreeing on a single distribution. We prove stegotexts remain indistinguishable from honest samples under this construction. Empirically, STEALTH decodes every message we sent for every receiver in the sender's model family, at every precision and quantization level, on smaller models, and on a different GPU architecture. STEALTH is even robust across different model families with separate vocabularies and tokenizers, decoding every message we tested. Our approach carries far more payload per token than prior robust schemes, and trained steganalyzers and a targeted statistical test both fail to distinguish its stegotexts from honest model output.

AI.tldr: STEALTH is a provably secure linguistic steganography scheme that stays decodable when the receiver's probabilities differ from the sender's due to precision, quantization, GPU architecture or parallel scoring. It decodes every tested message across receiver settings and carries more payload per token than prior robust schemes.
AI.motivation: Bit-exact provably secure steganography breaks when the receiver cannot recompute the sender's token probabilities exactly, and in three model families such schemes decode almost none of the messages under such mismatches.
AI.method: Each token is drawn with an exponential race driven by keyed pseudorandom noise, so a probability mismatch flips a token only when the race is close. A rateless spinal code decoded by beam search absorbs these flips, without sender and receiver agreeing on one distribution.
AI.result: STEALTH decodes every message sent for every receiver in the sender's model family, at every precision and quantization level, on smaller models and on a different GPU architecture. It also decodes every tested message across model families with different tokenizers. Trained steganalyzers and a targeted statistical test fail to distinguish its stegotexts from honest output.
AI.conclusion: The proof shows stegotexts remain indistinguishable from honest samples, and the scheme offers robust decoding with higher payload per token than prior robust schemes.

title: Kezek: Splitting Mono Two-Person Conversations into Per-Speaker Tracks for Full-Duplex Dialogue Data
comment: 18 pages, 15 tables, 2 figures. Code: this https URL ; weights: this https URL ; listening examples: this https URL
summary: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models learn turn-taking, overlaps and backchannels from conversations recorded with one channel per speaker, but most available conversational audio is a single mono mix. We present Kezek, a model that turns a mono recording of exactly two people into one track per person with the original length and timing; overlaps and short replies ("yeah", "mm-hm") stay on the track of the person who said them. Kezek decides who speaks when and who is who once for the whole recording (stage 1: a two-voice activity model guided by a speaker fingerprint trained to be insensitive to phase), and a conditioned time-domain separator only carries out that decision (stage 2), with outputs that always sum to the input. Standard separation metrics miss the failures that matter for dialogue data, so we report short-reply retention, leakage onto the other person's solo, channel swaps and coverage. Against the open pipeline pyannote -> DialogueSidon on the same recordings, Kezek keeps more short replies (0.83 vs. 0.69 on Open Yap test; 0.80 vs. 0.71 over the other's speech on unseen telephone speech from CallHome English), mostly because it returns the whole recording while the external pipeline drops part of it (on the audio both return, reply retention is about the same: 0.859 vs. 0.865 on Open Yap); it also leaks less, swaps channels less often, and runs 4-5 times faster (about 230 hours of audio per GPU-hour). We also report negative results and an ideal-mask ceiling that locate the remaining gap: quiet replies under a louder voice. Code and weights are released under permissive licences.

AI.tldr: Kezek splits a mono recording of exactly two speakers into one track per person with original length and timing. It keeps more short replies than the pyannote and DialogueSidon pipeline and runs 4 to 5 times faster, at about 230 hours of audio per GPU-hour.
AI.motivation: Full-duplex dialogue models need per-speaker channels, but most conversational audio is a single mono mix.
AI.method: Stage 1 is a two-voice activity model guided by a phase-insensitive speaker fingerprint, which decides who speaks when and who is who for the whole recording. Stage 2 is a conditioned time-domain separator that carries out that decision, with outputs that always sum to the input.
AI.result: Against pyannote followed by DialogueSidon, Kezek keeps more short replies: 0.83 versus 0.69 on Open Yap test, and 0.80 versus 0.71 over the other's speech on CallHome English telephone speech. On audio both return, reply retention is about the same (0.859 versus 0.865 on Open Yap). Kezek also leaks less, swaps channels less often and runs 4 to 5 times faster.
AI.conclusion: Kezek is a practical tool for producing per-speaker dialogue data, and the remaining gap lies in quiet replies under a louder voice. Code and weights are released under permissive licences.

title: AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems
comment: To be published on Annual Review Biomedical Data Science
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how biological research is done. Biological foundation models trained on millions of nucleotides, protein, and single-cell measurements predict protein structures, mutation effects, and cellular responses to genetic perturbations. Agentic systems, AI assistants built on large language models, can run multistep analyses from plain-language requests and increasingly call foundation models as tools. Yet it is often unclear when these models' outputs can be trusted. We frame this as a model's knowledge boundary: the range of inputs, tasks, and conditions over which its outputs are reliable. This review explains how foundation models are built and proposes that five design elements (data, architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme, and post-analysis) define this boundary. We examine evidence on where current models succeed or fail and present standardized descriptions of model limits so that researchers, and the agents acting for them, can use these tools reliably.

AI.tldr: This review frames the trustworthiness of biological foundation models as a knowledge boundary, the range of inputs, tasks and conditions where outputs are reliable. It proposes five design elements (data, architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme and post-analysis) that define this boundary.
AI.motivation: Biological foundation models and agentic systems that call them are increasingly used in research, but it is often unclear when their outputs can be trusted.
AI.method: The review explains how foundation models are built and proposes that five design elements define the knowledge boundary. It examines evidence on where current models succeed or fail.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results; the review examines evidence on where current models succeed and fail and presents standardized descriptions of model limits.
AI.conclusion: Standardized descriptions of model limits can let researchers and the agents acting for them use biological foundation models more reliably.

title: From Delegation to Coordination: Learning Efficient Multi-Agent Deep Research
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables
summary: Multi-agent deep-research systems use delegation to parallelize search and keep long tool traces out of the main agent's context. Yet delegation helps only when task allocation and subtask execution are coordinated: the main agent must issue useful subtasks, while subagents must return reliable evidence. Existing training either optimizes only the main agent or broadcasts the same team advantage to all agents, which can reward misleading subagent reports and penalize useful ones. We introduce LEAD-RL (Learning Effective Agent Delegation with Reinforcement Learning), a joint main-agent-subagent training framework with contribution-aware credit assignment. A training-time rubric evaluates the research utility of each subagent report and gates its inherited team advantage, while final-answer correctness remains the only team reward; no token, step, or speedup reward is used. Across five benchmarks and two model families, LEAD-RL improves answer quality. On BrowseComp, it improves accuracy by 2.49 percentage points and reduces critical-path cost by 24.5% over joint training with shared team credit. During validation, accuracy increases by 6.78 points at approximately constant critical-path cost. These results show that contribution-aware credit assignment improves the quality-efficiency trade-off of multi-agent deep research.

AI.tldr: LEAD-RL is a joint training framework for main agent and subagents in multi-agent deep research that uses contribution-aware credit assignment. It improves answer quality across five benchmarks, with a 2.49-point BrowseComp accuracy gain and 24.5% lower critical-path cost than joint training with shared team credit.
AI.motivation: Delegation helps deep research only when task allocation and subtask execution are coordinated. Existing training either optimizes only the main agent or gives the same team advantage to all agents, which can reward misleading subagent reports and penalize useful ones.
AI.method: A training-time rubric evaluates the research utility of each subagent report and gates the team advantage it inherits. Final-answer correctness is the only team reward, with no token, step or speedup reward.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks and two model families, LEAD-RL improves answer quality. On BrowseComp, accuracy improves by 2.49 percentage points and critical-path cost drops by 24.5% over joint training with shared team credit. During validation, accuracy rises by 6.78 points at approximately constant critical-path cost.
AI.conclusion: Contribution-aware credit assignment improves the quality-efficiency trade-off of multi-agent deep research.

title: A Compact xDAWN-Guided Spatio-Temporal Network with Filter-Bank Convolution for P300 Detection
summary: P300-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) enable communication by decoding stimulus-evoked EEG responses into character selections without requiring voluntary motor output. Reliable P300 detection remains difficult because of low response amplitude and signal-to-noise ratio, while practical spellers require accurate character selection with few stimulus repetitions and low computational cost. We propose a compact deep learning architecture that combines xDAWN spatial filtering for event-related potential enhancement and dimensionality reduction, a fixed frequency-selective filter bank, and convolutional feature learning for spatio-temporal EEG decoding. Depthwise-separable convolutions and progressive average pooling reduce computational complexity while retaining discriminative temporal information. The resulting target/non-target classifier contains only 5,100 trainable parameters. We evaluated the model on two public benchmarks, BCI Competition II Dataset IIb and BCI Competition III Dataset II, and compared it with established P300 decoding methods across different numbers of stimulus repetitions. The model achieved an information transfer rate of 17.8 bits/min with two repetitions on BCI Competition III and 40.5 bits/min on BCI Competition II, demonstrating a favorable accuracy-speed trade-off. These results suggest that combining domain-informed spatial and spectral priors with compact neural networks can support efficient P300 decoding for EEG-based BCI communication.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a compact P300 BCI decoder with xDAWN spatial filtering, a fixed filter bank and depthwise-separable convolutions, using 5,100 trainable parameters. It reaches 17.8 bits/min with two repetitions on BCI Competition III and 40.5 bits/min on BCI Competition II.
AI.motivation: P300 detection is hard because responses have low amplitude and low SNR, while practical spellers need accurate selection with few repetitions and low computational cost.
AI.method: The architecture applies xDAWN spatial filtering to enhance event-related potentials and reduce dimensionality, uses a fixed frequency-selective filter bank, and learns spatio-temporal features with convolutions. Depthwise-separable convolutions and progressive average pooling reduce computation.
AI.result: On BCI Competition II Dataset IIb and BCI Competition III Dataset II, the model reaches an information transfer rate of 17.8 bits/min with two repetitions on Competition III and 40.5 bits/min on Competition II, compared with established P300 decoding methods across repetition counts.
AI.conclusion: Combining domain-informed spatial and spectral priors with compact networks can support efficient P300 decoding for EEG-based communication.

title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models
summary: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.

AI.tldr: SALA learns latent actions from egocentric human videos by aligning them semantically with robot latents, using language similarity between unpaired clips. Its latent action supervision improves robot action prediction and real-world task success as pre-training and post-training data grow.
AI.motivation: Latent action models trained only with video reconstruction cluster latents by visual appearance rather than by underlying action, so human actions are hard to align with robot actions.
AI.method: Language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips estimate semantic similarities, which are turned into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents. Robot action reconstruction grounds the shared latent space in control, and the space supervises an embodied foundation model.
AI.result: Pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks. Post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.
AI.conclusion: Semantically aligned latent actions enable scaling along two axes, general pre-training and task-specific post-training, using human video without paired data.

title: Designing Institutions for Autonomous AI
summary: As autonomous AI agents increasingly interact in persistent populations, their collective capabilities and alignment depend not only on individual models, but also on the institutions governing their interactions. Yet AI research has largely focused on individual agents. In this Perspective, we argue that institutional design must become a distinct focus of AI research. Drawing on institutional political economy, social epistemology and organizational theory, we develop seven principles for designing AI institutions that sustain cooperation, enable reliable collective judgments and remain accountable to legitimate human purposes. These address reciprocal contributions, accountable authority, functional differentiation, epistemic pluralism, criticism and correction, human direction, and institutional adaptation. We illustrate their application through machine science, where autonomous research challenges institutions developed around human capabilities and constraints. We then propose an experimental research programme in which matched populations of AI agents operate under alternative institutional arrangements, and describe MoltJournal, an API-first journal for autonomous research agents, as an illustration of how such institutions can be made programmable and observable. Together, these contributions establish institutional design as a research agenda concerned not only with aligning autonomous agents, but with understanding how institutions can transform them into capable, reliable and accountable collectives.

AI.tldr: This perspective argues that institutional design should become a distinct research focus for autonomous AI agents and proposes seven principles for it. It also proposes an experimental programme comparing matched agent populations under different institutions, illustrated by the MoltJournal API-first journal.
AI.motivation: As autonomous agents interact in persistent populations, collective capabilities and alignment depend on the institutions governing them, yet AI research has focused largely on individual agents.
AI.method: Drawing on institutional political economy, social epistemology and organizational theory, the authors develop seven principles covering reciprocal contributions, accountable authority, functional differentiation, epistemic pluralism, criticism and correction, human direction, and institutional adaptation. They illustrate them through machine science.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experimental results; it proposes an experimental research programme and describes MoltJournal as an illustration of programmable, observable institutions.
AI.conclusion: Institutional design is set up as a research agenda concerned with turning autonomous agents into capable, reliable and accountable collectives.

title: Scalable Conversational Assessment: Chat-Based Exams with a Two-Agent LLM Pipeline
comment: Version submitted to SIGCSE TS 2027 (not accepted). A revised version is in preparation
summary: Oral exams are compelling because (1) students can be asked to provide their reasoning for an answer and (2) their interactive nature permits follow-up questions to resolve ambiguous answers. But oral exams scale poorly. In this paper, we present scalable conversational assessment, an LLM-based system that conducts interactive text-based conversations with students to assess their ability to make and support an argument. We use a two-agent architecture to separate concerns and reduce the likelihood that answers are leaked to the student: the interviewer interacts directly with the student, but only receives guidance about the next question to ask the student; the hidden evaluator knows the goals of the whole activity, tracks the student's progress using a rubric, and guides the interviewer on when to follow-up on the current question or proceed to the next question. The system was first tested using a collection of simulated students with LLM personas of a particular ability level or adversarial tactic (e.g., answer-extractors, prompt-injectors, confident fabricators). A novel element of this evaluation was that it required the use of a fictional assessment topic to prevent personas that shouldn't have information from using knowledge present in the LLM's pre-training. The system was also deployed in a small, elective AI literacy course in both formative and summative contexts. Through manual and post-facto AI review of the transcripts we identified opportunities to improve the follow-up question generation and ensure that grading only credited ideas that the student (and not the interviewer) contributed.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a scalable conversational assessment system in which a hidden evaluator and a student-facing interviewer, two LLM agents, conduct text-based oral-style exams. It was tested with simulated student personas and deployed in a small elective AI literacy course.
AI.motivation: Oral exams reveal student reasoning and allow follow-up questions, but they scale poorly.
AI.method: A two-agent architecture separates an interviewer, which talks with the student and receives only the next-question guidance, from a hidden evaluator that knows the full goals, tracks progress with a rubric, and decides when to follow up or move on. Evaluation used simulated personas, including answer-extractors, prompt-injectors and confident fabricators, on a fictional topic.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results. Transcript review identified improvements to follow-up question generation and to ensuring grading credits only ideas contributed by the student.
AI.conclusion: Two-agent conversational assessment is a promising scalable approach, and it needs refinement in follow-up generation and in attribution of credited ideas before wider use.

title: When Both Sides Adapt: The Challenges of Evaluating Interactive LLM Systems
summary: In interactive systems where users engage with LLMs, users are adaptive and, after observing LLM responses, can change their prompting strategy, as well as the type and difficulty of subsequent tasks. Thus model responses can influence the set of prompts on which the model is subsequently evaluated. We study the implications of this user adaptivity and prompt endogeneity for the evaluation of LLMs. We define two classes of estimands for comparing models: the common-distribution effect, which compares model performance on the same distribution of prompts, and the induced-distribution effect, which compares each model on the prompt distribution generated through user interaction. We show that offline benchmark evaluation and live A/B testing target different quantities, with the standard difference-in-means estimators for the two methods converging to the common-distribution effect and the induced-distribution effect, respectively. This distinction can affect decision-making: the two comparisons can rank models differently and lead to discrepancies in deployment recommendations. We characterize when such ranking reversals occur and provide a sufficient condition under which the rankings are guaranteed to agree. This result provides a practical heuristic for assessing whether offline evaluation is sufficient to reproduce the decision suggested by a live experiment. Third, we show, in a stylized linear model of interactions, that user adaptivity can increase variance in estimation. Finally, we discuss implications of user adaptivity for the interpretation of experiments and show that adaptivity creates a common mechanism leading to common evaluation challenges, such as reward hacking and novelty effects. Together, this work highlights the necessity of measuring both model performance as well as changes in the user behavior that the model induces.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that when users adapt their prompts after seeing LLM responses, offline benchmarks and live A/B tests can estimate different quantities and rank models differently. It characterizes when rankings reverse and gives a sufficient condition for agreement.
AI.motivation: In interactive systems, user adaptivity makes the prompts used for evaluation depend on the model's own responses, so standard evaluation may not reflect deployment behavior.
AI.method: Two estimands are defined: a common-distribution effect comparing models on the same prompt distribution, and an induced-distribution effect comparing models on the prompts generated through user interaction. The paper shows that standard difference-in-means estimators converge to these for offline benchmarks and A/B tests, respectively, and analyzes a stylized linear interaction model.
AI.result: The two comparisons can rank models differently and yield discrepancies in deployment recommendations. A sufficient condition guarantees agreement, and in a stylized linear model user adaptivity can increase estimation variance.
AI.conclusion: Measuring both model performance and the induced changes in user behavior is needed, since adaptivity also creates shared challenges such as reward hacking and novelty effects.

title: An Asynchronous Federated Learning Platform for Lung Adenocarcinoma Grading via Foundation Models and Structural Pruning
summary: Classification of lung adenocarcinoma into poorly differentiated (PD) and well-to-moderately differentiated (WMD) subtypes plays an important role in patient survival; however, consistent classification is difficult due to inter-observer variability among pathologists. Collecting data from multiple hospitals is also challenging due to patient privacy concerns. This study proposes a web-based federated learning system that shares only locally trained model weights without sharing patient data between institutions. The UNI2 foundation model and CLAM-SB were used to classify pathological whole slide images. A four-client federated learning system was constructed, and the NLST cohort was reserved exclusively for external validation. In centralized evaluation, joint training with CPTAC and TCGA outperformed single-institution training on external validation, confirming the necessity of multi-institutional data integration. FedAvg, FedProx, FedBN, and FedNova were compared as federated learning algorithms under identical experimental conditions. Test AUC ranked as FedBN, FedProx, FedNova, and FedAvg. FedNova showed the most balanced classification performance between PD and WMD. L1-norm structural pruning at 20%, 30%, and 40% sparsity was applied to reduce model transmission size. FedAvg, FedProx, and FedBN showed a tendency of decreasing Test AUC under pruning, while FedNova achieved improved Test AUC across all sparsity levels. A web-based application was developed supporting slide upload, local training, AI classification, and attention heatmap-based visualization. The combination of FedNova and 40% pruning was confirmed as a practical approach that improves communication efficiency and classification performance while protecting patient privacy.

AI.tldr: The study proposes a web-based federated learning system for classifying lung adenocarcinoma into PD and WMD subtypes, using UNI2 and CLAM-SB with structural pruning. FedNova with 40% pruning gives the best trade-off of communication efficiency and classification performance.
AI.motivation: Subtype classification of lung adenocarcinoma is affected by inter-observer variability, and multi-hospital data sharing is restricted by patient privacy, so the system shares only model weights.
AI.method: UNI2 and CLAM-SB classify whole slide images in a four-client federated system. FedAvg, FedProx, FedBN and FedNova are compared, and L1-norm structural pruning at 20%, 30% and 40% sparsity reduces model transmission size. The NLST cohort is held out for external validation.
AI.result: Joint training with CPTAC and TCGA outperforms single-institution training on external validation. Test AUC ranks FedBN, FedProx, FedNova and FedAvg in that order. FedNova gives the most balanced PD and WMD performance and improves test AUC at all sparsity levels, while FedAvg, FedProx and FedBN decline under pruning.
AI.conclusion: The combination of FedNova and 40% pruning is presented as a practical approach that improves communication efficiency and classification while protecting patient privacy, and a web application supports slide upload, local training and attention heatmaps.

title: Adversarial Risk in the Generative AI Era Necessitates Dropping the Small Epsilon Ball
comment: neurips 2026, 10 pages, position paper on adversarial risk, certified robustness
summary: Adversarial Machine Learning research is currently centered on the search for the epsilon-ball: minimal perturbations designed to fool models while remaining imperceptible to humans. We argue that this fixation on $\ell_p$ norms is a metrological trap that communicates a distorted perception of risk to defenders, one that is unaligned with real-world system vulnerabilities. This paradigm misleads defenders into optimizing for narrow, mathematical robustness at the expense of systemic security, while simultaneously incentivizing attackers to exploit non-overlapping alternative adversarial pathways. Ultimately, we argue that the dominance of the $\ell_p$ ball does not just fail to reduce harm---it may actively facilitate it by communicating a false sense of security against the wrong threats.

AI.tldr: The position paper argues that adversarial machine learning should move away from the small l_p epsilon-ball, which it calls a metrological trap that misrepresents real-world risk. It claims that focusing on this ball can leave systemic security gaps and may even facilitate harm.
AI.motivation: Adversarial ML research centers on minimal imperceptible perturbations under l_p norms, which the authors view as misaligned with real system vulnerabilities.
AI.method: The paper is an argument rather than an empirical study; it reasons that the l_p paradigm misleads defenders and incentivizes attackers toward non-overlapping alternative pathways. The abstract reports no experiments.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experimental results; its findings are argumentative claims about the effects of the l_p paradigm.
AI.conclusion: The dominance of the l_p ball may communicate a false sense of security against the wrong threats, so the field should drop it as the central frame.

title: StructRL: Model-Free Reinforcement Learning with Replay Graphs
summary: StructRL turns the experience collected during reinforcement learning into an explicit replay graph. Once the graph contains a path to the task goal, dynamic programming selects actions on the observed part of the state space; these actions form a graph policy that is defined only where the required transitions have been observed. StructRL transfers these actions to model-free learners: as action preferences for a DQN Q-model and as target directions along shortest observed paths for a SAC actor. For DQN on three sparse-reward MiniGrid tasks, final success rises from 0.10 to 0.90 (DoorKey), 0.10 to 0.80 (KeyCorridor) and 0 to 0.50 (ObstructedMaze); plain DQN does not catch up with three times the budget. For SAC on continuous PointMaze, graph-derived direction labels raise final success from 0.17 to 1.0 on seven matched runs that reached the goal. Distilling the graph policy into a fresh Q-model gives a DoorKey 6x6 controller that reaches the goal from 91% of reachable states, against 38% for plain DQN. Scaling experiments identify three bottlenecks: incomplete graph support, structural aliasing, and loss of graph information in high-dimensional inputs.

AI.tldr: StructRL builds an explicit replay graph from RL experience and uses dynamic programming on it to produce graph policies that transfer to DQN as action preferences and to SAC as target directions. On sparse-reward MiniGrid tasks DQN success rises from 0.10 to 0.90 on DoorKey and from 0 to 0.50 on ObstructedMaze.
AI.motivation: Model-free RL learns slowly with sparse rewards, and experience collected during learning is not reused in a structured way.
AI.method: Experience becomes a replay graph. Once the graph contains a path to the goal, dynamic programming selects actions on the observed part of the state space, forming a graph policy defined only where transitions were observed. This is transferred to a DQN Q-model as action preferences and to a SAC actor as target directions along shortest observed paths. A graph policy can also be distilled into a fresh Q-model.
AI.result: On three sparse-reward MiniGrid tasks, DQN final success rises from 0.10 to 0.90 on DoorKey, 0.10 to 0.80 on KeyCorridor and 0 to 0.50 on ObstructedMaze, and plain DQN does not catch up with three times the budget. On continuous PointMaze, SAC success rises from 0.17 to 1.0 on seven matched runs that reached the goal. A distilled DoorKey 6x6 controller reaches the goal from 91% of reachable states, against 38% for plain DQN.
AI.conclusion: Scaling experiments identify three bottlenecks: incomplete graph support, structural aliasing and loss of graph information in high-dimensional inputs.

title: Closing the Loop: Co-Evolving EM for Irregular Time Series Generation in Lifted Representations
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026; The first two authors contributed equally and are co-leading authors
summary: Regular time-series generation from irregular time series is typically reduced to one-shot imputation: complete each partial sequence once, freeze the completions, and train a generator on the resulting surrogate dataset. We show that this open-loop strategy is structurally flawed. Point imputers collapse ambiguous missing regions to conditional averages, while stochastic imputers become stale as the generator evolves; the binding constraint is therefore iteration, not imputer design. We introduce a co-evolving Monte Carlo EM framework that closes the imputer-generator loop. Each E-step samples missing values from the posterior of the current generator, and each M-step retrains the generator on these completions, preserving unconditional generator training. Since our diffusion prior operates in a lifted 2D representation while observations live in time-series space, we further introduce Posterior Sampling for Lifted Representations (PSLR), which enforces operator-consistent conditioning, uncertainty preservation, and manifold consistency during the E-step. Across ten datasets and four corruption regimes, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving over the strongest baselines by 59% in discriminative score, 15% in predictive score, 73% in Context-FID, and 71% in feature-correlation error. Ablations show that our approach reduces average discriminative score by 73% over single-step baselines, closing most of the remaining gap to the clean-data oracle. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes irregular time-series generation as a closed loop, co-evolving Monte Carlo EM that alternates sampling missing values from the current generator and retraining it. Across ten datasets and four corruption regimes it improves over the strongest baselines by 59% in discriminative score and 15% in predictive score.
AI.motivation: Standard one-shot imputation freezes completions once, but point imputers collapse ambiguous regions to conditional averages and stochastic imputers become stale as the generator evolves, so iteration is the binding constraint.
AI.method: The framework is a co-evolving Monte Carlo EM. Each E-step samples missing values from the current generator's posterior, and each M-step retrains the generator on these completions. Posterior Sampling for Lifted Representations (PSLR) enforces operator-consistent conditioning, uncertainty preservation and manifold consistency in a 2D lifted representation of the diffusion prior.
AI.result: Across ten datasets and four corruption regimes, the method improves over the strongest baselines by 59% in discriminative score, 15% in predictive score, 73% in Context-FID and 71% in feature-correlation error. Ablations show a 73% reduction in average discriminative score over single-step baselines.
AI.conclusion: Closing the imputer-generator loop closes most of the remaining gap to the clean-data oracle, so iterative co-evolution is central to generating regular series from irregular data.

title: Beyond Row-Level Prediction: Evaluating and Learning Composition for Reusable Table Representations
comment: Preprint. Under review
summary: Tables are compositional, with content spread across a schema, cell values, rows, and columns. Large-scale operations such as retrieval, overlap estimation, deduplication, and data curation need these local signals composed into one reusable embedding vector per table. Table representation methods, however, are mostly evaluated through row-level prediction or supervised downstream tasks, which do not measure table-level embedding quality directly. We introduce a benchmark that evaluates table-level embeddings through four desiderata: consistency under partial views, discriminability across label granularities, robustness to benign perturbations, and efficiency. Across twelve methods on synthetic and real corpora, lightweight schema- and text-based fingerprints are among the strongest. The sharpest contrast comes from two tabular foundation models, TabPFN and ConTextTab: although both are strong row-level predictors, their states, composed by mean, max, or three further parameter-free pooling rules, trail the strongest fingerprints. We therefore ask whether the gap lies in the encoder or in the compositional rule. Keeping ConTextTab frozen, we learn only the compositional rule over its cell states, using support-conditioned distribution matching (SCDM), a self-supervised loss we propose that matches the distribution of embedding similarities to the distribution of partition overlaps within and across tables. Across all fifteen head configurations, the learned rule raises the Spearman correlation between embedding similarity and partial-view overlap from 0.04 to 0.43-0.50 on synthetic data and improves triplet ranking, clustering, and retrieval, with smaller but systematic gains on real data. A downstream parent-table retrieval task confirms these findings. How local states are composed, and with what objective, substantially affects the quality of table-level embeddings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark for table-level embeddings based on four desiderata and proposes SCDM, a self-supervised loss that learns a compositional rule over frozen ConTextTab cell states. The learned rule raises the Spearman correlation between embedding similarity and partial-view overlap from 0.04 to 0.43 to 0.50 on synthetic data.
AI.motivation: Table representations are usually evaluated through row-level prediction or supervised tasks, which do not measure table-level embedding quality for retrieval, deduplication and curation.
AI.method: The benchmark tests consistency under partial views, discriminability across label granularities, robustness to benign perturbations and efficiency. SCDM matches the distribution of embedding similarities to the distribution of partition overlaps within and across tables, while the encoder stays frozen and only the compositional rule over cell states is learned.
AI.result: Across twelve methods, lightweight schema- and text-based fingerprints are among the strongest. TabPFN and ConTextTab trail them under mean, max or other pooling rules. With the learned rule over fifteen head configurations, the Spearman correlation rises from 0.04 to 0.43 to 0.50 on synthetic data and improves triplet ranking, clustering and retrieval, with smaller but systematic gains on real data.
AI.conclusion: How local states are composed, and the objective used, substantially affects table-level embedding quality, and the gap lies at least partly in the compositional rule rather than the encoder.

title: UniPipe: Unified Inference Serving and Fine-Tuning for Deadline-Constrained DNN Surrogate Workflows
summary: DNN surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate scientific workflows that must process high-rate sensor streams in near real time, exemplified by Ptychographic imaging at next-generation X-ray light sources. Such surrogates deliver 100-1000x higher throughput than iterative solvers, enabling faster steering of experiments. To preserve surrogate accuracy during an experiment, as the input distribution evolves, state-of-the-art deployments freeze the pretrained surrogate or run a separate CUDA context that fine-tunes concurrently with serving. However, multi-context concurrency causes significant contention on the GPU, inflating both the mean and the variance of inference latency, triggering deadline misses in workflows where sensor data has to be processed within a hard per-unit deadline. To address this challenge, we propose UniPipe, a single-context system that unifies inference serving and fine-tuning of a DNN surrogate on a single edge GPU. UniPipe is driven by three key insights: both serving and fine-tuning require a forward pass and can be fused into one; the per-sample latency of modern GPUs is non-linear in batch size; and the workload is repetitive across intervals, enabling offline scheduling. Specifically, UniPipe fuses training and inference data in a single forward pass with a selective backward pass on the training subset, and uses a polynomial-time scheduler that exploits the latency curve to compute the batch composition. We evaluate UniPipe on a real-world Ptychographic reconstruction workflow with sensor rates up to 5000 patterns/sec.; UniPipe lowers reconstruction MSE by up to 30% and inference MSE by up to 50% over a pretrained baseline, and reduces the deadline-miss rate by 13%-22% over a multi-context baseline. UniPipe's unified deployment reduces the latency spread from 106% to 57% of the mean, and increases total throughput compared to multi-context baseline.

AI.tldr: UniPipe is a single-context system that fuses inference serving and fine-tuning of a DNN surrogate on one edge GPU, avoiding multi-context contention. On a ptychographic reconstruction workflow it lowers reconstruction MSE by up to 30% and inference MSE by up to 50% over a pretrained baseline.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning a surrogate during an experiment, through a separate CUDA context, causes GPU contention that inflates the mean and variance of inference latency and causes deadline misses.
AI.method: UniPipe fuses training and inference samples in a single forward pass with a selective backward pass on the training subset. A polynomial-time scheduler uses the non-linear per-sample latency curve in batch size to compute batch composition, and offline scheduling exploits repetitive workloads.
AI.result: On a real ptychographic workflow with sensor rates up to 5000 patterns per second, UniPipe lowers reconstruction MSE by up to 30% and inference MSE by up to 50% over a pretrained baseline. It reduces the deadline-miss rate by 13% to 22% over a multi-context baseline and cuts latency spread from 106% to 57% of the mean.
AI.conclusion: A single-context unified deployment meets hard per-unit deadlines better than multi-context concurrency while also increasing total throughput.

title: SPIRE: Task-agnostic embodied continual learning through autonomous situation inference and causal motor-primitive reuse
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables (including appendix tables)
summary: Embodied continual learning requires controllers to infer changing situations, retain prior behavior and reuse motor skills without task labels or known boundaries. The challenge is deciding when to recover earlier behavior and which skills can support new learning. We introduce Situation-guided Primitive Integration for Recurrent Embodiment (SPIRE), a recurrent-spiking system that infers latent contexts from action-outcome evidence and learns context-specific motor actors online. Mature actors become protected sources that combine with a target-context residual to drive recurrent-spiking motor populations. Across coordinate, three-joint and hidden-force control, SPIRE maintained control, autonomously inferred situations, retained prior behavior and accelerated acquisition of an unseen source composition, reducing mean interactions to criterion by approximately 40% relative to matched fresh controllers. Rewinding compatible source actors impaired early acquisition in every matched intervention, demonstrating causal reuse. Against seven recurrent continual-learning and modular-control comparators, SPIRE achieved 2.4 times the mean prior-learning advantage of the strongest eligible task-free alternative selected for each paired stream. These results demonstrate autonomous recovery and causal reuse of motor skills for new learning in continuous embodied control.

AI.tldr: SPIRE is a recurrent-spiking embodied continual learning system that infers latent situations from action-outcome evidence and reuses protected motor actors without task labels. It reduces interactions to criterion by about 40% relative to fresh controllers and achieves 2.4 times the prior-learning advantage of the strongest eligible alternative.
AI.motivation: Embodied controllers must infer changing situations, retain prior behavior and reuse motor skills without task labels or known boundaries, and must decide when to recover earlier behavior and which skills can support new learning.
AI.method: SPIRE infers latent contexts from action-outcome evidence and learns context-specific motor actors online. Mature actors become protected sources that combine with a target-context residual to drive recurrent-spiking motor populations.
AI.result: Across coordinate, three-joint and hidden-force control, SPIRE maintains control, infers situations autonomously, retains prior behavior and accelerates acquisition of an unseen source composition, cutting mean interactions to criterion by about 40% against matched fresh controllers. Rewinding compatible source actors impairs early acquisition in every matched intervention. Against seven comparators, SPIRE achieves 2.4 times the mean prior-learning advantage of the strongest eligible task-free alternative.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate autonomous situation recovery and causal reuse of motor skills for new learning in continuous embodied control.

title: Generalize Then Personalize: Wearable-Based Heart Rate Forecasting Under Scarce Ruck-March Data
comment: IEEE BIBM 2026
summary: Heart rate (HR) forecasting may provide advance information about near-future cardiovascular response, potentially supporting physiological monitoring and workload-management decisions during ruck marching. However, robust model development is constrained by the difficulty of collecting large-scale ruck-march datasets, creating a scarce-data problem in which models must generalize across participants while adapting to individuals from limited personal data. To address this problem, we benchmark population-only training (POT), personalized-from-scratch training (PFST), and population-pretrained fine-tuning (PPFT) for HR forecasting during loaded ruck marching using data from eight active-duty U.S. Army medics across thirteen sessions. LSTM, Attention-LSTM, and CNN-LSTM backbones were evaluated against a persistence baseline at 30 s and 60 s horizons. Across all neural architectures and horizons, PPFT yielded lower mean MAE, RMSE, and endpoint MAE than both POT and PFST. Participant-level paired analysis after averaging across three training seeds showed that, relative to PFST, PPFT reduced trajectory MAE by 2.22-4.30 bpm and endpoint MAE by 1.24-2.88 bpm. All six trajectory-MAE comparisons remained significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{adj}$ = 0.0469), while four of six endpoint-MAE comparisons remained significant after adjustment. At 30 s, persistence achieved the lowest MAE (3.555 $\pm$ 1.274 bpm), while CNN-LSTM PPFT achieved the lowest RMSE (4.669 $\pm$ 1.916 bpm); LSTM PPFT achieved the lowest endpoint MAE (5.093 $\pm$ 2.365 bpm). At 60 s, Attention-LSTM PPFT achieved the lowest MAE (5.573 $\pm$ 1.939 bpm) and RMSE (7.134 $\pm$ 2.260 bpm), while CNN-LSTM PPFT achieved the lowest endpoint MAE (7.553 $\pm$ 2.357 bpm). These results suggest that population pretraining followed by participant-specific fine-tuning may provide a practical strategy for scarce-data wearable HR forecasting.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks population-only, personalized-from-scratch and population-pretrained fine-tuning for wearable heart rate forecasting during ruck marching, using data from eight soldiers across thirteen sessions. Population pretraining followed by fine-tuning gives the lowest errors across architectures and horizons, reducing trajectory MAE by 2.22 to 4.30 bpm relative to from-scratch personalization.
AI.motivation: Ruck-march datasets are hard to collect at scale, so models must generalize across participants while adapting to individuals from limited personal data.
AI.method: Population-only training (POT), personalized-from-scratch training (PFST) and population-pretrained fine-tuning (PPFT) are compared with LSTM, Attention-LSTM and CNN-LSTM backbones against a persistence baseline at 30 s and 60 s horizons. Results are averaged over three training seeds, with participant-level paired analysis and Holm adjustment.
AI.result: Across architectures and horizons, PPFT yields lower mean MAE, RMSE and endpoint MAE than POT and PFST. Relative to PFST, PPFT reduces trajectory MAE by 2.22 to 4.30 bpm and endpoint MAE by 1.24 to 2.88 bpm. All six trajectory-MAE comparisons remain significant after Holm adjustment (p_adj = 0.0469), and four of six endpoint comparisons do. At 30 s, persistence has the lowest MAE, while CNN-LSTM PPFT has the lowest RMSE and LSTM PPFT the lowest endpoint MAE. At 60 s, Attention-LSTM PPFT has the lowest MAE and RMSE.
AI.conclusion: Population pretraining followed by participant-specific fine-tuning may be a practical strategy for forecasting heart rate from wearables when data are scarce.

title: FOE-Dreamer: Deployment-Efficient Learning of Cyber Defense Policies in Operational Networks
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures. To appear in the proceedings of the Annual Computer Security Applications Conference (ACSAC)
summary: Autonomous cyber defense is widely studied with deep reinforcement learning, but most work trains policies inside simulators because learning requires many trial-and-error interactions. Simulator-based training carries a fidelity gap: trained policies face authentication delays, partial action failures, service dependencies, and user traffic patterns that the simulator did not represent, and degrade on transfer. Training directly in the network being defended removes the gap but makes every interaction slow and costly, so sample efficiency becomes the binding constraint. Model-based reinforcement learning has reduced sample requirements on games and physical robots by orders of magnitude by planning inside a learned world model, but it has not been applied to defenders trained in operational networks. We present FOE-Dreamer (Factored Opponent-Enhanced Dreamer), a model-based reinforcement learning framework that trains a defender online and directly in a network on cloud infrastructure, without a simulator stage. FOE-Dreamer separates three sources of variation in the latent state: a controllable component driven by defender actions, an exogenous component driven by benign user activity, and an opponent embedding inferred from defender-observable signals alone. Separating the components reduces the variance in policy gradients during planning in imagination. Against two scripted attacker profiles with user activity emulated by the GHOSTS framework on an 8-host OpenStack testbed, FOE-Dreamer trains within a 3-day budget on a single GPU and achieves about 2$\times$ better episode loss than Rainbow and IQN baselines under matched compute. Both the factoring and the opponent model contribute to the gain, and the learned latents are consistent with the intended separation.

AI.tldr: FOE-Dreamer is a model-based RL framework that trains a cyber defender online directly in an operational network, without a simulator stage. It separates controllable, exogenous and opponent latent components, and achieves about 2 times better episode loss than Rainbow and IQN baselines within a 3-day single-GPU budget.
AI.motivation: Simulator-trained cyber defense policies face a fidelity gap, and training directly in the defended network is slow and costly, so sample efficiency is the binding constraint.
AI.method: FOE-Dreamer learns a world model and plans in imagination. Its latent state is factored into a controllable component driven by defender actions, an exogenous component driven by benign user activity, and an opponent embedding inferred from defender-observable signals. Separating these reduces the variance of policy gradients during planning.
AI.result: Against two scripted attacker profiles, with user activity emulated by GHOSTS on an 8-host OpenStack testbed, FOE-Dreamer trains within a 3-day budget on a single GPU and achieves about 2 times better episode loss than Rainbow and IQN under matched compute. Both the factoring and the opponent model contribute to the gain.
AI.conclusion: Model-based RL can be applied to training defenders directly in operational networks, and the learned latents are consistent with the intended separation.

title: Machine Learning Moment Closure for the Boltzmann Transport Equation: Enforcing Hyperbolicity
summary: The Boltzmann transport equation describes particle transport across collisional regimes, but resolving its velocity dependence is expensive. Moment methods reduce this cost by evolving finitely many velocity moments, requiring a closure for unresolved higher-order moments. Data-driven closures can represent these moments accurately, yet without structural constraints they may produce complex characteristic speeds and unstable simulations. Learned Boltzmann closures with guaranteed hyperbolicity have so far been formulated in one spatial dimension; in multiple dimensions, hyperbolicity must hold in every direction simultaneously. We develop, to the best of our knowledge, the first data-driven closure for multidimensional Hermite moment systems of the linear Boltzmann equation that is hyperbolic by construction. The network learns a symmetric positive-definite symmetrizer shared by all spatial directions and restricted to a subspace that preserves the known lower-order transport equations; the unresolved rows follow from a symmetric completion. Every directional Jacobian thus has real eigenvalues and a complete set of eigenvectors for every network output and at any truncation order. The closure is trained only on spatial derivatives of unresolved moments from kinetic reference solutions, with no solver in the training loop, and evolved by a partially conservative discontinuous Galerkin method. In two-dimensional experiments in the transition and scattering-dominated regimes, a single learned third-order system with ten moments remains stable in all cases. Averaged over time, it is more accurate than the classical P7 and P15 truncations with 36 and 136 moments in every experiment, and its density error is about two orders of magnitude smaller than that of the P3 truncation with the same moments.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a data-driven closure for multidimensional Hermite moment systems of the linear Boltzmann equation that is hyperbolic by construction, by learning a symmetric positive-definite symmetrizer. A single learned third-order ten-moment system stays stable and is more accurate than P7 and P15 truncations in 2D tests.
AI.motivation: Moment methods need a closure for unresolved higher-order moments, and unconstrained learned closures may give complex characteristic speeds and unstable simulations. Learned closures with guaranteed hyperbolicity existed only in one spatial dimension.
AI.method: The network learns a symmetric positive-definite symmetrizer shared by all spatial directions, restricted to a subspace that preserves the known lower-order transport equations, with unresolved rows given by symmetric completion. The closure is trained on spatial derivatives of unresolved moments from kinetic reference solutions, without a solver in the loop, and evolved with a partially conservative discontinuous Galerkin method.
AI.result: In two-dimensional experiments in transition and scattering-dominated regimes, a single learned third-order ten-moment system remains stable in all cases. Averaged over time, it is more accurate than P7 and P15 truncations with 36 and 136 moments in every experiment, and its density error is about two orders of magnitude smaller than P3 with the same moments.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolicity by construction is achievable for learned multidimensional Boltzmann closures, and a small learned system can outperform classical higher-moment truncations in the tested regimes.

title: Social Engineering Attack Detection in Corporate Communications
summary: Social Engineering attacks continue to pose a significant risk to the corporate world with a growing level of sophistication. It is difficult to distinguish between authentic and phishing communication via email, chat, and phone. They pose a risk of exposing trade secrets and confidential communications and can create a chain of attack from lower-level employees up to executives. Therefore, we study this growing threat using real-world datasets to build baseline machine-learning models. Our TF-IDF models classify emails as phishing or safe, achieving accuracy above 90%. We build on this by exploring whether psychological manipulation and persuasion indicators can be measured to play a significant role in detecting phishing. Instead of relying solely on surface-level lexical features, we derive interpretable lexicon-based indicators of urgency, trust, greed, and other persuasion cues from the combined email dataset. By evaluating these manipulation-oriented features on their own, we measure how much signal they carry (ROC-AUC of 0.74 on a held-out test split) and test whether they transfer to held-out email sources.

AI.tldr: The study builds baseline ML models for corporate social engineering detection and shows that interpretable lexicon-based persuasion indicators carry signal on their own. TF-IDF models exceed 90% accuracy on phishing email classification, and the persuasion features reach ROC-AUC 0.74 on a held-out split.
AI.motivation: Social engineering attacks are hard to distinguish from authentic communication across email, chat and phone, and they threaten trade secrets and can escalate from junior staff to executives.
AI.method: TF-IDF baseline models classify emails as phishing or safe. Lexicon-based indicators of urgency, trust, greed and other persuasion cues are derived from the combined email dataset and evaluated alone, and tested for transfer to held-out email sources.
AI.result: TF-IDF models achieve accuracy above 90% on phishing classification. The manipulation-oriented features reach ROC-AUC of 0.74 on a held-out test split, and the abstract says transfer to held-out email sources is tested without reporting its outcome.
AI.conclusion: Psychological manipulation indicators carry measurable signal for phishing detection and may complement lexical features, though the abstract does not state whether they transfer to held-out sources.

title: Epigraph Form Reinforcement Learning-based Safe Trajectory Tracking Control for Connected and Autonomous Vehicles
summary: Safe trajectory tracking (STT) aims to enable autonomous vehicles to follow a reference trajectory accurately while avoiding collisions. This problem is particularly challenging for Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) in highly dynamic environments. Existing non-learning-based STT methods often use simplified vehicle and interaction models to meet real-time requirements, which may result in suboptimal tracking accuracy. Although Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) can help address this limitation, widely used Lagrangian DRL methods often suffer from unstable training because increasing Lagrange multipliers amplify policy-gradient magnitudes. To address these issues, we propose a novel reinforcement learning framework for STT, called STT Control Epigraph Form RL (STTC-EFRL). In this framework, the STT problem is formulated as an epigraph-form min-max optimization problem. Based on this formulation, we develop a learning mechanism that uses a decreasing scalar related to the epigraph to adjust the policy gradient descent direction without increasing the gradient magnitude, thereby improving training stability. We also develop a computationally efficient ray-casting method to compute a polyhedron scaling factor for safety quantification. Experimental results, including Vehicle-in-the-Loop tests, show that STTC-EFRL achieves higher tracking accuracy than the considered non-learning-based baseline and more stable training than widely used Lagrangian DRL methods, while satisfying safety requirements in connected environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes STTC-EFRL, a reinforcement learning framework for safe trajectory tracking of connected and autonomous vehicles that reformulates the problem as an epigraph-form min-max optimization. It reports higher tracking accuracy than a non-learning baseline and more stable training than Lagrangian DRL methods.
AI.motivation: Non-learning safe trajectory tracking methods use simplified vehicle and interaction models, which limits tracking accuracy, while Lagrangian DRL methods train unstably because growing Lagrange multipliers amplify policy-gradient magnitudes.
AI.method: The safe trajectory tracking problem is written as an epigraph-form min-max problem; a decreasing scalar tied to the epigraph adjusts the policy gradient direction without increasing its magnitude, and a ray-casting method computes a polyhedron scaling factor for safety quantification.
AI.result: In Vehicle-in-the-Loop tests, STTC-EFRL achieves higher tracking accuracy than the considered non-learning baseline and more stable training than widely used Lagrangian DRL methods, while satisfying safety requirements in connected environments.
AI.conclusion: The epigraph-form formulation offers a stable and accurate learning-based route to safe trajectory tracking for CAVs in highly dynamic environments.

title: A Transferable Pretrained 3D Model for Impedance Inversion with Sparse-Well Prior Conditioning
summary: Deep-learning-based seismic impedance inversion commonly requires retraining for each target survey, which may generalize poorly beyond the conditioning locations when well control is extremely sparse. We propose a transferable three-dimensional inversion framework that separates offline learning from target-survey deployment. A masked autoencoder first learns seismic structural representations from unlabeled multi-survey data, after which the frozen encoder is incorporated into an inversion network trained on synthetic geological models with sparse-well-derived low-frequency priors. During deployment, the complete inversion network remains fixed; the available conditioning well is used only to construct the low-frequency prior and align the global impedance range. Experiments on the Overthrust model show that the proposed method achieves the lowest full-volume NRMSE and reduces the P95 trace-wise NRMSE from 0.1310 to 0.1074 relative to the best target-trained baseline, indicating fewer localized large errors under different well locations. In a field survey with one conditioning well and three blind wells, it reduces the mean blind-well NRMSE by 20.95% relative to the target-trained U-Net while maintaining the highest correlation. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework transfers useful impedance information beyond the conditioning location with low deployment cost and without retraining the inversion network.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a transferable 3D seismic impedance inversion framework in which a masked autoencoder pretrained on unlabeled multi-survey data is frozen and combined with an inversion network trained on synthetic models, so that deployment to a new survey needs no retraining. It reports lower full-volume and tail errors on Overthrust and a 20.95% reduction in mean blind-well NRMSE on a field survey relative to a target-trained U-Net.
AI.motivation: Deep-learning impedance inversion usually must be retrained for each target survey and generalizes poorly away from the conditioning well when well control is extremely sparse.
AI.method: A masked autoencoder learns seismic structural representations from unlabeled multi-survey data; the frozen encoder is incorporated into an inversion network trained on synthetic geological models with low-frequency priors derived from sparse wells. At deployment the network stays fixed, and the conditioning well is used only to build the low-frequency prior and align the global impedance range.
AI.result: On the Overthrust model the method achieves the lowest full-volume NRMSE and reduces P95 trace-wise NRMSE from 0.1310 to 0.1074 relative to the best target-trained baseline. In a field survey with one conditioning well and three blind wells, mean blind-well NRMSE falls by 20.95% relative to the target-trained U-Net while correlation remains the highest.
AI.conclusion: Impedance information can be transferred beyond the conditioning location with low deployment cost and without retraining the inversion network, which suits sparse-well settings.

title: EASTAR: Event-Anchored Semantic and Task-Adaptive Region Representation Learning
comment: 13 pages. Accepted to the 43rd IEEE International Conference on Data Engineering (ICDE 2027)
summary: Urban region representation learning supports a wide range of urban analytics tasks by encoding regional functions and interactions, with human mobility serving as a central signal because it directly captures inter-region interactions. However, most mobility-based methods learn from aggregated origin-destination matrices, where trips driven by different activity purposes are mixed into purpose-agnostic interaction patterns. Although static urban attributes such as POIs and land use can enrich region-level semantics, they do not explicitly ground mobility interactions in activity-purpose signals. As a result, downstream adaptation is often performed over entangled embeddings, making it difficult to select task-relevant functional semantics. To address these limitations, we propose EASTAR, an event-anchored and task-adaptive framework for urban region representation learning. EASTAR treats offline activity events as sparse semantic anchors and uses them to factorize aggregated mobility representations into multiple purpose-related semantic channels. It further introduces free channels to capture latent mobility patterns not covered by event data and a global channel to preserve overall spatial structure. To adapt the learned channel space to different downstream objectives, EASTAR designs a task-adaptive prompt router that initializes task-channel relevance from LLM-derived priors and refines the routing weights through downstream supervision. Experiments on two real-world urban datasets across four prediction tasks show that EASTAR consistently outperforms representative baselines, achieving up to 39.15% reduction in MAE. Ablation and interpretability analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness of event anchoring, semantic channel construction, and task-adaptive routing.
