AI.tldr: The paper proposes EASTAR, an urban region representation learning framework that anchors human mobility to offline activity events and splits aggregated mobility into purpose-related semantic channels, with a task-adaptive prompt router. It reports consistent gains over baselines on two urban datasets across four prediction tasks, with up to 39.15% lower MAE.
AI.motivation: Mobility-based region representations learn from origin-destination matrices that mix trips of different activity purposes, and static attributes such as POIs and land use do not ground mobility interactions in activity purpose, so downstream adaptation works on entangled embeddings.
AI.method: Offline activity events serve as sparse semantic anchors that factorize aggregated mobility representations into purpose-related channels, plus free channels for latent patterns not covered by events and a global channel for overall spatial structure. A task-adaptive prompt router initializes task-channel relevance from LLM-derived priors and refines routing weights with downstream supervision.
AI.result: On two real-world urban datasets across four prediction tasks, EASTAR consistently outperforms representative baselines, reaching up to 39.15% reduction in MAE. Ablations and interpretability analyses support the contributions of event anchoring, semantic channel construction and task-adaptive routing.
AI.conclusion: Grounding mobility in activity-purpose events and routing channels by task yields more task-relevant urban region embeddings than purpose-agnostic mobility representations.

title: AI4Plasma I: Data-Efficient Surrogate Modeling of Capacitively Coupled Plasma Fields
summary: Reference capacitively coupled plasma (CCP) simulations provide spatially resolved plasma fields but are costly to generate across operating conditions. We compare the data efficiency of five surrogate architectures--Coordinate MLP, PCA-Net, U-Net, Fourier neural operator (FNO), and Transolver--for predicting RF-cycle-averaged electron density, ion density, electric potential, and electron temperature in 1D planar and 2D axisymmetric GEC CCP benchmarks. We assess the number of reference simulations needed to achieve 1% and 2% mean relative L2 error for parameter-interior and parameter-boundary test cases, and examine architecture-specific mechanisms. FNO achieves the lowest or joint-lowest reference-case requirement in seven of eight comparisons. In 1D, FNO reaches 1% interior error with 50 training cases, compared with 100 for Transolver and 200 for U-Net. In 2D, FNO and U-Net each reach 1% interior error with 100 cases; FNO and Transolver each reach 2% parameter-boundary error with 200 cases, compared with 400 for U-Net. At the stricter 1% 2D parameter-boundary target, Transolver requires 400 cases versus 800 for FNO. Additional analyses investigate FNO spectral modes and padding, U-Net skip connections, Transolver adaptive slicing, and PCA-Net projection versus prediction error. The results support FNO as a data-efficient baseline for the tested CCP settings, while showing that the preferred architecture depends on the accuracy target and operating-parameter region.

AI.tldr: The paper compares five surrogate architectures for predicting plasma fields in capacitively coupled plasma (CCP) simulations and measures how many reference simulations each needs to reach fixed error targets. FNO is the most data-efficient in most comparisons, though the preferred architecture depends on the accuracy target and operating region.
AI.motivation: Reference CCP simulations are costly to generate across operating conditions, so the number of simulations needed to train an accurate surrogate is a practical bottleneck that architecture comparisons often do not quantify.
AI.method: Coordinate MLP, PCA-Net, U-Net, Fourier neural operator (FNO) and Transolver are trained on 1D planar and 2D axisymmetric GEC CCP benchmarks to predict RF-cycle-averaged electron density, ion density, electric potential and electron temperature, and the number of training cases needed for 1% and 2% mean relative L2 error is measured for interior and boundary test cases.
AI.result: FNO has the lowest or joint-lowest requirement in seven of eight comparisons. In 1D, FNO reaches 1% interior error with 50 cases versus 100 for Transolver and 200 for U-Net. In 2D, FNO and Transolver reach 2% boundary error with 200 cases versus 400 for U-Net, and at a 1% 2D boundary target Transolver needs 400 cases versus 800 for FNO.
AI.conclusion: FNO is a data-efficient baseline for the tested CCP settings, but the best architecture depends on the accuracy target and the operating-parameter region.

title: From Forecasting to World Modeling: Can Temporal Foundation Models Recover Causal Response?
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Foundation Models for Temporal Systems (FMTS), non-archival. 15 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables
summary: A model that forecasts sales accurately can still mislead a retailer about how sales respond to a price change. We evaluate released tabular and time-series foundation models, as well as a foundation model pretrained specifically to estimate causal effects. We report three findings. First, forecast accuracy does not indicate the accuracy of the predicted effect of price, both on simulated data in which the true effect is known and on real retail sales records. Second, for the tabular foundation models, additional context improves forecasts but not the predicted effect of price. Third, instrumental variables, the standard remedy in econometrics, reduce this error only when supplied in a specific form and increase it for every model under confounding when supplied as raw instruments.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates released tabular and time-series foundation models, along with a foundation model pretrained to estimate causal effects, on whether they recover how sales respond to price. It finds that forecast accuracy does not indicate accuracy of the predicted price effect, and that instrumental variables help only in a specific form.
AI.motivation: A model that forecasts sales accurately may still mislead a retailer about the causal effect of a price change, and it is unclear whether foundation models trained for forecasting recover causal responses.
AI.method: Released tabular and time-series foundation models and a causal-effect pretrained foundation model are evaluated on simulated data with a known true price effect and on real retail sales records, with and without additional context and with instrumental variables supplied in raw or specific form under confounding.
AI.result: Forecast accuracy and accuracy of the predicted price effect diverge on both simulated and real data. For tabular foundation models, additional context improves forecasts but not the predicted price effect. Instrumental variables reduce error only when supplied in a specific form and increase error for every model under confounding when supplied as raw instruments.
AI.conclusion: Forecasting accuracy is not evidence of causal validity, so foundation models used for pricing decisions need separate causal validation.

title: Mask-Pattern Position Augmentation: Training-Free Long-Context Extrapolation for Diffusion LLMs
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 1 table, 1 algorithm
summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate by iteratively unmasking tokens with bidirectional attention, but rotary position embeddings (RoPE) still confine them to a fixed pretraining window. Existing training-free extrapolation, notably LongLLaDA, copies NTK-based RoPE scaling from autoregressive (AR) models and applies one static, length-only transform at every position and denoising step. That transplant ignores a signal unique to dLLMs: the evolving mask pattern of the partially decoded sequence. We propose Mask-Pattern Position Augmentation (MPPA). MPPA linearly interpolates indices into the pretrained window, then adds a per-position, per-step offset from cumulative mask density. The offset restores rotary phase resolution that interpolation collapses, and it shrinks as tokens are committed, so late steps see near-clean interpolated geometry. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct at twice its 4096-token window, MPPA reduces perplexity from 19.51 under standard decoding to 3.12 at 8192 tokens, below the in-window figure, with 100% passkey retrieval and unchanged needle-in-a-haystack accuracy. These preliminary $2\times$ results motivate mask-conditioned position engineering as a diffusion-native path to long-context generation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Mask-Pattern Position Augmentation (MPPA), a training-free method that extends the context window of diffusion LLMs by interpolating RoPE indices and adding a mask-density-dependent offset per position and denoising step. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct at twice its 4096-token window, it reports perplexity of 3.12 at 8192 tokens.
AI.motivation: Training-free extrapolation methods such as LongLLaDA copy NTK-based RoPE scaling from autoregressive models and apply one static, length-only transform, ignoring the evolving mask pattern that is specific to diffusion LLMs.
AI.method: MPPA linearly interpolates position indices into the pretrained window and adds a per-position, per-step offset computed from cumulative mask density. The offset restores rotary phase resolution lost to interpolation and shrinks as tokens are committed.
AI.result: On LLaDA-8B-Instruct at 2x its 4096-token window, MPPA reduces perplexity from 19.51 under standard decoding to 3.12 at 8192 tokens, below the in-window figure. It reaches 100% passkey retrieval and keeps needle-in-a-haystack accuracy unchanged.
AI.conclusion: The results are preliminary but suggest that mask-conditioned position engineering is a diffusion-native route to long-context generation.

title: PhysXAI: A Theoretical Framework for Diagnosing Physical Hallucinations in Weather Foundation Models
summary: Modern machine learning models for global weather forecasting achieve remarkable predictive accuracy, yet they frequently produce states that violate fundamental physical laws, including conservation of mass, hydrostatic balance, or spectral energy scaling. We term these outputs physical hallucinations and propose PhysXAI, a rigorous diagnostic framework that detects, localises, and attributes such inconsistencies. Unlike existing post-hoc metric suites, PhysXAI is a learnable system that explicitly decouples forecast error from physical plausibility. We formalise the problem through a novel joint condition on numerical and physical residuals, and introduce a multi-branch encoder that extracts representations from conservation, dynamical, spectral, cross-variable, and spatiotemporal residuals. A key innovation is a physics-consistency contrastive learning objective, which we theoretically show the latent representation to be approximately isometric to the physical residual space, ensuring that diagnostic decisions remain grounded in physically meaningful deviations. We further derive an adaptive multi-objective loss with gradient-based weighting to balance competing diagnostic objectives. The framework produces spatially resolved hallucination maps, violation-type classifications, and calibrated Bayesian uncertainty, enabling both detection and interpretable attribution of physical inconsistencies. We conduct a comprehensive comparative evaluation of PhysXAI across ERA5, WeatherBench 2, and MERRA-2, using forecasts from GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and NeuralGCM, with Python-written code and a fully reproducible experimental protocol. Our theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation establish PhysXAI as a principled framework for diagnosing physical hallucinations and advancing trustworthy AI for weather forecasting.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PhysXAI, a learnable diagnostic framework that detects, localizes and attributes physical hallucinations, meaning outputs of weather forecasting models that violate conservation, hydrostatic balance or spectral energy scaling. It evaluates the framework on forecasts from GraphCast, Pangu-Weather and NeuralGCM across ERA5, WeatherBench 2 and MERRA-2.
AI.motivation: Global weather forecasting models achieve high accuracy yet can produce physically inconsistent states, and existing post-hoc metric suites do not separate forecast error from physical plausibility.
AI.method: A multi-branch encoder extracts representations from conservation, dynamical, spectral, cross-variable and spatiotemporal residuals, trained with a physics-consistency contrastive objective and an adaptive multi-objective loss with gradient-based weighting; the framework outputs spatial hallucination maps, violation-type classes and Bayesian uncertainty.
AI.result: The abstract reports a comparative evaluation across three datasets and three forecasting models, with a theoretical argument that the latent representation is approximately isometric to the physical residual space. No quantitative results are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents PhysXAI as a principled framework for diagnosing physical hallucinations and supporting trustworthy AI for weather forecasting.

title: Probabilistic State Space Enumeration in Neural Network Computation
summary: Deep neural networks typically realize dense computation by propagating information through all intermediate channels, while many approximation methods rank and retain individual computational components. We ask whether dense neural computation can instead be represented exactly as an expectation over a combinatorial state space, and approximated by evaluating only its most probable configurations. We introduce a novel probabilistic state-space framework for Transformer MLPs. The framework partitions the intermediate dimension into channel groups, defines an input-dependent distribution over binary inclusion states, and uses importance-corrected masked outputs such that the full expectation exactly recovers the dense MLP output. The key algorithmic novelty is NORDER-II, which enumerates complete joint states in decreasing probability without constructing or sorting the exponentially large state space. Truncating this ordering yields an anytime approximation governed by cumulative probability mass and a state budget. On Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-2-2B, NORDER-II at a state budget of B=2048 achieves 92.4% and 93.8% MLP-output approximation accuracy, compared with 76.9% and 79.8% for Channel Top-k. When the first, middle, and last MLP layers are approximated jointly, WikiText-2 perplexity remains within 0.06% and 0.54% of dense inference. Relative to expected-count Grouped Top-k, NORDER-II yields 82.6% to 126.4% relative accuracy gains with only 0.18% to 0.19% additional local analytic FLOPs. These results establish the significance of joint-state structure beyond atomic salience and point to a new paradigm for neural computation: dense layers can be viewed as structured probabilistic inference over combinatorial computational states. This framework opens a path toward adaptive, probability-mass-controlled computation in pretrained neural networks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NORDER-II, which represents the dense MLP computation of Transformers exactly as an expectation over a probabilistic state space of channel-group inclusion states, and approximates it by enumerating the most probable states. On Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-2-2B at a budget of 2048 states, it reaches 92.4% and 93.8% MLP-output accuracy versus 76.9% and 79.8% for Channel Top-k.
AI.motivation: Common approximations of dense neural computation rank and retain individual components, ignoring joint structure among them, and it is unclear whether dense computation can be approximated through its most probable joint configurations.
AI.method: The intermediate dimension is partitioned into channel groups with an input-dependent distribution over binary inclusion states, and importance-corrected masked outputs make the full expectation equal the dense MLP output. NORDER-II enumerates complete joint states in decreasing probability without building or sorting the full state space, and truncation gives an anytime approximation controlled by probability mass and a state budget.
AI.result: With the first, middle and last MLP layers approximated jointly, WikiText-2 perplexity stays within 0.06% and 0.54% of dense inference. Relative to expected-count Grouped Top-k, NORDER-II yields 82.6% to 126.4% relative accuracy gains at 0.18% to 0.19% additional local analytic FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: Joint-state structure matters beyond individual component salience, and dense layers can be viewed as structured probabilistic inference, which opens a path to adaptive, probability-mass-controlled computation in pretrained networks.

title: When Does Causality Help in Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection?
summary: Causality-aware scoring is common in multivariate time-series anomaly detection, yet the literature rarely states when it helps. Holding one causality-guided autoencoder (DeCauAE) fixed, we vary graph quality, anomaly type and protocol against ground truth. Graph quality fixes the payoff: on a twenty-variable DAG the gain over a graph-free autoencoder decays as the graph is corrupted. Anomaly type fixes the target: the structural factor lifts window F1 from 0.800 to 0.976 where anomalies break conditional structure, and its advantage vanishes below a break severity s 0.3. Protocol fixes the ranking: point-adjusted F1 lets a random score match the full model, while range-aware VUS separates the autoencoder family from the classical baselines. On real benchmarks the causal module pays only where density makes a system eligible and cross-subsample reproducibility selects entities inside it; enabling it everywhere costs 0.012 VUS-ROC. The structural factor also transfers to classical detectors .

AI.tldr: The paper studies when causality-guided scoring helps multivariate time-series anomaly detection, using a fixed causality-guided autoencoder (DeCauAE) and varying graph quality, anomaly type and evaluation protocol. It finds that the benefit depends on graph quality, anomaly type and protocol, and that enabling the causal module everywhere costs 0.012 VUS-ROC on real benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Causality-aware scoring is common in multivariate time-series anomaly detection, but the literature rarely specifies the conditions under which it helps.
AI.method: With DeCauAE held fixed, the authors vary graph quality on a twenty-variable DAG against a graph-free autoencoder, anomaly type (including breaks of conditional structure with a break severity parameter), and protocol, comparing point-adjusted F1 with range-aware VUS against ground truth.
AI.result: On the twenty-variable DAG the gain over a graph-free autoencoder decays as the graph is corrupted. The structural factor raises window F1 from 0.800 to 0.976 where anomalies break conditional structure, but its advantage vanishes below break severity s = 0.3. Point-adjusted F1 lets a random score match the full model, while VUS separates the autoencoder family from classical baselines. The causal module pays only where density makes a system eligible and reproducibility selects entities; enabling it everywhere costs 0.012 VUS-ROC.
AI.conclusion: Causality helps anomaly detection only under specific graph quality, anomaly type and protocol conditions, so causal modules should be enabled selectively rather than everywhere.

title: Profile-Based Auditing of Domestic Violence Survey Selection Across South Asia
comment: Accepted at the AI4Science and New in ML Workshops, NeurIPS 2026
summary: Domestic violence (DV) data in the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) are collected through a specialized module whose household-level sampling and privacy requirements create a distinct observation process. We ask whether demographic, socioeconomic, and household characteristics form reproducible population profiles and whether these profiles contain information about selection into the DV module across South Asia. Using DHS Individual Recode data for 796,374 women aged 15-49 across Afghanistan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, and Pakistan, we harmonize 61 numeric and 8 categorical features, reduce the profile space with PCA, and identify six interpretable profiles. We then evaluate 22 machine-learning models under primary-sampling-unit-aware holdout validation. The best model, HistGradientBoosting, achieves ROC-AUC 0.9167 and PR-AUC 0.9612, versus 0.8475 and 0.9203 for a design-only baseline. Adding woman-level characteristics yields the largest incremental gain, while explicit interaction terms add little out-of-sample performance. Country-specific analyses reveal substantial heterogeneity, and leave-one-country-out evaluation shows that transferability of the incremental profile signal is limited. These results demonstrate that interpretable ML can audit differential coverage in sensitive survey modules beyond the formal sampling design.

AI.tldr: The paper audits which women are selected into the domestic violence (DV) module of Demographic and Health Surveys across five South Asian countries, using interpretable profiles and machine learning. The best model, HistGradientBoosting, reaches ROC-AUC 0.9167 against 0.8475 for a design-only baseline, but transfer across countries is limited.
AI.motivation: DV data in DHS come from a specialized module with its own sampling and privacy requirements, so the module forms a distinct observation process, and it is unknown whether selection into it can be predicted from population profiles.
AI.method: Individual Recode data for 796,374 women aged 15-49 in Afghanistan, India, Myanmar, Nepal and Pakistan are harmonized into 61 numeric and 8 categorical features, reduced with PCA into six interpretable profiles, and 22 machine-learning models are evaluated under primary-sampling-unit-aware holdout validation.
AI.result: HistGradientBoosting achieves ROC-AUC 0.9167 and PR-AUC 0.9612, against 0.8475 and 0.9203 for a design-only baseline. Woman-level characteristics give the largest incremental gain, explicit interaction terms add little out-of-sample, and country-specific results are heterogeneous. Leave-one-country-out evaluation shows limited transferability of the incremental profile signal.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable machine learning can audit differential coverage in sensitive survey modules beyond the formal sampling design, although the findings do not transfer reliably across countries.

title: Serving-Aligned Entire-Space Conversion Modeling via Click-Through Rate Knowledge Distillation
summary: Recommendation systems may use predicted click-through conversion rate (pCTCVR), the product of predicted click-through rate (pCTR) and post-click conversion rate (pCVR), to guide ranking decisions. Many pCVR models build on the Entire Space Multi-Task Model (ESMM), which jointly trains pCVR and auxiliary pCTR towers using pCTR and pCTCVR losses, but deploys only the pCVR tower. At serving time, this tower may be paired with a separately trained pCTR model, creating a training-serving mismatch in pCTCVR when its predictions differ from those of the auxiliary pCTR tower. In this paper, we use knowledge distillation (KD) from logged serving pCTR scores to supervise ESMM's auxiliary pCTR tower and improve training-serving pCTCVR alignment. We denote variants by KD-$\alpha$, where $\alpha$ controls the hard-label loss weight. On the Ali-CCP dataset, KD-0.3, the best variant on serving pCTCVR, increases ROC-AUC not only for serving pCTCVR but also for pCVR by 2.1% and 1.6%, respectively, and PR-AUC by 9.9% and 8.8%, respectively, relative to the ESMM baseline. We also test negative downsampling with 5% nonclick retention. Downsampled KD-0.3 increases mean AUC for serving pCTCVR and pCVR by 1.2% and 0.9%, respectively, -and PR-AUC by 8.5% and 4.5%, respectively, relative to downsampled ESMM.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using knowledge distillation from logged serving pCTR scores to supervise the auxiliary pCTR tower of ESMM, so that the trained pCVR tower matches the pCTCVR used at serving. On Ali-CCP, the best variant KD-0.3 improves ROC-AUC and PR-AUC over the ESMM baseline.
AI.motivation: ESMM trains pCVR and an auxiliary pCTR tower jointly but deploys only the pCVR tower, which may be paired with a separately trained pCTR model at serving time, creating a mismatch in pCTCVR between training and serving.
AI.method: Knowledge distillation from logged serving pCTR scores supervises ESMM's auxiliary pCTR tower, with variants named KD-alpha, where alpha is the weight of the hard-label loss. The authors also test negative downsampling with 5% nonclick retention.
AI.result: On Ali-CCP, KD-0.3 raises ROC-AUC for serving pCTCVR by 2.1% and for pCVR by 1.6%, and PR-AUC by 9.9% and 8.8% respectively, relative to ESMM. With downsampling, downsampled KD-0.3 improves mean AUC for serving pCTCVR and pCVR by 1.2% and 0.9%, and PR-AUC by 8.5% and 4.5%, relative to downsampled ESMM.
AI.conclusion: Distilling serving pCTR scores into ESMM's auxiliary tower improves training-serving alignment and pCVR accuracy, including under negative downsampling.

title: Knowledge Transfer for Conditional Flow Matching: Frozen Estimation and Adaptation
summary: Conditional generative modeling with limited target data can benefit from representations learned in a related source population. We develop a transfer learning framework for conditional flow matching that accommodates distinct source and target response distributions and dimensions. Two procedures exploit a representation learned from source data: TFM-Freeze estimates a target velocity head with the representation fixed, whereas TFM-Adapt jointly learns the head and a representation adaptation under a functional anchoring penalty. For explicit neural network classes, we establish bounds on conditional squared Wasserstein risk that account for source estimation, target fitting, representation mismatch, and numerical integration. When the source representation admits a smooth correction, adaptation replaces the frozen mismatch contribution by the cost of learning the correction and a controllable regularization bias. An information lower bound identifies regimes in which adaptation attains a strictly faster conditional squared Wasserstein risk rate than any generator restricted to the frozen context information. We also develop independent validation procedure for selecting among fitted conditional generators. We show that the selection procedure satisfies an oracle inequality, and the switching rule guarantees, with high probability, no increase in conditional energy risk relative to a target-only generator. Simulations and real data applications illustrate the gains from our proposed methods and the effectiveness of target validation in guarding against negative transfer.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a transfer learning framework for conditional flow matching from a related source population, with two procedures: TFM-Freeze, which keeps the source representation fixed, and TFM-Adapt, which also adapts the representation under a functional anchoring penalty. It gives Wasserstein risk bounds and a target-validation rule that guards against negative transfer.
AI.motivation: Conditional generative modeling with limited target data can benefit from a source population, but source and target response distributions and dimensions may differ, and transfer can hurt when the source is mismatched.
AI.method: A velocity head is estimated on the target with a frozen source representation (TFM-Freeze) or with the head and a representation correction learned jointly under a functional anchoring penalty (TFM-Adapt). Risk bounds account for source estimation, target fitting, representation mismatch and numerical integration, and an independent validation procedure selects among fitted generators.
AI.result: The authors show that adaptation can attain a strictly faster conditional squared Wasserstein risk rate than any generator restricted to the frozen context information in some regimes, and that the selection procedure satisfies an oracle inequality. The switching rule guarantees with high probability no increase in conditional energy risk relative to a target-only generator. Simulations and real data illustrate the gains.
AI.conclusion: Target validation can protect against negative transfer, and adapting the source representation can improve rates when the source representation admits a smooth correction.

title: PRELUDE: Separating Common Components from Target-Specific Dependencies for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables
summary: Multivariate time series forecasting often improves the prediction of a target by modeling the interactions among variables, and cross-variable modules such as cross-sectional pooling, inter-variable attention, and graph structures are used to construct such interactions. However, by intervening on the cross-variable reading of existing models at inference time, we find that although these models substantially reduce forecasting error through cross-variable interaction, their reading is nearly identical for all targets: the gain appears to come from dependencies among variables but mainly comes from the common component. We term this phenomenon spurious dependency and attribute it to common-component confounding: present in every variable, the common component affects how reading distinguishes sources, so that reading tends to be shared across targets and concentrates on a few similar averages; dependencies thus make up a small share of the read-in content, and a common component composed of several drivers is only partly captured. Theoretical analysis further shows that the common component and dependencies place different requirements on reading and should therefore be handled in different ways. Accordingly, we propose PRELUDE, a separated-reading framework that estimates the common component holistically through cross-sectional pooling and multiple common factors, and reads dependencies for each target via lead-lag relations in the innovation space obtained by prewhitening. Extensive experiments on 16 real-world datasets from four domains show that PRELUDE effectively mitigates spurious dependency and achieves the best overall performance: it attains the best MSE on 23 of the 24 short-horizon and air-quality settings and reduces the average MSE by 6.1% relative to the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PRELUDE, which separates the common component from target-specific dependencies in multivariate time series forecasting, arguing that existing cross-variable modules mostly capture a shared common component rather than dependencies. It reports the best MSE on 23 of 24 short-horizon and air-quality settings and a 6.1% average MSE reduction over the strongest baseline across 16 datasets.
AI.motivation: Cross-variable modules in forecasting models appear to read nearly the same content for all targets, so the reported gains seem to come from a common component rather than from dependencies among variables, a phenomenon the authors call spurious dependency.
AI.method: Interventions on the cross-variable reading of existing models at inference time support a common-component confounding explanation. PRELUDE estimates the common component holistically through cross-sectional pooling and multiple common factors, and reads dependencies for each target through lead-lag relations in the innovation space obtained by prewhitening.
AI.result: Across 16 real-world datasets from four domains, PRELUDE achieves the best MSE on 23 of 24 short-horizon and air-quality settings and reduces average MSE by 6.1% relative to the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Handling the common component and target-specific dependencies separately mitigates spurious dependency and improves forecasting performance overall.

title: Stealthy, High-Impact False Data Injection Attacks in Smart Grid Using Physics-Constrained GAN
comment: 10 pages
summary: False data injection (FDI) attacks can distort power system state estimation while retaining plausible measurement patterns. Existing FDI methods trade stealth for impact or vice versa. They often assume access to internal grids, all-bus sensing, or defender models. In this paper, we propose a detector-agnostic physics-constrained generative adversarial network (PCGAN) that learns decoupled power-flow sensitivities from historical measurements of deployed sensors. The learned active-power-angle and reactive-power-voltage-magnitude relationships guide perturbations restricted to compromised channels, while adversarial training promotes realistic spatiotemporal patterns. We implement PCGAN and seven existing FDI attacks on the IEEE 300-bus system using one year of observed hourly demand from PJM Interconnection, a regional transmission organization in the United States, and synthetic bus-level load profiles. We compare their performance across 10%, 30%, 60%, and 100% compromised sensors. Attack stealth is assessed against ten machine-learning (ML) detectors and conventional bad-data detection (BDD) methods, while physical impact is quantified through nonlinear alternating-current weighted least-squares state estimation. PCGAN achieves 84.28% mean ML evasion and 22.31% mean spatial load misperception across the four scenarios. Its mean stealth-impact trade-off score reaches 18.69%, compared with 5.61% for the strongest competing attack. PCGAN also achieves 83.45% chi-square BDD evasion and 86.02% largest-normalized-residual BDD evasion. These results demonstrate a favorable stealth-impact balance under varying sensor-access levels and provide challenging attack cases for evaluating FDI detectors.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PCGAN, a detector-agnostic physics-constrained GAN that generates false data injection attacks on smart grid state estimation using power-flow sensitivities learned from historical measurements. It reports 84.28% mean ML evasion and 22.31% mean spatial load misperception across scenarios on the IEEE 300-bus system.
AI.motivation: Existing FDI attacks trade stealth for impact or vice versa, and they often assume access to internal grid models, all-bus sensing or defender models.
AI.method: PCGAN learns decoupled active-power-angle and reactive-power-voltage-magnitude sensitivities from historical measurements of deployed sensors, restricts perturbations to compromised channels, and uses adversarial training to promote realistic spatiotemporal patterns. It is compared with seven existing FDI attacks at 10%, 30%, 60% and 100% compromised sensors.
AI.result: Against ten ML detectors and conventional bad-data detection, PCGAN achieves 84.28% mean ML evasion and 22.31% mean spatial load misperception. Its mean stealth-impact trade-off score is 18.69%, against 5.61% for the strongest competing attack, with 83.45% chi-square BDD evasion and 86.02% largest-normalized-residual BDD evasion.
AI.conclusion: PCGAN offers a favorable stealth-impact balance across sensor-access levels and provides challenging attack cases for evaluating FDI detectors.

title: Anytime-Valid Empirical Likelihood Inference from LLM Annotations with Adaptive Human Auditing
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate unlabeled data as a fast, low-cost alternative to human annotation. However, their outputs can be biased and miscalibrated relative to human labels, potentially leading to misleading analysis and inference. We propose AAELI (Adaptive Human Auditing and Anytime-Valid Empirical Likelihood Inference), an online framework for estimating the population mean of human labels under a limited auditing budget. AAELI uses LLM outputs to guide adaptive human auditing and combines them with audited labels through predictable empirical-likelihood $e$-processes to construct anytime-valid confidence sequences. Our main theoretical result shows that a predictably learned efficient projection preserves the first-order profile empirical-likelihood statistic under adaptive auditing, without requiring a prescribed convergence rate for the projection estimator. This yields an exactly anytime-valid betting construction whose continuous-mixture form incurs a scalar rather than vector-dimensional mixing penalty. Supporting results establish adaptive empirical-likelihood asymptotics and show that a learned audit rule attains the oracle variance within the stated class of augmented estimating-equation designs under the same audit-probability floor and long-run expected budget. Experiments on synthetic data and three real-world datasets demonstrate that AAELI maintains empirical anytime coverage while requiring fewer human audits than the strongest competing baseline to reach a target precision.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AAELI, an online framework that estimates the mean of human labels under a limited auditing budget by using LLM annotations to guide adaptive human audits, with anytime-valid confidence sequences from empirical-likelihood e-processes. It reports maintained anytime coverage and fewer human audits than the strongest baseline to reach a target precision.
AI.motivation: LLM annotations are cheap but may be biased and miscalibrated relative to human labels, which can mislead downstream inference, so an estimate of the human-label mean must be obtained with limited human auditing.
AI.method: AAELI uses LLM outputs to choose which items to audit adaptively and combines the audited labels through predictable empirical-likelihood e-processes. A predictably learned efficient projection preserves the first-order profile empirical-likelihood statistic under adaptive auditing, and a continuous-mixture betting construction gives anytime-valid confidence sequences.
AI.result: On synthetic data and three real-world datasets, AAELI maintains empirical anytime coverage and requires fewer human audits than the strongest competing baseline to reach a target precision. The abstract also states that a learned audit rule attains oracle variance within the stated class of designs.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive auditing guided by LLM outputs can give valid anytime inference on human-label means while reducing the human annotation cost.

title: DGPExplainer: Generating Prototype Sequence Explanations for Dynamic Graph Neural Networks
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been successfully applied to learning from graph-structured data. However, applying them to dynamic graphs-where nodes and edges evolve over time-presents significant challenges, particularly regarding explainability. While explanation techniques for static GNNs are well established, they do not readily extend to dynamic GNNs (DGNNs) due to the added complexity introduced by temporal dynamics and spatiotemporal dependencies, especially when generating model-level explanations. To address this gap, we introduce DGPExplainer, a post-hoc, prototype-based explainer specifically designed for DGNN models that transforms their complex decision-making processes into human-understandable, analogical, case-based explanations. DGPExplainer first employs local explanation methods to identify important elements within temporal snapshots of dynamic graph sequences. It then decomposes the graph at each time step into distinct prototypes, thereby symbolizing the dynamic graph sequence. Finally, we design a sequence generation method that uses these symbolized sequences to learn and generate class-specific dynamic graph pattern sequences that serve as prototype explanations. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method effectively produces prototype-based explanations for DGNN models across multiple classes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DGPExplainer, a post-hoc, prototype-based explainer for dynamic graph neural networks that produces class-specific prototype sequence explanations in the form of dynamic graph pattern sequences. It is evaluated on synthetic and real-world datasets across multiple classes.
AI.motivation: Explanation methods for static GNNs do not readily extend to dynamic GNNs, especially for model-level explanations, because of temporal dynamics and spatiotemporal dependencies.
AI.method: Local explanation methods identify important elements within temporal snapshots, each snapshot is decomposed into distinct prototypes that symbolize the dynamic graph sequence, and a sequence generation method learns class-specific pattern sequences from these symbolized sequences as prototype explanations.
AI.result: The abstract states that the method effectively produces prototype-based explanations for DGNN models across multiple classes on both synthetic and real-world datasets, without reporting quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Prototype sequences offer a case-based and human-understandable way to explain dynamic GNN decisions at the model level.

title: MOON-RL: Multi-Objective Optimization via Objective Space Navigation with Reinforcement Learning
comment: 66 pages, including appendices. Code, data and supplementary video links are provided in the manuscript
summary: Many engineering design problems involve multiple conflicting objectives and strict feasibility constraints. They are typically solved with population-based optimizers that require many evaluations and offer limited online control over where the search is focused. We present MOON-RL, a reinforcement-learning-based optimization framework that formulates constrained multi-objective search as preference-directed navigation in the objective space. In MOON-RL, a lightweight PPO policy receives objective-space and constraint-related observations and acts as an instance-specific adaptive search process. It learns how to update the design so that the current solution advances along a user-specified trade-off direction, while a simple meta-algorithm periodically resets the policy, resamples starting designs from a continuously updated archive of non-dominated solutions, and adjusts step-size and penalty schedules. We evaluate MOON-RL on real-world actuator-design problems and additional convergence-hard constrained benchmarks, comparing against established evolutionary algorithms under matched evaluation budgets. In focused search scenarios, MOON-RL achieves competitive performance in the region of interest, and ablation studies show that both the RL-driven adaptive sampling process and the meta-algorithm contribute to this behaviour, suggesting that repurposing RL training as objective-space navigation is a viable building block for interactive, preference-guided design tools. Additional experiments show that the framework also accommodates adaptive non-RL samplers, while PPO remains a strong choice for fixed-target, preference-directed objective-space navigation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MOON-RL, which casts constrained multi-objective design as preference-directed navigation in objective space, using a lightweight PPO policy that advances solutions along a user-specified trade-off direction. It reports competitive performance in the region of interest against evolutionary algorithms under matched budgets on actuator-design and constrained benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Engineering design problems with conflicting objectives and strict constraints are typically solved by population-based optimizers that need many evaluations and offer limited online control over where the search is focused.
AI.method: A PPO policy receives objective-space and constraint observations and learns to update designs along a trade-off direction, while a meta-algorithm periodically resets the policy, resamples starting designs from an archive of non-dominated solutions, and adjusts step-size and penalty schedules.
AI.result: On real-world actuator-design problems and constrained benchmarks, MOON-RL achieves competitive performance in the region of interest against established evolutionary algorithms under matched evaluation budgets. Ablations show that both the RL-driven sampling and the meta-algorithm contribute, and PPO remains a strong choice for fixed-target navigation.
AI.conclusion: Repurposing RL training as objective-space navigation is a viable building block for interactive, preference-guided design tools.

title: Regret Bounds for Quantum Linear Bandits
comment: 26 pages
summary: We study $d$-dimensional quantum linear bandits with bounded rewards, where the learner selects an action and queries its quantum reward oracle or its inverse in each round. For general action sets, existing algorithms achieve regret $O(d^{3/2}\operatorname{polylog}(T))$ over $T$ rounds. Prior work established a lower bound of $\Omega(d\log(1+T/d))$, leaving open whether the $d^{3/2}$ dependence in the upper bound is necessary. We resolve this question by proving a minimax lower bound of $\Omega(d^{3/2}\log(1+T/d^{3/2}))$. To prove this result, we construct a family of hard instances in which the reward gap of each action is proportional to its squared distance from the optimal action. We establish a posterior Fisher information bound for adaptive quantum queries with quantum memory, relating the information acquired about the optimal direction to the regret incurred. Viewing each selected action as an estimate of the optimal direction, we use a matrix Cramér--Rao argument to derive a lower bound on expected regret. When the action set is fixed and has size $K$, we propose two phased elimination algorithms, Soft-G-Elim and QG-Elim. We adapt quantum phase estimation to construct SoftQME, a mean estimator with small bias and controlled tails. Soft-G-Elim estimates the mean reward of every surviving action from independent SoftQME outputs on the support of an experimental design. Controlling the bias and fluctuations of these estimates yields regret $O(d\log T\log(dT)\sqrt{\log(KT)})$, reducing the $\log(KT)\log\log(dT)$ factor in the previous regret bound to $\sqrt{\log(KT)}$. QG-Elim further reduces this factor to $\min\{\sqrt{\log(KT)},\sqrt d\}$.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the d^{3/2} dependence in the regret of quantum linear bandits is necessary, by proving a minimax lower bound of Omega(d^{3/2} log(1+T/d^{3/2})). For fixed action sets it also proposes Soft-G-Elim and QG-Elim, which reduce a log factor in the previous regret bound.
AI.motivation: Existing algorithms achieve regret O(d^{3/2} polylog(T)) for quantum linear bandits, while the prior lower bound was Omega(d log(1+T/d)), leaving open whether the d^{3/2} dependence is necessary.
AI.method: Hard instances have reward gaps proportional to squared distance from the optimal action. A posterior Fisher information bound for adaptive quantum queries with quantum memory is combined with a matrix Cramer-Rao argument to lower-bound expected regret. For fixed action sets of size K, phased elimination algorithms use SoftQME, a quantum phase estimation based mean estimator with small bias and controlled tails.
AI.result: The minimax lower bound Omega(d^{3/2} log(1+T/d^{3/2})) matches the d^{3/2} dependence of the upper bound. Soft-G-Elim achieves regret O(d log T log(dT) sqrt(log(KT))), and QG-Elim further reduces the factor to min{sqrt(log(KT)), sqrt(d)}.
AI.conclusion: The d^{3/2} dependence is necessary for general action sets, and for fixed action sets the algorithms reduce the logarithmic dependence on K and T.

title: Protected Unbiased Sparsification: A Sharp Loewner Curve
comment: 44 pages, 11 figures. Code, protocols, and saved results are included as ancillary files
summary: Random sparsification replaces a probability vector by a random vector with few nonzero entries. We ask for unbiasedness, exact preservation of prescribed linear statistics, and a covariance guarantee for every downstream linear response. Let $p$ have $k$ positive coordinates, let $A$ specify the protected statistics, and let $d\le k-2$ be their effective rank. For every $d+1\le m\le k$, we construct an unbiased random probability vector $Q$ with at most $m$ nonzero coordinates, $AQ=Ap$ on every realization, and $\operatorname{Cov}(Q)\preceq h C_{p\mid A}$, where $h=(k-m)/((m-d)(k-d-1))$ and $C_{p\mid A}$ is the categorical covariance after optimal linear adjustment for the protected statistics. This coefficient is sharp uniformly over instances, even among biased estimators when error is measured by its second moment. A residual covariance bridge extends the concurrent unprotected curve to arbitrary pathwise linear protection. We also characterize instance-optimal constants for partitions with uniform weights within classes and derive bounds for peaked weights. For rational inputs, an exact Las Vegas sampler attains the curve within a factor $1+\epsilon$ in expected polynomial time. A separate fast block-pivotal sampler preserves block masses and is no worse in covariance order than independent sampling within blocks. Experiments illustrate the theory on synthetic weights and language-model attention. In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct decoding, the fast sampler preserves block masses, while comparisons with VarOpt remain statistically inconclusive and top-$m$ truncation scores highest on RULER.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs, for each target size m, an unbiased random probability vector with at most m nonzero coordinates that preserves prescribed linear statistics exactly and satisfies a sharp covariance bound. It also gives an exact sampler and a fast block-pivotal sampler, and illustrates them on language-model attention decoding.
AI.motivation: Random sparsification of a probability vector should be unbiased, exactly preserve protected linear statistics, and control the covariance of every downstream linear response, which existing methods do not jointly provide.
AI.method: For a vector p with k positive coordinates and protected statistics A of effective rank d, the paper builds an unbiased random vector Q with at most m nonzero coordinates such that AQ = Ap on every realization and Cov(Q) is bounded by h times the residual categorical covariance, with h = (k-m)/((m-d)(k-d-1)). A residual covariance bridge handles arbitrary pathwise linear protection.
AI.result: The coefficient h is sharp uniformly over instances, even among biased estimators under second-moment error. For rational inputs an exact Las Vegas sampler reaches the curve within a factor 1+epsilon in expected polynomial time. In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct decoding the fast sampler preserves block masses, while comparisons with VarOpt are statistically inconclusive and top-m truncation scores highest on RULER.
AI.conclusion: The covariance curve characterizes the best achievable trade-off between sparsity and variance under linear protection, and the fast sampler is practical for attention-style workloads.

title: A hybrid machine learning-analog framework for downscaling unprecedented climate extremes
summary: Extreme weather events are critical for climate impact assessments. While physical models can simulate unprecedented extremes, for example, through ensemble boosting, this approach is computationally demanding, often restricting output to coarse spatial resolutions. Probabilistic generative downscaling offers a solution by enabling efficient sampling from the entire climate distribution, including its extreme tails. Here, we first demonstrate that machine learning generated regional climate model heatwaves over Paris are physically realistic. We then leverage an emulated machine learning dataset to perform analog-based downscaling of coarse global climate model ensemble boosting events. Our hybrid framework effectively bridges high-resolution regional detail with rare-event sampling, providing an efficient tool for extreme event downscaling and capturing multi-model uncertainty.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid framework that combines machine learning emulation with analog-based downscaling to produce high-resolution samples of unprecedented climate extremes from coarse global climate model ensemble boosting events. It first shows that ML-generated regional climate model heatwaves over Paris are physically realistic.
AI.motivation: Physical models can simulate unprecedented extremes through ensemble boosting, but this is computationally expensive and usually restricts output to coarse resolution, while generative downscaling can sample the full climate distribution, including tails, more efficiently.
AI.method: An emulated machine learning dataset is used to perform analog-based downscaling of coarse global climate model ensemble boosting events, linking regional detail to rare-event sampling.
AI.result: The abstract reports that ML-generated regional climate model heatwaves over Paris are physically realistic and that the hybrid framework bridges high-resolution regional detail with rare-event sampling while capturing multi-model uncertainty. No quantitative results are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The framework is presented as an efficient tool for downscaling extreme events and representing multi-model uncertainty.

title: Learning Rate Transfer and Feature Learning Across Depth for Constrained Spectral Optimizers: Complete Scion
summary: Hyperparameter transfer across model depth is instrumental in training deep models, as it enables learning rates calibrated on shallow networks to be effectively applied to deeper architectures. The recent CompleteP framework establishes a $1/L$ residual scaling rule that demonstrates this for Adam-family optimizers. We study whether similar transfer extends to constrained optimization methods, specifically Frank-Wolfe and projected non-Euclidean normalized steepest descent, where updates are determined by linear minimization oracles. We derive scaling rules for these methods which confirm that the $1/L$ residual scaling applies, although the arguments differ from the Adam-family optimizers. Our analysis supports depth-wise transfer and width-wise transfer of the learning rate for the Scion algorithm while ensuring feature learning and avoiding the kernel-regime. In experiments on NLP transformers (nanoGPT on FineWeb), vision transformers (DeiT on ImageNet), and vision MLPs (MLP-Mixer on CIFAR-10), we observe learning rate transfer across depth and feature learning for appropriately chosen residual scaling.

AI.tldr: The paper derives scaling rules for learning rate transfer across depth and width in constrained spectral optimizers, specifically Frank-Wolfe and projected non-Euclidean normalized steepest descent, extending the CompleteP 1/L residual scaling beyond Adam-family optimizers. It applies these rules to the Scion algorithm and reports depth-wise learning rate transfer with feature learning in three transformer and MLP settings.
AI.motivation: CompleteP establishes a 1/L residual scaling rule for hyperparameter transfer across depth in Adam-family optimizers, but it is unknown whether similar transfer holds for constrained optimizers whose updates come from linear minimization oracles.
AI.method: Scaling rules are derived for Frank-Wolfe and projected non-Euclidean normalized steepest descent, and the analysis is applied to the Scion algorithm to support depth-wise and width-wise learning rate transfer while avoiding the kernel regime.
AI.result: In experiments on nanoGPT with FineWeb, DeiT on ImageNet and MLP-Mixer on CIFAR-10, learning rate transfer across depth and feature learning are observed for appropriately chosen residual scaling. The abstract does not give quantitative values.
AI.conclusion: The 1/L residual scaling applies to constrained spectral optimizers as well, although the arguments differ from those for Adam-family optimizers.

title: TabOmics: A Small, Open Tabular Foundation Model for Wide Omics Data
summary: Omics studies often produce tables with thousands to tens of thousands of molecular features and few samples. Tabular foundation models use diverse strategies to predict labels for such tables, with some relying on in-context learning, while approaches to wide tables may involve subsampling, grouping, or compressing features. We present TabOmics, a small, open family of tabular foundation models with 7.3M parameters, pretrained exclusively on synthetic tables. TabOmics processes all features retained after preprocessing jointly and derives predictions, attention-derived feature-importance scores, and test sample embeddings from the same forward pass. On 46 classification tasks from three benchmarks of high-dimensional, low-sample-size tables, TabOmics v2.5 with eight ensemble members achieves the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) among the evaluated models (0.943), outperforming TabPFN-3.5 with eight members on 32 tasks despite having about 30 times fewer parameters. With a single member, TabOmics v2.5 reaches a mean AUROC of 0.941, versus 0.942 for TabPFN-3.5 with eight members, with no significant paired difference under the reported task-level analysis. On synthetic tables, its feature-importance scores achieve feature recovery similar to that of TabPFN-Wide, and its predictions remain above chance at 30,000 features. On breast cancer tasks, the top ranked genes include PAM50 genes, which define the subtype labels, indicating concordance with the label definition rather than independent biological validation. The code, model weights, training recipes, and experimental artifacts are publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper presents TabOmics, a 7.3M-parameter open tabular foundation model pretrained only on synthetic tables and designed for wide omics data. Its eight-member ensemble reaches the highest mean AUROC (0.943) among the evaluated models on 46 high-dimensional classification tasks, with about 30 times fewer parameters than TabPFN-3.5.
AI.motivation: Omics tables have thousands to tens of thousands of features and few samples, and existing tabular foundation models rely on subsampling, grouping or compressing features, which may lose information.
AI.method: TabOmics processes all retained features jointly and produces predictions, attention-derived feature-importance scores and test sample embeddings in one forward pass. It is pretrained exclusively on synthetic tables.
AI.result: On 46 classification tasks from three benchmarks, TabOmics v2.5 with eight members reaches mean AUROC 0.943, outperforming TabPFN-3.5 with eight members on 32 tasks. A single member reaches 0.941 versus 0.942 for TabPFN-3.5 with eight members, with no significant paired difference. On synthetic tables its feature-importance recovery is similar to TabPFN-Wide, and predictions stay above chance at 30,000 features.
AI.conclusion: A small model pretrained on synthetic data can match or exceed larger tabular foundation models on wide omics tables, and the code, weights and recipes are publicly released.

title: MechBench: A Domain-Specific LLM Benchmark for Parallel Mechanisms
summary: Parallel mechanisms pose distinctive challenges to large language models (LLMs), as valid reasoning depends jointly on mechanism topology, loop closure, geometry, joint types, and modeling assumptions. Yet existing LLM benchmarks provide little systematic coverage of such domain-specific knowledge, constraint-sensitive analysis, and constructive design. To fill this gap, we introduce MECHBENCH, a 2,541-question benchmark for evaluating LLMs in parallel mechanisms across professional knowledge, mechanism analysis, and design. MECHBENCH contains standard and challenge tiers spanning six capability categories and nine executable analysis and design tasks. It is constructed through MECHFORGE, a domain-grounded framework that combines expert-organized knowledge, LLM-assisted question generation, programmatic instance generation, two-stage expert review, and task-aware scoring with exact matching, rubric-based evaluation, and program verification. We further develop MECHGPT as a diagnostic domain-adapted model. Experiments show that strong knowledge performance does not directly translate into executable mechanism reasoning: leading closed-service models achieve over 95 on the standard tier but only 47-60 on the challenge tier, while domain adaptation substantially improves MechGPT over its Qwen3-8B baselines but leaves a large gap in constrained analysis and design. These results establish MECHBENCH as a systematic testbed for measuring domain-specific LLM capabilities in mechanism science.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MechBench, a 2,541-question benchmark for evaluating LLMs on parallel mechanisms across professional knowledge, mechanism analysis and design, together with MechGPT, a domain-adapted model. Leading closed-service models score over 95 on the standard tier but only 47-60 on the challenge tier.
AI.motivation: Parallel mechanisms require reasoning that jointly depends on topology, loop closure, geometry, joint types and modeling assumptions, and existing LLM benchmarks give little systematic coverage of this domain-specific knowledge, constrained analysis and design.
AI.method: The benchmark is built through MechForge, which combines expert-organized knowledge, LLM-assisted question generation, programmatic instance generation, two-stage expert review and task-aware scoring with exact matching, rubric evaluation and program verification. It has standard and challenge tiers over six capability categories and nine executable tasks.
AI.result: Leading closed-service models score over 95 on the standard tier but 47-60 on the challenge tier. Domain adaptation substantially improves MechGPT over its Qwen3-8B baselines but leaves a large gap in constrained analysis and design.
AI.conclusion: Strong knowledge performance does not translate directly into executable mechanism reasoning, and MechBench serves as a testbed for domain-specific capability in mechanism science.

title: A Modified Glicko Model for Rating Soccer Clubs and National Teams Worldwide
comment: 39 pages, 4 figures, 14 tables
summary: Comparing soccer teams that rarely or never meet is a fundamental challenge in sports analytics: clubs play mostly within their national leagues, and national teams within their confederations. We propose a rating framework that places clubs and national teams worldwide on a common probabilistic scale. Building on a recent extension of Glicko with order effects and strength-dependent draw probabilities, we adapt the model to soccer with goal-scoring adjustments, a decomposition of home advantage, extra time, league-aware rating initialization and rules of promotion and relegation that do not inflate the levels of leagues; national teams start from the levels of their confederations. The models are evaluated on about 1.2 million club matches of 252 leagues from 166 countries (2000-2026) and 12.6 thousand national team matches (1998-2026). On held-out seasons, the modified Glicko model is clearly more accurate than Elo and as accurate as score-matrix models built on the goal expectations of a gradient boosting model, including the Dixon-Coles and Markov chain models, while it is substantially more accurate in international club matches. Averaging the predictions of the rating model and the Markov chain model is more accurate than either model alone. For national teams, the model is significantly more accurate than all baselines, especially in the final tournaments, where teams of different confederations meet. The resulting ratings are interpretable and can be used for player evaluation, transfer analysis and match forecasting. The match data, the ratings and the code are publicly available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a modified Glicko rating model that places clubs and national teams worldwide on a common probabilistic scale. It reports that the model is more accurate than Elo and as accurate as Dixon-Coles and Markov chain score-matrix models on held-out seasons, and that averaging it with the Markov chain model is more accurate than either alone.
AI.motivation: Clubs mostly play within national leagues and national teams within confederations, so teams that rarely or never meet are hard to compare directly.
AI.method: A recent Glicko extension with order effects and strength-dependent draw probabilities is adapted to soccer with goal-scoring adjustments, a decomposition of home advantage, extra time, league-aware rating initialization, and promotion and relegation rules that do not inflate league levels. National teams start from their confederation levels.
AI.result: On about 1.2 million club matches from 252 leagues in 166 countries (2000-2026) and 12.6 thousand national team matches (1998-2026), the model is clearly more accurate than Elo and as accurate as score-matrix models built on gradient boosting goal expectations, and substantially more accurate in international club matches. For national teams it is significantly more accurate than all baselines, especially in final tournaments.
AI.conclusion: The ratings are interpretable and can support player evaluation, transfer analysis and match forecasting.

title: MORA: Correcting Time Series Forecasts with Coarse Future Signals
comment: 33 pages, 3 figures
summary: Recent architectural advances have improved time-series forecasting. However, our analysis of forecasters with diverse architectures reveals a common pattern: a substantial share of residual energy is concentrated in a small number of low-frequency components. Simple linear probes further show that the forecasters' historical inputs still contain predictive information about errors in the forecast mean. Building on these findings, we propose Model-Output Residual Adaptation (MORA), a model-agnostic residual adapter that refines the outputs of frozen forecasters without requiring additional inputs. MORA estimates segment-wise means of the target sequence through structural extrapolation and learned estimation, rather than directly predicting backbone-specific residuals. It then converts discrepancies between these estimates and the corresponding statistics of the backbone forecast into stagewise corrections, scaling each update according to estimation reliability. Extensive experiments on twelve benchmarks with six forecasting backbones show average MSE reductions of 7.2% for long-term forecasting and 28.1% for short-term forecasting, with lower MSE in 96.2% of the 288 evaluated cases. The benefits also extend to three time-series foundation models evaluated at different context lengths. Together, these results demonstrate that predictable coarse-scale residuals can be effectively exploited to improve existing forecasts. Code repository: this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MORA, a model-agnostic residual adapter that refines the outputs of frozen time-series forecasters by correcting segment-wise means of the forecast using coarse future estimates. It reports average MSE reductions of 7.2% for long-term and 28.1% for short-term forecasting across twelve benchmarks and six backbones.
AI.motivation: Analysis of diverse forecasters shows that a substantial share of residual energy sits in a few low-frequency components, and linear probes show that historical inputs still predict errors in the forecast mean.
AI.method: MORA estimates segment-wise means of the target through structural extrapolation and learned estimation, rather than predicting backbone-specific residuals, converts discrepancies from the backbone's segment statistics into stagewise corrections, and scales each update by estimation reliability. It needs no additional inputs.
AI.result: Across twelve benchmarks with six forecasting backbones, average MSE falls by 7.2% for long-term and 28.1% for short-term forecasting, with lower MSE in 96.2% of 288 evaluated cases. Benefits also extend to three time-series foundation models at different context lengths.
AI.conclusion: Predictable coarse-scale residuals can be exploited to improve existing forecasts without retraining the backbones.

title: Overcoming the Resolution Limit: Significance-Aware Regularization for Intersectional Fairness
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Intersectional fairness requires evaluating models across fine-grained subgroups. However, as group definitions become more granular, the sample size per subgroup shrinks, causing fairness estimates to become increasingly unstable. Existing in-processing methods are certainty-blind: they penalize observed disparities without distinguishing statistically certified unfairness from sampling noise. This leads to fairness overfitting, where models sacrifice utility to "fix" spurious disparities in sparse regimes. To address this, we introduce the significant-excess metric family, a continuous, uncertainty-aware fairness score that measures only the portion of a subgroup's disparity exceeding what sampling variation can explain at a specific confidence level. Building on this metric, we propose SAFER (Significance-Aware Fairness Regularizer), a differentiable in-processing method that gates fairness penalties using a soft-count likelihood-ratio evidence statistic. SAFER satisfies a provable safety property: when every subgroup disparity lies well below the gate threshold, the unconstrained optimum is nearly stationary for SAFER. At that optimum, the back-propagated contribution of its significance-gated component is exponentially small, and the additional fairness contribution comes from a small ungated term with a fixed weight. Mechanism ablations across three benchmark datasets and purpose-built stress variants show that removing any component of SAFER (threshold smoothing, the significance gate, or a dense-tail term) produces the failure the theory predicts on at least one stress variant. In sparse intersectional settings, SAFER achieves a better fairness-utility Pareto frontier than the baseline methods, and it preserves utility when certified unfairness is absent.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SAFER, a differentiable in-processing fairness regularizer that penalizes only the part of a subgroup's disparity that is statistically significant, using a significant-excess metric family. It reports a better fairness-utility Pareto frontier than baselines in sparse intersectional settings and preserves utility when certified unfairness is absent.
AI.motivation: As intersectional subgroups become finer, their sample sizes shrink and fairness estimates become unstable, and existing certainty-blind in-processing methods penalize sampling noise, which causes fairness overfitting and loss of utility.
AI.method: A continuous, uncertainty-aware significant-excess fairness score measures the disparity exceeding what sampling variation explains at a given confidence level. SAFER gates fairness penalties with a soft-count likelihood-ratio evidence statistic, and a dense-tail term adds a small ungated contribution with fixed weight.
AI.result: Ablations on three benchmark datasets and stress variants show that removing threshold smoothing, the significance gate or the dense-tail term produces the failure predicted by theory on at least one stress variant. In sparse intersectional settings SAFER achieves a better fairness-utility Pareto frontier than baselines. The abstract also states a safety property: when all disparities lie well below the gate threshold, the unconstrained optimum is nearly stationary for SAFER.
AI.conclusion: Gating fairness penalties by statistical significance avoids fairness overfitting and preserves utility when no certified unfairness exists.

title: DETER: Suppression During Pretraining for Tamper Resistance
summary: Open-weight language models can acquire knowledge that could enable biological, chemical, or cyber misuse. Any attempt to limit such knowledge must remain effective after the model weights are released and can be fine-tuned. Unlearning applied after pretraining can be rapidly undone, whereas filtering the pretraining corpus offers greater resistance. We ask whether actively suppressing knowledge during pretraining can further increase the fine-tuning required to acquire it. Even simple gradient ascent interleaved with standard pretraining on the filtered corpus makes medical knowledge harder to acquire through adversarial fine-tuning than filtering alone or post-hoc unlearning. At 1B parameters, reaching the held-out PubMed loss of an unfiltered model requires over 20$\times$ as many PubMed fine-tuning tokens as after filtering alone. Retained knowledge is evaluated using both held-out data and downstream tasks. Across model sizes, varying suppression strength reveals an increasingly favorable trade-off between fine-tuning difficulty and held-out loss on retained pretraining data. These results point to pretraining as an effective stage for making unwanted capabilities harder to acquire through subsequent fine-tuning. Code is available at \href{this https URL}{\texttt{this http URL}}.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that actively suppressing medical knowledge during pretraining, by interleaving gradient ascent with standard pretraining on a filtered corpus, makes that knowledge harder to recover through adversarial fine-tuning than filtering alone or post-hoc unlearning. At 1B parameters, reaching the held-out PubMed loss of an unfiltered model needs over 20 times as many PubMed fine-tuning tokens as filtering alone.
AI.motivation: Open-weight models can acquire knowledge enabling biological, chemical or cyber misuse, and post-hoc unlearning can be quickly undone by fine-tuning, while corpus filtering is more resistant; the question is whether suppression during pretraining adds further resistance.
AI.method: Gradient ascent is interleaved with standard pretraining on a filtered corpus, with suppression strength varied across model sizes. Retained knowledge is evaluated on held-out data and downstream tasks.
AI.result: At 1B parameters, reaching the held-out PubMed loss of an unfiltered model requires over 20x as many PubMed fine-tuning tokens as after filtering alone. Varying suppression strength across model sizes shows an increasingly favorable trade-off between fine-tuning difficulty and held-out loss on retained data.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining is an effective stage for making unwanted capabilities harder to acquire through later fine-tuning.

title: The Illusion of Diversity: Aligning LLM Exploration via Effective Entropy
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has shifted the alignment paradigm of large language models from subjective preference to objective correctness, yet a fundamental disconnect persists between exploration diversity and reasoning validity. Existing strategies predominantly rely on "blind" entropy metrics, e.g., token-level or global sequence-level entropy, which structurally fail to distinguish between effective reasoning and potential hallucinations. This misalignment creates an illusion of diversity, where high entropy tends to signal chaotic degeneration rather than valuable exploration. To bridge this gap, we introduce Effective Entropy, a validity-aware entropy concept that quantifies diversity exclusively within the valid subspace and systematically filters out the noise of incorrect trajectories. Built on this concept, we instantiate VEPO, a simple Validity-aware Entropy Policy Optimization method that directly incorporates effective entropy into RLVR training. VEPO induces an adaptive attraction dynamic that drives up the probability of under-explored valid trajectories, a mechanism that matches the practical regime of large-scale autoregressive models where sequence probabilities remain extremely small. Experiments on six mathematical reasoning benchmarks with 1.5B and 7B DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen models show consistent aggregate accuracy gains over GRPO and competitive repeated-sampling success. A direct evaluation with matched correct counts finds more distinct strategies on commonly solved MATH500 problems, supported by paired statistical tests and three-seed training comparisons.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Effective Entropy, which measures exploration diversity only within valid reasoning trajectories, and VEPO, an RLVR method that uses it to drive exploration. VEPO gives consistent aggregate accuracy gains over GRPO on six math benchmarks with 1.5B and 7B DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen models.
AI.motivation: Token-level and global sequence entropy do not distinguish effective reasoning from hallucination or degeneration, so high entropy can create an illusion of diversity rather than valuable exploration.
AI.method: Effective Entropy quantifies diversity exclusively within the valid subspace and filters out incorrect trajectories. VEPO incorporates it directly into RLVR training, inducing an adaptive attraction dynamic that raises the probability of under-explored valid trajectories.
AI.result: Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks with 1.5B and 7B DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen models, VEPO shows consistent aggregate accuracy gains over GRPO and competitive repeated-sampling success. With matched correct counts on MATH500 it finds more distinct strategies, supported by paired statistical tests and three-seed comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Validity-aware entropy gives a more meaningful measure of exploration diversity for RLVR than blind entropy metrics.

title: Selective State-Space Neural Tucker Factorization for Temporal-aware Traffic Imputation
summary: Spatiotemporal traffic data imputation is a key task of intelligent transportation systems (ITS), and urban traffic data inherently exhibits strong long-term temporal dependencies. Therefore, accurate modeling of these long-term temporal dynamics is the core prerequisite for high fidelity traffic data imputation. However, existing traffic data imputation methods still suffer from inherent limitations in long-sequence modeling, such as gradient vanishing, low efficiency, and insufficient capability to capture long-range temporal correlations. To address these issues, this paper proposes a Selective State Space Neural Tucker Factorization model (S3NTF) for robust traffic data imputation. This model combines the Selective State Space mechanism with Neural Tucker Factorization to capture complex spatial correlations and long-term temporal dynamics. A state space-based time encoder is proposed to effectively extracts long sequence dependencies with linear complexity, while the latent spatiotemporal feature interaction learning module models high-order cross modal interactions based on Tucker decomposition. Extensive experiments on six real traffic datasets have shown that our model outperforms existing models in terms of accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes S3NTF, which combines a selective state space time encoder with Neural Tucker Factorization for spatiotemporal traffic data imputation. It reports better accuracy than existing models on six real traffic datasets.
AI.motivation: Traffic imputation depends on modeling long-term temporal dependencies, but existing methods suffer from gradient vanishing, low efficiency and limited capacity for long-range temporal correlations.
AI.method: A state-space-based time encoder extracts long sequence dependencies with linear complexity, while a latent spatiotemporal feature interaction module models high-order cross-modal interactions based on Tucker decomposition, together capturing spatial correlations and long-term dynamics.
AI.result: Experiments on six real traffic datasets show that the model outperforms existing models in accuracy. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Combining selective state space modeling with Tucker-based factorization is presented as a robust approach to traffic data imputation.
