title: One Hierarchy, Many Sports: Hierarchy-Aligned Multi-Task Learning for Next-Shot Prediction
summary: Next-shot prediction in racket sports requires learning from event data with different match structures, recorded attributes, and label vocabularies. Table tennis, badminton, and tennis nevertheless share a hierarchy in which shots form rallies and rallies form higher scoring units. We present MT-HTA, a hierarchy-aligned multi-task Transformer that uses this structure to jointly predict the attributes of the next shot. A temporal Transformer captures event progression, a feature-token path models interactions among semantic fields rather than along the time axis, and task-specific attention retrieves information from hierarchical summaries and player context. The architecture supports three- and four-level hierarchies and sport-dependent task sets. Across four datasets from three sports, the final MT-HTA achieves the highest mean task-averaged F1 among the compared main models. Ablations on table tennis support the combination of hierarchical encoding, task attention, and feature-token interaction. Additional modules alter the balance between classification scores and spatial error rather than improving every metric. These results support a reusable architecture for heterogeneous racket-sport event data. We release the code for reproducibility. this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MT-HTA, a hierarchy-aligned multi-task Transformer that jointly predicts the attributes of the next shot in table tennis, badminton and tennis using their shared shot-rally-score hierarchy. It reports the highest mean task-averaged F1 among the compared main models across four datasets from three sports.
AI.motivation: Next-shot prediction in racket sports must handle event data with different match structures, recorded attributes and label vocabularies, although the three sports share a hierarchy in which shots form rallies and rallies form higher scoring units.
AI.method: A temporal Transformer captures event progression, a feature-token path models interactions among semantic fields rather than along time, and task-specific attention retrieves information from hierarchical summaries and player context. The architecture supports three- and four-level hierarchies and sport-dependent task sets.
AI.result: Across four datasets from three sports, the final MT-HTA achieves the highest mean task-averaged F1 among compared main models. Ablations on table tennis support hierarchical encoding, task attention and feature-token interaction, and some additional modules trade classification scores against spatial error.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchy-aligned architecture offers a reusable design for heterogeneous racket-sport event data.

title: What Conformal Selection Can Certify in CRISPR Off-Target Design:Benchmark Leakage, Free Baselines, and a Finite-Sample Cohort Requirement
summary: Conformal selection promises distribution-free, finite-sample control of the error rate of a decision, and has been proposed as a safety layer for machine-learning CRISPR guide design. We ask whether such a certificate is attainable from the validated off-target data that exist. The constraint is arithmetic: a conformal p-value cannot fall below one divided by the calibration cohort size plus one, so a Benjamini-Hochberg selection certifies a single candidate only when that cohort is at least the candidate pool size divided by the tolerated error rate. Public cohorts supply ten validated guides, whereas a pool of two thousand at a ten percent error rate needs twenty thousand; the accepted set is consequently empty in over ninety-six percent of splits. Two benchmarking findings explain why this went unnoticed. The standard CIRCLE-seq file lists ten guides under eighty on-target strings, so grouping cross-validation on the sequence column trains and tests on one guide; corrected, pair-level discrimination and per-guide fidelity collapse. With that leakage removed, a training-free position-weight score and a bare count of near-match genomic sites are not beaten by a trained oracle. We give the corrected protocol, the baselines a new model must beat, and the cohort size a certified pipeline needs.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that conformal selection cannot certify a single CRISPR off-target candidate on the available validated data, because the calibration cohort is too small. It also finds that grouped cross-validation on the standard CIRCLE-seq file leaks guides across folds, and that a training-free position-weight score and a site-count baseline are not beaten by a trained oracle.
AI.motivation: Conformal selection promises finite-sample error control for ML-based CRISPR guide design, and the question is whether the validated off-target data are large enough to support such a certificate.
AI.method: The authors use the arithmetic bound that a conformal p-value cannot fall below 1/(n+1) for calibration size n, derive the cohort size needed for Benjamini-Hochberg selection, and audit the CIRCLE-seq benchmark for grouping leakage before comparing against training-free baselines.
AI.result: Public cohorts supply ten validated guides, whereas a pool of two thousand at a ten percent error rate needs twenty thousand, so the accepted set is empty in over 96% of splits. The CIRCLE-seq file lists ten guides under eighty on-target strings, and corrected pair-level discrimination and per-guide fidelity collapse after removing the leakage. A training-free position-weight score and a bare count of near-match genomic sites are not beaten by a trained oracle.
AI.conclusion: A certified pipeline would need a much larger validated cohort, and corrected benchmarking should use the training-free baselines a new model must beat.

title: Observations Drift, Structures Remain: Structural Pretraining with Time Alignment for Electromagnetic Signals
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Electromagnetic signal modeling is increasingly moving toward self-supervised pretraining on heterogeneous I/Q observations. However, an observed waveform is jointly shaped by signal generation, propagation environments, and acquisition processes, which mix reusable structural regularities with observation-specific variations. Existing methods usually pursue unified pretraining with reconstruction objectives on mixed observations. This heterogeneity creates two key mismatches for reconstruction pretraining: (1) appearance mismatch, induced by propagation-dependent waveform variations; and (2) temporal mismatch, induced by acquisition-dependent sampling coordinates. These mismatches make observation-specific appearances and sampling coordinates easier to reconstruct than stable signal structures, inducing observational shortcuts. We identify this failure mode as observation-biased pretraining. To address this, we propose Structural Pretraining with Time Alignment for heterogeneous EM signals. It mitigates temporal mismatch with RoPE-fs, which maps token positions to sampling-rate-normalized physical-time positions, and reduces reliance on appearance shortcuts by replacing waveform reconstruction with masked prediction of discrete structural units. These units are organized into atomic structural units and emergent structural units that capture variable-length compositional patterns beyond fixed patch boundaries. Across diverse EM benchmarks, our method improves both full-supervision and few-shot adaptation over existing EM pretraining baselines, showing that the learned representations better preserve structural consistency when observations drift in waveform appearance and temporal scale.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Structural Pretraining with Time Alignment for heterogeneous electromagnetic signals, which uses RoPE-fs for sampling-rate-normalized physical-time positions and replaces waveform reconstruction with masked prediction of discrete structural units. It reports improved full-supervision and few-shot adaptation over existing EM pretraining baselines.
AI.motivation: Reconstruction-based pretraining on heterogeneous I/Q observations suffers from appearance mismatch due to propagation and temporal mismatch due to acquisition sampling, which lead to observation-biased shortcuts instead of stable signal structure.
AI.method: RoPE-fs maps token positions to sampling-rate-normalized physical time, and waveform reconstruction is replaced by masked prediction of discrete structural units, organized into atomic units and emergent units that capture variable-length compositional patterns beyond fixed patch boundaries.
AI.result: Across diverse EM benchmarks the method improves both full-supervision and few-shot adaptation over existing EM pretraining baselines. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: The learned representations better preserve structural consistency when observations drift in waveform appearance and temporal scale.

title: Constructing and Validating Memorisation Audits for EHR Foundation Models
comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Beyond Private Training: The New Landscape of AI Privacy (InfPriv) and the Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026 Symposium, Findings Track
summary: Autoregressive electronic health record (EHR) foundation models may disclose training information at inference, yet clinical predictability makes patient-specific memorisation difficult to distinguish from generalisation. We evaluate fixed-window token reconstruction, sensitive-attribute disclosure, and random patient-level canaries in GPT-2-style models trained on MIMIC-IV, across early, best-validation, and final checkpoints. Reconstruction improves with additional context, but training--held-out differences remain small. Trajectory-unique prompts containing limited clinical information produce no excess sensitive disclosure for training patients. In a matched model with random binary patient-level canaries, training-patient label-recovery AUROC increases from 0.512 to 0.549 while held-out recovery remains at chance. An overfit 1,000-patient positive control achieves near-perfect recovery, confirming sensitivity to strong memorisation. These results reveal weak cohort-level memorisation but no reliable patient-level disclosure under the evaluated attacks. They motivate clinically grounded inference-time audits that can detect patient-specific memorisation in existing models without retraining with canaries.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether GPT-2-style autoregressive EHR foundation models trained on MIMIC-IV disclose patient-specific training information, using reconstruction, sensitive-attribute and canary-based audits. It finds weak cohort-level memorization but no reliable patient-level disclosure under the evaluated attacks.
AI.motivation: Clinical predictability makes patient-specific memorization hard to tell apart from generalization, so it is unclear whether these models disclose training information at inference.
AI.method: Fixed-window token reconstruction, sensitive-attribute disclosure and random patient-level binary canaries are evaluated across early, best-validation and final checkpoints. A matched model with canaries and a 1,000-patient overfit positive control are used as references.
AI.result: Reconstruction improves with more context but training-held-out differences remain small, and trajectory-unique prompts produce no excess sensitive disclosure for training patients. With canaries, training-patient label-recovery AUROC rises from 0.512 to 0.549 while held-out recovery stays at chance. The overfit positive control achieves near-perfect recovery.
AI.conclusion: The models show weak cohort-level memorization but no reliable patient-level disclosure, and inference-time audits can be used without retraining with canaries.

title: AI4Plasma II: Geometry-Aware Surrogate Modeling for Variable Electrode Gap GEC Plasmas
comment: 29 pages, 13 figures, 11 tables
summary: Industrial plasma process development requires broad exploration of operating and geometric parameters. Geometric parameters, particularly electrode spacing, affect discharge structure and processing uniformity. Exploring these parameter spaces through repeated high-fidelity simulations can be computationally expensive. Surrogate models can offer rapid predictions, but geometric variation complicates their application because the computational domain and discretization may change across samples. In this work, six geometry-aware surrogate models based on prescribed and learned geometry mappings, extended-domain representation, continuous coordinates, and geometry-native discretizations are compared in terms of their data requirements for accurate predictions of full plasma fields and ion density profiles near the wafer. The simulation dataset spans pressure, voltage, frequency, and electrode gap, with each reference case requiring an average simulation cost of 5.32 CPU h. To achieve a 2% mean error across the four plasma fields, prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO and Transolver require 100 training cases, compared with 250-1000 for the other models. Predicting ion density profiles near the wafer is more demanding and reveals larger differences among models, with prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO requiring the fewest training cases for the profile accuracy targets considered. To further reduce the data required for accurate predictions near the wafer, we introduce charge-separation weighting into the training loss, which reduces the prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO's minimum tested training requirement for a 5% profile error from 1000 to 100 cases. These results support prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO as a practical starting point for the variable-gap problem studied here when a suitable geometry mapping is available, while Transolver achieves the highest prediction accuracy with sufficient training data.

AI.tldr: The paper compares six geometry-aware surrogate models for plasma fields in GEC chambers with variable electrode gap, by their training-data requirements. Prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO and Transolver need 100 training cases for a 2% mean error, and charge-separation weighting reduces the Geo-FNO requirement for a 5% profile error from 1000 to 100 cases.
AI.motivation: Industrial plasma process development needs exploration of geometric parameters such as electrode spacing, but geometric variation changes the computational domain and discretization, which complicates surrogate modeling and high-fidelity simulations are expensive.
AI.method: Six geometry-aware surrogates based on prescribed and learned geometry mappings, extended-domain representation, continuous coordinates and geometry-native discretizations are compared, and a charge-separation weighting is added to the training loss. The dataset spans pressure, voltage, frequency and electrode gap, with an average of 5.32 CPU hours per reference case.
AI.result: For a 2% mean error across four plasma fields, prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO and Transolver need 100 training cases, versus 250-1000 for the other models. For ion density near the wafer, prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO needs the fewest cases, and charge-separation weighting cuts its requirement for a 5% profile error from 1000 to 100 cases.
AI.conclusion: Prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO is a practical starting point when a suitable geometry mapping exists, while Transolver gives the highest accuracy given enough training data.

title: Imputing Missing Near-Surface Air Temperature using Graph Attention Networks with Distance-Aware Edge Features
comment: 23 pages, 7 figures; LaTeX
summary: We introduce a graph attention network for reconstructing near-surface air temperature fields from incomplete observations. The model represents each grid cell as a node connected to its $k$ nearest neighbors, with attention weights that depend on node features, distance, and land-ocean transitions. This graph representation avoids the polar distortions associated with treating the globe as a flat latitude-longitude image, as most deep learning reconstruction methods do. This is particularly relevant for historical temperature records, which extend back to the mid-nineteenth century but remain incomplete, with the largest gaps early in the record and at high latitudes. We train our model on CMIP6 CESM2 historical simulations masked with the time-varying HadCRUT5 observational coverage from 1850 to 2014. We then compare our approach with ordinary kriging, GraphEM, and the LaMa inpainting network on a held-out realization. The graph model achieves the lowest spatial RMSE (0.997 K), 10.1% lower than LaMa and approximately 31% lower than kriging and GraphEM. The largest gains occur in the Arctic and Antarctic, while LaMa remains slightly more accurate in the densely observed tropics. The graph model's error also falls faster as coverage increases, so its advantage over LaMa grows by more than a third from the 1850s to the 2000s. An ablation study shows that the model's skill comes mainly from the geometric graph construction rather than from auxiliary physical covariates.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a graph attention network that reconstructs near-surface air temperature fields from incomplete observations by connecting each grid cell to its k nearest neighbors with distance- and land-ocean-aware edge features. On a held-out CMIP6 CESM2 realization it reaches the lowest spatial RMSE, 0.997 K, about 10.1% below LaMa and about 31% below kriging and GraphEM.
AI.motivation: Historical temperature records are incomplete, especially early in the record and at high latitudes, and most deep learning reconstruction methods treat the globe as a flat latitude-longitude image, which introduces polar distortions.
AI.method: Each grid cell is a node connected to its k nearest neighbors, with attention weights depending on node features, distance and land-ocean transitions. The model is trained on CMIP6 CESM2 historical simulations masked with time-varying HadCRUT5 coverage from 1850 to 2014 and is compared with ordinary kriging, GraphEM and the LaMa inpainting network.
AI.result: The graph model reaches spatial RMSE of 0.997 K, 10.1% lower than LaMa and about 31% lower than kriging and GraphEM. Gains are largest in the Arctic and Antarctic, while LaMa is slightly more accurate in the densely observed tropics. Its advantage over LaMa grows by more than a third from the 1850s to the 2000s, and an ablation shows that most of the skill comes from the geometric graph construction.
AI.conclusion: Geometric graph construction is an effective alternative to image-based inpainting for reconstructing historical temperature fields, especially at high latitudes.

title: GLCR: Global-Local Collaborative Routing for Multi-Task Electromagnetic Signal Processing
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables. Code available at this https URL
summary: Deep neural networks for electromagnetic signal processing are typically developed as single-task experts with fixed inputs and objectives, limiting cross-task transferability. Electromagnetic foundation models offer broader task coverage but incur substantial pretraining and inference costs. To balance accuracy and efficiency, we adopt model routing to dynamically dispatch unknown signals to matched experts within a heterogeneous pool. We construct HeteroSignal-7, a multi-task routing benchmark with 140,000 samples from seven datasets covering six task types, paired with seven classification and waveform-recovery experts and a unified evaluation protocol. We then propose GLCR, a two-stage routing method combining global dispatch with local discrimination of similar tasks. First, a lightweight one-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN) with an additive-margin head predicts one of seven routing classes. Second, a gradient-boosted-tree specialist uses four physical statistics to re-evaluate samples whose top two candidates match a confusion pair automatically identified from validation errors. The pipeline is trained across the full signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) range and requires neither SNR labels nor noise estimation at inference time. GLCR outperforms all 19 baselines, achieving 96.16% routing accuracy and a 76.30% system score, exceeding the respective second-best baselines by 1.16% and 1.14%. It achieves the lowest routing latency among the compared methods at 1.43 ms per sample and reduces expected overall system FLOPs by 5.9 times compared with executing all experts. This work provides a public evaluation platform and an efficient, reproducible baseline for heterogeneous expert routing in electromagnetic signal processing.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GLCR, a two-stage routing method that dispatches unknown electromagnetic signals to matched experts, combining a 1D CNN for global routing with a gradient-boosted-tree specialist for confusable tasks. It reports 96.16% routing accuracy and a 76.30% system score, and a 5.9-fold reduction in expected system FLOPs compared with running all experts.
AI.motivation: Single-task EM signal processing experts do not transfer across tasks, and EM foundation models incur high pretraining and inference costs, so model routing over a heterogeneous expert pool is proposed as a balance between accuracy and efficiency.
AI.method: A lightweight 1D CNN with an additive-margin head predicts one of seven routing classes. For samples whose top two candidates match a confusion pair identified from validation errors, a gradient-boosted-tree specialist uses four physical statistics to re-evaluate them. The method needs neither SNR labels nor noise estimation at inference.
AI.result: GLCR outperforms all 19 baselines, achieving 96.16% routing accuracy and 76.30% system score, exceeding the second-best baselines by 1.16% and 1.14%. It has the lowest routing latency among compared methods at 1.43 ms per sample and reduces expected overall system FLOPs by 5.9 times compared with executing all experts.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a public evaluation platform, HeteroSignal-7 with 140,000 samples, and an efficient, reproducible routing baseline for heterogeneous EM expert pools.

title: A Mechanistic Interpretability Study of an Astronomy Foundation Model
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. A condensed version was selected for an oral presentation at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpretability for Discovery
summary: Foundation models are increasingly used across the sciences, but whether their internal computations correspond to known scientific operations or proceed through different mechanisms remains unclear. Understanding these mechanisms is essential for assessing reliability, identifying failure modes, and learning new science from the models. We present, to our knowledge, the first causal mechanistic interpretability study of an astronomy foundation model, AION-1, focusing on its multimodal advantage in redshift prediction, where combining imaging with photometry outperforms photometry alone. We find that this advantage is largest for spatially extended and dust-attenuated galaxies, and that most of it is localized to the first of the encoder's twelve blocks. Within that block, how well a property is linearly decodable does not predict whether it can be localized. Spatial extent is causally used, and one attention head dominates linear probing for it, yet ablating that head has negligible effect on redshift prediction: the information is distributed across heads and is decodable again one layer after we erase it. Dust attenuation shows the opposite pattern: it is only weakly decodable anywhere in the encoder, yet a single head is necessary for most of the multimodal advantage, particularly for the most dust-attenuated galaxies, and keeping that head as the only active head in its block preserves nearly all of the advantage. None of the astrophysically motivated operations we tested explains what this head computes. Whether this reflects a limitation of current interpretability methods or a computation that does not correspond to any known astrophysical operation remains open, and resolving it is a prerequisite for using interpretability as a tool for scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a causal mechanistic interpretability study of the AION-1 astronomy foundation model, examining how it gains from combining imaging with photometry for redshift prediction. The multimodal advantage is largest for extended and dust-attenuated galaxies, and is partly localized to a single attention head that the authors could not explain with astrophysical operations.
AI.motivation: Whether foundation models in science use internal computations that correspond to known scientific operations, or other mechanisms, is unclear, and this matters for reliability, failure modes and scientific discovery.
AI.method: Causal interventions, such as ablations and linear probing, are applied to the encoder's twelve blocks to find where the multimodal advantage in redshift prediction is localized, and the authors test whether astrophysically motivated operations explain the heads' computations.
AI.result: Most of the multimodal advantage is localized to the first encoder block. Spatial extent is causally used and one head dominates linear probing for it, yet ablating that head has negligible effect because the information is distributed and decodable again one layer later. For dust attenuation, a single head is necessary for most of the advantage, and keeping only that head active in its block preserves nearly all of it.
AI.conclusion: None of the astrophysically motivated operations tested explains the dust-related head, and whether this reflects a limit of current interpretability methods or a computation with no known astrophysical counterpart remains open.

title: Beyond Reweighting: Certified Improvements from New Transitions in Discrete MCMC
comment: 43 pages, 9 figures
summary: Optimizing transition probabilities on a fixed grap may leave substantial limitations on the efficiency of reversible Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). We develop a framework for transition-support design that considers both allowed transitions and their stationary flows. For a fixed target distribution, observable, and node-flow budget, we derive a necessary and sufficient dual condition for support augmentation to strictly reduce the optimal value of the asymptotic variance, together with computable primal--dual certificates that establish improvements over every admissible original-support reweighting. We also construct a family in which adding a single edge reduces integrated autocorrelation time by an $\Omega(n)$ factor relative to optimal original-support weighting, demonstrating that structural limitations can impose arbitrarily large relative losses in estimation efficiency. To realize these gains, we investigate energy-informed edge selection and constrained stationary-flow optimization. Experiments on molecular and Ising state graphs distinguish the potential value of new transitions from the performance of kernels constructed on them: on identical augmented Ising supports, full weight optimization certifies strict improvements in 24/24 conditions, whereas degree-based Metropolis--Hastings weighting certifies none. Our results provide a principled approach to characterizing, certifying, and exploiting transition-support improvements in explicitly represented finite state spaces.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a framework for transition-support design in reversible MCMC, giving a necessary and sufficient dual condition under which adding transitions strictly reduces asymptotic variance. It shows that adding one edge can reduce integrated autocorrelation time by a factor of Omega(n) relative to optimal reweighting on the original support.
AI.motivation: Optimizing transition probabilities on a fixed graph may leave substantial efficiency limits, so the question is when enlarging the set of allowed transitions yields gains that reweighting cannot achieve.
AI.method: For a fixed target, observable and node-flow budget, the authors derive a dual condition and computable primal-dual certificates for support augmentation. They investigate energy-informed edge selection and constrained stationary-flow optimization on molecular and Ising state graphs.
AI.result: On identical augmented Ising supports, full weight optimization certifies strict improvements in 24 of 24 conditions, whereas degree-based Metropolis-Hastings weighting certifies none. A constructed family shows that a single added edge can reduce integrated autocorrelation time by an Omega(n) factor.
AI.conclusion: Characterizing and certifying transition-support improvements can yield substantial efficiency gains, and the choice of weights on new transitions matters as much as the transitions themselves.

title: The Noise Floor of a Quantization Comparison: Engine, restart, batch and kernel drift, measured against 8-bit and 4-bit effects in two decision models
comment: 21 pages, 1 figure. Code and data: this https URL
summary: A quantized model is usually judged by comparing it with its BF16 original, but that comparison changes more than the weights. It often changes the serving engine, it always runs on a different server instance, it may change how requests are batched, and on some stacks the library selects a different kernel depending only on which packages import. We measure each of these sources on the same 2,400 public decisions for two of Cloudflare's decision models, Clef-flash (9B) and Clef (27B), on an NVIDIA GB10, and state every quantization effect as the excess over them. Sources that are not quantization move between 0 and 0.92% of decisions. this http URL restarts are bit-identical on every record for both models. vLLM restarts flip 0, 5 and 20 decisions at BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 on Clef-flash and 4, 0 and 22 on Clef; a third instance of Clef's quantized builds (exploratory) leaves FP8 at 0 and puts NVFP4 at 4 to 22, depending on which two instances are compared. An engine change at BF16 flips 6 to 16, a batch-size change 8 to 15, and the Gated DeltaNet kernel transformers selects unasked 10 to 14. Quantization inside one engine moves more: for Clef-flash and Clef, 0.88% and 1.04% at Q8_0, 2.12% and 1.62% at FP8, 5.79% and 3.50% at Q4_K_M, and 5.79% and 5.67% at NVFP4. On both models, every 4-bit interval excludes every non-quantization source. Two of our five pre-registered predictions failed, and the same two fail when the tests are rerun on the 27B: FP8 is not inside restart noise, and changing engine moves fewer decisions than 8-bit quantization does. Accuracy hides most of this. Over the full 31,275 public questions, Clef's Q4_K_M build moves accuracy by a net six questions (-0.02 points [-0.20, +0.16]) while 436 of its decisions get worse (exploratory), and NVFP4 costs Clef-flash 0.95 points and Clef 0.65. We release the code, quantization recipes, per-record outputs and the pre-registration.

AI.tldr: The paper measures the noise floor of comparing a quantized LLM with its BF16 original, separating non-quantization sources such as engine, restart, batch size and kernel changes from quantization effects in two Cloudflare decision models, Clef-flash (9B) and Clef (27B). Non-quantization sources flip 0 to 0.92% of decisions, while 4-bit quantization flips 3.50% to 5.79%.
AI.motivation: A quantized model is usually compared with its BF16 original, but that comparison also changes the serving engine, server instance, batching and sometimes the kernel selected by the library, so the measured difference may not reflect quantization alone.
AI.method: The same 2,400 public decisions for each model are run on an NVIDIA GB10, with each non-quantization source measured and each quantization effect reported as the excess over those sources. Five pre-registered predictions are tested, and accuracy is checked over 31,275 public questions.
AI.result: vLLM restarts flip 0, 5 and 20 decisions at BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 on Clef-flash, and 4, 0 and 22 on Clef. Engine change at BF16 flips 6 to 16 decisions and batch-size change 8 to 15. Quantization flips 0.88% and 1.04% at Q8_0, 2.12% and 1.62% at FP8, 5.79% and 3.50% at Q4_K_M, and 5.79% and 5.67% at NVFP4 for Clef-flash and Clef. Two of five pre-registered predictions failed. NVFP4 costs Clef-flash 0.95 accuracy points and Clef 0.65.
AI.conclusion: Every 4-bit effect exceeds every non-quantization source, though FP8 falls within restart noise and per-decision changes can hide accuracy-neutral shifts, so accuracy alone understates quantization effects.

title: SpaceMCP: Vision Language Model Spatial Reasoning via Model Context Protocol
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the 2nd Workshop on Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Despite impressive advances in large language models (LLM), vision-language models (VLM) still exhibit limited spatial reasoning capabilities. Recent progress in feed-forward 3D reconstruction has enabled precise, real-time geometric understanding from visual inputs. In this work, we propose SpaceMCP, a framework that leverages these advances to introduce an MCP-style paradigm for spatial reasoning. Our approach augments a VLM with structured function calls, allowing it to query a scene graph for spatial information such as distances, object positioning, and camera properties. The scene graph is constructed in real time using feed-forward 3D reconstruction to recover metric geometry, combined with open-vocabulary segmentation to identify and localize relevant objects within the scene. Paired with the VLM's strong reasoning capabilities, the VLM is able to combine this primitive information to solve more complex spatial tasks. Without any training, SpaceMCP achieves state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench and VSTI-Bench, outperforming recent spatially post-trained VLMs and improving its base VLM by 15-22 points per benchmark. We argue that, given the contrast between the relatively slow progress in native VLM spatial reasoning and the rapid advances in feed-forward 3D computer vision, this paradigm offers a promising path forward for enabling robust spatial reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SpaceMCP, which augments a vision-language model with structured function calls that query a real-time scene graph built from feed-forward 3D reconstruction and open-vocabulary segmentation. Without training, it reports state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench and VSTI-Bench, improving its base VLM by 15-22 points per benchmark.
AI.motivation: VLMs still show limited spatial reasoning, while feed-forward 3D reconstruction now provides real-time metric geometry, and the paper asks whether this can be exploited through an MCP-style interface.
AI.method: The VLM calls functions that query a scene graph for distances, object positions and camera properties. The scene graph is built in real time from feed-forward 3D reconstruction for metric geometry and open-vocabulary segmentation for localizing objects, and the VLM combines these primitives to solve complex spatial tasks.
AI.result: Without any training, SpaceMCP achieves state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench and VSTI-Bench, outperforming recent spatially post-trained VLMs and improving its base VLM by 15-22 points per benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Combining fast 3D reconstruction with VLM reasoning through structured tool calls is a promising path to robust spatial reasoning, given the faster progress of 3D vision.

title: Characterizing Predictive Multiplicity in Ranking and Its Fairness Implications
comment: 32 pages, 6 figures
summary: Prediction problems often admit competing models that achieve comparable performance yet produce conflicting outputs, a phenomenon known as predictive multiplicity. While this challenge has been extensively studied in classification tasks, its implications remain largely unexplored in ranking frameworks, which are critical for high-stakes societal decisions such as the allocation of welfare resources and social assistance. This paper investigates the phenomenon of predictive multiplicity in score-based ranking problems. We introduce formal definitions to capture multiplicity in ranking settings, supported by foundational theoretical guarantees. Furthermore, we examine the dual relationship between predictive multiplicity and algorithmic fairness in ranking problems: we analyze how model multiplicity can act as a potential source of unfairness, while demonstrating how exploring this decision space provides a principled avenue for discovering less discriminatory rankings. Finally, we complement our theoretical contributions with insightful empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets, validating our analytical findings and illustrating their practical implications. Taken together, this work highlights the real-world relevance of predictive multiplicity in ranking and sheds light on the potential of leveraging this effect to achieve fairer outcomes.

AI.tldr: The paper studies predictive multiplicity in score-based ranking, where competing models with similar performance produce conflicting rankings, and shows how this multiplicity relates to ranking fairness.
AI.motivation: Predictive multiplicity has been studied for classification but not for ranking, even though rankings drive high-stakes decisions such as welfare and social assistance allocation.
AI.method: The authors give formal definitions of multiplicity for ranking, prove foundational theoretical guarantees, and analyze how multiplicity can cause unfairness while exploring the set of near-optimal models to find less discriminatory rankings.
AI.result: Theoretical results are complemented by empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets that validate the analytical findings.
AI.conclusion: Predictive multiplicity matters for ranking, and exploring the space of equally good models offers a principled route to fairer ranking outcomes.

title: Orbit: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on IT Operations Reasoning
summary: LLMs now support IT operations (ITOps), but benchmarks rarely show why a model fails. We present ORBIT, a benchmark of ITOps questions in three formats, namely multiple-choice, open-ended, and troubleshooting, with each question accompanied by a reference answer and a recorded source. An audit found template defects in about a tenth of the generated items, so we drop them and rebuild the troubleshooting format from real practitioner threads with accepted answers. Under one independent judge, five LLMs answer most multiple-choice items correctly, between a third and just over half of the open-ended items, and a minority of the troubleshooting items, even under a more lenient root-cause rubric. When models judged their own answers, they accepted many answers to defective items, so we use one independent judge for every model. Word overlap with the question finds the correct option for more than half of the multiple-choice items. ORBIT is a diagnostic aid for selecting and supervising assistants rather than a deployment test.

AI.tldr: ORBIT is a benchmark of IT operations questions in multiple-choice, open-ended, and troubleshooting formats, each with a reference answer and recorded source, used to evaluate LLMs with one independent judge.
AI.motivation: Existing IT operations (ITOps) benchmarks rarely show why a model fails, and self-judged evaluation is unreliable.
AI.method: The authors audit generated items, drop those with template defects, rebuild the troubleshooting format from real practitioner threads with accepted answers, and score every model with a single independent judge.
AI.result: Under the independent judge, five LLMs answer most multiple-choice items correctly, between one third and just over half of open-ended items, and a minority of troubleshooting items. Models accepted many answers to defective items when judging themselves, and word overlap with the question alone finds the correct option for more than half of multiple-choice items.
AI.conclusion: ORBIT is a diagnostic aid for selecting and supervising assistants rather than a deployment test.

title: Sensitivity-Aware Surrogate Modeling with Random Feature Expansions
summary: Random feature expansions (RFEs) provide a flexible approach to surrogate modeling, but their accuracy depends on the distribution used to sample features. We propose spike-and-slab random feature expansions (SAS-RFE) to learn the feature sampling distribution from sensitivity analysis. The method employs a spike-and-slab distribution that assigns probabilities to the inclusion of individual inputs in randomly sampled Fourier features. These inclusion probabilities are determined by estimates of total Sobol' sensitivity indices, rather than by explicitly selecting important inputs or interaction terms. An information theoretic criterion shows that the total Sobol' indices yield a distribution that approximates the input interaction structure of the model. An iterative algorithm updates the sampling probabilities using sensitivity estimates from successive RFE surrogates. Analytical formulas for the Sobol' indices of random Fourier feature expansions enable these updates without additional evaluations of the target function. Numerical experiments on six benchmark problems, with up to 100 input dimensions, demonstrate improvements in surrogate approximation and sensitivity estimation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes spike-and-slab random feature expansions (SAS-RFE), which learn the feature sampling distribution for surrogate models from estimated total Sobol' sensitivity indices.
AI.motivation: The accuracy of random feature expansion surrogates depends on the sampling distribution of the features, which is usually not tuned to the model's input structure.
AI.method: Inclusion probabilities of inputs in Fourier features follow a spike-and-slab distribution set by total Sobol' indices; an iterative algorithm updates these probabilities using analytical Sobol' index formulas for random Fourier features, requiring no extra target evaluations.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on six benchmark problems with up to 100 input dimensions show improved surrogate approximation and sensitivity estimation.
AI.conclusion: Learning the sampling distribution from sensitivity analysis gives a more accurate and efficient random feature surrogate, supported by an information-theoretic argument that total Sobol' indices approximate the model's interaction structure.

title: SAME: Semantic Watermark Embedding for Open-Source Large Pretrained Models
summary: Open-source large pretrained models (LPMs) have become increasingly valuable assets for model development and downstream applications, but their accessibility also facilitates unauthorised copying and modification. To protect their intellectual property (IP), existing approaches typically embed tailored trigger-response patterns as watermarks for ownership verification. However, such trigger designs need to be tailored to task-specific data that constrain their transferability across downstream tasks, and are not durable under subsequent benign fine-tuning. To address these limitations, we propose SemAntic waterMark Embedding (SAME), which introduces a semantically meaningful private vocabulary that enables flexible composition of adaptive and persistent watermarks. Specifically, SAME introduces a fixed private vocabulary that assigns each native token a private embedding counterpart, while aligning the semantic expressiveness of the two vocabularies within the model's representation space. This alignment allows private tokens to be flexibly composed into semantic triggers that elicit meaningful responses, enabling adaptive watermarks beyond predefined trigger-response pairs. By grounding the private vocabulary in the model's native semantics, SAME couples the watermark with its evolving semantic capabilities, allowing this connection to be preserved throughout downstream fine-tuning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAME provides reliable and robust watermarks across LPMs of varying scales and architectures, enabling effective ownership verification for IP protection.

AI.tldr: SAME embeds a semantically meaningful private vocabulary in open-source large pretrained models to create adaptive, persistent watermarks for ownership verification.
AI.motivation: Existing trigger-response watermarks are tied to task-specific data, do not transfer well across downstream tasks, and are not durable under benign fine-tuning.
AI.method: SAME assigns each native token a private embedding counterpart and aligns the two vocabularies in the model's representation space, so private tokens compose into semantic triggers that elicit meaningful responses.
AI.result: Experiments across large pretrained models of varying scales and architectures show reliable and robust watermarks that enable ownership verification.
AI.conclusion: Grounding the watermark in the model's native semantics keeps it linked to the model's capabilities through downstream fine-tuning, giving effective intellectual property protection.

title: Sparse PCA with Overlapping Supports: NP-Hardness and an FPTAS
summary: In sparse principal component analysis (SPCA) with several components, each must be sparse and all must be pairwise orthogonal. When the supports of the components overlap, these two requirements interact. For a covariance matrix of fixed rank, polynomial-time algorithms with optimality or approximation guarantees are known for one component, and for several components with disjoint supports or with a common support. We study the general model, with individual sparsity constants and arbitrary support overlaps. We are given a rational $n\times r$ matrix $R$ and $d$ sparsity constants $s_i \le n$, and the goal is to find an $n\times d$ matrix $X$ with orthonormal columns that maximizes $\|R^\top X\|_F^2$, such that column $i$ has at most $s_i$ non-zero entries. Here $RR^\top$ plays the role of the covariance matrix and has rank at most $r$. We show that SPCA is NP-hard even when $r = d = 2$, but admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) when $r$ and $d$ are fixed. The returned solution has exactly orthonormal columns, and its entries are real algebraic numbers in an exact representation. For fixed $\epsilon$, the number of steps of the algorithm is linear in $n$ up to a polylogarithmic factor. Our approach reduces SPCA to a sparse version of the orthogonal Procrustes problem, that is, to maximizing a linear function over the feasible region of SPCA. We show that this problem is NP-hard even for $d = 2$, and we give an FPTAS for it when $d$ is fixed. This FPTAS combines approximate dynamic programming over the rows, two-column updates that restore exact orthogonality, and an exact computation of the few variables for which these updates are not available.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that sparse PCA with arbitrarily overlapping component supports is NP-hard even for rank 2 and two components, and gives a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) when the rank and number of components are fixed.
AI.motivation: Earlier polynomial-time guarantees for sparse PCA covered only one component, disjoint supports, or a common support, not the general overlapping case.
AI.method: The problem is reduced to a sparse version of the orthogonal Procrustes problem, and the FPTAS combines approximate dynamic programming over rows, two-column updates that restore exact orthogonality, and exact computation of a few variables.
AI.result: The returned solution has exactly orthonormal columns with real algebraic entries, and for fixed epsilon the number of steps is linear in n up to a polylogarithmic factor.
AI.conclusion: The general overlapping case is hard in the worst case, but it admits an efficient approximation scheme when the rank and the number of components are fixed.

title: Fewer Expert Transfers Without Changing Routing: Expert Eviction for MoE Offloading
comment: AXIOM workshop (Foundations of Efficient Deep Learning) at NeurIPS 2026. 11 pages, 2 figures. Code and data: this https URL
summary: A mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model uses only a few experts per token, so a server can keep most expert weights in CPU memory and copy an expert to the GPU when the router requests it. Recent methods train the router to keep the same experts for several tokens, and treat fewer routing switches as a proxy for fewer copies. We measure the trade-off directly, in a harness that performs and times real CPU-to-GPU copies for OLMoE-1B-7B. On an L40S GPU, every tested policy that holds an expert set fixed and decodes faster than the least-recently-used (LRU) cache increases next-token loss by at least 0.067 nats. A change that leaves every routing decision intact does better: when the cache must evict an expert, evict the one whose next use lies farthest in the future. This rule copies 2.1x fewer experts than LRU at no loss in quality and is within 3.5% of the fewest copies possible. It needs future requests; the next sixteen tokens of demand recover 96% of its reduction, whereas a rule based on counts of past requests recovers 27%.

AI.tldr: The paper measures the trade-off between routing stability and expert copies in mixture-of-experts offloading, and shows that Belady-style eviction (evict the expert whose next use is farthest in the future) copies far fewer experts than LRU without changing routing.
AI.motivation: Recent methods train routers to keep the same experts across tokens and treat fewer routing switches as a proxy for fewer CPU-to-GPU expert copies, but this proxy was not measured directly.
AI.method: The authors use a harness that performs and times real CPU-to-GPU copies for OLMoE-1B-7B on an L40S GPU, comparing expert-fixed policies with cache eviction rules, and test a future-aware rule against count-based rules.
AI.result: Every tested policy that holds the expert set fixed and decodes faster than LRU increases next-token loss by at least 0.067 nats. The future-aware rule copies 2.1x fewer experts than LRU at no loss in quality and is within 3.5% of the minimum possible copies. Sixteen tokens of future demand recover 96% of its reduction, versus 27% for a count-based rule.
AI.conclusion: Better eviction that keeps routing decisions intact reduces copies more effectively than changing the router, but the best rule needs future request information.

title: Your Hypergradient is Skewed: Antithetic Neumann Estimation for Bilevel Optimization
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Bilevel optimization is a core tool in practical machine learning workflows, including hyperparameter tuning, data reweighting, robust learning, reinforcement learning, and imbalanced classification. Hypergradient computation requires the inverse of the inner Hessian, typically estimated via a truncated Neumann series. While existing analyses focus on bias and variance, we show that the product structure of the Neumann series introduces a third source of error: skewness. We identify that, unlike ordinary gradients, whose asymmetry is suppressed by mini-batch averaging, the Neumann estimator amplifies skewness across factors, with the third-moment error growing, under weak contraction, with truncation depth, inner condition number, and per-factor noise asymmetry. This arises in many practical settings such as corrupted labels, outliers, heterogeneous or class-imbalanced datasets. To address this, we introduce the Antithetic Neumann Estimator (ANE), which pairs each Hessian sample with a mirrored counterpart around a reference Hessian and averages the resulting inverse-Hessian estimates. With an exact reference, the antithetic product retains only even-order noise, eliminating all odd-order perturbation terms; with an approximate reference, the residual odd-order contribution is bounded linearly in the reference error. ANE requires only a modification of the Hessian vector step and combines with existing stochastic or variance-reduced bilevel methods. We instantiate ANE-SGD and ANE-VR, the latter adding recursive variance reduction. Across robust regression, data cleaning, offline reinforcement learning, and imbalanced classification, ANE-based methods improve on stochastic and variance-reduced baselines on every task (20 seeds each), lowering loss by 4 to 25% relative to the best baseline; the largest gains, on robust regression, are a 25% lower test loss and a 54% higher test r-squared.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies skewness as a third error source in the truncated Neumann series used for hypergradient estimation in bilevel optimization, and proposes the Antithetic Neumann Estimator (ANE) to cancel odd-order error terms.
AI.motivation: Analyses of Neumann-based hypergradient estimators focus on bias and variance, but the product structure of the series amplifies skewness, which mini-batch averaging does not suppress.
AI.method: ANE pairs each Hessian sample with a mirrored counterpart around a reference Hessian and averages the inverse-Hessian estimates; the authors instantiate ANE-SGD and ANE-VR, the latter with recursive variance reduction.
AI.result: With an exact reference, all odd-order noise terms vanish; with an approximate reference, the residual is bounded linearly in the reference error. Across robust regression, data cleaning, offline RL, and imbalanced classification (20 seeds each), ANE-based methods lower loss by 4 to 25% relative to the best baseline, with the largest gains on robust regression: 25% lower test loss and 54% higher test r-squared.
AI.conclusion: Correcting the skewness of the Neumann estimator improves bilevel optimization across several tasks and combines with existing stochastic and variance-reduced methods.

title: Owned Edits to a Shared Decision Rule: Learning Private Exceptions as Typed, Gated, Withdrawable Weight Edits
comment: 58 pages, 7 figures. Every reported value is generated from a versioned results ledger (release r8)
summary: Organisations that apply the same published decision rule often hold private evidence that the rule is wrong for their own cases, and will not pool it. We describe a learning mechanism for that setting whose unit of change is an owned edit. The published rule is compiled exactly into a small ReLU network, a structured prior. Each party's learner searches a small typed space of declarations, a few named values such as subject, scope, form and size, and proposes one only when its own records pass a selection-aware evidence gate. The learning is that gated search around the prior. In two analyses registered before they ran, on synthetic data with 20 sampled hidden truths, the learner at 30 records per party was non-inferior, within 2 points, to all seven tuned baselines (a confined gradient learner, Ditto, FedRep, federated averaging, two pooled networks and pooled gradient-boosted trees), scoring 96.6% against 91.7% for the unchanged rule; the same search without the prior or the gate scored 84.0%. In a third registered test, typed edits over a network trained on shared records beat that network alone by 5.4 points and the same edits over the published rule by 3.1. An acceptance body recomputes each edit from its declaration and writes it into units reserved for that party, so by construction an edit changes no decision about any other subject, withdraws exactly, discloses at most log2 of the typed space's size in bits, and can hide nothing beyond its declared values. We report where it loses: truths shared by all parties, relaxations, ten records, a pre-stated gate criterion that failed in both runs, and a language model given the records that decided about as accurately on one draw. On a rule-only base, a table of owned exceptions makes the same decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes learning private exceptions to a shared decision rule as typed, gated, and withdrawable weight edits, so each organisation can correct the rule for its own cases without pooling data.
AI.motivation: Organisations applying the same published rule may hold private evidence that it is wrong for their cases, but will not share that evidence.
AI.method: The published rule is compiled exactly into a small ReLU network that serves as a prior; each party searches a small typed space of declarations and proposes an edit only when its own records pass a selection-aware evidence gate, and an acceptance body recomputes each edit and writes it into units reserved for that party.
AI.result: On synthetic data with 20 hidden truths, the learner with 30 records per party is non-inferior, within 2 points, to seven tuned baselines, scoring 96.6% against 91.7% for the unchanged rule and 84.0% for the same search without the prior or gate. In a third test, typed edits over a shared-record network beat that network alone by 5.4 points and the published rule by 3.1 points. The authors also report failure cases, including a pre-stated gate criterion that failed in both runs.
AI.conclusion: Gated, typed, owned edits allow private corrections to a shared rule that do not change other parties' decisions, can be withdrawn exactly, and reveal limited information, with the stated limitations.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Inventory Control under Regime-Switching Demand: A Controlled Comparison of LSTM, MLP, and (s,S) Policies
summary: Classical inventory policies such as (s,S) are provably optimal under stationary demand but cannot adapt when demand switches between hidden regimes, and memoryless deep reinforcement learning policies, confined to a fixed observation window, cannot maintain a belief over latent demand structure. We ask whether a recurrent policy offers a measurable advantage over both a memoryless policy and a classical baseline under regime-switching demand, and how that advantage scales with supply-chain lead time. We build a custom Gymnasium environment in which daily demand is generated by a two-state hidden Markov process with Poisson emissions, so that the regime is known at evaluation time but hidden from the agent. An optimised (s,S) heuristic, an MLP PPO agent, and an LSTM Recurrent PPO agent are trained under matched compute and evaluated at lead times of 0, 3, 6, and 10 days over 30 deterministic episodes each. The recurrent policy outperforms both alternatives at every lead time, and its margin over the MLP widens monotonically with lead time, from parity at lead time 0 to 2.17$\times$ at lead time 10. Principal component analysis of the LSTM hidden state explains the widening gap: the representation shifts from encoding a binary regime indicator at short lead times to encoding multi-step pipeline state at long lead times. Recurrent memory becomes the decisive architectural factor as the credit-assignment horizon lengthens.

AI.tldr: The paper compares an LSTM recurrent PPO policy, an MLP PPO policy, and an optimised (s,S) heuristic for inventory control under hidden two-state regime-switching Poisson demand across several lead times.
AI.motivation: Classical (s,S) policies are optimal only under stationary demand and memoryless deep RL policies cannot maintain a belief over latent demand regimes, so the value of recurrent memory is unclear.
AI.method: The authors build a custom Gymnasium environment with a hidden Markov demand process and Poisson emissions, train all three policies under matched compute, and evaluate them at lead times of 0, 3, 6, and 10 days over 30 deterministic episodes each, with PCA of the LSTM hidden state.
AI.result: The recurrent policy outperforms both alternatives at every lead time. Its margin over the MLP widens monotonically with lead time, from parity at lead time 0 to 2.17x at lead time 10. PCA shows the LSTM state shifts from encoding the regime indicator to encoding multi-step pipeline state.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent memory becomes the decisive architectural factor as the credit-assignment horizon grows with supply-chain lead time.

title: Riordan Arrays as Structured Operators for Artificial Intelligence
summary: Riordan arrays have traditionally been studied as infinite lower-triangular matrices that encode generating-function transformations and combinatorial relationships. This note proposes a complementary direction: using Riordan arrays as structured operators in artificial intelligence and data analysis. For a data sequence with generating function $A(z)$, a Riordan array $(g(z),f(z))$ produces the transformation \[ A(z)\longmapsto g(z)A(f(z)). \] This yields a parameterized family of causal linear operators that combine convolution, substitution, and multiscale mixing. The resulting structure may support parameter-efficient neural-network layers, variable-length sequence models, interpretable recurrent systems, invertible architectures, and models for hierarchical or recursively generated data. We explain what the infinite-dimensional viewpoint does and does not provide, outline several possible architectures, identify theoretical and numerical challenges, and propose an initial experimental program. The aim is not to claim that Riordan arrays are appropriate for all data, but to identify settings in which their algebraic structure supplies a useful inductive bias.

AI.tldr: The note proposes Riordan arrays as structured causal linear operators for AI and data analysis, transforming a generating function A(z) into g(z)A(f(z)) to combine convolution, substitution, and multiscale mixing.
AI.motivation: Riordan arrays are usually studied as combinatorial infinite lower-triangular matrices, and their use as operators in neural and sequence models has not been explored.
AI.method: The paper frames Riordan arrays as parameterized operators, explains what the infinite-dimensional viewpoint does and does not provide, and outlines candidate architectures and an initial experimental program.
AI.result: No empirical results are reported; the note identifies theoretical and numerical challenges and possible settings for the operators.
AI.conclusion: The algebraic structure may supply a useful inductive bias for parameter-efficient, variable-length, or hierarchical models, but the note does not claim suitability for all data.

title: WELP : Weighted Ensemble in the LooP for committor learning
comment: NeurIPS 2026
summary: Understanding how complex molecular systems transition between metastable states is a central challenge in computational chemistry and biophysics. A key tool for characterizing these transitions is the committor function: the probability that a trajectory initiated from a given configuration reaches one state before another. Because the committor encodes both the progress and the mechanism of a transition, it is an ideal collective variable (CV). Learning it, however, requires sampling the rare transitions it describes. We address this circular dependency with a ``WE-in-the-loop'' framework that couples committor learning with weighted ensemble (WE), an enhanced sampling method that uses a CV to drive transition dynamics. Our framework alternates between the two: WE simulation generates transition data for training a neural network committor with a self-consistent loss, and the learned committor then serves as an improved CV for subsequent WE simulation. Across a two-channel 2D system, alanine dipeptide, and chignolin, our framework consistently outperforms greedy baselines, highlighting the importance of principled exploration. We also curate a public benchmark of empirically determined committor values for alanine dipeptide. Together, the framework and benchmark provide a new method for studying rare transitions in high-dimensional molecular systems and a standard for evaluating committor learning methods.

AI.tldr: WELP couples committor learning with weighted ensemble (WE) sampling in a loop, so that WE generates transition data for a neural committor and the learned committor then drives further WE simulation.
AI.motivation: Learning the committor requires sampling the rare transitions it describes, which creates a circular dependency between the collective variable and the sampling.
AI.method: The framework alternates WE simulation with training a neural network committor using a self-consistent loss, and the learned committor serves as an improved collective variable for the next WE round; the authors also curate a public committor benchmark for alanine dipeptide.
AI.result: Across a two-channel 2D system, alanine dipeptide, and chignolin, the framework consistently outperforms greedy baselines.
AI.conclusion: Principled exploration in the loop provides a method for studying rare transitions in high-dimensional molecular systems and a benchmark for evaluating committor learning.

title: PhysICL: In-Context Learning of Physical Fields on Unstructured Meshes from Procedural Priors
summary: Engineering design studies produce a few tens to a few hundred simulations of one problem, each on its own mesh, and their surrogates are retrained for every study. Tabular foundation models instead infer a new task from its examples in one forward pass, after pretraining on synthetic tasks. We demonstrate the feasibility of in-context learning for physical field prediction on unstructured meshes. A single model, PhysICL, pretrained solely on procedural tasks, predicts fields, with quantiles, directly on each query mesh from labeled simulations, without updating its weights. The same checkpoint accepts variable numbers of context examples, scalar inputs and input fields, and any number of output fields, while mesh size and connectivity can vary within a task. Its procedural prior draws generic laws and boundary-element physical models on morphed 2D and 3D template meshes, evaluated only at the points the model samples, fast enough that tasks generated on the fly by CPU workers keep the GPUs busy throughout pretraining. On five PLAID datasets never seen in pretraining, its field error decreases as the context grows and, from $K = 32$, is below that of the nearest context simulation on every dataset and context draw. It is on par with per-dataset reduced-order models on two of them, behind them where the fields are low-rank. On AhmedML surfaces with a median of 1.1 million nodes, twenty times the largest pretraining mesh, its fixed spatial budgets keep the peak GPU memory at $K = 64$ at 4.27 GiB, against 4.07 GiB on the 6,000-node meshes of 2D\_MSHE. Finally, on 2D\_MSHE, far from the prior, fine-tuning on procedural tasks that reproduce its geometry and loads, without any of its outputs, at a tenth of the pretraining cost, divides the stress error by 2.7.

AI.tldr: PhysICL performs in-context learning for physical field prediction on unstructured meshes, using a model pretrained only on procedural tasks to predict fields from labeled simulations without weight updates.
AI.motivation: Engineering design studies run few tens to hundreds of simulations of one problem on different meshes, and surrogates are retrained for each study, whereas tabular foundation models infer new tasks from examples in a single forward pass.
AI.method: A single model is pretrained on procedural priors built from generic laws and boundary-element physical models on morphed 2D and 3D template meshes, and it predicts fields with quantiles directly on each query mesh from a variable number of context examples.
AI.result: On five unseen PLAID datasets, field error decreases as context grows and, from K = 32, is below that of the nearest context simulation on every dataset and draw. It is on par with per-dataset reduced-order models on two datasets and behind them where fields are low-rank. On AhmedML surfaces with a median of 1.1 million nodes, peak GPU memory at K = 64 is 4.27 GiB, against 4.07 GiB on 6,000-node 2D_MSHE meshes. Fine-tuning on procedural tasks reproducing 2D_MSHE geometry and loads divides the stress error by 2.7 at a tenth of the pretraining cost.
AI.conclusion: Procedural pretraining enables in-context physical field prediction on unstructured meshes with fixed memory budgets, with reduced accuracy where fields are low-rank.

title: Subject-Held-Out Evaluation of Deep Ground Reaction Force Estimators Across Two Laboratories: Leakage and Cross-Laboratory Transfer
comment: 15 pages (9 main + 6 supplementary), 5 figures. Submitted to IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics. Code and run outputs: this https URL
summary: Deep networks that estimate ground reaction forces and centers of pressure from motion-capture markers are validated within one laboratory, in a seldom-stated coordinate frame, and sometimes with trial-level splits that put the same person in the training and the test set. We measured what each practice costs, and whether such models transfer between laboratories. Three sequence models (convolutional, convolutional-recurrent, and convolutional-transformer) were evaluated on two independent datasets, locomotion (6 subjects) and occupational patient handling (10 subjects), under one pipeline, one tuning procedure, three seeds, and four protocols: trial-level split, leave-one-subject-out, pooled two-laboratory training with matched held-out subjects, and cross-laboratory transfer. At a fixed configuration, trial-level splits overstated the subject-held-out coefficient of determination by +0.040 to +0.194; on occupational data the overstatement exceeded every difference between architectures. With subjects held out, the three models reached values between 0.583 and 0.804; the leader differed between datasets, and gaps lay within subject-to-subject variability. Pooling the laboratories changed neither dataset on matched subjects. Transfer between laboratories was below chance in both directions, including the vertical force, which no in-plane rotation can affect. Leaving force targets in the plate frame while inputs were heading-aligned cost 0.57 of locomotion anteroposterior-force explained variance, enough to make that force look hardest; a Newton's-law correlation detected the mismatch before training. Split protocol and target frame changed reported accuracy more than architecture did. Learned force estimators should be validated with subjects held out, checked for frame consistency before training, and tested across laboratories before deployment claims are made.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that trial-level splits overstate accuracy for deep ground reaction force estimators, and that cross-laboratory transfer fails in both directions, so models need subject-held-out, frame-consistent, cross-lab validation.
AI.motivation: Deep GRF and centre-of-pressure estimators are often validated within one laboratory, in an unstated coordinate frame, and with trial-level splits that place the same person in training and test sets.
AI.method: Three sequence models (convolutional, convolutional-recurrent, and convolutional-transformer) are evaluated on locomotion (6 subjects) and occupational patient handling (10 subjects) data, with one pipeline, three seeds, and four protocols: trial-level split, leave-one-subject-out, pooled two-lab training, and cross-lab transfer.
AI.result: Trial-level splits overstate the subject-held-out coefficient of determination by +0.040 to +0.194, more than architecture differences on occupational data. With subjects held out, the models reach 0.583 to 0.804, with gaps within subject-to-subject variability. Pooling labs changes neither dataset on matched subjects. Cross-lab transfer is below chance in both directions. Using plate-frame force targets with heading-aligned inputs costs 0.57 of explained variance on locomotion anteroposterior force, and a Newton's-law correlation detects this mismatch before training.
AI.conclusion: Split protocol and target frame affect reported accuracy more than architecture, so force estimators should be validated with subjects held out, checked for frame consistency, and tested across laboratories.

title: Protocol-Aware Auditing of Domain-Blind Feature Attribution in Network Intrusion Detection
comment: Accepted as a poster at the LXAI Research Workshop, NeurIPS 2026; 6 figures
summary: Feature-attribution methods can query rule-violating network states through perturbations, coalitions, references, paths, and ablations, making explanations and their evaluation sensitive to model behavior outside the operational domain. We formalize this failure mode as domain blindness and prove valid-query invariance: when models agree on the required oracle information within a declared rule-valid set, a procedure confined to that set returns the same attribution. We instantiate one protocol-aware query-control principle in LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, and DeepLIFT and audit paired configurations across four NIDS datasets and three classifier families. In six settings where standard LIME reports perfect top-feature repeatability, PA-LIME reveals substantial variability, with a mean of 0.575. Under FGSM followed by protocol repair, PA-DeepLIFT and PA-IG achieve the largest attribution-similarity curve areas, 0.452 and 0.413, while mean within-PA rank agreement rises to 0.366 from 0.217. PA-XAI therefore turns structured domain assumptions into explicit, testable controls for explanation auditing; support modeling, raw-flow reconstruction, and adaptive explanation attacks provide complementary validation layers.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes domain blindness in feature attribution for network intrusion detection, proves valid-query invariance, and proposes protocol-aware variants (PA-LIME, PA-SHAP, PA-IG, PA-DeepLIFT) that confine attribution queries to a rule-valid set.
AI.motivation: Attribution methods can query network states that violate operational rules through perturbations, coalitions, references, paths, and ablations, which makes both explanations and their evaluation unreliable.
AI.method: The authors prove that when models agree on the required oracle information within a declared rule-valid set, a procedure confined to that set returns the same attribution, and they apply this control to LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, and DeepLIFT across four NIDS datasets and three classifier families.
AI.result: In six settings where standard LIME reports perfect top-feature repeatability, PA-LIME shows substantial variability with a mean of 0.575. Under FGSM followed by protocol repair, PA-DeepLIFT and PA-IG achieve the largest attribution-similarity curve areas, 0.452 and 0.413, and mean within-PA rank agreement rises to 0.366 from 0.217.
AI.conclusion: Structured domain assumptions can be turned into explicit, testable controls for explanation auditing, with further validation layers suggested for support modeling, raw-flow reconstruction, and adaptive attacks.

title: Imitating the Imperfect: Offline-to-Online Robust Imitation Learning from Heterogeneous Demonstrators
summary: Imitation learning (IL) typically relies on large-scale offline demonstrations collected from multiple human or algorithmic demonstrators. However, most existing approaches assume these demonstrators are homogeneous or near-optimal experts, a convenient but unrealistic assumption in real-world applications. In practice, demonstrations are often collected from heterogeneous demonstrators with unknown and varying levels of expertise, resulting in highly mixed-quality data. In this work, we study a challenging yet practical setting of imitation learning from such heterogeneous imperfect demonstrators. We propose Latent Expertise and Optimality Scoring based Imitation Learning (LEOS-IL), a principled framework that jointly learns (i) a state-action optimality scoring model and (ii) latent expertise levels for each demonstrator from unlabeled suboptimal offline demonstrations. The learned scoring model is then integrated into an online policy optimization procedure, where the agent is trained to maximize estimated optimality scores while its online rollouts are iteratively leveraged to refine the scoring model, thereby mitigating distributional shift during online adaptation. We further provide theoretical guarantees for optimality score identification and conditional optimal occupancy and policy recovery under explicit sufficient conditions. Experiments on continuous control benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms existing baselines across highly heterogeneous and low-quality demonstration regimes.

AI.tldr: LEOS-IL is an offline-to-online imitation learning framework that learns state-action optimality scores and latent demonstrator expertise from unlabeled, heterogeneous, suboptimal demonstrations, then refines the scores during online policy optimization.
AI.motivation: Most imitation learning methods assume homogeneous or near-optimal demonstrators, which is unrealistic when demonstrations come from mixed-quality sources.
AI.method: The framework jointly learns a state-action optimality scoring model and latent expertise levels for each demonstrator, integrates the scores into online policy optimization, and uses online rollouts to refine the scoring model against distribution shift.
AI.result: The authors give theoretical guarantees for optimality score identification and for conditional optimal occupancy and policy recovery under explicit sufficient conditions. On continuous control benchmarks, the method consistently outperforms existing baselines in highly heterogeneous and low-quality demonstration regimes.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modeling demonstrator expertise and state-action optimality makes imitation learning robust to heterogeneous imperfect demonstrations.

title: A Unified Interpretable Semantic Framework for Multi-Modal Fiber Sensing Under Data Scarcity
summary: We propose a unified interpretable semantic framework for multi-modal fiber sensing under data scarcity. The framework maps heterogeneous measurements from state of-polarization (SOP) monitoring, distributed acoustic sensing (DAS), and optical time-domain reflectometry (OTDR) into a shared set of physics-grounded semantic descriptors capturing impulsiveness, persistence, structural characteristics, and energy concentration. Inference is performed through reasoning over semantic class profiles, optionally assisted by retrieval of semantically similar examples to resolve ambiguity and support adaptation without model retraining. Experimental validation on real SOP, DAS, and OTDR datasets demonstrates robust performance across sensing modalities, achieving accuracies of 95.0%, 91.1%, and 94.6%, respectively, while providing transparent and physically interpretable decisions. The proposed framework establishes a unified and data efficient approach for optical fiber sensing in evolving and data scarce deployment environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a semantic framework that maps SOP, DAS, and OTDR fiber sensing measurements into shared physics-based descriptors and classifies them by reasoning over class profiles, reporting accuracies of 95.0%, 91.1%, and 94.6%.
AI.motivation: Fiber sensing measurements from different modalities are heterogeneous, and data scarcity limits learning-based classifiers in changing deployment environments.
AI.method: Measurements are mapped to descriptors of impulsiveness, persistence, structural characteristics, and energy concentration, and inference reasons over semantic class profiles, optionally aided by retrieval of similar examples without retraining.
AI.result: On real SOP, DAS, and OTDR datasets, the framework achieves 95.0%, 91.1%, and 94.6% accuracy respectively, with decisions that are interpretable.
AI.conclusion: The shared semantic descriptors offer a data-efficient and interpretable approach for optical fiber sensing under data scarcity. The abstract does not compare these results against baselines.
