Split conformal prediction reached its nominal coverage in all 24 settings I tested (within 0.006), but the sets were large when accuracy was low: at 90% coverage, temperature-scaled sets contained on average 63% (Qwen, English), 78% (Qwen, Arabic), 86% (Jais, English) and 89% (Jais, Arabic) of the options. The margin between the top two option probabilities separated correct from incorrect answers best for Qwen on English (AUROC 0.734) and worst for Jais on Arabic (0.579). Answering only the 20% most confident questions lowered Qwen's English error from 0.439 to 0.098. Jais showed a strong prior for option C (49% of English and 60% of Arabic predictions). Scoring Latin letters only cut the Arabic share to 29% but left accuracy, raw ECE and AUROC nearly unchanged. Because the two benchmarks differ in subject, level and number of options, I do not attribute differences between languages to language itself. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper studies calibration and conformal prediction for two open-weight 7B LLMs answering medical multiple-choice questions in English (MedMCQA) and Arabic (MedAraBench), finding raw probabilities overconfident and temperature scaling removing most of the calibration error.
AI.motivation: Accuracy alone does not show when a medical LLM answer can be trusted, and little is known about uncertainty for Arabic medical QA.
AI.method: The author evaluates Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Jais-adapted-7B-chat in 4-bit precision on 2,816 English and 4,927 Arabic questions, applying temperature scaling and split conformal prediction and measuring expected calibration error (ECE) and AUROC of option-probability margins.
AI.result: Accuracy is 0.561 (English) and 0.430 (Arabic) for Qwen, and 0.369 and 0.308 for Jais. Raw ECE is 0.242 to 0.486, and temperature scaling removes 82% to 93% of it. Conformal sets reach nominal coverage in all 24 settings, but are large at low accuracy, averaging 63% to 89% of options at 90% coverage. Answering the 20% most confident questions lowers Qwen's English error from 0.439 to 0.098. Jais has a strong prior for option C.
AI.conclusion: Temperature scaling fixes most miscalibration, but uncertainty is informative only where accuracy is high, and the author does not attribute language differences to language itself because the benchmarks differ in subject, level and option count.

title: Sustainable Federated Fine-Tuning with LoRA: Environmental Impact and Performance Footprint
comment: Accepted author manuscript for publication in the Proceedings of the 2027 IEEE Consumer Communications & Networking Conference (CCNC 2027), Las Vegas, Nevada, USA, January 9-12, 2027
summary: Federated Learning (FL) with Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) enables efficient adaptation of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its energy and carbon costs across hardware remain poorly understood. We evaluated federated Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on NVIDIA A40, RTX 6000 Ada, and A100 GPUs using a $2^2$ full factorial design with 135M/360M models and 10/100 local steps. CodeCarbon tracked energy and estimated CO$_2$-equivalent emissions. Descriptive allocation of variation assigned 84.8-91.2% of energy and emissions variation to local steps within these ranges. On A40 and RTX 6000 Ada, configurations with fewer steps achieved comparable accuracy with roughly 6-8-fold lower energy consumption and higher accuracy per kWh. These findings support smaller local budgets for energy-efficient federated fine-tuning within the evaluated setting.

AI.tldr: The paper measures the energy and carbon cost of federated LoRA fine-tuning of LLMs across three GPUs and finds that the number of local steps accounts for most of the variation, with fewer steps giving much better energy efficiency at comparable accuracy.
AI.motivation: The energy and carbon costs of federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning across hardware are poorly understood.
AI.method: A 2^2 full factorial design is run on NVIDIA A40, RTX 6000 Ada and A100 GPUs with 135M and 360M models and 10 or 100 local steps, with energy and CO2-equivalent tracked by CodeCarbon and variation allocated descriptively.
AI.result: Local steps account for 84.8% to 91.2% of energy and emissions variation. On A40 and RTX 6000 Ada, configurations with fewer steps reach comparable accuracy with roughly 6 to 8 times lower energy use and higher accuracy per kWh.
AI.conclusion: Smaller local step budgets support energy-efficient federated fine-tuning within the evaluated range.

title: Factored One-sided Adam-Moment for Practical and Scalable SOAP
comment: NeurIPS 2026. 17 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Second-order optimizers (e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP's dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP's dense second moment, and we measure only a 15-20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP's optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP's gains need not require SOAP's cost. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: FOAM is a lightweight SOAP variant that drops the output-side Kronecker factor and uses factored second-moment estimation, aiming to match SOAP and Muon in LLM pre-training loss at close to AdamW cost.
AI.motivation: Second-order optimisers such as Shampoo and SOAP converge faster per step than AdamW but remain costly, with substantial optimiser-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead.
AI.method: FOAM uses input-only preconditioning, which removes one Kronecker factor and one eigendecomposition, and replaces SOAP's dense rotated second moment with a factored row-by-column estimator.
AI.result: FOAM matches SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across 124M to 760M parameter LLM pre-training, uses half of SOAP's optimiser state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and tolerates a three-fold learning-rate range. The measured K-FAC violation is 15% to 20%.
AI.conclusion: SOAP-like gains can be obtained at a much lower cost, with the approximation shown to be nearly lossless empirically.

title: Time Flies When You Parallelise: Pareto-efficient Time Series Foundation Models with Linear Recurrences
summary: Time series foundation models have demonstrated strong zero-shot forecasting performance, but computational efficiency remains a central architectural challenge. Temporal self-attention incurs quadratic cost in the number of temporal tokens, while nonlinear recurrent state transitions restrict parallel computation along the temporal dimension. We introduce ci-proto, a family of time series foundation models based on Mamba-3, whose linear state recurrences support chunk-wise parallel-in-time computation during training, and inference costs that scale linearly with sequence length. The architecture alternates recurrent temporal processing with cross-variate attention, supporting multivariate probabilistic forecasting with past-only and future-known covariates. Across fev-bench's 100 forecasting tasks, ci-proto XL sets a new state of the art among time series foundation models. The five ci-proto variants also make up the entire Pareto frontier for mean scaled quantile loss and mean absolute scaled error against both parameter count and median runtime.

AI.tldr: ci-proto is a family of time series foundation models built on Mamba-3 linear recurrences that alternate temporal recurrence with cross-variate attention, reaching state-of-the-art results on fev-bench and forming the Pareto frontier on accuracy versus cost.
AI.motivation: Temporal self-attention is quadratic in sequence length, and nonlinear recurrent transitions prevent parallel computation over time.
AI.method: The architecture uses linear state recurrences that allow chunk-wise parallel-in-time training and linear-cost inference, alternating these with cross-variate attention, and supports probabilistic multivariate forecasting with past-only and future-known covariates.
AI.result: On fev-bench's 100 forecasting tasks, ci-proto XL sets a new state of the art among time series foundation models. The five variants make up the entire Pareto frontier for mean scaled quantile loss and mean absolute scaled error against parameter count and median runtime.
AI.conclusion: Linear recurrences with cross-variate attention give a time series foundation model family with a better efficiency-accuracy trade-off than prior designs.

title: Capacity-Constrained Delayed Feedback for Online Conformal Risk Control
summary: Online conformal risk control (OCRC) enables reliable uncertainty quantification in machine learning by converting model outputs into prediction sets with long-term risk guarantees. These guarantees, however, hinge on the assumption that the loss of each round is revealed immediately and losslessly. In practice, feedback may be delayed, and limited resources may prevent tracking all pending predictions, causing some feedback to be lost. To address this challenge, we develop capacity-aware OCRC (CA-OCRC), a framework that jointly determines how to allocate limited tracking feedback capacity and how to construct prediction sets. CA-OCRC is based on a randomized tracking policy that samples a proxy delay to decide whether, and for how long, feedback for the current round is tracked. CA-OCRC updates the prediction sets via inverse probability weighting, compensating for the possibility of feedback lost due to delays and limited tracking capacity. We analyze risk bounds for both arbitrary and stochastic delays, revealing a trade-off between receiving more feedback and avoiding capacity saturation. Building on these bounds, we optimize the proxy delay distribution, showing scaling laws for the tracking capacity that ensure the same long-term risk as OCRC with unlimited feedback. Experiments on medical imaging, natural language processing, computer vision, and wireless communications show the effectiveness of CA-OCRC as compared to existing OCRC mechanisms.

AI.tldr: CA-OCRC is an online conformal risk control method that allocates limited feedback-tracking capacity through a randomised policy and corrects for delayed or lost feedback with inverse probability weighting, retaining the long-term risk guarantee of unlimited-feedback OCRC.
AI.motivation: Existing online conformal risk control assumes losses are revealed immediately and losslessly, which fails when feedback is delayed and tracking capacity is limited.
AI.method: A randomised tracking policy samples a proxy delay to decide whether and how long to track each round's feedback, and the prediction sets are updated by inverse probability weighting. Risk bounds are derived for arbitrary and stochastic delays, and the proxy delay distribution is optimised.
AI.result: The abstract gives no numerical results. It reports experiments on medical imaging, NLP, computer vision and wireless communication tasks showing gains over existing OCRC mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Scaling laws for tracking capacity are shown, and the method keeps the same long-term risk as unlimited-feedback OCRC, with a trade-off between receiving more feedback and avoiding capacity saturation.

title: Near-Optimal Regret for Oracle-Efficient Adversarial Contextual Bandits
summary: We study contextual bandits with $K$ actions, a class of $N$ policies, and i.i.d.\ contexts from a distribution that the learner can sample. For any sequence of loss functions fixed before play, we give an oracle-efficient algorithm with expected regret $O(\sqrt{KT\log(2N)}\,\log(2KT))$ against the best policy in hindsight on the realized contexts. This improves the $T^{2/3}$ dependence on the horizon in prior oracle-efficient bounds and achieves the optimal regret rate in this setting up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm perturbs policy scores using a Poisson sample of auxiliary contexts. At each sampled context, the perturbation assigned to an action is a Laplace noise draw multiplied by a scale specific to that context and action. We show that choosing these scales to minimize a convex objective determined by past observations yields the stated regret bound. We further approximate the minimizing scales by projected stochastic gradient descent using only an exact offline cost-sensitive optimization oracle that returns the optimum value. Since the table of scales can be large, the algorithm represents the SGD iterates implicitly by storing the random draws that determine each update and evaluates the scales only at queried contexts. Both the oracle complexity and the remaining resource bounds are polynomial in $T$, $K$, and $\log(2N)$.

AI.tldr: The paper gives an oracle-efficient algorithm for adversarial contextual bandits with regret O(sqrt(KT log(2N)) log(2KT)), improving the T^{2/3} dependence of earlier oracle-efficient bounds to near-optimal rates.
AI.motivation: Prior oracle-efficient methods for contextual bandits achieve only T^{2/3} regret, which is far from the optimal rate in this setting.
AI.method: The algorithm perturbs policy scores using a Poisson sample of auxiliary contexts, with Laplace noise scaled per context and action. The scales minimise a convex objective and are approximated by projected SGD using only an exact offline cost-sensitive optimisation oracle, with SGD iterates stored implicitly through their random draws.
AI.result: The expected regret against the best policy in hindsight is O(sqrt(KT log(2N)) log(2KT)), and the oracle complexity and resource bounds are polynomial in T, K and log(2N).
AI.conclusion: Oracle-efficient methods can reach near-optimal regret for adversarial contextual bandits, up to logarithmic factors.

title: Bellman Contraction under MMD: A Unified Framework
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 88 pages, 18 figures, 13 tables
summary: We introduce a mathematical framework for studying contraction of the distributional Bellman operator under Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). We show that contraction reduces to conditional positive definiteness of an associated kernel constructed from the base kernel, which we call the Bellman difference kernel. Focusing on radial kernels, we use Schoenberg's theorem to connect this condition to Bernstein functions. This gives contraction criteria that hold in any dimension and can be verified analytically or tested numerically. Our framework unifies known results for the Gaussian RBF, power-distance, and multiquadric kernels. A numerical search identifies 11 new kernels that induce contraction. We also propose chaining, a general construction that produces kernels inducing contraction with any prescribed factor. To reconcile theory with practice, we show that contraction on a set only requires conditional positive definiteness on that set. This explains why the RBF kernel can remain a valid choice when rewards are bounded, despite its lack of global contraction. Finally, we identify a fundamental tradeoff between contraction rate and discriminative power, where kernels that contract faster tend to discriminate less between distributions. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper gives a framework for contraction of the distributional Bellman operator under MMD, reducing contraction to conditional positive definiteness of a derived kernel, and it identifies 11 new contracting kernels together with a chaining construction.
AI.motivation: Existing contraction results for distributional Bellman operators under MMD are known for only a few kernels, and their scope is not systematically understood.
AI.method: The authors define a Bellman difference kernel built from the base kernel, use Schoenberg's theorem and Bernstein functions for radial kernels, perform a numerical search, and introduce chaining to produce kernels with any prescribed contraction factor.
AI.result: The framework unifies known results for the Gaussian RBF, power-distance and multiquadric kernels and identifies 11 new contracting kernels. Contraction on a set needs only conditional positive definiteness on that set, which explains the RBF kernel's use for bounded rewards. A trade-off exists between contraction rate and discriminative power.
AI.conclusion: Faster-contracting kernels discriminate less between distributions, so kernel choice in distributional RL trades contraction against discrimination.

title: Using an energy pixels approach to estimate the size a 2nd Generation DEL must be to train a high-resolution binding model
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures
summary: DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) are commonly used to find small-molecule binders to a target protein. But the hard part is no longer finding a hit. It is building a machine-learning model good enough to guide the medicinal chemistry that follows, one that can resolve the shift in affinity when a chemist changes a single atom. Such a model needs two things from its training data: dense sampling of the small patch of chemical space around the hit, and an adequate number of genuinely tight binders within it. A diverse naive DEL gives neither. It samples an enormous space, so any one neighborhood is covered far too thinly, and the tightest binders are rare. A model trained on that naive DEL data must extrapolate to binders tighter than any it has seen, and that is where models can fail. One way to get training data with both properties is a second-generation DEL built around the hit. We ask how complex that library must be. We treat binding as a sum of small, independent interactions, called pixels on the target and antipixels on the ligand. From the spread of affinities measured in the naive library, with no structural information and nothing yet synthesized, we estimate the complexity such a library must have to supply that dense sampling and those tight binders. The method does two useful things. It turns the number of tight binders a model needs into the number of compounds a library must contain. And it estimates the expected yield of a randomly designed second-generation DEL, so the gain from designing the library with machine learning or active learning can be measured against a baseline, without the expense of a control library as large as the experiment itself.

AI.tldr: The paper estimates how complex a second-generation DNA-encoded library (DEL) must be to train a high-resolution binding model, using an energy-pixel model fitted to the affinity spread of a naive library without structural data.
AI.motivation: A naive DEL samples chemical space too thinly and contains too few tight binders for training an accurate model around a hit, so a second-generation library built around the hit is needed, but its size is unknown.
AI.method: Binding is modelled as a sum of small independent interactions between target pixels and ligand antipixels. From the spread of affinities in the naive library, the authors estimate the complexity needed for dense sampling and enough tight binders.
AI.result: The abstract reports no numerical results. It states that the method converts the number of required tight binders into a library size and estimates the expected yield of a randomly designed second-generation library as a baseline for measuring the gain from ML or active learning design.
AI.conclusion: The method gives a way to size second-generation DELs and to benchmark ML-guided library design without building a control library as large as the experiment.

title: Paper-Faithful Federated Learning: Scientific Checks for Practitioner and Agent Development
comment: 13 pages, 2 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Federated learning experiments can produce reasonable-looking results even when the experiment implementation differs from the intended experimental protocol. Small errors in configuration, data partitioning, aggregation, randomness, evaluation, or checkpoint recovery may therefore affect a comparison without causing the program to fail. We present FedBrew, a research codebase for controlled and reproducible federated learning experiments. Its focus is controlled simulation with checks of specified conditions of the intended experimental protocol. FedBrew uses configuration checks, identifiable client data partitions, checkpoint recovery checks, self-describing run records, and development-time checks of scientific conditions. These checks assess, for example, whether client partitions are disjoint and exhaustive and aggregation weights match the prescribed rule; numerical and recovery checks examine non-finite client model states and interrupted runs. The same structure also provides clear extension points and automated checks for new algorithms, datasets, models, and tasks, whether they are added by researchers or AI coding agents. FedBrew therefore supports reproducible and inspectable FL experiments through checks of specified software and scientific conditions and the run records associated with reported results.

AI.tldr: FedBrew is a research codebase for controlled, reproducible federated learning experiments that adds configuration, partition, checkpoint and numerical checks so that implementation errors that deviate from the intended protocol are caught.
AI.motivation: Federated learning experiments can produce plausible results even when the implementation departs from the intended protocol, through errors in configuration, partitioning, aggregation, randomness, evaluation or checkpoint recovery, and these errors usually do not cause crashes.
AI.method: The codebase provides configuration checks, identifiable client partitions, checkpoint recovery checks, self-describing run records, and development-time checks of scientific conditions. Examples include verifying that client partitions are disjoint and exhaustive and that aggregation weights match the prescribed rule, and checking for non-finite client states and interrupted runs. It also offers extension points with automated checks for new algorithms, datasets, models and tasks.
AI.result: The abstract describes the checks and run records but reports no experiments or quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The structure supports reproducible and inspectable federated learning experiments, including when extensions are written by researchers or AI coding agents.

title: Support-Constrained Offline Policy Improvement for Pediatric ECMO from Limited Clinical Data
summary: Managing children on ECMO (Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation) requires balancing short-term physiological stability with the long-term goal of preventing neurological injury. Standard reinforcement learning can propose risky, out-of-distribution actions, while imitation learning is limited to reproducing clinician behavior. We introduce Support-Constrained Fitted Q-Iteration (FQI-SC), an offline reinforcement learning framework that cautiously improves upon expert behavior by restricting optimization to empirically supported state-action pairs and defaulting to the clinician baseline in low-data regions. On 78 pediatric trajectories totaling over 6,000 hours of clinical data, we evaluate our framework using Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE) and a behavioral disagreement. Additionally, we formalize the performance-safety trade-off by introducing a unified Balance Score ($S(\pi)$). Our empirical evaluation shows that support-constrained policy improves the Balance Score by 38\% relative to FQI, improves estimated value by 1.28 FQE units over imitation learning, and reduces disagreement with clinician actions by 71\% relative to FQI.

AI.tldr: FQI-SC is an offline reinforcement learning method for pediatric ECMO that improves on clinician behaviour by restricting optimisation to empirically supported state-action pairs and defaulting to the clinician baseline in low-data regions.
AI.motivation: Standard reinforcement learning can propose risky out-of-distribution actions, while imitation learning only reproduces clinician behaviour, so a method that improves cautiously on experts is needed for ECMO management.
AI.method: The authors introduce Support-Constrained Fitted Q-Iteration, which optimises only over empirically supported state-action pairs, evaluated with Fitted Q-Evaluation and a behavioural disagreement measure. A Balance Score S(pi) formalises the performance-safety trade-off.
AI.result: On 78 pediatric trajectories totalling over 6,000 hours, the support-constrained policy improves the Balance Score by 38% relative to FQI, improves estimated value by 1.28 FQE units over imitation learning, and reduces disagreement with clinician actions by 71% relative to FQI.
AI.conclusion: Support-constrained offline RL can give a safer policy improvement over clinician behaviour from limited clinical data.

title: ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs
comment: 48 pages, 14 figures, 26 tables. Companion paper to "AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics" (Sharpe et al., 2026)
summary: A foundational principle of physics is that all coordinate systems are equally valid: the behavior of a PDE-governed system does not depend on the origin or orientation of the frame, nor on the units or mesh used to write it down, and neither should a surrogate model. Yet the neural surrogates with the lowest errors on today's aerodynamics benchmarks lack these invariances and fail under simple transformations of the same problem: for models trained on PDEs of cars in one pose (i.e., translation and rotation) and from one mesher, rotating the full PDE raises the surface-pressure error from 4% to more than 100%, and re-sampling its boundary raises it to about 30%. We introduce ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention), a slice-attention transformer for steady, boundary-driven PDEs in which no learned operation receives a coordinate and every sum over the boundary is a quadrature. Positions enter only as distances and relative angles to learned slice anchors, lengths are measured in a unit computed from the boundary, and interior points query the boundary through a tree-accelerated learned kernel without influencing one another. With every boundary cell a token and an exact boundary read, ISLA is equivariant to rigid motions and reflections, invariant to the units of its declared data, and consistent under mesh refinement, while at every setting each query is independent of all other queries. On AeroZoo, 2,816 flows that vary in shape, size, speed, and boundary conditions, its mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are at least 3.1 and 3.3 times lower than any baseline's. On AirfRANS its errors are second only to those of a boundary-integral model (GLOBE) and at least 1.6 times lower than those of Transolver and GeoTransolver.

AI.tldr: ISLA is a slice-attention transformer for steady boundary-driven PDEs that is equivariant to rigid motions and reflections and invariant to units, and that reduces surface-pressure and velocity errors on aerodynamic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The lowest-error neural surrogates for aerodynamics lack coordinate invariances and fail under simple transformations of the same problem, with surface-pressure error rising from 4% to over 100% when a car is rotated.
AI.method: ISLA encodes positions only as distances and relative angles to learned slice anchors, measures lengths in a unit computed from the boundary, treats each boundary cell as a token with exact boundary reads, and lets interior points query the boundary through a tree-accelerated learned kernel without interacting with one another.
AI.result: On AeroZoo's 2,816 flows, mean reference-scaled velocity and pressure errors are at least 3.1 and 3.3 times lower than any baseline. On AirfRANS, errors are second only to GLOBE, a boundary-integral model, and at least 1.6 times lower than Transolver and GeoTransolver.
AI.conclusion: Building invariances and quadrature into the architecture gives a boundary-driven surrogate that is robust to frame, units and mesh changes while improving accuracy on aerodynamic benchmarks.

title: A Convex-Analytic Reformulation for Poisoning Attacks on Logistic Regression
summary: We study data poisoning attacks on logistic regression with $\ell_2$-regularization, where an attacker chooses the features of a fixed number of injected observations with prescribed labels to maximize the logistic loss on the clean training data. Strong convexity of the defender's problem yields an exact reformulation through its first-order optimality conditions. Using convex conjugacy of the softplus function, we replace the sigmoid relations by a single convex optimality-gap inequality and express the attacker's objective as a concave function. A change of variables makes the stationarity condition affine, leaving bounded bilinear equalities as the only nonconvex constraints. We derive finite bounds on all variables involved in these equalities, including a global bound on the coefficient norm and tighter bounds obtained by preprocessing based on convex optimization. Experiments on eight binary classification datasets evaluate attack effectiveness and compare the two reformulations when solved with \textsf{SCIP}. Attacks obtained by local optimization degrade predictive performance on most datasets, while the convex-analytic formulation produces substantially stronger reported dual bounds within a fixed time limit.

AI.tldr: The paper gives an exact convex-analytic reformulation of data poisoning attacks on l2-regularised logistic regression, replacing the nonconvex bilevel problem with bounded bilinear constraints that yield stronger dual bounds in a fixed time limit.
AI.motivation: Attacks on logistic regression are typically found by local optimisation, which degrades predictive performance on most datasets but offers no certified bounds on attack strength.
AI.method: Strong convexity of the defender's problem gives an exact reformulation via first-order optimality conditions. Convex conjugacy of softplus replaces the sigmoid relations with a convex optimality-gap inequality, and a change of variables makes stationarity affine, leaving bounded bilinear equalities as the only nonconvex constraints. Finite variable bounds and convex-optimisation preprocessing are derived, and the two formulations are solved with SCIP.
AI.result: Local optimisation degrades predictive performance on most of eight binary classification datasets, and the convex-analytic formulation gives substantially stronger reported dual bounds within a fixed time limit.
AI.conclusion: The convex-analytic reformulation gives a more tractable and certifiable way to analyse poisoning attacks on logistic regression.

title: Enhancing Preference Detection using Eye Movement Cascade and Multilayer Combinatorial Fusion
comment: Published in the Proceedings of the 26th Annual International Conference of the Global Business and Technology Association (GBATA), 2026, pp. 969-980
summary: Understanding how visual attention influences human preference formation is a fundamental problem in consumer behavior and cognitive science. In this work, we investigate how eye movement patterns can be used to predict preference decisions when subjects compare two alternatives. To address this problem, we analyze an eye-tracking dataset, where subjects view pairs of face images and their gaze behavior is recorded throughout the decision process. We model this problem using multiple machine learning classifiers and apply the Multi-layer Combinatorial Fusion (MCF) framework to iteratively combine diverse models. The MCF framework expands models to a large pool of model fusions and then reduces them based on cognitive diversity, repeating this process across layers until diversity diminishes. Experimental results show that MCF significantly improves performance over individual models. The best single model achieves a Pre@k of 0.90, which is improved to 0.9143 after the first layer of MCF, and further increased to 0.9286 in the second layer. This progression demonstrates that the second layer not only surpasses the performance of the first layer but also outperforms the best individual model, highlighting the effectiveness of leveraging diversity through multi-layer fusion.

AI.tldr: The paper uses eye-movement features and Multi-layer Combinatorial Fusion (MCF) to predict preference decisions between paired face images, with fusion raising Pre@k from 0.90 for the best single model to 0.9286 after two layers.
AI.motivation: Understanding how visual attention shapes preference formation matters for consumer behaviour and cognitive science, and single classifiers may not capture the diversity of gaze patterns.
AI.method: Several machine learning classifiers are trained on an eye-tracking dataset of subjects comparing pairs of face images, and MCF expands a pool of model fusions, reduces them by cognitive diversity, and repeats across layers until diversity diminishes.
AI.result: The best single model reaches Pre@k of 0.90, which rises to 0.9143 after the first MCF layer and 0.9286 after the second. The second layer outperforms both the first layer and the best individual model.
AI.conclusion: Multi-layer fusion guided by diversity improves preference prediction from gaze data beyond any individual model.

title: AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics
comment: 35 pages, 13 figures, 23 tables. Lead authors: Peter Sharpe and Carmelo Gonzales. Companion paper to "ISLA: A Coordinate-Free, Measure-Weighted Transformer for Boundary-Driven PDEs" (Sharpe, 2026). Dataset to be published shortly at this https URL
summary: Neural surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are trained and ranked on datasets that each vary one design family in one flow domain. Such datasets cannot test the least that an aerodynamic foundation model must do: predict CFD-quality incompressible flow in seconds for new shapes in new enclosures. On DrivAerML, larger models and longer training barely lower Transolver's error; doubling the training cases cuts it by about 12% up to 400 cases, exhausting the dataset. We introduce AeroZoo, a benchmark and training corpus of 3,815 time-mean solutions to the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations with a transition model, across seven geometry families, eight enclosure configurations and Reynolds numbers from $10^3$ to $10^8$. Each sample poses a well-posed PDE problem in the form a solver receives it: the boundary meshes grouped by condition type, the prescribed values and the fluid properties. The 2,816 samples with a stable time mean form the canonical benchmark: two tasks, engineering metrics and 22 frozen splits, disjoint in geometry, that hold out geometry families, enclosures, boundary-condition layouts and Reynolds ranges. On the random split, boundary-condition tokens cut GeoTransolver's median velocity error from 76.9% to 8.4% of the inlet speed in single-seed runs (uniform inlet flow: 11.0%). ISLA, a transformer for boundary-driven PDEs, reaches 5.3% over four seeds, about 4 times the change from a finer mesh. On the same test samples, a held-out geometry family barely changes ISLA's error relative to uniform flow, and a held-out enclosure or boundary-condition layout raises it 2.4 to 9.2 times. The data and the scoring code will be released.

AI.tldr: AeroZoo is a benchmark and training corpus of 3,815 RANS-based aerodynamic flow solutions across seven geometry families, eight enclosures and Reynolds numbers from 10^3 to 10^8, designed to test whether neural CFD surrogates generalise to new shapes and new enclosures.
AI.motivation: Neural CFD surrogates are trained and ranked on datasets that vary one design family in one domain, so they cannot test whether a model can predict flow for new shapes in new enclosures, and error on DrivAerML barely falls with larger models or longer training.
AI.method: The authors release 3,815 time-mean RANS solutions with a transition model, of which 2,816 form the canonical benchmark. It has two tasks, engineering metrics and 22 frozen splits that are disjoint in geometry and hold out geometry families, enclosures, boundary-condition layouts and Reynolds ranges. The solver inputs are given as well-posed PDE problems.
AI.result: With boundary-condition tokens, GeoTransolver's median velocity error on the random split falls from 76.9% to 8.4% of inlet speed in single-seed runs, against 11.0% for uniform inlet flow. ISLA reaches 5.3% over four seeds. Held-out enclosures or boundary-condition layouts raise ISLA's error 2.4 to 9.2 times.
AI.conclusion: Generalisation to unseen enclosures and boundary-condition layouts is much harder than to unseen geometry families, and the benchmark exposes this gap. The data and scoring code will be released.

title: Symmetry in Time: A Representation Theory of Linear Recurrent Memory
summary: State space models (SSMs) are an emerging alternative to Transformers. SSMs offer linear-time inference and parallel training, but most implementations make the parallel scan efficient by making the recurrence diagonal: each channel of the hidden state is multiplied by an input-dependent real or complex number. These numbers commute, so the state records which inputs occurred but not their order. We formalize this with representation theory, which explains and fixes the state-tracking failures previously reported for SSMs. The state update defines a linear representation of the monoid of input sequences, and we show that an SSM tracks a group at every sequence length exactly when that group is a quotient of the group generated by its transition matrices. Two consequences follow. Diagonal real- and complex-valued SSMs can track only commutative groups, while the transition matrices of any SSM that can track a group must split into independent blocks over the real, complex, and quaternion numbers. We then introduce HyperSSM, which adds quaternion channels while keeping linear-time inference and parallel training. Trained only on final answers, HyperSSM solves the group tasks of recent state-tracking benchmarks exactly with at most five state numbers. This includes $S_5$ with 32 generators, where previous SSMs are at chance, and HyperSSM generalizes to sequences 25 times longer than those seen in training. Because the theory says what the transitions must encode, the learned weights of the linear recurrence can be interpreted directly. We demonstrate this by recovering the calibration of a real gyroscope, the rotations of imperfect qubit gates and the geometry of protein backbones.

AI.tldr: The paper uses representation theory to show that diagonal SSMs can track only commutative groups, and introduces HyperSSM, which adds quaternion channels and solves group state-tracking tasks, including S5, with a small state.
AI.motivation: Most SSM implementations use diagonal recurrences for parallel scans, so the state records which inputs occurred but not their order, which explains reported state-tracking failures.
AI.method: The state update is treated as a linear representation of the monoid of input sequences, and an SSM tracks a group exactly when that group is a quotient of the group generated by its transition matrices. HyperSSM adds quaternion channels while keeping linear-time inference and parallel training.
AI.result: HyperSSM solves recent state-tracking benchmark group tasks exactly with at most five state numbers, including S5 with 32 generators where previous SSMs are at chance, and it generalises to sequences 25 times longer than those seen in training. The learned weights are recovered for a real gyroscope's calibration, imperfect qubit gate rotations and protein backbone geometry.
AI.conclusion: The theory determines what the transition matrices must encode, which makes the learned recurrence interpretable and supports quaternion-block SSMs for group tracking.

title: Physically Interpretable Basin Selection in Discrete-Variable Origami Design
summary: Automatic differentiation has enabled rapid progress on continuous-variable mechanical design problems, but gradient-based optimization still struggles with discrete variables. The standard approach is to optimize using a continuous relaxation of the choices, then commit to the nearest discrete design at the end. Why this procedure selects unfavorable basins is poorly understood. Here, we introduce a practical, interpretable design problem inspired by origami, in which automatic differentiation is used to design shapes with a target functional behavior. Each origami sheet has a fixed geometry, and a bilevel optimization framework tunes which one of four discrete hinge types to place at each fold. Baseline gradient-based design settles into basins with a large discretization gap: relaxed optimization solves 97% of runs, but the final, discrete solutions succeed only half the time. We find that the gap can be relieved with a surprisingly simple modification. An initialization prior uniformly biased toward the stiff, flat hinge option boosts the final solve fraction from 49% to 69%. Applying the prior adds no additional compute and leaves the optimization process unchanged. Compared to the baseline, sheets produced with the prior have greater geometric compatibility and mechanical stiffness. Directly penalizing frustration and floppiness in the outer loss function produces an even greater improvement than the prior does, raising the solve fraction to 78% and indicating that these properties help distinguish the unfavorable basins. Our results demonstrate that loss landscapes for mechanical design can have physically meaningful basins that are not robust to discretization and cause solves to fail. Targeting these basins' physical signatures, even with just an initialization bias, helps avoid them.

AI.tldr: The paper studies why gradient-based design of origami with discrete hinge choices fails, showing that a prior biased toward the stiff flat hinge and a penalty on frustration and floppiness raise the final solve fraction from 49% to 69% and 78%.
AI.motivation: Relaxed optimisation solves 97% of runs, but after rounding to discrete hinges only half of the final designs succeed, because the optimiser settles in basins with a large discretisation gap.
AI.method: A bilevel optimisation framework chooses one of four hinge types at each fold of a fixed-geometry origami sheet. The authors compare a baseline with an initialisation prior biased toward the stiff, flat hinge and with direct penalties on frustration and floppiness in the outer loss.
AI.result: The initialisation prior raises the solve fraction from 49% to 69% at no added compute, and the penalty raises it to 78%. Prior-based designs show greater geometric compatibility and stiffness than the baseline.
AI.conclusion: Some loss-landscape basins for mechanical design are not robust to discretisation, and targeting their physical signatures can help avoid them.

title: Two mathematical models of knowledge distillation
summary: Many hypotheses compete to explain the successes of knowledge distillation. To help address this, we propose and analyze a mathematical model of distillation, which suggests that distillation's performance comes not from obtaining better models but from easier to optimize landscapes. For generalized linear models trained with stochastic gradient descent, we prove that distillation fits performant student models asymptotically more quickly than non-distilled models. In rank-1 matrix approximation, we characterize conditions on the target matrix under which gradient descent with distillation converges strictly faster than training on the supervised objective. The theory helps delineate the ways distillation provides benefits (i.e., in optimization speed, not in generalization), and experiments on real datasets corroborate the theoretical predictions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a mathematical model of knowledge distillation and argues that distillation speeds up optimisation rather than improving generalisation, proving faster convergence for generalised linear models under SGD and for rank-1 matrix approximation.
AI.motivation: Many competing hypotheses explain distillation's success, and the authors want to test whether its benefit lies in better models or in easier optimisation.
AI.method: The authors analyse SGD on generalised linear models with distillation targets and gradient descent on rank-1 matrix approximation, characterising conditions under which distillation converges faster, and check the predictions on real datasets.
AI.result: For generalised linear models trained with SGD, distillation fits performant student models asymptotically faster than non-distilled training. In rank-1 approximation, distillation converges strictly faster under characterised conditions on the target matrix. Experiments on real datasets corroborate these predictions.
AI.conclusion: Distillation helps in optimisation speed rather than generalisation, according to the theory.

title: Towards a Theory of Learnability via Debate
summary: Debate has been recently proposed as a training protocol that is hoped to produce more aligned models even as model capabilities scale. The idea is that the human, instead of providing supervision in the form of labels, judges a debate between two models that compete to prove the correctness of opposite labels. It can be shown that functions of a much higher computational complexity can be correctly judged in this way, compared to the complexity of functions that can be directly evaluated using a computationally weak evaluator. This suggests that perhaps debate can be used to teach very complicated functions to models. However, previous work has largely ignored the fact that this is a training protocol, and simply analyzes the game being played between the two debaters for a known judge. We take the first steps towards understanding the learning problem implicit within the protocol, by formulating it as an online learning problem. We show that once we formulate the learning problem precisely, there are cases where the best way to learn given access to a judge is different from running an adversarial debate. This motivates us to define a cooperative version of the protocol, whose learnability we characterize using a combinatorial dimension. We also consider the possibility of the human judge being fallible and occasionally judging the debate incorrectly. We show that a small number of errors in judgement can lead to a large error in learning.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates debate-based training as an online learning problem, showing that the best learning strategy with a judge can differ from adversarial debate, proposing a cooperative protocol with a combinatorial characterisation, and showing that a few judging errors can cause large learning errors.
AI.motivation: Prior debate analyses treat the protocol as a game between debaters for a known judge, ignoring that it is also a training protocol, and the learnability of the induced learning problem is unclear.
AI.method: The authors formulate the learning problem precisely as online learning, define a cooperative variant of debate, characterise its learnability with a combinatorial dimension, and analyse a fallible judge that sometimes judges incorrectly.
AI.result: The abstract reports theoretical results only: cases where adversarial debate is not the best learning strategy, a characterisation of cooperative learnability, and a finding that a small number of judging errors can lead to a large learning error.
AI.conclusion: Debate as a training protocol needs its own learning-theoretic analysis, and judge reliability is critical to it.

title: Internalizing Investment Mandates: A Neurosymbolic RL Approach to Portfolio Allocation
comment: Accepted at ICAIF '26
summary: Institutional portfolios operate under investment policy statements that specify asset allocation constraints, often conditioned on market regime information. Deep reinforcement learning has been shown to optimize financial performance but typically does not enforce rule compliance, making it unsuitable for real-world deployment. Existing neurosymbolic methods such as Probabilistic Logic Policy Gradient (PLPG) offer constraint-satisfying reinforcement learning (RL) via differentiable symbolic supervision but assume a finite, discrete action space. We present a PLPG-inspired continuous allocation method that estimates the probability that the policy's own executed action satisfies the investment mandate, using reparameterized Monte Carlo sampling, and adds it to the training objective. No post-hoc enforcement mechanism intercepts actions at inference time and compliance is learned by the agent. Audited directly on deterministic mean actions with no correction, the policy reduces violations of a six-rule regime-conditional mandate from 96-98% for unconstrained RL and 33.4% for a reward-penalty baseline to 4.8%, showing that a continuous-action neurosymbolic policy can substantially internalize a symbolic mandate.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a continuous-action neurosymbolic RL method that learns to satisfy an investment mandate through a differentiable compliance probability in the training objective, reducing violations of a six-rule mandate from 96-98% to 4.8% without inference-time correction.
AI.motivation: Deep RL for portfolios does not enforce investment policy rules, and existing neurosymbolic methods such as PLPG assume finite discrete action spaces.
AI.method: The method estimates the probability that the policy's own executed action satisfies the mandate using reparameterised Monte Carlo sampling, adds it to the training objective, and applies no post-hoc action interception.
AI.result: Audited on deterministic mean actions without correction, violations of a six-rule regime-conditional mandate fall from 96-98% for unconstrained RL and 33.4% for a reward-penalty baseline to 4.8%.
AI.conclusion: A continuous-action neurosymbolic policy can largely internalise a symbolic mandate through training alone.

title: Null-Corrected Conditional Coverage in Materials Property Prediction: A Five-Dataset Replication
comment: N pages, 15 tables. Extends and partly revises arXiv:2608.07589. Submitted to Data-Centric Engineering. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Uncertainty quantification for materials property prediction increasingly reports conditional coverage, coverage within strata of the predicted value, alongside marginal coverage. The worst-bin statistics used for this are downward-biased in finite samples, a known defect that applied materials work does not generally correct for. We replicate a single-dataset conditional coverage study across five regression datasets (n = 437 to 21,263), seven interval methods and 50 random splits each, correcting the worst-bin statistic against its expected value under exact conditional validity. The null is simulated from realized per-bin test counts and referenced to each method's own marginal coverage, separating marginal miscalibration from uneven coverage. On the smallest dataset the correction runs from 0.061 to 0.096, between a third and two thirds of the shortfalls actually reported, against 0.009 to 0.011 on the two largest. Split conformal prediction's failure survives the correction on four of five datasets; two conclusions of the antecedent study do not. Conformalized quantile regression, characterized there as a negative case, fails on one dataset only. Cross-fitted normalized conformal prediction, grouped there with the successful methods, fails on three of five. Group-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction stays below our significance criterion on every dataset, yet exceeds the null on three of five under an octile refinement of the variable it calibrates on. A level-matched ablation locates that uniformity in group-conditional calibration rather than in the elevated quantile level, and removes Mondrian's apparent width cost entirely. Conditional coverage evaluations should report the null distribution of the worst-bin statistic used, the method's realized marginal coverage, and the resolution of the evaluation partition relative to any partition the method calibrates on.

AI.tldr: The paper replicates a conditional coverage study of uncertainty methods on five materials regression datasets and shows that correcting the worst-bin statistic for its finite-sample downward bias changes several earlier conclusions.
AI.motivation: The worst-bin statistic for conditional coverage is downward-biased in finite samples, and applied materials work does not generally correct for this.
AI.method: The authors replicate across five regression datasets (n = 437 to 21,263), seven interval methods and 50 random splits each, simulating the null from realised per-bin test counts and referencing it to each method's marginal coverage.
AI.result: On the smallest dataset the corrected shortfall ranges from 0.061 to 0.096, against 0.009 to 0.011 on the two largest. Split conformal failure survives on four of five datasets. CQR fails on one dataset and cross-fitted normalised conformal on three of five. Mondrian conformal exceeds the null on three of five datasets under an octile refinement.
AI.conclusion: Conditional coverage evaluations should report the null distribution of the worst-bin statistic, realised marginal coverage and the resolution of the evaluation partition.

title: Credal Wrapper for Uncertainty Modelling in Sparse Geological Data
comment: 28 pages, 4 figures, 10 tables
summary: Machine learning models for mineral exploration are trained on a few hundred sparse, expensive samples and used to decide where to drill next, so their epistemic uncertainty (EU), the part that more data could remove, matters as much as their predictions. Yet EU cannot be measured on real data, because the counterfactual that defines it is never observed, so estimators are graded by proxies such as out-of-distribution detection and calibration. We contribute a general simulation protocol that makes EU directly computable for a given model and can grade any EU estimator. It separates two estimands the literature conflates, reducible error and estimator spread, builds an oracle reference for each in a synthetic prospectivity field sampled by clustered drilling surveys, and compares uncertainty measures of an identical ensemble within each simulated world. We use it to ask when credal (imprecise-probability) measures are more faithful than Bayesian model averaging (BMA) in the sparse, low-class regime of geological classification. The credal interval width recovers the epistemic ordering better than BMA when members are few, confirming the small-ensemble advantage reported for credal wrappers; the advantage vanishes by M = 10 and reverses at M = 40. Secondly, the choice of credal functional matters more than the choice between credal and BMA. Lastly, the credal advantage does not widen as training data are thinned, so it compensates for few posterior samples rather than few data. On real drill-hole geochemistry from South Australia, a resampling oracle reproduces the first finding. The protocol applies to any EU estimator whose data-generating process can be simulated.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a simulation protocol that makes epistemic uncertainty computable for geological classifiers and uses it to show that credal wrappers beat Bayesian model averaging only for small ensembles.
AI.motivation: Epistemic uncertainty for mineral exploration models cannot be measured on real data because its counterfactual is never observed, so estimators are only graded by proxies.
AI.method: The protocol simulates a synthetic prospectivity field with clustered drilling surveys, separates reducible error from estimator spread, builds an oracle for each, and compares uncertainty measures on the same ensemble within each simulated world.
AI.result: The credal interval width recovers the epistemic ordering better than BMA when there are few members. The advantage vanishes by M = 10 and reverses at M = 40. The choice of credal functional matters more than credal versus BMA, and the advantage does not widen as training data are thinned. A resampling oracle reproduces the first finding on real South Australian drill-hole geochemistry.
AI.conclusion: Credal advantages mainly compensate for few posterior samples rather than few data, and the protocol can grade any EU estimator whose data-generating process can be simulated.

title: Clustering trajectories of modelled estimates: an uncertainty-aware framework, with an application to global cardiovascular disease burden, 1990 to 2023
comment: 19 pages, 8 figures
summary: Modelled health estimates such as those of the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study are increasingly used in secondary analyses designed for observed data. However, trajectory clustering typically ignores published uncertainty, selects the number of clusters using criteria blind to it, and assigns countries to groups with unwarranted certainty. We propose an uncertainty-aware framework that separates trajectory level from shape, quantifies membership probabilities by perturbing estimates within their uncertainty intervals, selects clusters based on stability under uncertainty, and examines the roles of development, region, and measurement quality. Applied to age-standardised cardiovascular disease DALY rates for 201 countries from 1990-2023 (GBD 2023), the framework identified two stable trajectory types, whereas the gap statistic selected three. The additional cluster was poorly supported (median membership probability 0.70) and disappeared once uncertainty was considered. The retained clusters had similar burdens in 1990 but diverged markedly over time: a stalled-improvement group of 78 countries (median change $-8\%$, 40 of them in sub-Saharan Africa) and a sustained-decline group of 92 countries ($-52\%$). Thirty-one countries remained unclassified because their memberships were uncertain. Results were reproduced using mortality rates, a 2000-2023 analysis window, and bootstrap resampling. Among countries with the narrowest uncertainty intervals, a third well-supported trajectory emerged in former Soviet and Eastern European countries. These findings show that uncertainty affects both the number and composition of trajectory clusters. Ignoring it risks over-interpreting unstable groups and overstating confidence in country classifications. Incorporating published uncertainty and measurement quality should become standard practice when clustering modelled health estimates.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an uncertainty-aware clustering framework for modelled health estimates and applies it to GBD cardiovascular DALY trajectories for 201 countries, finding two stable groups where the gap statistic selects three.
AI.motivation: Trajectory clustering of modelled estimates such as GBD usually ignores published uncertainty, chooses cluster numbers without it, and assigns countries with unwarranted certainty.
AI.method: The framework perturbs estimates within their uncertainty intervals to compute membership probabilities, and selects clusters by their stability under uncertainty. It also examines the roles of development, region and measurement quality.
AI.result: Two stable trajectory types are found, while the gap statistic selects three. The third cluster has median membership probability 0.70 and disappears under uncertainty. One group of 78 countries shows stalled improvement, with median change of -8% and 40 countries in sub-Saharan Africa. The other of 92 countries shows sustained decline of -52%. Thirty-one countries remain unclassified. Results hold for mortality rates, a 2000-2023 window and bootstrap resampling.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty affects both the number and composition of trajectory clusters, and it should be included when clustering modelled health estimates.

title: Enhancing Resolution and Reliability with Attention Mechanisms in Nuclear Accident Surrogate Modeling
comment: Code and supplementary material: this https URL
summary: Severe accident (SA) analysis of nuclear power plants relies on system codes such as MAAP, whose computational cost limits large-scale applications including dynamic probabilistic safety assessment and reinforcement learning. This study proposes the Accident Binary-Continuous Transformer (ABC-Transformer), a decoder-only surrogate combining causal self-attention with temporal attention pooling. It jointly embeds continuous thermal-hydraulic variables with binary safety-system and severe accident management guideline (SAMG) states, enabling 5-minute-resolution forecasting over 72-hour transients. Trained on 11,000 MAAP simulations of a total loss of component cooling water scenario for the OPR1000, it achieved lower one-step teacher-forcing error than CNN and recurrent baselines at fine resolutions. Autoregressive reliability was characterized as a full per-scenario distribution over 1100 held-out scenarios. For scheduled-sampling (SS) training, the median $R^2$ is $0.947 \pm 0.006$ and $3.8 \pm 1.0$% of scenarios fail ($R^2<0$; mean $\pm$ SD over four training seeds), while errors accumulate with rollout length. A Mahalanobis self-distance computed from each surrogate rollout, before comparison with the MAAP reference, ranks these failures (ROC-AUC 0.895, reference seed). A threshold at the 40th percentile of calibration scores accepts $36.8 \pm 0.5$% of 550 evaluation scenarios, with no accepted rollout below $R^2 = 0$ for any seed, and routes the rest to MAAP.

AI.tldr: The ABC-Transformer is a decoder-only surrogate for MAAP severe-accident simulations that forecasts 72-hour transients at 5-minute resolution and uses a Mahalanobis self-distance to flag rollouts likely to fail.
AI.motivation: System codes such as MAAP are too expensive for large-scale uses such as dynamic probabilistic safety assessment and reinforcement learning.
AI.method: The model combines causal self-attention with temporal attention pooling and jointly embeds continuous thermal-hydraulic variables with binary safety-system and SAMG states. It is trained on 11,000 MAAP simulations of a total loss of component cooling water scenario for the OPR1000.
AI.result: The median R^2 under scheduled sampling is 0.947 plus or minus 0.006, with 3.8 plus or minus 1.0% of 1,100 held-out scenarios failing (R^2 < 0). The Mahalanobis self-distance ranks failures with ROC-AUC 0.895. A 40th-percentile threshold accepts 36.8 plus or minus 0.5% of 550 evaluation scenarios with no accepted rollout below R^2 = 0, and routes the rest to MAAP.
AI.conclusion: Surrogate rollouts can be screened for reliability, with the accepted subset trusted and the remainder passed to the full code.

title: Quantifying Methodological Inflation in Clinical Machine Learning: A Cross-Modality Audit of Subject-Level Leakage and Nested Feature Selection for Parkinson's Disease
summary: Reported accuracy in Parkinson's disease (PD) machine learning can reflect the evaluation protocol rather than real signal. We ask how much evaluation choices inflate performance by comparing naive and rigorous protocols on voice, telemonitoring and blood-transcriptomic datasets. Subject-aware splitting reduced voice AUROC from 0.892 to 0.780 and telemonitoring R^2 from 0.105 to -0.037; Random Forest recovered neither gap. Supervised probe selection before splitting inflated transcriptomic AUROC from 0.711 to 0.998. A nested 50-probe panel matched a 1,000-probe panel (0.811 versus 0.844), and recruitment-wave batch structure was detected. Future work should validate a stable panel on an independent cohort.

AI.tldr: The paper audits Parkinson's disease machine learning on voice, telemonitoring and blood-transcriptomic data and shows that subject-level leakage and supervised probe selection inflate reported performance.
AI.motivation: Reported accuracy in PD machine learning may reflect the evaluation protocol rather than real signal.
AI.method: The authors compare naive and rigorous protocols on three datasets, using subject-aware splitting, nested feature selection and comparisons of probe panels, and they check for batch structure by recruitment wave.
AI.result: Subject-aware splitting reduces voice AUROC from 0.892 to 0.780 and telemonitoring R^2 from 0.105 to -0.037, and Random Forest recovers neither gap. Supervised probe selection before splitting inflates transcriptomic AUROC from 0.711 to 0.998. A nested 50-probe panel matches a 1,000-probe panel (0.811 versus 0.844), and recruitment-wave batch structure is detected.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation choices can inflate PD performance substantially, and a stable panel should be validated on an independent cohort.

title: Learning Nonlinear Transient Dynamics in Fluid Flow Networks with the Neural Basis Method
comment: 28 pages, 5 figures. Under review
summary: Fluid flow networks, from pipeline infrastructure to biological vasculature, are governed by nonlinear edgewise hyperbolic laws coupled through continuity and conservation at junctions. Many-query tasks require rapid evaluation across unseen parametric settings, but conventional methods re-solve the system for each query at prohibitive cost. Existing physics-informed neural approaches impose the governing equations through penalty losses over generic neural approximators; these losses act only as optimization surrogates, with no guarantee that their reduction reduces solution error, and the resulting optimization is prone to ill-conditioning, particularly for hyperbolic systems. Building on the "representation-then-projection" principle of the neural basis method, we introduce a new approach for modeling fluid flow networks. Fixed neural bases define the representation space on each edge, while projection of the discretized equations determines the expansion coefficients, embedding edgewise laws into a conservative formulation. Edge subdomains are coupled through non-overlapping domain decomposition, and a neural operator learns, directly in this reduced space, the parametric map to the expansion coefficients. On looped and branching network topologies, we reproduce references with relative $L^2$ errors below 0.02%, whereas the physics-informed neural network baseline fails. Across unseen boundary conditions in both interpolation and extrapolation, we maintain mean pressure errors below 1% and mean flux errors below 3.3%, while the physics-informed DeepONet baseline reaches 8-18% pressure errors and 85-95% flux errors. These results highlight the framework's potential for real-time monitoring, design exploration, and uncertainty quantification of fluid flow networks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the neural basis method for fluid flow networks, using fixed neural bases on each edge with projection of the discretised equations and a neural operator in the reduced space, achieving pressure errors below 1% and flux errors below 3.3% on unseen boundary conditions.
AI.motivation: Conventional solvers must re-solve each query, and physics-informed neural networks impose governing equations through penalty losses that do not guarantee lower solution error and are ill-conditioned for hyperbolic systems.
AI.method: Fixed neural bases define the representation on each edge, projection of discretised equations gives the expansion coefficients in a conservative formulation, edges are coupled by non-overlapping domain decomposition, and a neural operator learns the parametric map to coefficients.
AI.result: On looped and branching networks the method reproduces references with relative L2 errors below 0.02%, while the PINN baseline fails. On unseen boundary conditions, mean pressure errors stay below 1% and mean flux errors below 3.3%, while the PI-DeepONet baseline reaches 8 to 18% pressure error and 85 to 95% flux error.
AI.conclusion: The framework is promising for real-time monitoring, design exploration and uncertainty quantification of fluid networks.

title: Modeling Drug Overdose Mortality Levels Using Social Vulnerability Indicators in U.S. Counties: A Double Machine Learning Approach for Causal Analysis
summary: Drug poisoning mortality (DPM) remains a leading cause of death among working-age Americans, and its burden falls unevenly across communities. Existing county-level studies of social vulnerability and overdose have largely reported predictive or associational relationships, while the shape of the adjusted exposure-response relationship between overall social vulnerability and mortality remains unclear. We examined the CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and county drug poisoning mortality across three two-year windows spanning 2016-2021. The associational analysis compared linear regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost models of log mortality using period-specific SVI subfeatures and county covariates. The selected XGBoost models were interpreted with SHAP values. The double machine learning (DML) analysis estimated the exposure-response relationship between SVI and DPM and tested the linearity restriction. Socioeconomic vulnerability contributed positively to predicted mortality, with disability and unemployment among the strongest subfeatures, while racial and ethnic minority composition contributed negatively in all three periods. Summing the four theme contributions reduced the overall-index attribution by 34% to 36%, indicating substantial offsetting. Linearity was rejected in every window ($p < 10^{-26}$). The adjusted relationship increased through the middle of the SVI distribution and declined in the upper tail. This pattern remained stable both before and after the outbreak of the epidemic. Overall SVI therefore captured meaningful variation in overdose mortality but did not function as a uniformly increasing risk scale across its full range. Component-level interpretation and current overdose surveillance provide important context for interpreting the composite index.

AI.tldr: Using double machine learning on CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index data for U.S. counties, the paper finds that the adjusted relationship between social vulnerability and drug poisoning mortality rises through the middle of the index and falls in the upper tail, so linearity is rejected.
AI.motivation: Existing county-level studies of social vulnerability and overdose are mostly predictive or associational, and the shape of the adjusted exposure-response relationship is unclear.
AI.method: The authors compare linear regression, Random Forest and XGBoost models of log mortality over three two-year windows from 2016 to 2021, interpret the XGBoost models with SHAP, and estimate the exposure-response curve with double machine learning, testing linearity.
AI.result: Socioeconomic vulnerability contributes positively to predicted mortality, while racial and ethnic minority composition contributes negatively in all three periods. Summing theme contributions reduces the overall-index attribution by 34% to 36%. Linearity is rejected in every window (p < 10^-26), and the pattern is stable before and after the epidemic outbreak.
AI.conclusion: The composite SVI captures meaningful variation in overdose mortality but is not a uniformly increasing risk scale across its full range, so component-level interpretation is needed.

title: Can a search hold its own bar? In-loop deflation and its exploits in autonomous strategy discovery
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Corrections for backtest overfitting such as the deflated Sharpe ratio are applied after a search ends: the searcher maximises raw performance and a separate procedure deflates the reported winner. Autonomous searches driven by large language models perform many implicit backtests before reporting, so this paper asks what changes when the correction moves inside the loop and the acceptance threshold is indexed to the running count and dispersion of the search's own trials. The threshold then becomes an object the search can optimise against: we show analytically that a naive in-loop bar admits a variance-dilution effect, in which mediocre near-duplicate candidates lower the bar because the ledger's dispersion falls faster than its trial-count factor grows. We propose two defences, a pre-registered variance floor and a monotone high-water-mark bar, and evaluate the construction under a protocol frozen before any run, with every in-loop decision replaying exactly from its recorded trace. Across 53 audited hundred-candidate searches over two frontier models, two universes, and two feature spaces, the gated search reports "no certifiable discovery" on 36 of 37 runs, un-gated controls report a strategy on all 16, and every arm's out-of-sample confidence interval includes zero. Supporting studies find that state-based stopping reaches the same outcome after 8 to 9 trials at about a twelfth of the trial budget while an adaptive budget adds nothing, that a controlled stress test reproduces the dilution effect and both defences, and that a hundred nominal trials collapse to 6 to 8 effectively independent return streams. We scope these results to the analysed system.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that when a backtest-overfitting correction such as the deflated Sharpe ratio is moved inside an LLM-driven search loop, the acceptance threshold can be gamed through variance dilution, and it proposes a variance floor and a high-water-mark bar as defences.
AI.motivation: Corrections for backtest overfitting are normally applied after a search ends, but autonomous LLM searches perform many implicit backtests before reporting, so an in-loop threshold can be optimised against by the search itself.
AI.method: The authors analyse a naive in-loop bar that is indexed to the running trial count and dispersion, and propose a pre-registered variance floor and a monotone high-water-mark bar. They evaluate them under a frozen protocol across 53 audited searches of 100 candidates over two frontier models, two universes and two feature spaces.
AI.result: The gated search reports no certifiable discovery in 36 of 37 runs, while ungated controls report a strategy in all 16. Every arm's out-of-sample confidence interval includes zero. State-based stopping reaches the same outcome after 8 to 9 trials at about one-twelfth of the budget, and 100 nominal trials collapse to 6 to 8 effectively independent return streams.
AI.conclusion: In-loop corrections can be gamed through variance dilution, and the proposed defences restore conservative behaviour for the analysed system only.

title: Modelling the occurrence and reporting dynamics of weather-related home insurance claims
summary: We study the occurrence and reporting dynamics of weather-related claims in private home insurance, combining detailed portfolio and claim information with publicly available high-resolution weather data. Existing approaches typically start from an identified severe weather event, such as a hailstorm, and model the dynamics of the claims caused by that event. In practice, however, claims arise under moderate as well as severe conditions, and the claims handling process runs continuously. An insurer therefore requires insight into the occurrence and reporting of claims on every calendar day. Modelling all calendar days jointly poses two challenges: recently occurred claims are only partially reported, and days with severe weather are rare while accounting for a large share of the claims. We propose a multi-regime EM-XGBoost framework that addresses both: an expectation-maximisation setup accounts for the incurred-but-not-reported (IBNR) claims, while a data-driven regime structure lets the occurrence and reporting dynamics differ across weather conditions. In a case study on a Dutch home insurance portfolio, we compare single- and two-regime specifications for two spatial resolutions: the country as a whole, and its individual regions. We find that the regional two-regime model outperforms the regional single-regime model as well as both national models, indicating that the benefit of a multi-regime setting depends on a sufficiently granular spatial resolution. We also show that daily covariates constructed from hourly weather observations, capturing the duration and the intra-day timing of severe weather, improve both the occurrence and the reporting model.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-regime EM-XGBoost framework for daily occurrence and reporting of weather-related home insurance claims, handling incurred-but-not-reported claims and separate regimes for different weather conditions, and finds the regional two-regime model performs best in a Dutch case study.
AI.motivation: Existing models start from identified severe events, whereas claims arise on every day under moderate and severe conditions, and recent claims are only partly reported while severe-weather days are rare but account for many claims.
AI.method: An expectation-maximisation setup accounts for IBNR claims, and a data-driven regime structure lets occurrence and reporting differ across weather conditions. Single- and two-regime specifications are compared at national and regional resolutions, with daily covariates built from hourly weather observations.
AI.result: The regional two-regime model outperforms the regional single-regime model and both national models. Daily covariates capturing the duration and intra-day timing of severe weather improve both the occurrence and reporting models.
AI.conclusion: The benefit of a multi-regime setting depends on sufficiently granular spatial resolution, and hourly-derived weather covariates help.

title: Probe Before You Preach: Conformal Ambiguity Sets and Neuro-Symbolic Counterfactual Probing for Diagnosing Algebraic Misconceptions in Middle School Mathematics
comment: 19 pages, 1 figure. Theoretical framework, method, and public-graph audit; withdrawn hardcoded offline/classroom outcome tables omitted; classroom study proposed for future validation
summary: Distinct mathematical misconception rules can produce the same incorrect answer, making diagnosis from a single response ambiguous. We formalize this algebraic collision and derive a conditional Bayes error bound; internally generated reasoning does not add student-specific information beyond its inputs under an explicit conditional-independence assumption. We propose Mondrian Adaptive Conformal Misconception Sets (MACMS) and Symbolic-Verified Counterfactual Micro-Probing (Sym-EIG). MACMS has curriculum-group marginal coverage under exchangeability, not a per-student correctness guarantee.
