Sym-EIG searches for probes whose outputs separate modeled candidate rules; identification additionally depends on the candidate set and response model. An audit of a local public Eedi graph finds 2,118 of 2,258 linked constructs associated with at least two misconception IDs; construct-level associations alone do not establish same-answer collisions. Other project performance tables require recomputation because their script assigns numerical results directly. No diagnostic performance or classroom learning benefit is claimed here. A classroom study is proposed for future validation.

AI.tldr: The paper formalises algebraic misconception diagnosis from single responses, proposes MACMS conformal misconception sets and Sym-EIG counterfactual probes, and audits an Eedi graph, while stating that no diagnostic performance or learning benefit is claimed.
AI.motivation: Different misconception rules can produce the same wrong answer, so diagnosis from one response is ambiguous.
AI.method: The authors derive a conditional Bayes error bound under a conditional-independence assumption, propose Mondrian Adaptive Conformal Misconception Sets (MACMS) with curriculum-group marginal coverage, and Symbolic-Verified Counterfactual Micro-Probing (Sym-EIG) that searches for probes separating candidate rules.
AI.result: An audit of a public Eedi graph finds 2,118 of 2,258 linked constructs associated with at least two misconception IDs, but construct-level associations alone do not establish same-answer collisions. Other performance tables need recomputation, and no diagnostic performance or classroom benefit is claimed.
AI.conclusion: The framework is a formal basis for diagnosis, and a classroom study is proposed as future validation.

title: Provenance-tracked, experimentally validated neural operator surrogates of three-dimensional laser melting with keyholes and free-form paths
comment: Main text: 44 pages, 13 figures, 7 tables. Supplementary Information: 19 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables
summary: A three-dimensional thermo-fluid-dynamic simulation of laser melting resolves the melt pool and vapor depression but costs from one to thousands of core-hours per track. We train FNO, RIGNO and GAOT neural operators that predict the temperature, melt-pool and free-surface fields. Our datasets comprise 3D temperature and melt geometry fields covering lack-of-fusion to keyhole conditions under varied laser power, scan speed, beam radius, beam shape and preheat, and include free-form scan paths with speed changes and up to four beams. We generate them with FLOW-3D WELD, using solver settings validated against published measurements for four materials. We implement an AiiDA framework to store the provenance of every simulation, model and evaluation, so each tabulated metric traces back to the solver and model inputs behind it. On held-out simulations, the best architecture scores below 2 % relative temperature error on quasi-steady straight tracks, below 4 % on single-beam free-form paths and about 5 % with two to four beams. Inference takes under a second per predicted arbitrary time step on our single-GPU setup. We extend a surrogate trained on Ti-6Al-4V to Inconel 718 by growing its training set autonomously, and the extended models reach a relative temperature error of about 3 % or less on both Inconel 718 and Ti-6Al-4V. At 20 Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 conditions held out of training, the two-alloy RIGNO predicts melt-pool and vapor-depression depths within 30 % of published measurements, and its depths differ from FLOW-3D at the same conditions by 2 % on average. Furthermore, these results provide a scalable framework which can readily be applied to computationally intensive simulations in fields other than laser melting.

AI.tldr: The paper trains FNO, RIGNO and GAOT neural operators as surrogates for 3D FLOW-3D laser melting simulations with keyholes and free-form paths, achieving below 2% to about 5% relative temperature error and sub-second inference, and it adds AiiDA provenance tracking.
AI.motivation: A 3D thermo-fluid simulation of laser melting costs from one to thousands of core-hours per track, which limits design and exploration.
AI.method: The authors generate datasets with FLOW-3D WELD covering lack-of-fusion to keyhole regimes and free-form paths with speed changes and up to four beams, train FNO, RIGNO and GAOT, store provenance of every simulation and model with AiiDA, and extend a Ti-6Al-4V surrogate to Inconel 718 through autonomous training-set growth.
AI.result: On held-out simulations the best architecture scores below 2% relative temperature error on straight tracks, below 4% on single-beam free-form paths and about 5% with two to four beams. Inference takes under a second per time step. The extended models reach about 3% or less error on both alloys, and the two-alloy RIGNO predicts melt-pool and vapour-depression depths within 30% of published measurements on 20 held-out conditions.
AI.conclusion: The provenance-tracked neural operator framework is scalable and could be applied to other computationally intensive simulations.

title: Beyond the First Hit: Towards Tight Guarantees for $k$-means++
comment: 48 pages, 1 figure (3 panels). Exact-arithmetic certificate data and verification code included as ancillary files
summary: Let $R_k$ be the worst-case ratio between the expected cost of the $k$ seeds chosen by $k$-means++ and the optimal $k$-means cost. In their seminal paper introducing $k$-means++, Arthur and Vassilvitskii (SODA 2007) showed that $2\ln k\le R_k\le8(\ln k+2)$, and Makarychev, Reddy and Shan (NeurIPS 2020) improved the upper bound to $5(\ln k+2)$. We prove $R_k\le\frac{1163}{233}+2.108\,H_{k-2}$ for every $k\ge3$ by a computer-assisted argument, and $R_k\le5+2.3139\,H_{k-2}$ for every $k\ge2$ by a short analytic argument; here $H_j$ is the $j$th harmonic number. Since $H_{k-2}\le1+\ln k$, this lowers the leading coefficient of $\ln k$ from $5$ to $2.108$. We also determine $R_2=5$ and $R_3=185/32$ exactly; both are suprema that are approached but not attained. On the lower side we prove $R_k\ge2(1+H_{k-1})$ for every $k$, and give a second family of lower bounds that is larger than this for $2\le k\le18$. Previous analyses bound the expected cost of a cluster just after it is first sampled by a constant times its optimal cost, and then charge that cost for the rest of the run. We instead track how a cluster's cost evolves after its first hit: a cluster left with a large residual cost is likely to be sampled again before it accumulates much of the logarithmic charge, and each repeat repairs it.

AI.tldr: The paper tightens the analysis of k-means++ by proving new upper bounds on its worst-case approximation ratio, R_k <= 2.108 H_{k-2} + 1163/233 with a computer-assisted argument, and lower bounds that are exact for k = 2 and k = 3.
AI.motivation: Earlier analyses bound the expected cost just after a cluster is first sampled and charge that cost for the rest of the run, leaving a gap between the known bounds on the leading logarithmic coefficient.
AI.method: The authors track how a cluster's cost evolves after its first hit, so that repeat samplings repair large residual cost, and they combine a computer-assisted argument with an analytic argument.
AI.result: The upper bound R_k <= 1163/233 + 2.108 H_{k-2} for k >= 3 lowers the leading coefficient of ln k from 5 to 2.108, and R_k <= 5 + 2.3139 H_{k-2} holds for k >= 2. R_2 = 5 and R_3 = 185/32 are determined exactly. A lower bound of 2(1 + H_{k-1}) holds for all k, with a second family larger for 2 <= k <= 18.
AI.conclusion: Tracking post-hit cost evolution gives a tighter analysis of k-means++, although the logarithmic coefficient is not yet matched by the lower bound.

title: The norm, not the labels: training and evaluating finite-element surrogates for stress analysis in the energy norm
comment: 45 pages, 6 figures; supplementary material (37 pages, 4 figures) appended
summary: Finite-element surrogates predict the stresses of a new design in one evaluation, but are usually trained on solutions with a displacement loss and compared by it, although engineering decisions rest on stresses. Application in engineering: stress analysis of perforated plates and solids with cavities, parametric families in which holes concentrate stress. Contribution to artificial intelligence: training and evaluating such surrogates in the energy norm, with or without solutions, and screening their predictions without solutions. For linear elastostatics, minimising the assembled discrete potential energy is exactly supervised regression in this norm: the energy gap of a prediction is the strain energy of its stress error. A displacement loss under-weights the stiff modes that carry the strains. In pre-registered comparisons, changing only the norm of the supervised loss cut a three-dimensional transformer's median energy-norm error 7.5-fold and its median von Mises error 6.1-fold; in two dimensions it more than halved the von Mises error, also on held-out instances. In three dimensions, the transformer trained on the energy alone came within a factor of 1.3 of the energy-norm-supervised one in median energy-norm and von Mises error. It was more accurate than the displacement-supervised one on all five metrics in every seed. Given the stiffness matrix, a Ritz projection was more accurate than the label-free transformer, in the seed means, on every metric but peak stress. No network transferred to a substantially finer mesh. The energy ranks predictions of a load case, and its sign flags those worse than the zero field.

AI.tldr: The paper trains and evaluates finite-element surrogates for linear elastostatic stress analysis in the energy norm, showing that changing only the training norm reduces a 3D transformer's median energy-norm error 7.5-fold and von Mises error 6.1-fold.
AI.motivation: Surrogates predict stresses that matter for engineering decisions but are trained and compared with a displacement loss, which under-weights the stiff modes that carry strains.
AI.method: For linear elastostatics, minimising the assembled discrete potential energy equals supervised regression in the energy norm, so the authors train with energy-norm supervision, with or without labelled solutions, and screen predictions using the energy gap. They compare pre-registered settings on perforated plates and solids with cavities in 2D and 3D.
AI.result: Energy-norm supervision reduces median energy-norm error 7.5-fold and median von Mises error 6.1-fold in 3D, and more than halves von Mises error in 2D. The energy-only transformer comes within a factor of 1.3 of the energy-supervised one in 3D. Given the stiffness matrix, a Ritz projection beats the label-free transformer on every metric except peak stress. No network transfers to a substantially finer mesh.
AI.conclusion: The energy norm is a better training and evaluation target for stress surrogates, and the energy sign flags predictions worse than the zero field.

title: Conformal Risk Certificates for Portfolio Optimization Under Uncertainty: A Gated Reinforcement-Learning Approach
comment: 26 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Submitted to Annals of Operations Research
summary: Reinforcement-learning portfolio policies can optimize allocations from prices, covariances, and prior positions, yet they lack a calibrated, replayable mechanism for certifying that a proposed allocation respects a bounded risk envelope before execution. Regulators increasingly expect automated portfolio systems to provide exactly this kind of pre-trade audit trail, interpretable risk limit, and human-oversight mechanism. Gated Conformal Semantic Risk Control addresses this gap by separating return-seeking allocation from text-conditioned downside-risk verification. An instruction-tuned language model maps timestamped disclosures into schema-validated semantic risk states over macro, liquidity, earnings, and sector channels. These states induce correlated ellipsoidal factor-shock uncertainty sets whose conformal radii are calibrated by rolling finite-sample prediction over localized semantic nonconformity buckets. An asymmetric second-order cone gate then checks each raw PPO proposal against a certified worst-case semantic loss budget. The gate stays inactive for compliant proposals and intervenes only when that budget is exceeded. In walk-forward out-of-sample tests on nine liquid U.S. Select Sector SPDR ETFs, Raw PPO earns a 12.7% annual return while incurring a 4.05% semantic violation rate. Gated-CSRC removes all observed out-of-sample semantic limit breaches while retaining an 11.7% annual return. This 100-basis-point auditable safety premium is smaller than the yield loss imposed by unconditional hard projection, and exact McNemar testing confirms the compliance gain at $p < 10^{-15}$. Loughran-McDonald lexicon controls and time-shuffled text controls fail to reproduce this certificate.

AI.tldr: Gated Conformal Semantic Risk Control (Gated-CSRC) separates PPO portfolio allocation from text-conditioned downside-risk verification, using conformal ellipsoidal uncertainty sets and a second-order cone gate, removing all observed out-of-sample semantic limit breaches while keeping 11.7% annual return against 12.7% for raw PPO.
AI.motivation: RL portfolio policies lack a calibrated, replayable mechanism to certify that an allocation respects a bounded risk envelope before execution, which regulators increasingly expect.
AI.method: An instruction-tuned language model maps timestamped disclosures into schema-validated semantic risk states over macro, liquidity, earnings and sector channels. These induce ellipsoidal factor-shock sets with conformal radii from rolling calibration in semantic nonconformity buckets, and an asymmetric second-order cone gate checks each PPO proposal against a worst-case semantic loss budget.
AI.result: On nine U.S. Select Sector SPDR ETFs in walk-forward tests, raw PPO earns 12.7% annually with a 4.05% semantic violation rate, while Gated-CSRC earns 11.7% with no observed breaches. Exact McNemar testing gives p < 10^-15 for the compliance gain. Loughran-McDonald lexicon and time-shuffled text controls fail to reproduce the certificate.
AI.conclusion: A gated conformal risk layer can provide an auditable compliance premium of about 100 basis points, smaller than the yield loss of unconditional hard projection.

title: Beyond Foreign-Key Connectivity: Semantic Relationship Representation for Relational Deep Learning
summary: Relational databases encode information through tables and primary--foreign key constraints. Although recent Relational Deep Learning (RDL) approaches represent these databases as heterogeneous graphs, a foreign-key connection primarily specifies structural connectivity between records. Its semantic interpretation may involve additional information that is not explicitly represented by connectivity alone. This paper introduces a conceptual framework for constructing relationship-aware representations from relational databases. The framework distinguishes three complementary aspects: (i) schema-defined relationship semantics, including endpoint types and foreign-key roles; (ii) association entities and explicitly available relationship-level attributes; and (iii) contextual information describing the temporal and structural circumstances of a connection. We formulate a Relationship Representation Construction (RRC) protocol that maps relational schema elements and database records to node representations, relationship descriptors, and contextual representations. A key principle of the protocol is semantic ownership: attributes are assigned to records, relationships, or context according to their meaning, rather than merely their physical location in a database table. Ambiguous attributes are not automatically promoted to relationship features. The resulting representations can be incorporated into existing relational graph learning architectures through relationship-conditioned message passing. The proposed framework is complementary to recent work on relational message passing, graph transformers, and task-dependent graph construction. We discuss its conceptual foundations, illustrate the construction protocol using a multi-table database, and identify research questions and empirical evaluations required to establish its potential benefits.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a conceptual framework and a Relationship Representation Construction protocol for relational deep learning that treats foreign-key links as more than connectivity, assigning attributes to records, relationships or context by their meaning.
AI.motivation: RDL methods represent relational databases as heterogeneous graphs, but a foreign-key connection specifies only structural connectivity and may carry semantics that are not represented.
AI.method: The framework separates schema-defined relationship semantics, association entities with relationship-level attributes, and contextual temporal and structural information. The RRC protocol maps schema elements and records to node representations, relationship descriptors and context, with a semantic ownership principle, and feeds them into relationship-conditioned message passing.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experiments. It illustrates the protocol on a multi-table database and lists research questions and empirical evaluations still required.
AI.conclusion: The framework is complementary to existing relational message passing and graph transformer work, and its benefits remain to be empirically established.

title: A New Framework for Quantum Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 28 pages, 3 figures; includes appendices and NeurIPS paper checklist
summary: Quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) has emerged as a promising approach for controlling quantum systems and accelerating learning tasks with quantum resources. However, most existing QRL formulations still retain a classical reinforcement learning interface: states and actions are often encoded in computational bases and rewards are extracted through measurements. This interface is restrictive for genuinely quantum environments: choosing a measurement can discard entanglement information, while repeated intermediate measurements collapse the evolving state and require costly re-preparation. This motivates a fully QRL framework in which the agent, environment, rewards, and return accumulation are all quantum. In this paper, we take a step toward this goal and introduce a new QRL framework in which both the policy and the environment are modeled by conditional quantum channels. We then propose a quantum policy-gradient algorithm for parameterized conditional quantum channels with a trainable control basis. We also derive finite- and infinite-horizon gradient estimators using a new parameter-shift rule. This rule is needed because policy parameters are shared across repeated interaction blocks and the infinite-horizon objective is not a finite circuit; rather than shifting every occurrence and evaluating the whole trajectory, our estimator shifts only one sampled policy block. Sampling this block from a geometric distribution yields an unbiased gradient estimator under bounded rewards. Finally, we establish convergence of the resulting stochastic gradient-ascent procedure to stationary points under standard smoothness and step-size assumptions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a fully quantum reinforcement learning framework in which the policy and environment are conditional quantum channels, with a quantum policy-gradient algorithm, a new parameter-shift estimator that samples one policy block from a geometric distribution, and convergence to stationary points.
AI.motivation: Most QRL formulations keep a classical interface in which states and actions are encoded in computational bases and rewards come from measurements, which discards entanglement and forces costly re-preparation for genuinely quantum environments.
AI.method: Both policy and environment are modelled as parameterised conditional quantum channels with a trainable control basis. The parameter-shift rule shifts only one sampled policy block, with the block drawn from a geometric distribution, giving an unbiased gradient estimator under bounded rewards for the infinite-horizon objective.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experimental numbers. It claims unbiased finite- and infinite-horizon gradient estimators and convergence of stochastic gradient ascent to stationary points under standard smoothness and step-size assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The framework is a step toward fully quantum reinforcement learning with theoretically grounded policy-gradient training.
